Affiliations: IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca Lucca Italy; BBVA Research Madrid Spain; IUSS, University School for Advanced Studies of Pavia Pavia Italy; Climate Finance Alpha ‐ CLIMAFIN Paris France
Abstract: ABSTRACT Our paper presents a causal machine learning (ML) methodology to study the heterogeneous effects of economy‐wide shocks and applies it to the impact of the COVID‐19 crisis on exports. This method is applicable in scenarios where, due to the pervasive nature of the shock, it is difficult to identify a control group that is not affected by the shock and to determine ex ante differences in shock intensity across units. In particular, our study investigates the effectiveness of different ML techniques in predicting firms' trade and, by building on recent developments in causal ML, these predictions are used to reconstruct the counterfactual distribution of firms' trade under different COVID‐19 scenarios and investigate the heterogeneity of treatment effects. Specifically, we focus on the probability of Colombian firms surviving in the export market under two different scenarios: a COVID‐19 setting and a non‐COVID‐19 counterfactual situation. On average, we find that the COVID‐19 shock decreased a firm's probability of surviving in the export market by about 20 percentage points in April 2020. We study the treatment effect heterogeneity by employing a classification analysis that compares the characteristics of the firms on the tails of the estimated distribution of the individual treatment effects.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: When Technology Meets Inequality: The Persistent Effects of Distance Education on Gender Gaps in Rural China
Authors: Xiaodong Zheng, Binyang Lou, Yanran Zhou
Affiliations: Modern Business Research Center Zhejiang Gongshang University Hangzhou China; School of Economics Zhejiang Gongshang University Hangzhou China; Tailong Finance School Zhejiang Gongshang University Hangzhou China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the persistent effects of China's Modern Distance Education Program (MDEP), a large‐scale educational technology initiative that provided access to high‐quality instruction for over 100 million rural primary and junior high school students. Utilising two nationally representative surveys and employing a cohort‐based triple‐difference (DDD) identification strategy, we demonstrate that MDEP significantly narrowed the gender gap in educational attainment. The programme's effects exhibit a cumulative pattern, intensifying with greater exposure duration and investment intensity. We further find that MDEP facilitated gender‐equitable access to public educational resources and weakened son‐preference distortions in household educational investment, thereby improving educational outcomes for rural girls. These educational gains also translated into persistent reductions in gender disparities in labour market outcomes, with MDEP‐exposed rural women experiencing greater improvements in formal employment, digitally intensive occupations and wages than comparable men.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: The inclusion of transaction costs in conservation compensation schemes as illustrated with tigers
Authors: V. Prakash, Y. Zhang, R.A. Gitzen, C.A. Lepczyk
Abstract: Human expansion into wildlands has intensified human-wildlife conflicts (HWC), resulting in a need for mitigation. Compensation, a mitigation tool, faces challenges due to underestimated costs, including transaction costs. We developed a framework to identify transaction costs based on successful post-conflict compensation scheme elements, focusing on Verification, Process, and Compensation. As part of this framework, we identified key parameters determining transaction costs. We applied this framework to quantify transaction costs in a human-tiger conflict (HTC) compensation scheme near Pilibhit Tiger Reserve, India, by surveying HTC-affected persons or their families in 2022. Most participants were unaware of the compensation process, found it difficult, and expressed dissatisfaction with government agencies. The average waiting cost at the 2022 USD rate was $583 per claimant, with a 101-day delay, and total transaction costs exceeded 40% of the compensation amount received. Because compensation increased with claimant effort rather than need, awareness, or socioeconomic status, the results point to an equity concern: administrative burdens disproportionately reward those able to navigate costly processes. Therefore, reducing procedural barriers is essential to ensure fair and equitable access to compensation schemes. This framework provides a scalable tool to improve conservation compensation programs globally by identifying interventions that reduce transaction costs, thereby alleviating the impacts of HWCs across diverse regions and species.

Title: Are the blue and the green natural allies? Mapping the public foundations of just transition worldwide
Authors: Mengqi Xie, Sijeong Lim
Abstract: A Just Transition, with its dual goals of environmental sustainability and social equity, has gained global prominence and has been adopted as a formal policy agenda by governments and intergovernmental organizations. While broad and meaningful public support for both goals is crucial to effective implementation, research on public attitudes has largely focused on developed Western countries or specific vulnerable populations. To address this gap, we examine whether and how support for environmental protection aligns or conflicts with backing for progressive redistribution across a diverse range of developed and developing countries. We posit that access to economic safety nets enables broader alignment at the population level (i.e., breadth of support), while post-materialist values and lived endorsement of the welfare state foster stronger individual-level alignment (i.e., depth of support). Our analysis, covering 95 countries from 2005 to 2022, finds support for these expectations. First, the population share of Green-Blue progressives supporting both goals is notably smaller in developing countries with high economic insecurity. Second, one’s environmental and redistributive attitudes in much of the Global South are unaligned or negatively correlated, in contrast to the positive individual-level alignment observed in developed countries, particularly among post-materialists and in generous welfare states. Regional variation is also significant: Europe ranks high in breadth and shows significant depth; North America shows strong depth but no significant breadth; East Asia demonstrates wide breadth but comparatively shallow depth. Sub-Saharan Africa lags significantly on both dimensions. This global variation calls for context-sensitive Just Transition policies that account for distinct socioeconomic realities.

Title: The security unlock: How rural social pension makes people more entrepreneurial?
Authors: Lingran Yuan, Jiong Zhu
Abstract: Previous literature on the determinants of entrepreneurship has not explored the role of social pension. Leveraging variation in the roll-out timing of a universal rural pension program across Chinese counties, our analysis, at both the individual and aggregate levels, reveals that pension provision led to an increase in entrepreneurship among the younger generation. We show that this effect operates through two primary channels: an intergenerational transfer channel and a local demand channel. Specifically, the pension program mitigates upward transfers from adult children to elderly parents, while boosting local consumer demand, which exerts a demand-side “pull” effect on enterprise establishment. Our findings may shed new light on the interplay between pension, intergenerational resource allocation, and entrepreneurial activity.

Title: Skepticism without scrutiny: Verification and information manipulation
Authors: Suli Zheng, Bo Wang

Title: Fed information shocks and option-implied expectations
Authors: Adam Harper, Yilun Lu

Title: Emission intensity in models with production under financial frictions
Authors: Xiang Shi, Jun Yu
Abstract: Financially constrained firms emit more per unit of output, yet standard production models need not reproduce this pattern. We develop a heterogeneous-firm model with collateral constraints, combining post-production abatement or clean-capital substitution with capital- or output-based emissions. With proportional output-based emissions, tighter financing raises intensity locally only for constrained firms that actively abate; clean-capital substitution leaves it constant. Under linear capital-based emissions, post-production abatement produce opposite pattern for low-net-worth firms; clean-capital substitution matches the pattern locally only when the cleaner capital mix reduces intensity more than production expansion raises it. Our results provide guidance for quantitative green-transition models with financial frictions.

Title: Distribution-free bounds on double marginalization under α-concave demand
Authors: Qianqian Wen, Kayson Hu
Abstract: Under successive monopoly, how far can the retail price rise above the integrated monopoly price when only demand curvature is known? We work with α[jls-end-space/]-concave demand: demand whose α[jls-end-space/]-th power is concave, with log-concavity as the case (Formula presented). Demands whose α[jls-end-space/]-th power, or logarithm when (Formula presented), is affine (the α[jls-end-space/]-affine demands) yield the ratio (Formula presented), but it is not tight: the manufacturer’s optimal wholesale price can strictly exceed the integrated monopoly price. The tight bound (Formula presented) solves an explicit equation and is approached, never attained, by smoothed truncated α[jls-end-space/]-affine demands; approximately 3.15 for log-concave and 1.71 for concave demand.

Title: The genericity of obvious manipulations under the Egalitarian Walrasian rule when preferences are linear
Authors: Pierre Bardier, Bach Dong-Xuan, Van-Quy Nguyen
Abstract: We study the incentives properties of one of the central solutions to the problem of allocating divisible commodities among equally entitled agents, namely the Egalitarian Walrasian rule (EW), when agents have linear preferences. The EW rule being manipulable on this domain, we ask whether it is, at least, immune to obvious manipulations , in the sense of Troyan and Morrill (2020). Unfortunately, the answer is negative. This manipulability result is generic since we show that any agent for whom all the commodities are desirable has an obvious manipulation.

Title: Cost pressure, cash cycle, and trade credit
Authors: Anywhere Sikochi
Abstract: Prior research shows that firms respond to cost pressures by absorbing the costs or passing them through to customers. I show that firms can also respond by managing their cash conversion cycle through adjusting trade credit policies. Longer payment terms are a form of financing subsidy such that firms can recapture the subsidy by adjusting collection from customers and payment to suppliers. I document that cost pressure is associated with shorter cash conversion period, primarily driven by increasing accounts payable days. The results generally do not vary depending on firms’ choice to absorb costs or pass them through to customers.

Title: IP governance and patent renewal decisions: Evidence from U.S. public firms
Authors: Chen-Ting (Chris) Lien, Shao-Yin Wu
Abstract: Which patents do firms allow to lapse, and who governs the decision? A U.S. patent remains in force only if its owner pays three scheduled maintenance fees. Many patents lapse; renewal records show which, but not how the choice is made. We hand-collect the IP-governance structures (board-level IP committees and dedicated IP officers) of all 7,735 patent-holding U.S. public firms over 1985–2019. Linking these to patent market values (Kogan et al. 2017) and USPTO maintenance-fee records, we measure how closely each firm’s lapse decisions align with the market’s valuation. We document five stylized facts. First, lapsing is pervasive: 41 percent of firms let at least one patent lapse. Second, alignment varies widely: the lapsed patents’ average value rank is the 59th percentile, with a standard deviation of 24 percentile points across firm-years. Third, formal IP governance is rare: 2.4 percent of firms have an IP committee. Fourth, committee firms’ lapse decisions come closest to the market’s ranking: their lapsed patents average the 51st percentile of value, against the 59th for other firms. Fifth, the association is concentrated in the committee form rather than in an officer title. Within firms, better-aligned years are followed by higher market value and investment. The facts mark patent renewal as a common, widely varying, and largely ungoverned margin of intangible-asset management.

Title: A walk down memory lane: How memories influence stock investment and information processing
Authors: Giovanni Burro, Alessandro Castagnetti, Alessandra Cillo, Giovanni Paolo Crespi
Abstract: Propensity to invest in stocks is highly heterogeneous, with many households avoiding stock market participation altogether. This heterogeneity is difficult to reconcile with standard economic theory. We study the role of memories in shaping investment decisions and in influencing how individuals incorporate stock-related information. Across two experiments, participants invest in a stock and are compensated based on its actual price realization. In the first experiment, we verify that activating memories prior to investing systematically shifts investment behavior. Participants asked to recall stock market–related memories before the investment task make more polarized choices: recalling positive memories increases investment relative to recalling non-positive ones, while activating non-positive memories lowers investment compared with not activating them. The second experiment reveals our central finding: the effect of information critically depends on the type of memory activated. All participants recall a memory before investing, after which some receive positive and truthful information about the stock. Information meaningfully increases investment only among participants who recalled non-personal memories; in contrast, recalling personal memories completely eliminates the response to information. We show that this sharp interaction cannot be explained by changes in beliefs, overconfidence, or mistrust in experts. Instead, it can be rationalized within a selective memory framework.

Title: Matching for risk-taking: Overconfident bankers and government-protected banks
Authors: Andreas Haufler, Bernhard Kassner
Abstract: We set up a simple theoretical model in which banks with varying degrees of government support are matched with CEOs that have different degrees of overconfidence. The channel through which the matching occurs is the share of bonus payments offered by banks in their profit-maximizing contracts. This yields a sequence of hypotheses when CEOs can freely choose risk levels: banks with more government support incentivize their CEOs more and this disproportionately attracts overconfident CEOs. In equilibrium this in turn leads to an assortative matching between overconfident managers and banks with a larger bailout probability. We then test the hypotheses derived from this model for U.S. data spanning both the Great Financial Crisis and the Covid Crisis. Our results confirm the hypotheses from our theoretical model for normal years, but not during crises and periods of enhanced regulation.

Title: Infrastructure remembers: network continuity and the making of divided Jerusalem, 1943–1962
Authors: Shlomi Efrati
Abstract: How does a city’s public transit network withstand the shocks of political partition, mass immigration, and the redrawing of international borders? Urban history has traditionally marginalized public transportation as a passive background rather than an active driver of a city’s spatial evolution. To address this gap, this study reconstructs the bus network of the Jewish HaMkasher cooperative — the city’s dominant urban operator from 1931 until its absorption into Egged in the 1960s — across two pivotal snapshots: 1943, under late British Mandate rule, and 1962, in the divided city, when the network was confined to the western sector. The reconstruction draws on a previously unexplored corpus of primary documents from the Egged Archives (which hold the HaMkasher records) and the Jerusalem Municipality Archives, including 1943 distance tables, a 1962 cartographic map, and detailed administrative records from the District Motor Regulatory Board. Methodologically, this archival data was georeferenced and transformed into line-level graphs, ultimately creating unified network models for both time periods. By computing both degree and betweenness centrality for every stop, the study maps the underlying structural roles within the network. A null-model comparison preserving each stop’s arrivals and departures shows that the resulting concentration of brokerage on the western corridor reflects the historical configuration rather than the reconstruction’s topology. Furthermore, the severe disruption of the 1949 armistice line provides analytic leverage for weighing infrastructural inertia against the persistent geographic constraints of Jerusalem’s mountainous terrain and its fixed commercial core. The findings reveal a continuity beneath the era’s dramatic geopolitical ruptures. Long before the 1948 partition, the Jaffa Road corridor already functioned as a pivotal structural bridge. Rather than forcing a total reorganization of the transit system, the Armistice Line activated vulnerabilities already latent within it. Consequently, the post-1948 westward expansion relied on this preexisting corridor, and the grafting of new immigrant neighborhoods onto the system quantitatively manifested as arrested polycentrism. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the spatial logic of a transit infrastructure can outlast — and quietly constrain — the profound political and demographic transformations of the city it serves.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: On the exact solution of the cycle packing problem
Authors: Reem A. Al-Jarallah, Marcos Roboredo, Eduardo Uchoa, A. Ridha Mahjoub
Abstract: In the Cycle Packing Problem (CPP), we are looking for the maximum number of edge-disjoint cycles on a given graph. For this problem, we present a Branch-and-Cut-and-Price (BCP) algorithm based on a set-packing formulation strengthened with Rank-1 cuts. Cycle variables are generated dynamically by solving pricing subproblems modeled as constrained shortest path problems on directed graphs. The algorithm is executed in three phases: a root phase, MIP-based heuristic phase, and a complete BCP phase. To demonstrate the robustness of the proposed algorithm, we present extensive computational experiments on 1000 benchmark instances with up to 100 nodes, showing that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the best existing exact method.

Title: Support, resistance, and technical trading
Authors: Keisuke Teeple
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Navigating abatement technology transition: the interplay of endogenous emissions and technological progress
Authors: Jianxin Guo
Abstract: This paper develops a tractable continuous-time optimal control model to investigate when enterprises should transition to advanced abatement technologies under binding carbon constraints. By formalizing the dynamic interplay between exogenous technological progress and the compounding penalties of endogenous emission accumulation, we analytically determine the optimal transition timing and the corresponding piecewise abatement trajectories. We show that a key growth trade-off emerges: while high-growth environments increase emissions accumulation and strengthen near-term compliance pressure, they also raise the option value of waiting for cheaper advanced technologies. The optimal transition timing is therefore determined by the balance between these two forces, rather than by static cost comparisons. Furthermore, we demonstrate that intertemporal abatement allocation is jointly shaped by discounting and technological learning, leading to non-trivial within-regime dynamics. Finally, we introduce the concept of a strategic pivot point, which captures whether parameter changes induce a reallocation of abatement effort toward earlier or later periods within each technological phase. This provides a unified interpretation of how firms adjust their mitigation paths in response to changes in market conditions and environmental policy stringency.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Isolated or interconnected? An equilibrium framework for swarm electrification in rural energy planning
Authors: N. Ouanes, T. González Grandón, I. Fagerli, S.A. Gabriel
Abstract: Swarm electrification–the interconnection of isolated decentralized energy systems for local energy sharing– could accelerate rural electrification, yet it remains largely absent from major initiatives that still prioritize solar home systems and centralized mini-grids. To determine when swarm interconnection is most justified, we develop a techno-economic decision-support framework, introducing three heterogeneity indexes: budget heterogeneity (BHI), demand shape diversity (SDI), and demand peak diversity (PDI). We use these indexes to investigate how heterogeneity increases the value of interconnection in the swarm-grid setting. We translate model outputs into policy-relevant indicators, e.g., avoided investment and added social welfare, and combine these into a single benefit ratio (BR). Using mixed complementarity problem (MCP) models–common in market and other equilibrium settings–we simulate decentralized energy trading under two competitive assumptions: perfect competition and Cournot competition, thus deriving tariff levels endogenously. We also include a central-planning benchmark where prices are exogenously fixed. Results from a Madagascar case study indicate that heterogeneity reshapes the economic rationale for interconnection. Demand differences yield at least 3% avoided investment through more efficient allocation and reduced oversizing, and complementary load-profiles increase energy sharing more than fivefold. Budget heterogeneity dominates, inducing over fifteen times more energy sharing by redistributing investments across nanogrids. Different market designs highlight a profitability-affordability trade-off: payback periods as short as 1.5 years are maximized under cost-recovery-oriented settings, imposing higher tariffs and underscoring the need for governance mechanisms aligned with energy-justice objectives. This framework offers practical guidance for a more adaptive and socially-inclusive rural electrification.

Title: Corporate climate risk perception and labor income share: Empirical evidence from China
Authors: Zhongyang Chen, Zhiwen Wang, Min Yang
Abstract: This study, utilizing data from Chinese A-share listed companies between 2009 and 2023, reveals that corporate perceptions of climate risk significantly lower the labor income share by influencing employment adjustments and capital deepening. Transition risk perception operates mainly through employment reductions and workforce restructuring, while physical risk perceptions predominantly decrease average wages; both types increase the capital-labor ratio. The impact is stronger in labor-intensive, high-carbon industries, disaster-prone areas, and large, highly leveraged firms, but less so where government-market relations are more integrated. Additionally, higher perceived risks tend to widen internal inequality by increasing executives' compensation share and continuously reducing that of regular employees. These findings highlight corporate climate risk perception as a new driver of declining labor income share, shedding light on how climate change influences income distribution at the micro level.

Title: Shock amplification and delayed recovery in resource economies: The role of fiscal policy reform
Authors: Livingstone S. Geoffroy Boko, Sylvain Eloi Dessy
Abstract: This paper examines how global commodity price shocks propagate through resource-dependent economies, with a focus on the interaction between extraction costs and domestic policy responses. We develop a simple framework in which high-cost producers are more exposed to negative price shocks, but the persistence of their response depends on investment conditions and policy environments. We test these predictions using the 2014–2016 oil price collapse, comparing Alberta—one of the world’s highest-cost oil producers—to a synthetic control constructed from lower-cost jurisdictions. Alberta experienced significantly larger declines in hydrocarbon output, investment, and per capita GDP, along with a more prolonged recovery. However, placebo analyses for other high-cost jurisdictions reveal no comparable declines, indicating that cost structure alone is insufficient to explain the observed contraction. Exploiting within-province variation, we further show that Alberta’s response to the 2015 shock differs markedly from its response to the 2009 collapse, despite an unchanged cost structure. Event-study estimates indicate that the post-2015 decline is closely associated with contemporaneous fiscal policy changes. While policy responses may be endogenous, the combined evidence points to a transmission mechanism in which domestic policy shapes—and potentially amplifies—the effects of external shocks in high-cost environments.

Title: Calibrating fiscal policy signals for ammonia fuel adoption in shipping
Authors: Xin Mao, Jiadong Shi, Kum Fai Yuen
Abstract: Ammonia is a promising zero-carbon shipping fuel, yet uptake remains sluggish. This study calibrates budget-constrained fiscal instruments to promote shipowner adoption and sustain diffusion while ensuring supplier profitability, supply stability, and government payoff. We develop a two-layer Stackelberg model with the government as leader and shipowners and fuel suppliers as followers. In the static layer, the optimum is identified by gridding tax and subsidy; in the dynamic layer, ODEs track 100-month trajectories. Results show an interior optimum within the fiscal corridor at 99 , 79 , delivering 99.996 % static adoption, an equilibrium price of USD 1 , 080 / t , and about 87.06 % penetration. Dynamics converge stably, with learning-driven price declines and rising composite government utility. The optimum serves as a policy anchor: maintain the carbon tax as a long-run signal and front-load then phase down the subsidy as adoption increases. Within the corridor, fiscal parameters are adaptively adjusted to observed adoption, profitability, and net fiscal burden.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Heterogeneous bus ridership responses to micro-scale built environment: Evidence from explainable AI
Authors: Andy Angxi Xie
Abstract: Despite the inherent complexity of urban mobility, conventional methodologies often oversimplify the associations between transit demand and built environment, leaving nonlinearity and behavioral asymmetries obscured. This study integrates computer vision and explainable artificial intelligence (XGBoost-SHAP) to decode how the micro-scale built environment affects multidimensional bus ridership. Six environmental visual proxies were extracted through semantic segmentation from 3,736 street view imagery, and subsequently analyzed alongside 8.6 million ridership records over one month across 934 bus stops in Shenzhen, China. Four models distinguish temporal-behavioral patterns (weekday peak vs. weekend off-peak, boarding vs. alighting). The results reveal behavioral heterogeneity: stronger correlations were observed in boarding than alighting demand, while weekend discretionary trips exhibit greater sensitivity to micro-environmental quality than weekday mandatory trips. By quantifying nonlinear threshold effects and diminishing marginal utilities, this study develops a spatial screening matrix that supports planners in flagging environmental mismatches and advancing transit-demand-oriented, data-driven transportation planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Modeling Taxi-Metro Competition: Uncovering Nonlinear Influences of Trip and Built Environment Factors
Authors: Xiang Liu, Guocong Zhai, Hongtai Yang, Donggen Wang, Mark Zuidgeest, Hongliang Ding, Xiaobo Liu
Abstract: Understanding taxi-metro competition is crucial for optimizing the modal split where both modes serve overlapping origin-destination (OD) pairs. This study examines the nonlinear factors associated with taxi-metro competition strength in Chengdu, defined as the proportion of taxi trips among the combined taxi and metro trips for each OD pair. To account for bounded competition strength, we propose a hybrid model combining Beta regression with Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (Beta-BART), which achieves better predictive performance than gradient-boosted decision trees and BART. The results show that OD distance has the highest relative importance (6.2%) and that competition strength declines sharply as OD distance increases to about 7.5 km, with little change beyond this distance. Furthermore, land use mix exhibits an inverted-U association, with competition strength peaking near 0.80. Practically, these nonlinear patterns can inform more targeted transport planning. Methodologically, the framework provides a template for modeling proportional transportation outcomes with bounded distributions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: To what extent do green roads generate ecological gains?
Authors: Bojun Zhang, Lin Huang, Jiangwen Fan, Yuhao Wu, Haiyan Zhang, Yuxin Qiao, Xiaochuang Bu, Xinran Miao, Yagang Tong
Abstract: Road expansion in fragile plateau regions can cause multidimensional ecological disturbance, yet the relative performance of green-road sections remains uncertain. We assessed the Tongsai Expressway on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau using a matched-reference structure–quality–function framework integrating propensity score matching, land-cover- and distance-stratified gain analysis, and exploratory interpretable machine learning. Green-road sections showed selective rather than universal gains. Statistically supported gains were concentrated in Green Road 2, particularly woodland quality indicators (NDVI, NDBSI, WET) at 300–500 m and grassland water conservation (12.470–18.618 mm) at 100–500 m, whereas structural and composite-index gains lacked consistent support. Variation in estimated road eco-effects was associated with road distance, land cover, elevation, climate, and built-up proximity. Climate-enhanced matching and equal-primary-dimension weighting retained the main patterns. Because this is a single-corridor, non-replicated case study with section-specific spatial and temporal contexts, the findings represent case-specific associations rather than causal effects of individual green-road measures.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The effects of global and local heterogeneity on cooperation in multi-level public goods: experimental evidence
Authors: Tjaša Bjedov, Simon Lapointe, Thierry Madiès, David Masclet, Jean-Christian Tisserand
Abstract: Using an artefactual field experiment in a bilingual Swiss state with participants speaking different languages, this paper investigates how both heterogeneity and majority and minority statuses influence cooperation in a repeated multiple-level public good game in which participants can simultaneously contribute to a global good and local goods. Heterogeneity is based on language by using two native groups, German and French speakers, as our subject pool. We find that group heterogeneity has a negative effect on cooperation, which is mainly driven by a decrease in contributions to local public goods while contributions to the global good are not affected. The lower contributions to the local goods in the heterogeneous treatments are mainly due to lower contributions by majority members while the minority members contribute similar amounts to the reference group or even more. Furthermore, we observe that the impact of heterogeneity on contributions is magnified for individuals who are members of a linguistic minority in their real life. Finally, our article has implications for managerial and public policy, highlighting the fact that global heterogeneity can affect cooperation behaviors in local groups, even when they are homogeneous.

Title: Maxmin expected utility as resulting from disagreement among experts
Authors: Shiri Alon, Gabrielle Gayer
Abstract: This paper characterizes the Maxmin Expected Utility (MEU) model of Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989) in an environment a´-la Savage, based on information in the form of expert evaluations. The decision maker is assumed to consult with experts whose preferences abide by Savage’s Subjective Expected Utility theory. While the tastes of experts are aligned with those of the decision maker, their prior probabilities may vary, introducing ambiguity into the framework. The decision maker’s derived set of priors is contained in the convex hull of the experts’ subjective probabilities (or models). Thus, no ambiguity prevails when probability is unanimous according to all the experts. We conclude by characterizing methods for updating the decision maker’s beliefs when an expert’s evaluation is discarded.

Title: JUE Insight: Immigration and native intergenerational mobility in the United States
Authors: Veli M. Andirin
Abstract: Immigration continues to shape the economic and political debate in the United States. Yet, we surprisingly know little about the impact of immigration on the economic mobility of native children. Using recent data on changes in mobility and an identification strategy based on initial settlement patterns of immigrants, I study whether the large increase in the immigrant population between 1980 and 2010 had an impact on native intergenerational mobility. Despite concerns about immigration hurting native children, I find that the impact of immigration on native mobility is statistically insignificant. Moreover, I can rule out economically large effects. I show that this result can be explained by the insignificant impact of immigration on socioeconomic mechanisms previously associated with intergenerational mobility, such as parental employment or incarceration rates.

Title: Editorial Board
The rise and fall (and rise) of the Affordable Care Act: Varying impacts on coverage over time and place
Authors: Gabriella Aboulafia, Jonathan Gruber, Benjamin D. Sommers

Title: IDSSFlex: An Intelligent DSS for the Design and Evaluation of Flexible Manufacturing Systems
Authors: D. Borenstein
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A robust optimization approach for the urban last-mile network of high-speed rail logistics integrating drone delivery
Authors: Shengdong Li, Li Shi, Chuijiang Guo, Jingshuai Yang, Changan Xu, Wenqing Li
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Dynamic Greentech/product innovation and pricing regulation in a monopoly exhibiting network externality
Authors: Shengbiao Ma, Shoude Li, Huiquan Li
Affiliations: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Hunan University of Technology and Business; Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; School of Finance and Economics, Qinghai University
Abstract: This paper aims to investigate the control optimisation issues concerning Greentech and product innovation within a monopolistic framework, particularly for goods exhibiting network effects. The unique characteristics of our study include: (i) differentiating between the efforts directed at Greentech innovation, specifically in (a) replacement technology innovation, which entails a radical transformation in the nature of emissions-producing products, and (b) abatement technology innovation, which mitigates pollution levels without altering the fundamental aspects of the technology integrated into the final product, and (ii) analysing a specific scenario in which the scale of the network is directly correlated with consumer demand. Our primary findings reveal that: (i) under certain conditions, there exists the unique saddle-point equilibrium of the system under both monopolistic and socially optimal decision-making; (ii) the impact of efforts in Greentech and product innovation on price and output depends on the level of product quality and emissions; (iii) equilibrium innovation efforts rise with stronger network effects and larger market size, but decrease as environmental tax rates rise, and (iv) to encourage the monopolist’s engagement in Greentech development, the social planner must set the environmental tax rate above the marginal damage caused by end-of-pipe emission.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Multi-objective sustainable closed-loop agricultural supply chain optimization under uncertainty respecting water circularity: olive products
Authors: Ahmad Attar, Ali Zahedi, Amirhossein Salehi-Amiri, Navid Akbarpour
Abstract: Abstract Driven by economic fluctuation and environmental concerns, the agricultural sector urgently requires integrated closed-loop supply chain (CLSC) models that balance profitability with sustainability. Current literature often overlooks simultaneous economic and environmental objectives, particularly concerning water circularity and reverse logistics in the olive industry. This study addresses this gap by proposing a novel bi-objective mixed integer linear programming model designed to minimize both the total supply chain cost (encompassing procurement, facility setup, operation, storage, and transportation) and total water consumption. Uncertainty regarding product yield, influenced by factors like climate and soil, is systematically incorporated using the possibilistic programming approach. The comprehensive network explicitly models forward flows, reverse logistics, package recovery, and rich wastewater utilization. This complex mathematical problem is solved using four rigorously tuned multi-objective metaheuristics (NSGA-II, NRGA, MOVNS, and MOSA). Applied to a real-world olive network case study, the model demonstrated major reductions in logistics costs, waste production, and water use. A critical finding reveals that the most impactful leverage point for water and cost efficiency lies upstream in cultivation practices (e.g., irrigation management and pest control), rather than downstream industrial recovery, providing actionable guidance for sustainable supply chain management. This research delivers a unified decision framework for water-aware CLSCs under uncertainty.

Title: Endogenous stabilization of maritime intermodal networks under disruption dynamics: a capacity-geometry framework
Authors: Nam Anh Quach
Abstract: Maritime intermodal networks are increasingly exposed to disruptions that reduce link throughput, terminal storage, and port–hinterland operating capacity. This study develops a Capacity-Geometry Framework in which such shocks are represented as contractions of the joint flow–queue feasible region. The recovery problem is formulated through a variational inequality and a projected dynamical system coupling congestion-sensitive flow adjustment with node-level queue imbalance. Under convexity of the disrupted feasible set, strong monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity of the network response operator, and an admissible stabilization parameter, the projected dynamics converge exponentially to a unique disrupted equilibrium. Numerical experiments on a controlled three-node network, an OpenStreetMap-derived Hai Phong port–hinterland topology, and stylized global and ASEAN networks demonstrate feasibility restoration, queue moderation, and convergence across multiple network scales. Controlled benchmarks show that the proposed dynamics substantially outperform passive and purely local capacity-repair responses while approaching the operational recovery quality of a globally informed centralized benchmark. Sensitivity tests across ten disruption-severity levels show progressively longer feasibility-recovery times as capacity contraction intensifies, while scalability experiments indicate near-linear growth in projected-update runtime over state dimensions from 3 to 3,000. The framework therefore provides a mathematically explicit basis for studying decentralized feasibility recovery after maritime capacity shocks.

Title: Risk-taking by CEOs: Role of exposure to social violence in early childhood
Authors: Cindy Xinyi Shen, Wanli Zhao
Abstract: Utilizing the Cultural Revolution as the source of social violence, we explore the effect of childhood and early adolescence (ages 5–15) experience of social violence on CEO’s risk-taking behavior. We document that CEOs who experienced higher levels of social violence during this formative period are less likely to engage in M&A and innovation activity. Our results are robust to alternative explanations and statistical exercises. Further analyses show that this effect takes effect by affecting people’s mental health. Given that our treatment is distinct from the events in prior studies (e.g., natural disasters or economic depression), this study enriches our understanding of the origin of managerial risk-taking incentives.

Title: Geopolitical shocks and household financial distress in Europe: The Russia–Ukraine war
Authors: Anastasios Evgenidis, Apostolos Fasianos, Fang Yao
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of a major geopolitical risk shock, comparable in scale to the outbreak of the Russia–Ukraine war, on household financial distress in five European countries. We combine a VAR, household survey data, and theoretical insights to develop macro–micro simulations that quantify how such shocks influence household balance sheets. The VAR traces the macroeconomic effects of a surge in geopolitical risk, which we apply to household-level data using the HFCS. We find the shock is associated with elevated inflation, tighter monetary policy, higher mortgage rates, and falling house prices. Our simulations show these dynamics significantly increase financial distress, with variation across countries. We incorporate endogenous consumption responses and show that adjustments driven by interest rate exposure, inflation, and housing wealth play a key role in shaping household resilience. We also document that younger and lower-income households tend to increase consumption following the shock, exacerbating their financial vulnerability.

Title: Target the Vulnerable? An Analysis of Rapid Rehousing Prioritization
Authors: Nick Arnosti, Felipe Simon
Affiliations: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota 55455; School of Economics and Business, University of Chile, Santiago 8330015, Chile
Abstract: We model the problem facing a policymaker who must allocate rapid rehousing support to people experiencing homelessness and wishes to minimize the steady-state social cost of homelessness. Support is often given to the most vulnerable applicants or to applicants most likely to remain housed. Although these approaches can be effective in some cases, in general, they may result in a homeless population that is arbitrarily larger than what could be achieved by an optimal policy. We propose an alternative priority queue that is approximately optimal. We then study a family of policies where the policymaker does not differentiate between agents based on their characteristics. Within this family, first-in, first-out (FIFO) queues best target the most vulnerable. If the most vulnerable households benefit most from housing assistance, then an FIFO queue minimizes the expected unhoused population. Conversely, a last-in, first-out queue is optimal if the least vulnerable households benefit most from housing assistance. Finally, we expand our model to allow households to choose among several allocation systems. We show that even in this larger family of policies, if the most vulnerable households are also the ones that most benefit from housing assistance, an FIFO queue minimizes the expected unhoused population. History: This paper has been accepted for the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design. Funding: This work was supported by the National Science Foundation CAREER AWARD [Grant 2339912; CAREER: Efficient and Equitable Housing Allocation (University of Minnesota, Twin Cities)].

Title: A Nonasymptotic Theory of Seminorm Lyapunov Stability: From Deterministic to Stochastic Iterative Algorithms
Authors: Zaiwei Chen, Sheng Zhang, Jimmy Zhang, Shaan Ul Haque, Siva Theja Maguluri
Affiliations: Edwardson School of Industrial Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47906; Amazon Web Services, Inc., Santa Clara, California 95054; H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial & Systems Engineering, Georgia Tech, Atlanta, Georgia 30332
Abstract: We study the problem of solving fixed-point equations for seminorm-contractive operators and establish foundational results on the nonasymptotic behavior of iterative algorithms in both deterministic and stochastic settings. In the deterministic setting, we present a fixed-point theorem for seminorm-contractive operators, showing that the iterates converge geometrically to the kernel of the seminorm. In the stochastic setting, which is our main focus, we analyze stochastic approximation (SA) algorithms under seminorm-contractive operators and Markovian noise, providing a finite-sample analysis for various step size choices. A benchmark for equation solving is linear systems of equations, in which the convergence behavior of fixed-point iteration is closely tied to the stability of linear dynamical systems. In this special case, our results provide a characterization of system stability with respect to a seminorm, linking it to the solution of a Lyapunov equation in terms of positive semidefinite matrices. In the stochastic setting, we establish a finite-sample analysis for linear Markovian SA without requiring the Hurwitzness assumption. Our theoretical results offer a unified framework for deriving finite-sample bounds for reinforcement learning algorithms in the average reward setting, including TD([Formula: see text]) for policy evaluation (which is a special case of solving a Poisson equation) and Q-learning for control. Funding: This work was partially supported by the National Science Foundation [Grants EPCN-2144316, CPS-2240982, CMMI-2112533], a seed grant from Georgia Tech, and an award from Raytheon Technologies. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.2025.0920 .

Title: Arrested development: analyzing popular resistance against the arrest of war-criminals in DR Congo and Liberia
Authors: Anders Themnér, Rosalie Biaba
Abstract: International war crimes trials have become a common feature of post–civil war politics, sparking debate about the effectiveness of such interventions. A key shortcoming in the literature is its neglect of the critical moment when wartime leaders are arrested and that such incarcerations sometimes trigger public resistance that can put peace at risk. In this paper, we contribute to the literature on war crime tribunals by asking: when and how do subelites mobilize followers to protest the arrest of former wartime leaders? Drawing on insights from the protest movement literature, we hold that large-scale protests often require elite involvement. We argue that demonstrations are especially likely when subelites possess limited autonomy in the aftermath of war—lacking independent sources of financing and constrained by identity politics. In such contexts, the cost of remaining passive is high, compelling subelites to mobilize protests to maintain their standing among followers. To assess this argument, we compare the incarcerations of Jean-Pierre Bemba in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Charles Taylor in Liberia. Our analysis draws on original, in-depth interviews with key informants in both countries. The paper contributes by unpacking the conditions under which local actors contest international criminal justice interventions.

Title: Cash transfers and social preferences of children
Authors: Johannes Haushofer, Magdalena Larreboure, Sara Lowes, Leon Mait
Abstract: We study the effects of a large unconditional cash transfer program on social preferences of children in rural Kenya using a randomized controlled trial. We measure the social preferences of 4022 children with survey questions and incentivized behavioral games three years after the cash transfer. First, we find no persistent economic effects of the program. Additionally, we find no consistent evidence that children from the treatment group or that children from the spillover group are more or less prosocial than children from the control group. However, we find some evidence of reduced psychological well-being among adults and children in spillover households.

Title: Inductive inference for restricted stochastic dominance
Authors: David M. Kaplan, Xin Liu
Abstract: Conventional first-order stochastic dominance tests have two important limitations: non-rejection does not provide strong evidence of dominance, and the simple “reject” or “not reject” decision loses much information. Instead, we learn inductively about the set of values on which one CDF lies below another (restricted stochastic dominance). With high asymptotic probability, this set is contained within our outer confidence set and contains our inner confidence set. These confidence sets provide a richer picture than a global test’s single binary decision, and a large inner confidence set provides strong evidence of restricted stochastic dominance. Our theory allows generic non-iid sampling.

Title: Liquidity withdrawal before scheduled macroeconomic announcements
Authors: Guanchen Lv, Weidong Li, Yaqiong Zhou
Abstract: This note tests whether displayed liquidity deteriorates before scheduled macroeconomic announcements. Using millisecond-level E-mini S&P 500 futures order-book data at 78 announcement times in 2024, we find that spreads widen by 5.3% and best-quote depth falls by 8.7% in the final ten seconds before release, relative to minutes 1–10 before release. These changes persist locally and are not mirrored in 58 matched pseudo-windows without material scheduled releases. During the first ten seconds after release, message-sequence classification assigns 31.2% of absolute midquote adjustment to execution-driven depletion and 64.0% to cancellation-driven depletion and explicit non-trade quote updates. The findings are consistent with anticipatory liquidity withdrawal.

Title: Shared parental leave, male board directors, and firm performance: A corporate governance perspective
Authors: Ylva Baeckström, Onur Kemal Tosun
Abstract: To explore a broader dimension of board gender diversification, we investigate whether increased gender-equal government policy in relation to shared parental leave (SPL) affects the governance behavior of male board directors. We analyze the influence of the 2015 UK SPL policy using data on 1930 UK firms and semi-structured interviews with board directors. Consistent with social influence theory, we observe changes in male directors’ governance decisions after SPL. Attributable to better corporate governance, financial performance improves in firms with predominantly male boards. Director interviews reveal increased board level focus on gender equality and SPL, often facilitated by considerate, yet powerful, male directors. Broadening research on corporate governance and gender, our study suggests the positive influence of increased commitment to gender equality on the corporate governance behavior of the predominant cohort of male directors. For board gender diversity to contribute to meaningful performance improvements diversity must be embedded at deep organizational levels, and women directors must be granted sufficient power to effect strategic change. Governments need to ensure gender egalitarian policies foster structural equality and encourage fathers to take parental leave. In addition to focusing on gender representation targets, firms must address boardroom gender power imbalance.

Title: Competing for commoditization or platforming for de-commoditization: The role of salient thinking
Authors: Qingyuan Zhu, Jiong Sun, Guowei Liu
Abstract: Consumer preferences are often context-dependent, with attention naturally drawn to a product’s most prominent attribute. Applying the behavioral framework of “salient thinking,” this paper examines how firms strategically design channel architecture to manipulate consumer focus. We reveal a fundamental asymmetry in the incentives for firms to transition from direct competitors to cooperative complementors. Under direct competition, markets often devolve into a “commoditized,” price-salient equilibrium. However, we demonstrate that relative product quality allows firms to escape this trap. When a lower-quality firm resells a premium competitor’s product, the resulting contrast shifts consumer focus from price to quality; this “de-commoditization” fosters a market environment that can overcome double marginalization, particularly when quality-production costs remain moderate. Crucially, this mechanism is structurally asymmetric: it fails if the high-quality firm acts as the reseller, as low-quality firms prefer price-salient competition. These insights provide a novel, cognition-driven rationale for why premium and budget brands selectively co-locate in modern retail ecosystems.

Title: Robustness-led and stability-responsive rescheduling: A Stackelberg game-theoretic formulation
Authors: Man Li, Shuqi Li, Junpeng Wang, Xuanfei Wang, Junwei Wei, Qinmin Yang, Xiangmin Zhang
Abstract: Scheduling under disruptions poses a fundamental challenge in operations research, as decision makers must hierarchically prioritize system robustness while responding with schedule stability in real time. Existing rescheduling approaches typically rely on symmetric or weighted formulations, which obscure the leader-follower decision asymmetry inherent in disruption management and fail to provide a principled coordination mechanism between robustness and stability. This study formulates disrupted rescheduling as a hierarchical decision-making problem and proposes a Stackelberg game-theoretic formulation grounded in bilevel optimization. The structure explicitly models robustness as the Leader’s strategic objective and stability as the Follower’s responsive objective, thereby capturing the endogenous priority structure observed in practical rescheduling decisions. A baseline schedule is first constructed via multi-objective optimization to define the feasible and performance-relevant region for subsequent adjustments. Under disruptions, rescheduling decisions are then derived through backward induction by characterizing the subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE) of the Stackelberg game, yielding sequential and priority-aware responses that coordinate stability within robustness-led constraints. Computational experiments on standard benchmark instances demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a robustness-stability coordination unattainable by conventional strategies. In particular, the Stackelberg-based model attains robustness levels statistically indistinguishable from robustness-dominant complete rescheduling, while simultaneously improving schedule stability by an average of 39.52% relative to stability-oriented right-shift rescheduling. These results indicate that explicitly modeling rescheduling as a hierarchical bilevel game enables superior performance continuity under disruptions. The study contributes to the literature by introducing a decision-theoretic perspective on rescheduling under disruptions, establishing Stackelberg games as a unifying framework for robustness-stability coordination, and offering a transferable modeling paradigm for complex scheduling problems with hierarchical priorities.

Title: Heuristics for balancing cost and diversity in wire harness routing layouts
Authors: T. Karlsson, E. Åblad
Abstract: This paper addresses the harness dissimilarity problem—a generalization of the path dissimilarity problem—in which the goal is to select ℎ dissimilar yet low-cost wire harness routing layouts, providing alternatives for engineering decision-making. Our approach involves two stages: first, generating a diverse pool of candidate routings; second, constructing subsets of size ℎ that are well-distributed along an approximated Pareto front. We analyze three methods for generating the candidate pool: the iterative penalty method, the pathway reward method, and NSGA-II. To approximate a Pareto front for the bi-objective problem of maximizing diversity while minimizing the total cost of selected candidates, we propose a weighted-sum constructive heuristic combined with local search, which outperforms a GRASP metaheuristic from related work. The method is also evaluated against an exact solver for small instances.

Title: Introduction to the special issue honoring Michel Juillard’s contribution to macroeconomics
Authors: Thomas Lubik, Isabelle Salle, Gauthier Vermandel
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Diagnostic expectations and cryptocurrency returns
Authors: Weijia Xue, Chunyang Zhou
Abstract: This paper studies whether standard tokenomics can account for the strong hourly return reversals observed in cryptocurrency markets. Using 319 Binance USDT pairs, we document pervasive short-horizon negative return predictability: past one-hour returns forecast subsequent one- to four-hour returns with negative coefficients for most coins, including BTC and ETH. We then show that a benchmark tokenomic model with rational expectations cannot generate this pattern because equilibrium token prices follow a geometric Brownian motion and therefore exhibit no non-overlapping return predictability. To explain the data, we introduce diagnostic expectations (DE) as the only wedge relative to the rational benchmark. Recent news shifts perceived platform productivity through a representativeness term and induces price overshooting, which is subsequently corrected as sentiment mean-reverts. The model matches the observed reversal pattern, implies that sentiment is priced in equilibrium, and generates endogenous boom-bust dynamics. We also show that the framework extends tractably to settings with heterogeneous coins and demand.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: History-dependent monetary policy – less is more
Authors: Olena Kostyshyna, Luba Petersen, Jing Yang
Abstract: History-dependent monetary policies (HDMP) can potentially address the challenges that standard monetary policy frameworks face, especially at the ELB. Using controlled laboratory experiments, we identify several vulnerabilities in HDMP. Our analysis of experimental data shows that a weakened expectations channel can undermine HDMP. Experimental participants’ expectations feed off past data; they are not forward-looking and do not internalize the stabilization properties or future make-up strategies of HDMP. Conditional on these expectations, we highlight two risks associated with HDMP: inflation overshoots under average inflation targeting and deflationary spirals under price level targeting and nominal GDP level targeting. However, effective central bank communication through medium-term macroeconomic projections can improve the performance of price level targeting.

Title: Economy-wide and international spillovers of the economic impacts of climate change
Authors: Maksym Chepeliev, Dominique van der Mensbrugghe, Toon Vandyck
Abstract: Estimates of the economic consequences of climate change diverge widely and are influenced by methodological choices. Here, we explore different approaches to quantifying economic damages by leveraging a structural model of the global economy. We decompose macroeconomic outcomes by region, factor, and sector to reveal differences between top-down aggregate productivity shocks and a bottom-up representation of impact channels. While aggregate economic outcomes are comparable, region-specific results differ substantially between approaches at the tails of the distribution, driven by divergent international trade responses. Allowing for economic adaptation in production and trade flows, our findings indicate that international spillovers raise global welfare losses from climate change by 1%–7% relative to the sum of domestic impacts. Overall, our results suggest that a disaggregated representation of climate change impact channels is important for improving the understanding of aggregate economic outcomes and for informing effective adaptation policies that account for international trade spillovers.

Title: Carbon emissions intensity and idiosyncratic volatility: Evidence from Indian firms
Authors: Ushmeet Kaur, Wasim Ahmad
Abstract: Climate change has become an increasingly important source of financial risk, attracting growing interest in how carbon emissions are priced in equity markets. Although the literature is expanding, firm-level evidence from emerging markets remains limited. In this paper, we examine whether corporate carbon emissions intensity predicts future idiosyncratic stock return volatility among Indian listed firms over the period 2009–2023. We find that firms with higher CO 2 emissions intensity, measured as Scope 1 and Scope 2 carbon-dioxide-equivalent (CO 2 e) emissions scaled by revenue, exhibit significantly higher one-period-ahead idiosyncratic stock return volatility. Specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in emissions intensity increases annualised idiosyncratic volatility by 1.32 percentage points, representing 4.6% of the sample mean. The relationship is driven primarily by direct (Scope 1) rather than purchased energy (Scope 2) emissions and is stronger for firms covered by India’s Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme and during periods of elevated economic policy uncertainty, but weaker for firms that use renewable energy. We also find evidence that stock illiquidity is a potential channel through which carbon emissions influence future firm-specific stock return risk. The results remain robust to alternative measures of emissions intensity and risk, sample-selection corrections, a lead test, an instrumental-variables analysis, and additional robustness checks. Overall, our findings suggest that firm-level carbon emissions are an important determinant of firm-specific stock return risk in an emerging equity market.

Title: The impact of Daylight Saving Time (DST) on electricity consumption in Iran
Authors: Amirhossein Rafati Sahneh Saraei, Ali Jadidzadeh
Abstract: Daylight Saving Time (DST) shifts clock time relative to daylight and routine activities, with ambiguous effects on electricity consumption: later evening daylight may reduce lighting demand but may also affect cooling, heating, and activity-related load. This paper evaluates the effect of DST on electricity consumption in Iran using nationwide hourly load data from 2015 to 2021, weather and calendar controls, and a Regression Discontinuity in Time (RDiT) design around legally fixed spring-forward and fall-back transition dates. We distinguish local boundary effects from the season-average daily effect over the full DST-active period. The national season-average daily ATE is positive, corresponding to a 2.24% increase in national daily electricity consumption during DST, but is not statistically significant at the 5% level under Newey–West inference. In contrast, the boundary RDiT estimates reveal significant local discontinuities: the spring-forward transition is associated with a 3.87% increase in residualized electricity consumption, while the DST-normalized fall-back estimate indicates an 11.14% decrease under DST relative to standard time. These transition-specific effects should not be netted out to infer the full-season effect. Heterogeneity analyses show that effects vary across tariff periods and consumer categories, with stronger spring-forward responses during on-peak hours and different fall-back responses for RECs and EDCs. Overall, the results do not support a simple electricity-saving interpretation of DST in Iran; the estimated effect depends on the estimand, timing of demand, and consumer composition.

Title: Route-informed planning for medium- and heavy-duty truck charging infrastructure in California
Authors: Runhua (Ivan) Xiao, Miguel Jaller, Anmol Pahwa, Claudio B. da Cunha
Abstract: California freight electrification depends as much on charging access and corridor planning as on vehicle adoption. Public agencies and fleets need evidence on whether depot and public charging networks can support truckload operations without increasing empty repositioning, modeled charging-stop requirements, and route infeasibility. This study develops an operations-based freight charging assessment for mixed diesel and battery-electric truck operations and applies it to controlled California truckload scenarios. Rather than optimizing final station sites, the framework evaluates predefined depot-adjacent and public fast-charging sites through route feasibility, total and deadhead VMT, modeled charging stop rows, active charging locations, and cost-accounting indicators. The results are scenario-level route-record comparisons and do not reflect observed daily truck operations or session-level charging dwell measurements.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Data-driven modelling of passenger-car stock electrification: validation and cross-country scenarios
Authors: Dominik Fink, Harald Lerch, Vladislav Kemka, Pavel Žlábek, Jan Kovanda
Abstract: Electrification policy targets new registrations, but the transition of the national passenger-car stock depends jointly on BEV adoption and vehicle retirement. This study models both, using the Czech Republic as an ageing-market case. A power-law registration function is calibrated on Czech data for 2016–2024 and benchmarked against five reference countries; a fixed-lifetime stock-turnover model, with an age-structured extension, then gives post-2035 trajectories. The adoption parameter α is a reduced-form capacity measure reflecting affordability, policy continuity and charging access. Adjusted MAPE is 6.1–17.2 % with R 2 above 0.92; the Czech in-sample fit gives MAPE 5.8 %, R 2 0.974, α cal 0.034 and n cal 2.81. Vehicle lifetime alone sets the nominal replacement horizon r d = r 0 + L: 2047 for L = 12 years, 2055 for L = 20, while α scn = 0.10–0.40 governs the stock trajectory, not the terminal year. Results are scenario comparisons, not forecasts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Supervised dimension reduction for autoregressive time series based on sliced inverse regression
Authors: Ying Liao, Yifan Huang, Zhigen Zhao, Yisha Xiang
Abstract: Supervised dimension reduction is crucial for time series analysis, yet standard methods often ignore temporal dependencies, leading to information loss and suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we extend the conventional sliced inverse regression (SIR) method to propose an effective dimension reduction (EDR) framework for autoregressive (AR) time series. Within this framework, we introduce two ways (denoted by SIR-T-1 and SIR-T-2) to more efficiently utilize the available data by leveraging AR structures. SIR-T-1 incorporates lagged information by establishing an equivalence between the conditional covariance matrices of current and lagged observations. SIR-T-2 employs a weighted aggregation scheme to combine EDR directions estimated from multiple lags. Extensive simulation experiments show that SIR-T-1 significantly outperforms the basic SIR in prediction accuracy and robustness, particularly in challenging scenarios with small sample size, high noise, and nonlinearity. SIR-T-2 proves to be an effective approximation for time series with low noise levels. A case study on superconductor data demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves 28.6%–63.9% lower prediction error than SIR for data-limited manufacturing stages, confirming its practical utility. The results underscore that leveraging AR structures is essential for EDR in time series and the resulting EDR directions provide practical insights for real-world applications.

Title: Projection Uniqueness in Data Envelopment Analysis with No Free Disposability
Authors: Yongbin Pan, Haoxiang Liu, Ya Chen, Liang Liang

Title: A unified deep reinforcement learning framework for solving the heterogeneous fleet vehicle routing problem
Authors: Shihong Huang, Shengjie Wang, Lei Gao, Hong Ma, Zhanluo Zhang, Feng Zhang, Weihua Zhou
Abstract: The Heterogeneous Fleet Vehicle Routing Problem (HFVRP) incorporates diverse vehicle capacities, fixed costs, and variable travel costs, making routing decisions highly sensitive to vehicle selection. Most existing Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) methods assume homogeneous fleets, leading to suboptimal performance when applied to HFVRP. To address this, we investigate HFVRP under complex constraints and develop a unified DRL framework capable of solving the problem across diverse settings. We formulate a Mode-Switching Markov Decision Process, modeling the generation of HFVRP solutions as a single-stage autoregressive decision process. Accordingly, we propose a Mode-Switching Cross-Semantic Multi-View framework (MS-CSMV), a unified architecture featuring a cross-semantic encoder and a multi-view decoder that effectively addresses diverse problem constraints and captures the complex mapping relationships between vehicle heterogeneity and customer node attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MS-CSMV significantly outperforms state-of-the-art neural solvers and achieves a favorable balance between solution quality and computational efficiency, producing solutions within seconds. Furthermore, the framework exhibits robust zero-shot generalization capabilities across large-scale instances and previously unseen problem variants.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Data-driven robust optimization for emergency facility deployment under ambiguous demand position
Authors: Yuchen Li, Daniel Zhuoyu Long, Jianghua Zhang
Abstract: Under the uncertainty of disaster locations, the deployment of emergency facilities is a core challenge, which directly determines the efficiency of emergency response and thereby reduces the time required to deliver emergency services. To address the spatial uncertainty of future demand points, we propose a cluster-wise Wasserstein distance-based spatial ambiguity set via historical demand clustering to characterize future demand distribution. We first formulate a distributionally robust optimization model for locating emergency facilities from the perspective of minimizing the transport distance. Then from the target-oriented decision-making perspective, we propose a cluster-wise robust satisficing model to maximize the robustness to the uncertainty of achieving a specified satisfactory target transport distance. A solution technique based on row-and-column generation is proposed to tackle the large-scale discrete models efficiently. We conduct numerical experiments to verify the validity of the discretization method in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy under the proposed algorithm. The results show that the robust satisficing model has better average performance than the benchmark models. Finally, the robust satisficing framework is applied to deal with a real case of locating emergency facilities in Sichuan, an earthquake-prone region of China.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Real-time yard slot allocation for outbound containers in an automated container terminal based on deep reinforcement learning
Authors: Weixuan Niu, Yanwei Zhang, Mengyu Tang, Yuhan Song, Heng Huang, Suikai Li, Yu Tian
Abstract: Efficient yard slot allocation for outbound containers is paramount to enhancing ship loading efficiency in automated container terminals (ACTs), where the perpendicular yard layout and the twin yard crane (YC) configuration are widely deployed. In such ACTs, the storage of an arrived outbound container relies on a twin-YC relay process where the container is initially stacked in a temporary handshake slot by the landside YC and subsequently remarshalled to a seaside slot by the seaside YC, presenting a complex relay-type yard slot allocation problem (RYSAP). This problem essentially comprises two decision-making processes: Decision 1 allocates a handshake slot for an arrived outbound container, while Decision 2 selects an outbound container from the handshake area and allocates a seaside slot for it. Structurally, each decision-making process is decomposed into two hierarchical stages: Stage 1 constructs a stack-set to bound the decision space for Stage 2, and Stage 2 determines the specific slot within the stack-set. To cope with the uncertainties in container arrivals and decision triggering, this problem is addressed in real time via a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based method. For Stage 1, the stack-set selection strategy is designed to construct the stack-set at each decision-making point. For Stage 2, a DRL method is proposed for specific slot allocation, aiming to reduce the number of blocking containers and enhance space utilization. By integrating the two interconnected decision-making processes, a comprehensive Markov Decision Process (MDP) is formulated. Crucially, the mathematical expectation of the number of future blocking containers at the current state is incorporated into the reward function, thereby guiding the DRL agent to learn a forward-looking policy. To accelerate training convergence and enhance policy performance, a Double Dueling Deep Q-Network with effective random exploration (D3QN-ERE) is developed. Numerical experiments verify the effectiveness, stability, and favorable generalization capability of the proposed method. Further analysis of the experimental results provides some suggestions for improving the yard operation and management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: When Should Service Firms Engage in Co‐Opetition? Reliability, Pricing, and Market Dynamics
Authors: Zichen Liu, Qi Fu, Zhaotong Lian
Affiliations: Faculty of Business Administration University of Macau Macao SAR China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates strategic repair co‐opetition between two rival service providers with unreliable servers. We develop a two‐stage queueing game, where in Stage 1, the competing firms select their repair mode: either operating independent repair teams (competition) or sharing resources (co‐opetition). In Stage 2, they set service prices for delay‐sensitive customers. We analyze how these repair modes influence steady‐state service availability, pricing equilibria, and profitability. Our findings reveal that sharing resources does not universally improve service capacity; the outcome depends on the firms' relative repair efficiency. Additionally, although higher availability increases maximum throughput, it simultaneously intensifies price competition. Consequently, firms' preferences are contingent on market demand. When demand is high, the capacity benefits dominate, driving firms to choose the repair mode that yields higher availability. Conversely, in low‐demand scenarios, firms favor the mode with lower availability to restrict capacity and soften price competition. In markets with intermediate demand, asymmetric pricing equilibria tend to drive firms toward divergent repair modes, preventing the formation of co‐opetition. Finally, we show that while a social planner prefers higher capacity to maximize welfare, independent firms may strategically restrict capacity, leading to a divergence from the social optimum.

Title: Reinforcement learning for train marshalling in flat yards: a decision transformer approach
Authors: Amit Kumar, T. M. Rofin, Milind Akarte
Abstract: Railway freight transportation plays a vital role in sustainable logistics, offering a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative to road transport. Within this domain, shunting yard operations are critical for forming outbound trains by rearranging wagons. This paper addresses the train building by a single shunting engine problem, a challenging operational problem observed in flat shunting yards, where a single engine must reassemble wagons into a predefined sequence using a minimal number of moves. We develop a simulation-based framework using the Gymnasium library to model the physical and operational constraints of a realistic rail yard environment. This simulation serves as the foundation for a Hybrid Model that combines the simulation model with three solution approaches which are then explored and evaluated. First, an online deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent using the proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm, which learns by interacting with the environment Second, a recursive search heuristic (RSH) method that mimics rule-based operational strategies. Third, a decision transformer (DT) model that utilizes offline trajectory data to learn a sequence-to-action mapping, leveraging recent advances in attention-based architectures. A dataset of RSH generated trajectories is used to train the DT model, allowing it to perform effectively without online environment interaction. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on multiple problem instances of varying complexity, comparing the quality of the generated shunting plans, training times, and policy generalization capabilities. The results show that while the PPO performs competitively on small instances, it struggles with scalability. DT performs similar to RSH in small instance and outperforms PPO in all problem instances, offering a promising approach for deploying such trained Artificial Intelligence agents in operational setting. This study demonstrates the potential of Hybrid Model paradigm by combining simulation, heuristic search, and both online DRL and offline DT sequence modelling techniques for addressing complex combinatorial optimization problems.

Title: Privatization Under Political Ties
Authors: Matteo Broso
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Management University of Brescia Brescia Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT I study a product differentiation model with endogenous entry where a politically connected public firm competes with a private one. Consumers are heterogeneous in their willingness to pay. I argue that—because of political ties—the public firm may mimic the preferences of the consumer with the median willingness to pay. I show that as privatization (i.e., the weight on profits in the public firm's objective function) increases, the equilibrium market structure shifts from a welfare‐inefficient public monopoly to a duopoly.
