Title: Measuring perceived long-distance accessibility
Authors: Milan L. Moleman, Bert van Wee
Abstract: Over recent years, perceived accessibility has gained interest, yet is primarily studied in the context of daily travel. Relatively little is known about perceived long-distance accessibility, that is, the perceived ability to reach distant destinations of at least 100 km away. This paper develops and tests a measurement scale for perceived long-distance accessibility using data collected in 2025 among long-distance travellers in the Netherlands. First, we conduct an exploratory factor analysis to identify the underlying factors of perceived long-distance accessibility. Next, we apply a confirmatory factor analysis to validate the factor solution. Lastly, we explore relations between perceived long-distance accessibility levels and background information (among others, gender, age, educational attainment, employment status, household income, and level of urbanity) using a linear regression model and latent class analysis. Our analysis reveals four key dimensions of perceived long-distance accessibility among Dutch long-distance travellers: travel options, digital skills, needs and desires, and time availability. Overall, the measurement scale developed in this paper allows to quantitatively identify differences in levels of perceived long-distance accessibility among individuals, which in turn equips policymakers and practitioners with insights necessary to promote a more inclusive long-distance passenger transport system.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Designing transport systems for people with non-visible disabilities
Authors: Chu Shi Qi Chloe, Mikela Chatzimichailidou
Abstract: The accessibility and inclusivity of transport systems are critical to promoting health, equity, and participation, and require an understanding of the experiences and diverse needs of all users. Persons with disabilities, who are recognised as vulnerable road users, face elevated transport risks and increased challenges in navigating transport environments, often resulting in reduced accessibility and participation. Among them, individuals with non-visible disabilities experience compounded challenges, arising not only from the functional limitations of their impairments, but also from social and systemic obstacles due to the unseen nature of their conditions. Despite this, mobility studies specifically focusing on non-visible disabilities – conditions in which impairments are not outwardly apparent – remain limited and fragmented, often confined to condition-centric studies. This scoping review aims to identify the barriers and impacts experienced by individuals with non-visible disabilities when using transport systems, and to highlight key considerations for future interventions. Three non-visible disabilities – autism, dementia, and anxiety disorders – were selected to guide the literature search and analysis. Findings reveal the heterogeneity across the three selected conditions, along with common mobility barriers such as confusion and complexity in transport systems, and the overwhelming nature of the travel environment. Consequently, individuals across the three selected conditions often modify their travel behaviour and reduce social participation. The review identifies key principles for inclusive design, including people-centric planning, systemic integration of support and training, and an emphasis on actionable design changes to create accessible environments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: QUBO formulations for parallel machine scheduling
Authors: Frank Phillipson, Yoseph Y. Hutten
Abstract: This paper investigates several Quadratic Unconstrained Binary optimisation (QUBO) formulations for the parallel machine scheduling problem (Formula presented) with the goal of assessing their suitability for quantum annealing and related heuristic optimisation methods. Three QUBO models are constructed, ranging from formulations derived from classical integer and one-hot encodings to a more compact load-balancing based representation. Extensive computational experiments using Simulated Annealing (SA) and Quantum Annealing (QA) reveal substantial differences in scalability and solution quality among the formulations. The alternative load-balanced model consistently yields near-optimal makespans, typically within 1%–3% of the theoretical lower bound, highlighting its stability and effectiveness compared to the more penalty sensitive formulations, whose performance deteriorates for larger instances. Sensitivity analyses further reveal that the appropriate selection of penalty weights and problem-specific parameter tuning significantly influences both solution accuracy and computational effort in QUBO formulations. While current quantum hardware limitations restrict experimentation to small problem sizes, the findings illustrate how compact QUBO designs can better exploit quantum optimisation frameworks. The insights gained in this study provide practical modelling guidelines for future quantum scheduling research and lay the groundwork for extending QUBO-based approaches to more complex scheduling environments.

Title: A time-varying approach to assessing fiscal cyclicality: The role of the European fiscal framework
Authors: Giovanni Carnazza, Francesco Tomasone
Abstract: This paper offers new empirical insights into the relationship between the European fiscal framework and the cyclical stance of fiscal policy in EMU countries. By employing a Time-Varying Coefficient (TVC) model, we generate country- and year-specific measures of fiscal cyclicality from 1995 to 2019. We then quantify the evolving intensity of fiscal rules through a country- and year-specific composite index and examine its relationship with fiscal cyclicality via panel regressions with multiple estimators, including a robust IV-GMM specification that addresses endogeneity concerns. This dual-framework strategy enables us to capture the distortion introduced by real-time revisions and identify a significant procyclical bias in peripheral countries, which is largely masked when ex post data are used. In other words, our findings reveal a marked asymmetry: while the estimated relationship between fiscal rules and cyclicality is neutral or mildly countercyclical in core countries, it is significantly procyclical in peripheral ones when real-time data are considered. These results have important implications for the revised European fiscal framework, as the new indicator (i.e., net expenditure) continues to rely on cycle-sensitive variables and may therefore perpetuate the same structural basis. Our analysis calls for a deeper reconsideration of the methodology used to estimate potential output in the EU. By demonstrating how the interaction between fiscal rules and real-time macroeconomic estimates can generate unintended policy outcomes, this study contributes to a more informed debate on the future of fiscal governance in the euro area.

Title: The macroeconomic effects of a greener technology mix
Authors: Fabrizio Ferriani, Andrea Gazzani, Filippo Natoli
Abstract: What are the macroeconomic implications of a technology-driven green transition? Leveraging granular data on the universe of patents granted in the U.S., we construct a monthly green-innovation indicator defined as the share of U.S. patents filed since 1980 that are classified under climate change mitigation categories. After purging this measure from the effects of oil shocks, credit conditions, and other predictable macroeconomic components, we use it in a structural VAR model as a proxy for reallocation from brown to green innovation and we document that a positive green-innovation shock generates a temporary negative supply effect: industrial production falls, unemployment rises and consumer prices increase, reflecting lower aggregate productivity. These short-run costs, however, are not permanent and the negative implications for economic activity and prices dissipate in the medium run. Technology adjustment leads to a persistent decline in the emissions intensity of output and a shift in energy mix towards renewables, resulting in an overall Pareto improvement for the economy. Our findings are independent of variations in national and international climate policy commitments and point to a dynamic trade-off: greening the technology mix is costly in the short run, but it delivers lasting environmental gains without permanent macroeconomic losses.

Title: Bidding strategies for energy storage operators in a 100% renewable electricity market: A game-theoretic approach
Authors: Arega Getaneh Abate, Dogan Keles, Xiufeng Liu, Salim Hassi, Xiao-Bing Zhang
Abstract: Large-scale energy storage is expected to be a pivotal source of flexibility in electricity systems supplied entirely by renewable energy sources (RES). However, its strategic role in market-based dispatch remains insufficiently understood. In a 100% RES market setting, storage can improve adequacy and renewable utilization by shifting energy across time. It can also acquire market power as the main flexible, price-making technology. In this paper, we develop a Cournot competition model in which storage operators choose quantity bids to maximize profit in a stylized day-ahead electricity market supplied only by RES. Market clearing is represented through residual-demand blocks so that renewable intermittency appears as an intertemporal arbitrage opportunity for storage operators. We formulate the storage operators’ problem in two tractable ways: (ii) a continuous reformulation based on demand blocks, and (ii) an equivalent mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model with big- M linearization. Nash equilibria are computed with an iterative best-response procedure and benchmarked against a centralized social planner problem to quantify efficiency losses from strategic behavior. The model is calibrated to Denmark’s DK1 bidding zone using 2024 day-ahead data and 2030 renewable-capacity and demand projections. The results show that storage reduces imbalances and improves welfare relative to a no-storage case. Concentrated ownership also creates incentives to withhold flexibility, raise prices, and slow the reduction of unmet demand and curtailment. These findings position storage as both a stabilizing resource and a potential source of market power, highlighting the importance of market designs that jointly consider competition, concentration, and capacity deployment in high-RES systems.

Title: From terroir to quality: Handling the run for efficiency across time and space for Italian agri-food firms
Authors: Anna Rita Dipierro, Pierluigi Toma
Abstract: In the actual increasingly competitive market for agricultural firms, the ability to turn inputs into outputs named efficiency has to be pursued by exploiting quality. We conceive quality as a game changer within the per se complex agriculture-environment link. We aim at exploring the critical junctures between efficiency, quality and territorial riskiness, considering space-sensitive products, whose quality is certified as linked to the terroir. We employ an integrated methodological approach of efficiency analysis, causal inference and machine learning. A conditional nonparametric efficiency estimator is assisted by the causal evaluation of the certification effects on efficiency over time, through difference-in-differences technique and genetic matching. Also, a machine learning technique called feature selection is used to make out-of-sample prediction of the efficiency score. The approach is applied to 1133 Italian agri-food firms, measured over 24 internal and external characteristics from 2015 to 2020. Italy stands for a best-practice in the quality products market, despite increasing territorial vulnerability. We question and later find that the collaboration – which is needed to sell certified products of origin – is a vital expedient to run for efficiency over time and by less-caring of spatial threats. Results are relevant for researchers, and promote some win-win strategies for governors and producers in a long-term oriented vision of the sector.

Title: Navigating blockchain assimilation in supply chain organisations: an integrated institutional and innovation assimilation perspective
Authors: Colin Callinan, Trevor Clohessy, Amaya Vega, Graham Heaslip
Affiliations: Atlantic Technological University Department of Business and Marketing, , Sligo; Atlantic Technological University Department of Electronic, Software and Advanced Manufacturing Engineering, , Galway; Atlantic Technological University Department of Enterprise and Technology, , Galway; Atlantic Technological University Faculty of Engineering and Computing, , Galway
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how institutional pressures shape the adoption, assimilation and integration of blockchain technologies in supply chain organisations. By combining Gallivan’s innovation assimilation model with institutional theory, the paper explains why blockchain projects frequently stall or regress. Design/methodology/approach Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with blockchain vendors, adopters and ecosystem actors are triangulated with a systematic literature review to map institutional influences across assimilation stages. Findings The analysis identifies four institutional mechanisms; network legitimacy, coordinated uncertainty reduction, institutional paradoxes and cross-organisational cognitive reframing which collectively explain non-linear and uneven assimilation trajectories. Regulative, normative and cognitive pressures function as both enablers and constraints at different stages, particularly during routinisation and infusion. Practical implications The findings provide managers and policymakers with guidance on reducing institutional friction, aligning incentives across supply chain tiers and supporting stable governance and assurance structures required for sustained blockchain integration. Originality/value The study advances supply chain management research by showing how multi-tier governance, power asymmetries and certification regimes shape blockchain assimilation. It offers a multi-level explanation for why blockchain rarely progresses beyond early pilots into embedded, long term practice.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Integration of planning and scheduling in silicon industry: A bi-level perspective
Authors: Zuocheng Li, Aodong Ma, Rongjuan Luo
Affiliations: Kunming University of Science and Technology, Kunming; School of Logistics and Management Engineering, Yunnan University of Finance and Economics, Kunming
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Editorial: Reproducibility at the International Journal of Forecasting
Authors: Pierre Pinson, Christophe Pérignon, Olivier Akmansoy, Nesrine Dali, Bahman Rostami-Tabar

Title: Beyond circularity: Topological and temporal limits of the circular economy
Authors: Nicolas Merveille
Abstract: The circular economy has established itself as a dominant sustainability paradigm, yet the formal properties of its foundational metaphor, the circle, remain unexamined. This paper identifies two analytically distinct constraints embedded in the dominant circular imaginary. The first is topological: when the operative metaphor functions as a single closed loop, it reproduces the cycle graph, a one-dimensional structure with zero redundancy and minimal resilience. The second is temporal: the assessment apparatus associated with circularity operates within quantitative, sequential time (chronos) and renders qualitative, heterogeneous temporalities (kairos) structurally invisible. The claim defended here is specific. Sustainability paradigms generally pose time as a problem left open; the circular economy's founding metaphor figures time as resolved (return, cycle, regeneration) while its apparatus operationalizes only chronos. This blindness is not general ignorance but performative contradiction. Empirical evidence from three continents (African solar projects, Mexican circular assessment, Peruvian extraction) substantiates the diagnosis. We propose a polyrhythmic completion structured as a wheel, with Doughnut Economics as the rim, regeneration as the hub, and ArtefactKairos (institutional devices for temporal composition) as the spokes, operationalized through the Temporal Composition Diagnostic (TCD), a four-step governance protocol. The TCD is applied to a published sugar beet pulp biorefinery assessment that models feedstock as a fixed daily input without addressing the seasonal harvest sustaining it, then calibrated ex ante against the Antamina mining region in Peru. In both settings it reveals what standard assessment cannot detect and specifies the institutional clauses it would generate.

Title: Beyond generation: Clean energy accommodation and health-related defensive expenditure among Chinese households
Authors: Jing-Yue Liu, Xiang-Jie Liu, Yue-Jun Zhang
Abstract: The social value of clean electricity depends not only on how much is generated but also on whether power systems can absorb and deliver it for use rather than curtail it. This study examines whether improved clean energy accommodation reduces households' health-related defensive expenditure. Using China's Plan on Clean Energy Accommodation as a quasi-natural experiment and micro-panel data from the China Family Panel Studies for 2012–2022, we find that the policy reduced residents' out-of-pocket medical expenditure in policy-targeted regions by about 18% on average, with larger reductions among rural residents and in regions facing larger pre-policy accommodation gaps. Consistent with this reduction, supporting evidence indicates that the policy reduced renewable curtailment, increased realized clean electricity output, and improved ambient air quality; it was also associated with cleaner household energy use and more frequent exercise, especially in rural areas. These gains, however, were unevenly distributed, with larger effects in net electricity-exporting and resource-rich regions, areas with limited healthcare service capacity, and among lower-income, male, and middle-aged residents. An illustrative calculation suggests potential annual savings of RMB 261.2 billion (US$38.3 billion) in out-of-pocket medical expenditure across the policy-targeted regions. These findings underscore the importance of clean energy accommodation and provide evidence to inform policies aimed at translating renewable electricity into more equitable household welfare gains.

Title: A bi-level optimization model for urban bicycle lane planning with a globally optimal branch-and-price-and-cut algorithm
Authors: Lexing Zhang, Michael W. Levin, Mobina Nankali
Abstract: Cycling safety remains a major challenge because riders are frequently exposed to mixed traffic, which suppresses cycling adoption and limits the growth of sustainable mobility. To address this issue, we model the problem as a Stackelberg game in which the planner seeks to minimize cyclists’ exposure to mixed traffic while users respond by choosing routes that minimize their perceived travel times, and we develop a bilevel network design model that selects protected bicycle lanes under a construction-length budget to reduce cyclists’ unprotected exposure. The model is solved using a branch-and-price-and-cut framework with finite-convergence and global-optimality guarantees. Experiments on several benchmark city-scale networks demonstrate that the approach effectively lowers exposure and can solve practical urban networks to small certified optimality gaps within reasonable computation times. The results further show that key algorithmic parameters shape both the resulting network designs and the computational performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The (hidden) Samaritan contest
Authors: Rabah Arezki, Youssouf Camara, Frederick Van Der Ploeg, Grégoire Rota-Graziosi

Title: The macroeconomic effects of purely forward-looking uncertainty shocks: Evidence from the euro area
Authors: Svetlana Rujin
Abstract: If the underlying data-generating process operates at a higher frequency than observed data, timing and dynamic restrictions in structural vector autoregressions (SVARs) may be misspecified. Building on Berger et al. (2020), I propose an alternative identification scheme that jointly relaxes the zero-impact restriction on realized volatility and the zero-lag restrictions on macroeconomic variables in the volatility block, estimated with a richer twelve-lag specification. Applied to euro area data, the identified shocks depress real activity gradually and with a delay, unlike the macro-neutral U.S. evidence, though they account for only a modest share of real fluctuations.

Title: Weaponized reputation: Experimental evidence on the misuse of coordinated punishments
Authors: Haihan Yu
Abstract: This paper experimentally studies how coordinated punishment can be misused. In a repeated trust game with public reputation, we compare a silent commitment treatment, where Agents privately choose a review threshold (the minimum payment required for a positive review), with a public commitment treatment, where the review threshold is observable before Principals choose payments. Public commitment significantly reduces cooperation: effort and payments fall relative to silent commitment. Public commitment also turns posted review thresholds into more enforceable demands: Principals are substantially more likely to meet visible thresholds. Successful zero-effort extraction, in which an Agent exerts no effort but sets a positive review threshold met by the Principal’s payment, is significantly more frequent under public commitment. Coordinated punishments can therefore discipline misconduct, but may also create tools for extortion.

Title: A rational bubble model with momentum
Authors: Feng Liu, Joseph S. White
Abstract: Standard rational greater-fool models (e.g., Allen et al., 1993; Liu and Conlon, 2018) generate bubbles but do not generate momentum. Behavioral models with bounded rationality (e.g., Hong and Stein, 1999) generate momentum but do not generate rational bubbles. We expand an existing rational greater-fool model to show how momentum emerges during asset bubbles.

Title: Geopolitical risk and fiscal financing capacity in E7 economies: does institutional quality matter?
Authors: Umar Farooq, Mosab I. Tabash, Abdulrahman Alomair, Abdulateif A. Almulhim
Abstract: This study examines whether geopolitical risk (GPR) affects tax revenue mobilization (TXR) in E7 economies and whether institutional quality (INQ) helps mitigate this effect. Using annual data for China, India, Brazil, Russia, Mexico, Indonesia, and Türkiye over 1985–2024, the study employs the Cross-Sectionally Augmented Autoregressive Distributed Lag (CS-ARDL) estimator, with Fully Modified Ordinary Least Squares (FMOLS) used for robustness. The results indicate that geopolitical risk significantly reduces tax revenue mobilization, while stronger institutional quality improves revenue performance. Moreover, the interaction between GPR and INQ is positive and significant, confirming that institutional quality weakens the adverse effect of geopolitical risk on tax revenue. The findings highlight the importance of institutional capacity in strengthening fiscal resilience and sustaining government financing capacity during periods of geopolitical uncertainty.

Title: The exchange rate puzzle and the systematic component of monetary policy: Evidence from Mexico
Authors: Jesús Eduardo López-Mares, Rogelio Varela-Llamas, Juan Manuel Ocegueda-Hernández
Abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate puzzle following contractionary monetary policy shocks in a small open economy. Using a Bayesian SVAR for Mexico, we compare three cumulative identification schemes: pure sign restrictions on impulse response functions (IRFs), a closed-economy Taylor-type rule with contemporaneous sign and zero restrictions, and an exchange-rate-augmented rule. Neither pure sign restrictions nor the closed-economy rule yields a precisely estimated overshooting pattern—only the augmented rule does. Robust to alternative specifications, these results suggest that omitting the exchange rate from the systematic component of monetary policy may hinder shock identification in small open economies.

Title: Endogenous depopulation and economic growth
Authors: Alberto Bucci, Klaus Prettner
Abstract: Fertility rates have declined dramatically across almost all high-income countries over the past decades. In some countries, population growth is already negative and many more are projected to exhibit negative population growth in the future. This raises concerns about potential economic prospects. Indeed, endogenous and semi–endogenous growth models imply that a shrinking workforce would lead to declining income growth and, perhaps, even to stagnation. We include an endogenous quantity/quality trade–off between fertility and human capital accumulation in these models to assess the extent to which a declining number of people (i.e., workers) may be compensated by increasing education. We demonstrate that economic growth does not necessarily decline with population shrinkage: in many scenarios, human capital investment can offset demographic headwinds and sustain technological progress.

Title: Approximately efficient resource allocation: A theoretical and experimental evaluation
Authors: Nicole Immorlica, Robizon Khubulashvili, Sera Linardi, Brendan Lucier, Joshua Mollner, Glen Weyl
Abstract: Matching mechanisms that elicit strength of preference can exhibit efficiency gains over those that do not. To quantify these gains, we propose a measure of approximate ex-ante Pareto efficiency. We use this notion to quantify the efficiency improvement of the raffles mechanism (which we define) over the deferred acceptance mechanism (DA). We complement our theoretical analyses with experimental results. Using human subjects, we find that the raffles mechanism yields higher average payoffs as predicted by the theory, despite the fact that subjects play only approximately optimal strategies.

Title: Fare evasion strategies, perceived safety, and travel choices in public transport: evidence from a vignette experiment
Authors: Benedetto Barabino, Martina Carra, Jérémy Celse, Roberto Ventura
Abstract: Fare evasion poses persistent challenges for public transport systems, with implications for financial sustainability, social norms, corporate image, and perceived safety and security. While deterrence strategies such as increasing inspection frequency or fine severity are widely used, their effects on passengers’ perceptions and behavioural spillovers remain weakly evidenced. This study examines how anti–fare evasion cues influence travel preferences, perceived safety and security, and fare‐evasion intentions, accounting for time of day and competition from a ride‑sharing service (RSS). Four research questions were examined through a vignette‑based randomised experiment. Participants chose among a non‑manipulated bus route, a manipulated route (enforcement or service cue), and an RSS alternative across seven conditions crossing enforcement cues (inspection, fines, neutral) and period (day/night). The results showed that the effects of anti–fare evasion cues were small and statistically uncertain. Neither inspections nor fines produced clear improvements in perceived safety or security (RQ1), and the enforcement type showed no consistent direct effect on the choice of the manipulated route (RQ2). Night-time conditions did not meaningfully change safety or risk perceptions, nor did they reliably moderate the association between perceived route safety and route choice (RQ3). Fare evasion was more frequent at night and less frequent on the manipulated route yet contrasts between Fine and Inspection treatments remained small and imprecisely estimated (RQ4). The RSS garnered only 3.73% choices amid price differentials. Thus, deterrence failed to bolster reassurance or ridership proxies, with choices driven by safety and security perceptions independently of cues. Night primarily led to increased evasion without corresponding gains in safety and security. Policies should pair targeted enforcement with service enhancements, particularly nocturnal, in multimodal contexts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Underestimation of the costs of owning and running a car
Authors: Adam Joachim Shier, Shane Timmons, Peter D. Lunn
Abstract: Car ownership and use appears less responsive to cost increases and income declines than might be expected, a pattern often attributed to habit formation and lifestyle adjustment. An additional explanation is that motorists may underestimate how much they spend on owning and running a car, but there is little empirical evidence testing this possibility. Using a representative sample of 801 motorists, we compare intuitive estimates of the annual motoring costs with detailed itemised expenditure across all major fixed (e.g., tax, insurance) and variable (e.g., fuel/charging, parking) costs over the same period. Total reported costs are almost 50% higher than motorists intuit. Median intuitive costs were €2,000, while median itemised costs were €2,923, excluding purchase price and depreciation. Most motorists (over 70%) exhibit this underestimation bias, with similar rates across engine types and socio-demographic groups. These findings are consistent with recall failures and salience bias when motorists consider the costs of owning and running a car, with potential implications for the persistence of car ownership. Improving the visibility and aggregation of motoring costs may complement fiscal and infrastructural measures aimed at supporting sustainable modal shift.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Container shipping disruptions and the economics of decarbonization
Authors: Hugo Morão
Abstract: This paper examines how containerized shipping disruptions affect macroeconomic and financial conditions for decarbonization. The analysis identifies supply chain shocks using exogenous price surcharges from major container carriers in a structural vector autoregression. Supply chain disruptions weaken the economic case for clean energy investment through three channels. Policy uncertainty raises the Transition Risk Index while depressing carbon prices on impact. Clean technology costs rise and suppress expected decarbonization investment returns. Damage to climate policy credibility advantages fossil fuel interests. Carbon prices fall on impact before recovering as substitution toward more carbon-intensive production raises allowance demand. Expected decarbonization investment returns remain depressed while fossil fuel stocks appreciate, as markets price in weaker future climate policy. Supply chain vulnerabilities generate persistent headwinds for the energy transition that operate through financial market channels.

Title: Trading electrons: Predicting DART spread spikes in ISO electricity markets
Authors: Emma Hubert, Dimitrios Lolas, Ronnie Sircar
Abstract: We study the problem of forecasting and optimally trading day-ahead versus real-time (DART) price spreads in U.S. wholesale electricity markets. Building on the framework of Galarneau-Vincent et al., we extend spike prediction from a single zone to a multi-zone setting and treat both positive and negative DART spikes within a unified statistical model. To translate directional signals into economically meaningful positions, we develop a structural and market-consistent price impact model based on day-ahead bid stacks. This yields closed-form expressions for the optimal vector of zonal INC/DEC quantities, capturing asymmetric buy/sell impacts and cross-zone congestion effects. When applied to NYISO, the resulting impact-aware strategy significantly improves the risk-return profile relative to unit-size trading and highlights substantial heterogeneity across markets and seasons.

Title: Deployment-oriented validation of vessel energy efficiency inference for maritime decarbonisation policy
Authors: Xun Yang, Ran Yan
Abstract: AI-based vessel fuel-consumption models are used for emission accounting, compliance screening, and decarbonisation planning, but their reported accuracy depends on how validation is designed. Using high-frequency data from 27 ocean-going vessels, this study tests whether random mixed validation overstates model performance. We compare it with maritime use-case tests for later-period prediction, unseen trips, unseen vessels, cross-type transfer, and data-scarce transfer. Across 64 model-task combinations, use-case-aligned held-out errors are 9.18 percentage points higher on average than random mixed-validation estimates. Prediction error also reverses direction across settings, indicating that accuracy metrics alone can hide policy-relevant over- or under-estimation. In a container-ship CII case study, rating accuracy ranges from 34.4% to 71.7%, while 11.7% to 100.0% of action-required D/E vessel-years are missed. These results indicate that regulatory and planning applications require validation aligned with the intended maritime use case, with reporting of both error magnitude and bias direction.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Do aviation hazard rankings overlook conservation-concern birds in U.S. wildlife strikes?
Authors: Amir Rafe, Subasish Das
Abstract: Airports concentrate aircraft and birds in shared space, making wildlife strikes a flight-safety problem and a documented source of avian mortality. We analyze 343,997 U.S. wildlife-strike records from 1990 to 2025 with a framework that corrects for reporting growth, models per-strike severity, and ranks species by aviation hazard and conservation status. A detection-aware count model bounds the true rise in the strike rate between 3.4 and 8 fold, below the widely cited fourteen-fold rise in the reported rate. A random-parameters ordered probit shows that engine ingestion and body mass dominate severity, with the mass effect growing more variable at higher impact speeds. Conservation weighting shifts 112 of 310 ranked species by more than 30 places, elevating aerial insectivores, migratory warblers, and grassland passerines, including the Vulnerable Chimney Swift. The results support region- and season-specific mitigation that protects aircraft and declining birds together.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Challenges in comparing measured and modelled annual average noise levels around airports
Authors: Rebekka C. van der Grift, Alireza Amiri Simkooei, Mirjam Snellen
Abstract: Aircraft noise has a significant impact on communities near airports. To regulate noise, annual average levels such as L den are modelled across large areas. This study examines the consistency between L den predicted by the European Civil Aviation Conference Doc 29 model and measurements from noise monitoring terminals around Amsterdam Airport Schiphol from 2017 to 2024. While strong correlations confirm Doc29′s suitability for system-level assessments, systematic biases persist, with nighttime levels L night generally overestimated and L den underestimated. Three potential sources were identified: difference between modelled and flown tracks, background noise influencing measured levels, and undetected flights, particularly for quieter aircraft and in low noise regions. Accounting for these factors improves correlation and reduces deviation between measurements and predictions. These results demonstrate promising methods for enabling noise model validation near airports. Further improvements in detection methods and operational modelling will increase the robustness of noise assessments and better support evidence-based policy development around major airports.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Pragmatism, not ideology: drivers of e-bike sharing usage intensity
Authors: Michael Stiebe, Frank Christian Krysiak, Widar von Arx, Benjamin Weggelaar
Abstract: What drives usage intensity among registered e-bike sharing system (EBSS) users – distinguishing power users from dormant registrants – remains underexplored despite its importance for system viability. We link survey responses from 1,844 registered users to their individual trip histories within an operational dataset of 1.4 million trips from free-floating S-Pedelec and dock-based e-bike sharing systems operating concurrently in Basel, Switzerland. Using Gaussian Mixture Model clustering and an ordered logit model, we find that usage is highly concentrated (Gini = 0.77) and primarily substitutes public transport. Pro-environmental self-identity negatively associates with high-intensity user (“power-user”) status. Instead, intensive use is associated with multimodal integration and perceived functional superiority over public transport. System design distinguishes two distinct pragmatic archetypes: dock-based “routine optimizers” and free-floating “flexibility maximizers”. These findings suggest EBSS policy should emphasize multimodal integration and service reliability calibrated to EBSS’s genuine but bounded role in sustainable urban mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Trade and uneven development: evidence from China’s tea exports
Authors: Xinsheng Cui, Ruixia Cui, Guangbin Cheng
Abstract: Why could the expansion of international trade contribute to industrial development in one part of the world while reinforcing Malthusian forces in another? We examine this question through the dramatic expansion of Chinese tea exports to Western markets between 1776 and 1910. Exploiting variation in local exposure to changes in national tea exports based on agro-climatic suitability and trade costs, we show that greater export exposure increased population growth. The demographic response operated through a relaxation of preventive checks, reflected in earlier marriage and higher fertility. In contrast, tea exports generated no persistent gains in per-capita income or human capital. The findings suggest that the gains from international trade can be absorbed primarily through demographic expansion in economies subject to Malthusian forces, shedding light on the uneven developmental consequences of global economic integration.

Title: Recovery strategies for disrupted seaside planning in container terminals: a systematic review
Authors: Fabricio Niebles-Atencio, Eduardo Lalla-Ruiz, Stefan Voß

Title: Synchronous production and intralogistics of smart assembly cell line under graduation intelligent manufacturing system
Authors: Shiquan Ling, Binyang Liu, Mingxing Li, Daqiang Guo, Ting Qu, Zhen He, George Q. Huang, Ming Li

Title: Managing a continuous-time make-to-stock system with finite resources
Authors: Qian Luo, Qingguo Bai, Jianxin Fang, Nicholas Yeo
