Title: A new school bus location routing problem with mixed loads and bus stop selection
Authors: Willem Gerhard Meiring, Jan H. van Vuuren
Affiliations: Stellenbosch University

Title: Intrafirm integration versus separation in product and digital service competition
Authors: Li Li, Mengqing Zhang
Affiliations: Sun Yat-Sen University

Title: Profile Bayesian optimization for expensive computer experiments
Authors: Courtney Kyger, James Fernandez, John A Grunenwald, James Braun, Annie S Booth
Affiliations: Department of Statistics, Vriginia Tech; Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, NC State University

Title: Are international diversification benefits still achievable? turn on machine learning
Authors: Ana Sofia Monteiro, Silva Nuno, Helder Sebastião
Abstract: This study uses multivariate Machine Learning—Dynamic Conditional Correlation (DCC) models to dynamically forecast returns and covariances. The resulting forecasts are then used to select international diversified portfolios. Using weekly data on 77 national stock and bond indexes from August 2001 to July 2022, we show that some of these models lead to large economic gains. Most notably the proposed Random Forest—DCC model and a combination of two and four best-performing Machine Learning portfolios substantially enhance portfolio performance and the certainty equivalent of constant relative risk-averse investors. International diversification is most beneficial for investors from America, Asia–Pacific, Middle East, Africa, and Europe namely from 2014 to 2022. The results also point out that most of the economic advantages come from investing in emerging markets.

Title: A sustainability-aware optimization framework for port-hinterland truck scheduling
Authors: Ali Mokhtari-Moghadam, Trung Thanh Nguyen, Massoud Mohsendokht, Jin Wang, Zaili Yang
Abstract: Abstract Ports are critical gateways for trade and regional growth but also generate substantial externalities such as emissions, congestion, and safety risks. Growing maritime transport and port throughput intensify long-haul diesel truck traffic on hinterland access roads, causing peak-hour bottlenecks, long queues, and higher environmental impacts. Despite many proposed operational strategies, these challenges remain insufficiently addressed. This paper develops a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model for sustainable port-hinterland truck scheduling within an integrated chassis-based remote gate (CRG) and battery-electric trucks (BET) framework for short-haul transport. Using a major UK port case study with real traffic data, the model minimizes total logistics costs, including fixed investments, transport, waiting and idling times for short- and long-haul trucks, and $$\hbox {CO}_2$$ CO 2 emissions. To handle large-scale instances, a two-stage adaptive genetic algorithm (TS-AGA) is proposed and benchmarked against the MILP and a two-stage simulated annealing approach. Collaborative and non-collaborative scheduling strategies are compared to assess the benefits of coordinated decision-making. Results show that collaborative scheduling reduces total system costs by about 13.6% by better synchronizing long-haul diesel truck arrivals with short-haul battery-electric truck operations. Sensitivity analysis further examines how long-haul travel-time uncertainty affects congestion and economic performance. Overall, the proposed MILP model and TS-AGA solution approach demonstrate that coordinated truck scheduling can substantially improve the operational efficiency and sustainability of CRG-BET-based port-hinterland systems. By jointly optimizing long-haul and short-haul operations under collaborative and uncertainty-aware strategies, the study offers a practical and scalable scheduling methodology to reduce logistics costs, congestion, and emissions while supporting sustainable port-city connectivity.

Title: An extension of Harsanyi’s linear tracing procedure for selecting a proper equilibrium
Authors: Lingxuan Tang, Yiyin Cao, Chuangyin Dang
Abstract: Proper equilibrium refines Selten’s perfect equilibrium by imposing a stricter requirement on trembles, which introduces computational challenges, especially in large games. Given the foundational role of Harsanyi’s linear and logarithmic tracing procedures in equilibrium selection theory, this paper introduces extensions of these procedures to select proper equilibria in normal-form games. We propose an extension of the linear tracing procedure by constructing a perturbed game with continuously differentiable polynomial functions, where each player optimizes a linear combination of the payoff function based on the strategies given by others and the payoff function based on a prior belief about the strategies. By applying the optimality condition, fixed-point argument, and variable transformation to the perturbed game, we establish the existence of a smooth path starting from a unique point and approaching a proper equilibrium. To enhance procedural efficiency, we develop an extension of the logarithmic tracing procedure tailored to approximate the extension of the linear tracing procedure. Additionally, we incorporate a continuously differentiable exponential function into the perturbed games and utilize error-bound analysis to establish smooth paths to proper equilibria. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency and stability of our methods.

Title: A predictive maintenance framework based on conservative remaining useful life method
Authors: Junjie Zhu, Butong Li, Xufeng Zhao
Abstract: Prediction accuracy alone does not guarantee economically effective maintenance decisions. For safety-critical and high-availability equipment, optimistic remaining useful life (RUL) estimates may delay maintenance and increase failure risk, whereas excessive conservatism may cause premature intervention and loss of usable life. This study develops a decision-oriented predictive maintenance framework based on conservative remaining useful life (CRUL) estimation to determine an appropriate level of conservatism. The framework integrates an asymmetric Insurance Factor (IF), case-specific conservatism selection, and uncertainty-aware maintenance decision-making. A hybrid 1D-CNN–Informer model is employed to capture both local degradation patterns and long-range temporal dependencies. The asymmetric loss provides a statistical interpretation of conservative prediction by estimating a lower conditional expectile, with larger IF values assigning greater penalties to optimistic errors. Maintenance lead-time uncertainty is further incorporated into the decision process, and the IF is selected by minimizing the maintenance cost rate, thereby balancing corrective-maintenance risk against premature intervention and unused RUL. Experiments on an aircraft-engine degradation dataset show that the proposed predictor achieves competitive RUL estimation performance, while the CRUL-based decision framework consistently reduces maintenance costs compared with traditional maintenance strategies.

Title: The industrial geography of Eurasia in the 20th century: Soviet planners meet Tsarist fundamentals
Authors: Marvin Suesse, Iris Wohnsiedler
Abstract: How responsive is the location of economic activity to shocks? This paper uses a new data set on the location of factories in the Russian Empire (1890, 1908) and the Soviet Union (1989), supported by modern nightlight data, to explore the forces determining the spatial location of industrial production in Eurasia over the long twentieth century. Over this period, the region experienced a radical shift in its economic system from market to central planning and back again. Production was also subjected to various shocks, including war and the associated relocation of firms, forced population movement, and infrastructure investments. We assess to what extent these shocks changed the role of agglomeration effects, local labour inputs and market access in determining industry location. We find that shocks to labour fundamentals shifted the economy to new spatial equilibria. Nonetheless, the shifts were small in magnitude and these forces were not powerful enough to eradicate the path-dependent effects of Tsarist locations that were still evident in the industrial structure of the region even a century later. These results suggest the impact of even severe shocks to a spatial equilibrium to be modest at the aggregate level.

Title: Fiscal Constraints and the Power of Words: Does High Debt Mute the Fed?
Authors: Athanasios Andrikopoulos, Apostolos G. Katsafados, Steven Ongena
Affiliations: University of Sussex Business School Brighton UK; Athens University of Economics and Business Athens Greece; Department of Finance University of Zurich Zurich Switzerland; Swiss Finance Institute Zurich Switzerland; KU Leuven Leuven Belgium; Norwegian University of Science and Technology, NTNU Business School Trondheim Norway; CEPR London UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We test whether high public debt is associated with reduced effectiveness of Federal Reserve communication. Using voice sentiment measures extracted from FOMC press conference Q&A sessions, we estimate local projections and find that high debt significantly attenuates the estimated association between voice sentiment and industrial production. The attenuation is particularly strong for hawkish (anger) and dovish (happiness) emotional tones, and for overall positive voice sentiment. Our results are robust to a series of robustness checks, including alternative lag lengths, monetary policy controls, and textual sentiment as a control. These results align with fiscal constraint theories and extend recent evidence on debt and monetary policy transmission, suggesting that elevated public debt weakens not only conventional interest‐rate policy but also the power of forward guidance and central bank signaling.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Operational disruption, resource reconfiguration, and AI integration in hospital equipment-as-a-service operations
Authors: Soumyatanu Mukherjee, Sayan Mukherjee, T.C. Edwin Cheng
Abstract: This study examines how disruption exposure relates to adaptive responses in hospital Equipment-as-a-Service (EaaS) operations, focusing on resource reconfiguration and the depth of AI workflow embedding. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view, supported by resource orchestration logic and a behavioral theory of the firm lens, we test a disruption-to-adaptation framework in which disruption exposure is associated with resource reconfiguration and AI integration, while technical complexity and trust condition these relationships. We use a field-grounded, between-subjects, scenario-based role-playing experiment with 320 hospital decision-makers from India-based hospitals across Bihar, Maharashtra, and West Bengal. The scenarios were developed from field engagements documenting disruption episodes involving CT outages, network delays, patient surges, staffing bottlenecks, and vendor coordination. The results show positive associations of disruption exposure with resource reconfiguration and AI integration. Resource reconfiguration is, in turn, positively associated with AI integration, and a supplementary indirect-effect analysis identifies it as a significant complementary pathway that accounts for approximately 18.6% of the total association linking disruption exposure to deeper AI embedding. Technical complexity strengthens the relationships of disruption exposure with both resource reconfiguration and AI integration. Trust strengthens the direct relationship between disruption exposure and AI integration but does not significantly alter the relationship between reconfiguration and AI integration. The findings contribute to production and service operations research by showing that AI-enabled service platforms support disruption response not merely through technological sophistication, but through timely reconfiguration of workflows, roles, and coordination routines.

Title: Prescribed burning and localized human health: A stochastic bioeconomic model for wildfire mitigation
Authors: Ewa Z. Vick, Benjamin A. Jones, Shana McDermott
Abstract: In this paper, we examine the localized smoke health trade-off associated with prescribed burning as a wildfire mitigation policy. Prescribed burning is frequently justified on the basis that it generates less smoke than the wildfires it helps to mitigate; however, research on this topic remains limited, largely due to challenges in obtaining suitable data. This analysis addresses this gap by presenting the first bioeconomic-health model of prescribed burning that incorporates a stochastic wildfire component, with a focus on four distinct forest types distributed across the continental United States. The analysis focuses on localized smoke-related health impacts for a representative community located downwind of a treated hectare, allowing us to isolate the immediate smoke-related health costs of prescribed burning and compare them with the expected reductions in future wildfire smoke-related health impacts from that same hectare. Under the model assumptions, the results indicate that the localized smoke-related mortality damages associated with prescribed burning exceed the expected reductions in future wildfire smoke-related mortality damages on a per-hectare, per-100,000 population basis, with substantial variation across forest types. These results address an important externality associated with prescribed burning in that nearby communities in the Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) may repeatedly experience smoke exposure from prescribed fires, while many additional benefits of prescribed burning, including reductions in wildfire spread, property losses, and ecosystem damages, may accrue over larger spatial scales or to populations outside the treated area.

Title: Between toolkit and theory: A critical review of social metabolism
Authors: Manuel González de Molina, Juan Infante-Amate, Víctor M. Toledo
Abstract: Social Metabolism (SM), rooted in Marx's concept of Stoffwechsel and systematisedsystematized by Fischer-Kowalski for sustainability science, has generated a rapidly growing body of literature encompassing over 4700 publications. From its inception, SM carried a dual ambition: to develop biophysical accounting tools capable of measuring the economy in tons and joules rather than solely in monetary units, and to build a comprehensive theory of socio-ecological change. Yet methodological ambition has largely overshadowed the theoretical one, and the research communities that have developed around SM remain fragmented. No systematic theoretical characterization of these schools of thought currently exists. This paper proposes such a characterization. Building on a comprehensive bibliometric corpus of over 4700 publications retrieved from OpenAlex (the search protocol is given in the Supplementary Material), we conduct a critical qualitative review that identifies four main schools of SM: the Vienna School (VS/MEFA), the Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis school (MuSIASEM), the Metabolic Rift school (MR), and the Social Agrarian Metabolism school (SAM). We compare them across six analytical dimensions: terminology and definitions, epistemological scope, operational tools, stock/flow vs. fund/flow approaches, main applications, and the integration of social variables. Our approach is deliberately theoretical: we examine not only how each school measures biophysical flows, but how it conceptualizes the relationship between society and nature and how far it has developed SM as a genuine socio-ecological theory. We conclude by identifying key challenges, including the need to recover the original theoretical ambition of SM as a comprehensive framework for understanding socio-ecological change.

Title: Participation builds trust, not framing: insights from a national energy-transition experiment
Authors: Kevin Goes, Louison Thépaut, Niek Mouter, Emile Chappin, Sjoerd Kluiving
Abstract: Institutional trust is a critical determinant of public cooperation in the energy transition, yet little is known about how different framings of government communication influence trust in practice. This study reports results from a large-scale national experiment (N ≈ 3000) embedded in a Participatory Value Evaluation (PVE) on heat-transition policy. Participants were randomly assigned to one of six value-based framing conditions, or a control group: environmental, financial, or stability messaging, each presented by either local or national government. Trust in government was measured before and after the intervention, enabling a Difference-in-Differences analysis complemented by Latent Profile Analysis and Honest Causal Forests. Across all specifications, value-based framing failed to increase trust and, in some cases, reduced it, with the local-stability frame showing the most consistent negative effect. Trust responses varied strongly across latent trust profiles but not across demographic groups, indicating that predispositions toward government, rather than socio-demographic characteristics, drive communication sensitivity. In contrast, participation in the PVE itself produced a modest and robust increase in trust independent of the framing treatment. These findings suggest that participatory decision tools may strengthen trust, whereas value-laden communication risks unintended negative effects.

Title: Political career incentives and the environmental costs: Evidence from China’s promotion tournaments
Authors: JingXuan Xu, Hao Xu, Guangrong Ma
Abstract: This paper shows that promotion incentives for county-level cadres in China are an important driver of air pollution deterioration. Building on the multi-winner tournament model proposed by Clark and Riis (1998), we predict an inverted-U-shaped relationship between the number of counties within a prefecture and the promotion incentives for county-level cadres. Using the length of small rivers as an instrumental variable for the number of counties within a prefecture, our empirical analysis identifies a robust inverted-U-shaped relationship between the number of counties and air pollution levels, suggesting that promotion incentives significantly exacerbate air pollution. Further analysis reveals that, in pursuit of economic growth, local cadres tend to relax environmental regulations and attract more pollution-intensive firms. In regions where cadres’ performance evaluation places less emphasis on economic growth, the inverted-U-shaped relationship does not exist. These findings suggest that local cadres’ career incentives stimulate economic growth at the expense of the environment.

Title: Energy poverty and health: Evidence from European countries
Authors: Martina Celidoni, Raffaele Miniaci, Paola Valbonesi
Abstract: We estimate the effect of energy poverty on a range of subjective and objective health outcomes among older Europeans using ex-ante harmonized microdata from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe. To address potential endogeneity concerns, we exploit regional weather-based Eurostat data on Heating Degree Days to construct two instrumental variables for energy poverty. Our findings indicate that energy poverty has detrimental effects on both physical and mental health. Ordinary Least Squares estimates show that individuals experiencing energy poverty are more likely to report poor health, chronic lung conditions, and score higher on assessments of depressive symptoms and cognitive decline, while also displaying lower grip strength and a higher probability of sarcopenia. Instrumental variable estimates confirm a clinically significant negative effect on physical health, with energy poverty substantially reducing grip strength among older individuals. From a policy perspective, our results highlight the importance of integrating energy affordability into climate and decarbonization strategies. Policies that increase residential energy costs without adequate compensatory measures may unintentionally worsen heating deprivation and generate adverse health consequences, particularly within ageing societies.

Title: Reputation, punishment and the enforcement of social norms
Authors: David F. Jackson
Abstract: Reputation and social punishment are key mechanisms for norm enforcement, yet existing research often conflates or treats them in isolation. We distinguish reputational punishment as the automatic loss of trust-based interactions following defection, from social punishment, the voluntary avoidance in interactions maintained independently from reputation. Integrating both in a model of informal enforcement, we show that social punishment complements reputation when it is too weak to support cooperation alone, but as reputation strength increases, it substitutes for social punishment, resulting in an inverted-U-shaped relationship between punishment and reputational strength. The mechanism provides a novel motivation for third-party punishment driven by how reputation amplifies punishment threats across an agent’s network. Payoffs depend on the distribution of interaction stakes, determining how many new transactions punishment facilitates. We consider social structure by defining ingroups by their capacity to independently enforce trust, implying incentives to renegotiate from universal to localised norms. However, when community enforcement is insufficient, ingroup members may impose additional punishment on defectors, mimicking collective reputation. Extending the model to regulate multiple norms within a single domain has distinct implications for punishment intensity, and the model’s equilibria provide a mechanism rationalising the inconsistent cross-cultural relationship between cooperation and enforcement intensity. The framework contributes to the literature on informal enforcement, social capital, and social norms by explaining how the nature and intensity of interactions and the costs of complying with a community’s norms influence patterns of social enforcement and norm compliance across different social structures.

Title: Windows of change as precursors to changing travel behaviour aligned with sustainable mobility
Authors: David A. Hensher, John D. Nelson, Edward Wei, Thiranjaya Kandanaarachchi, Camila Balbontin, Chinh Ho, Corinne Mulley, Wen Liu
Abstract: There is an increasing focus on ways in which we can achieve behavioural change associated with improved sustainability outcomes in the transport sector. In societies where the car is the dominant passenger transport mode with all of its associated interpretations of convenience, we continue to search for ways to change travel habits that result in a switch out of the car in favour of public transport and active modes. Beyond the existing research on mobility biographies, this study proposes the concept of “Windows of Change” (WoC), representing the cycle of key events driving travel behaviour changes of individuals. The study demonstrates that WoC works in ways that support sustainability outcomes. We categorise the WoC into four broad classes: lifestyle and household changes (e.g., changes in living arrangements, family structure, or personal habits); work and commuting-related changes (e.g., changes in employment, workplace incentives or commuting patterns); transport and mobility changes (e.g., changes in vehicle ownership, public transport use or travel habits); and social and environmental considerations (including awareness and influence of others). In particular, the study applies a series of negative binomial count models to identify the relationship between the key events in WoC and modal one-way trip frequency in a typical week associated with the WoC period, after controlling for various socioeconomic effects and country dummy variables. Data is collected from over 4,000 respondents spread across Australia, Finland, New Zealand, the United States, the United Kingdom, Singapore, and Sweden, investigating respondents’ local travel behaviour changes over the period 2023–2025, showing the concept of WoC can be applied across countries and cultural contexts. The findings provide a rich array of policy advice on what key WoC influences suggest actionable ways to support the switch to more sustainable modes, and what remain as clear barriers to achieving such an outcome.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Exploring road users’ perceptions of fatbikes and riders’ behaviours in the Netherlands: Implications for public acceptability
Authors: Soyeon Kim, Dennis Andreoli, Marjan Hagenzieker
Abstract: Fatbikes, electric fat-tire bicycles, are increasingly visible in the Netherlands. Although fatbikes are classified within the broader electric bicycle (e-bike) category, fatbikes may be perceived as a distinct and riskier mobility mode than conventional e-bikes. As this perception can affect public acceptability, it creates a challenge for their integration into urban mobility systems. Yet empirical evidence on the perceptions and acceptability of fatbikes remains limited. This study examines Dutch road users’ perceptions of fatbike riders and their behaviour, and how these perceptions are associated with the public acceptability of fatbikes, based on an online survey of 508 respondents. Results show that fatbike riders are perceived negatively, often associated with youth and reckless riding behaviour. Compared to regular e-bike riders, fatbike riders are viewed as engaging more frequently in traffic violations and unsafe behaviours. Public acceptability of fatbikes is also considerably lower than that of e-bikes, which are perceived more neutrally. Interestingly, public transport and scooter users are more likely to view fatbikes as an alternative mode of transport. These findings suggest that policy responses need to address the behaviours and concerns that shape acceptability, rather than focus solely on the vehicle category. Policy implications, therefore, include behaviour-focused measures, such as enforcement and education to promote safe riding and prevent illegal modifications, as well as public information campaigns that clarify lawful and safe fatbike use. This study contributes to ongoing discussions on new mobility by providing empirical evidence and policy guidance for safer, more sustainable urban transportation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Artificial intelligence and rent sharing between airlines and workers: evidence from the U.S. Airline industry
Authors: Fecri Karanki, Anming Zhang
Abstract: Has the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution already begun to reshape the airline labor market? Following the COVID-19 pandemic, airline workers experienced rapid wage increases amid acute labor shortages. At the same time, the emergence of generative AI after 2022 introduced new technological expectations that may have altered bargaining conditions. This study examines how the distribution of quasi-rents between airlines and workers has evolved over the period 2000–2024. We construct feasible wage benchmarks based on a Nash rent-sharing framework and embed them within a two-tier stochastic frontier model to measure deviations from these benchmarks. This approach allows us to quantify how observed wages reflect shifts in surplus distribution rather than changes in wage levels alone. The results reveal a long-run decline in worker-side rent extraction, with a pronounced shift after 2022. Despite rising wages and continued labor market tightness following the COVID-19 recovery, observed wages increasingly fall below feasible benchmarks, indicating that airlines retain a growing share of quasi-rents. An occupation-weighted AI exposure index, interpreted as a measure of expected technological substitution, shows that higher exposure is associated with larger worker-side wage shortfalls relative to the benchmark. This pattern is particularly pronounced at low-cost carriers, where more standardized operations generate broader exposure across routine cognitive tasks. Overall, the findings suggest that technological expectations associated with generative AI may have already shifted bargaining outcomes in favor of airlines, even in the presence of labor shortages. The study contributes to the literature by providing the first empirical evidence linking AI-related exposure to rent-sharing dynamics in the airline industry within a unified bargaining-frontier framework, highlighting the distributional implications of technological change.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Editorial Board
Diffusion and imitation learning-assisted memetic algorithm for energy-efficient hybrid flow shop scheduling problem with variable speed
Authors: Weiyao Cheng, Yiying Yang, Leilei Meng, Peng Wu
Abstract: The hybrid flow shop scheduling problem (HFSP) is prevalent in practical production environments. With growing energy expenditure and increasing ecological concerns, energy-efficient scheduling has emerged as an important research topic. Modern production systems often feature machines with variable-speed capabilities, allowing jobs to be processed at different speed levels. While this offers additional scheduling flexibility, it introduces a trade-off between production efficiency and energy consumption. Therefore, this study investigates the energy-efficient HFSP with variable speeds (EEHFSP-S), aiming to minimize both the makespan and total energy consumption. To address this problem, first, a novel mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model is first formulated. Unlike existing MILP formulations, the designed model introduces auxiliary variables to linearize the products of decision variables, making it solvable by IBM CPLEX. Then, a diffusion and imitation learning-assisted memetic algorithm, termed DILMA, is proposed. In DILMA, a diffusion model is trained to learn the distribution of high-quality solutions and generate a promising initial population. Furthermore, ten knowledge-based local search operators are developed based on problem characteristics, considering both critical and non-critical operations. To further enhance local search effectiveness, an imitation learning model is trained to adaptively select suitable operators for solutions. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed MILP model and demonstrate that DILMA outperforms existing algorithms in approximating high-quality Pareto fronts.

Title: Original sin redux: A model-based evaluation
Authors: Boris Hofmann, Nikhil Patel, Steve Pak Yeung Wu
Abstract: Using a two-country model, this paper shows that the shift from foreign currency to local currency external borrowing does not eliminate the vulnerability of EMs to foreign financial shocks but instead results in “original sin redux.” A monetary tightening abroad is propagated to EM financial conditions through a tightening of foreign lenders’ financial constraints, driven in part by currency mismatches on their balance sheets. Foreign exchange intervention and capital flow management measures can mitigate global financial spillovers to EMs in the short run and a larger domestic investor base can reduce the vulnerability in the longer run.

Title: A new horizon? The effect of a national education reform on student achievement and the academic environment
Authors: Yaniv Reingewertz, Adi Shany
Abstract: This study analyzes the effect of the New Horizon educational reform on student achievements and on the academic environment in schools. New Horizon is a broad-based national reform initiated by the Ministry of Education and gradually implemented in elementary and lower-secondary schools in Israel beginning in 2008. The main elements of the reform are an increase in the time teachers spend in school, additional small-group instruction time (individual hours), an increase in teachers’ and principals’ salaries and posing higher requirements and incentives for professional development. We use a difference-in-differences (DID) approach to evaluate the effects of the reform on a multitude of outcomes related to student achievements and to measures of school academic environment. We find that in the short run, about two years after it was first implemented, the New Horizon reform has increased student test scores, mainly in math and English. In addition, the reform has improved a number of the school-learning environment’s attributes. We also find that the reform has had no effect on school violence and on the general level of students’ satisfaction with school. Furthermore, we explore how specific components of the reform are related to our findings. ∗We thank the Israel’s Ministry of Education and the National Authority for Measurement and Evaluation in Education (RAMA) for allowing access to restricted data at the Ministry online protected research lab. Many thanks to Haim Gat, Sonia Perez, Orna Simhon, and Mira Lahak who provided much insight and information on the New Horizon reform. We thank Eliad Trefler and Ariela Knaani from the Ministry online protected research lab for their great assistance. We are grateful to Victor Lavy, Josh Angrist, and Analia Schlosser for helpful comments and suggestions. Shany acknowledges financial support from the Council of Higher Education of Israel and the Department of Economics of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Corresponding author: Adi Shany: adi.shani@mail.huji.ac.il

Title: How does harassment alter cycling satisfaction? Insights from London
Authors: Khashayar Kazemzadeh, Amir Pooyan Afghari, Ahmadreza Faghih Imani, Jonas De Vos
Abstract: Cycling satisfaction is a key factor in increasing cycling mode share, particularly in low-cycling contexts such as England. Satisfaction is subjective and shaped by both observable conditions and unobserved psychological factors. One important but understudied factor is harassment, which can take many forms (e.g., verbal, physical, sexual, racial, or identity-based) and may strongly influence cyclists’ experiences. This study develops a quantitative framework to examine how harassment affects cycling satisfaction through a latent variable representing harassment-related experiences, using survey data from 1,525 cyclists in London. Results show that cyclists who feel stressed, unsafe, or threatened are significantly more likely to report dissatisfaction, even after controlling for socio-demographic factors. Harassment-related perceptions are strongly associated with traffic exposure, lighting conditions, and accumulated near-miss or collision experiences. These findings demonstrate that cycling satisfaction is significantly associated with harassment-related perceptions and highlight the need to incorporate harassment-sensitive measures into cycling level-of-service evaluations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Contextualising the impact of street slopes on pedestrian accessibility for sustainable mobility
Authors: Vasileios Milias, Panagiotis G. Tzouras, Ioanna Vourdanou, Konstantinos Markos, Konstantinos Kepaptsoglou, Alexandros Nikitas
Abstract: Proximity-based planning has become a central paradigm in transport policy, guiding the design of sustainable, accessible, and liveable cities. This shift has driven the development of various methods for assessing pedestrian accessibility, reflecting the central role of walking as the most sustainable mode. Yet, the impact of street slopes on accessibility is often neglected and remains poorly understood. This study identifies two systematic biases: a slope-speed bias, caused by assuming flat terrain, and a slope-preference bias, reflecting behavioural aversion to slopes. We compare three models: (a) slope-agnostic, (b) slope-adjusted with gradient-dependent speeds, and (c) slope-preference incorporating walking preferences across walking propensity groups. Applied in Athens, Greece, results show that slope-agnostic models overestimate accessibility by approximately 6–8% on average. Accounting for walking preferences introduces an additional 33–40% reduction for low-propensity walkers across destination types. The proposed framework offers a transferable approach for integrating terrain sensitivity into accessibility analysis.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Editorial Board
Shattered dreams: the economic impact of eliminating DACA
Authors: Phillip Connor, Francesc Ortega
Abstract: Abstract Since 2012, the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program has provided temporary relief from deportation and a work permit for undocumented youth. In recent years, DACA renewals have faced slower processing, mounting legal challenges, and the ongoing risk of revocation. We present a novel imputation for immigrant status, which identifies likely DACA recipients, and provide estimates of the income losses stemming from the potential elimination of the program. Because recipients are young, current earnings understate their lifetime contribution to the U.S. economy; our estimates account for this, and for uncertainty around key calibration parameters. We estimate that losing work authorization could lower the earnings of the average DACA recipient by nearly $$\$9900$$ $ 9900 annually, or $$\$5.3$$ $ 5.3 billion for the approximately 540,000 recipients in 2023. Incorporating a likely feasible volume of removals, affecting half of the DACA-eligible population, raises annual losses to $$\$48,000$$ $ 48 , 000 per recipient and $$\$23.0$$ $ 23.0 billion in the aggregate. Lifetime losses in such a scenario reach $$\$260$$ $ 260 billion nationwide ( $$\$544,000$$ $ 544 , 000 per affected individual).

Title: Towards environmental and economic sustainability through interorganisational postponement: a relational perspective
Authors: Trung Hieu Le, Lorenzo Bruno Prataviera, Heather Dawn Skipworth, Abhijeet Ghadge
Affiliations: Phenikaa University Faculty of Business Administration, Phenikaa School of Business and Economics, , Hanoi, , and School of Management, Cranfield University, Cranfield, UK; University of Verona Department of Management, , Verona, , and School of Management, Cranfield University, Cranfield, UK; Cranfield University School of Management, , Cranfield
Abstract: Purpose Firms face increasing pressure to reduce environmental impacts while maintaining cost-effective supply chains (SCs). Postponement has emerged as a promising strategy, yet existing research offers inconsistent evidence on its environmental and economic implications. In addition, the implementation of postponement relies on interorganisational collaboration, yet the relational processes underlying this implementation remain underexplored. This study aims to examine how interorganisational postponement is implemented and how it supports the joint pursuit of environmental and economic sustainability. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the relational view (RV), the study analyses an in-depth single case of a UK-based multinational manufacturer implementing interorganisational postponement with three suppliers. Using a process-based approach, we examine interviews, internal documents and operational data to trace how the four sources of relational rents enable the implementation of postponement and how underlying relational mechanisms connect these sources to sustainability outcomes over time. Findings Interorganisational postponement implementation is enabled by complementary resources and capabilities, relation-specific assets, knowledge-sharing routines and effective governance, which operate through underlying relational mechanisms including resource convergence and divergence, asymmetric investment adaptation, information-processing capabilities and formalised governance. These mechanisms explain how partner fit changes, investment commitments adapt, knowledge is processed across firms and governance becomes more formalised as operational complexity increases. Through these mechanisms, interorganisational postponement contributes to sustainability rents, reflected in joint environmental and economic gains such as lower emissions, reduced waste, tariff savings and improved transport efficiency. Originality/value The study offers a relational and processual understanding of postponement’s role in sustainable SC management by moving beyond a firm-centred, static view to explain how it unfolds across the SC. It illustrates how interfirm resources and relational mechanisms shape whether environmental and economic outcomes are jointly created and preserved. Accordingly, it extends the RV by providing a more nuanced understanding of the established sources of relational rents and the underlying relational mechanisms through which these sources evolve and contribute to sustainability rents, highlighting how interorganisational collaboration can co-create environmental and economic value through the implementation of postponement.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Optimal dynamic content bandwidth allocation in shoppertainment live streaming
Authors: Zhehong Hao, Jianxiong Zhang, Xiaoqing Fan

Title: Human–robot collaborative order picking with synchronisation constraints
Authors: Shuai Liu, Man Wang, Yaoyao Ku, Hao Dong

Title: Designing a blood supply chain network with temporary mobile facilities in natural disasters by a relax-and-fix approach: a case study
Authors: Mahdi Bastan, Reza Tavakkoli-Moghaddam, Mahdi Hamid, Niaz Wassan, Hamed Fazlollahtabar
Affiliations: Sharif University of Technology; University of Tehran; Istinye University; Amirkabir University of Technology (Tehran Polytechnic); Sultan Qaboos University; Damghan University

Title: Sim-approaches for the stochastic clustered team orienteering problem
Authors: Daniele Ferone, Paola Festa, Tommaso Pastore
Abstract: Abstract This paper introduces the Stochastic Clustered Team Orienteering Problem (SCTOP), a variant of the recently defined CluTOP where travel times are non-negative random variables. This problem aligns with the growing interest in prize-collecting problems and the challenge of optimizing routes under uncertainty. To address the Stochastic CluTOP, we propose a Simheuristic method integrating Monte Carlo simulations within an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (SimALNS). Additionally, we incorporate two policies, Continuous and Reactive, to adaptively manage the maximum route length in route generation process. The proposed approaches are validated on a well-established benchmark of the scientific literature to test the benefits of including Monte Carlo simulations in the route-design process and to evaluate the possible contributions of the two policies in case of higher profit variances. The results demonstrate that the Monte Carlo simulation allows SimALNS to consistently achieve higher stochastic performance compared to its deterministic counterpart. Moreover, the results highlight that across all algorithms tested, the Reactive strategy is the most effective.

Title: Models, constructive heuristics, and benchmark instances for the flexible job shop scheduling problem with nonlinear routes and position-based learning
Authors: Kennedy A. G. Araujo, Ernesto G. Birgin, Débora P. Ronconi
Abstract: Abstract This paper addresses the flexible job shop scheduling problem with nonlinear routes and position-based learning effect. In this variant of the flexible job shop scheduling problem, precedence constraints of the operations constituting a job are given by an arbitrary directed acyclic graph, generalizing the classical case in which a total order is imposed. Additionally, it is assumed that a worker performing an operation at a machine undergoes a learning process: the more times a worker has performed an operation, the faster he or she will be able to complete it on subsequent repetitions. Mixed integer programming and constraint programming models are presented and compared in the present work. In addition, sets of benchmark instances and constructive heuristics are introduced. The problem we study here corresponds to modern problems of great relevance in the printing industry. The framework we introduce aims to assist authors in the design of novel, effective, and efficient methods. Instances with optimal solutions provide a means to evaluate the quality of solutions found by other methods. Constructive heuristics serve two purposes. First, they provide an initial solution to off-the-shelf exact methods, offering a warm start when addressing instances of the proposed models. They also lay the groundwork for developing algorithms, such as list scheduling, neighborhoods, local searches, and ultimately, metaheuristics.

Title: Natural catastrophes and the dynamics of default hazard: evidence from contract-level credit data
Authors: Rosella Castellano, Federico Cini, Giulio Mariani, Saverio Storani
Abstract: This study examines the association between natural catastrophes and contract-level default hazard in Italy. We combine granular credit contract data from Experian Italia S.p.A. with EM-DAT disaster records matched at the province-month level over 2000–2025. Default is defined as the first transition from performing to non-performing status, identified by three or more missed installments. We estimate semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards models with time-varying catastrophe exposure, province and sector stratification, interaction terms, catastrophe-time indicators, and robustness controls for calendar-year and month-of-year effects. The results show no robust increase in default hazard during the catastrophe month or the first six months thereafter. Higher hazard ratios emerge in selected later windows, most consistently between seven and twelve months after the event. Sectoral characteristics explain baseline heterogeneity, whereas sector-specific differences in the persistent catastrophe component are limited. Territorial heterogeneity is more pronounced. The findings highlight delayed and geographically differentiated credit-risk patterns following natural catastrophes.

Title: Error Estimation for SAA Solutions to Compound and Risk-Averse Stochastic Programs
Authors: Volker Krätschmer
Affiliations: Faculty of Mathematics, University of Duisburg-Essen, D-45127 Essen, Germany
Abstract: This paper is a study on solutions of the sample average approximation method to solve compound stochastic programs. We derive nonasymptotic upper estimates for probabilities of the approximation errors. The results depend on the sample size and use explicit terms rather than unspecified universal constants. They allow for immediate conclusions about nonasymptotic rates for the optimal solutions. Additionally, the results can be used to construct nonasymptotic confidence regions for solutions of compound stochastic programs. In the special case of classical risk-neutral stochastic programs, we end up with upper estimates of deviation probabilities for M-estimators, and their nonasymptotic rates. Moreover, we may also demonstrate how to apply the results to sample average approximation of risk-averse stochastic programs. In this respect we consider stochastic programs expressed in terms of absolute semideviation risk measures and Average Value at Risk. The investigations are based on concentration inequalities from a recent contribution by the author. The line of reasoning does not rely on pathwise analytical properties of the objectives. In particular, continuity or convexity in the parameter is not imposed in advance as usual in the literature on the sample average approximation method. The main results also apply to objectives with Hölder continuous paths. Moreover, they also work for objectives whose paths are piecewise Hölder continuous, as, for example, in two-stage mixed-integer programs.

Title: Distributional properties of cost allocation rules in multi-family energy retrofits: Evidence from 4 million apartments
Authors: Jakub Sokołowski, Stefan Bouzarovski
Abstract: Collective decisions to retrofit multi-family residential buildings require co-owners to agree on how the total cost is divided among dwellings, yet the distributional properties of alternative allocation rules have been insufficiently investigated at scale. Using harmonised Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) microdata covering over 4 million apartments in almost 450,000 buildings across Poland, England and Wales, and the Netherlands, we simulate five allocation rules: area-proportional, progressive-area, emissions-proportional, inefficiency-proportional, and Shapley-value allocation. For each building, we evaluate the resulting cost-share distributions using within-building inequality indices, size-progressivity measures, and cooperative-game-theoretic stability criteria. We find that performance-based rules produce within-building Gini coefficients 2 to 11 times higher than area-proportional allocation, with systematic variation across national building stocks. These rules are also less proportional in terms of dwelling size, assigning larger cost shares to smaller dwellings than their floor-area shares warrant. The Shapley rule, often advocated on cooperative-game-theoretic grounds, routinely allocates more to a single dwelling than that dwelling's stand-alone retrofit cost. The results show that cost-allocation rules generate distributional and stability consequences at policy-relevant magnitudes. For retrofit governance in multi-owner buildings, allocation design should therefore be treated as a central component of policy implementation rather than a technical-administrative choice.

Title: Advanced vehicle data sharing and privacy protection: When does regulation improve welfare?
Authors: Zhenmin Qiu, Yuanguang Zhong, Yanxi Li, Zixi Wen, Dan Zhu
Abstract: This paper examines how government data regulations influence advanced vehicle firms’ pricing and product quality decisions, consumers’ data-sharing behavior, and social welfare. We develop a game-theoretic framework involving the government, an advanced vehicle firm, and consumers under three scenarios: (i) consumers do not share data, (ii) consumers share data without regulation, and (iii) consumers share data with government regulation. The analysis yields several insights. First, while government regulation enhances privacy protection, it also restricts the advanced vehicle firm’s ability to utilize consumer data, relative to the unregulated data-sharing scenario, resulting in lower product quality and price. Second, when either the cost coefficient or the privacy loss is very low or very high, data sharing leads to higher profits and greater consumer surplus than no sharing. However, at intermediate levels, the increasing cost of personalization outweighs its benefits, making non-sharing more preferable. Third, moderate regulation can alleviate privacy concerns while preserving data value. Although stronger data regulation initially enhances consumer trust, excessive regulation increases technological costs, thereby reducing overall social welfare. Based on this, we further extend our model by allowing consumers to partially share data. A counterintuitive finding is that more consumer data does not necessarily increase firm profit. This indicates that, compared with mandatory full data sharing, data-sharing flexibility can improve consumers’ participation incentives by enabling them to better trade off personalization benefits against privacy loss, thereby expanding effective demand and potentially increasing firm profit despite reduced data collection.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: How to mitigate the effect of cross-border supply chain disruption on SMEs’ resilience?
Authors: Xin Zheng, Hao Liu, Zhiqiang Wang, Yun Chen
Abstract: Cross-border supply chain disruptions are increasingly posing significant challenges to global operations. However, their impact on firm resilience, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), has been insufficiently investigated. This study examines how SMEs react to cross-border supply chain disruptions. Drawing on a panel sample of 10,501 firm-quarter observations of SMEs listed on China’s ChiNext market, we find that cross-border supply chain disruptions negatively affect SMEs’ resilience. Furthermore, this effect is significantly mitigated when SMEs effectively orchestrate three key resources: alternative suppliers (relational resources), governmental financial support (financial resources), and digital technology (technological resources). Our study advances logistics and transportation literature by uncovering the specific effects of cross-border supply chain disruptions on SMEs’ resilience. Moreover, our study extends resource orchestration theory into the context of cross-border supply chain disruption by showing that SMEs build resilience through orchestrating relational, financial, and technological resources.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Traffic forecasting considering burst disturbances based on spatial-temporal graph neural impulsive differential equations
Authors: Hongtao Li, Bowei Su, Junfang Tian, Haina Zhang, Wenzheng Liu
Abstract: Traffic forecasting, as a cornerstone task in intelligent transportation systems, plays a vital role in alleviating urban congestion, optimizing traffic management, and improving travel efficiency. However, in real-world traffic systems, smooth and continuous variations driven by routine commuting patterns often coexist with abrupt disturbances caused by accidents, signal transitions, and unexpected events. Although capturing such mixed dynamics is of significant practical importance, it has not been fully explored in existing studies. To address this challenge, we propose a spatial-temporal graph learning framework (ST-GINDE) incorporating an impulse-like modulation neural ordinary differential equation module. The model formulates traffic dynamics as a continuous-time evolution process on spatial-temporal graphs, enabling unified modeling of temporal evolution, spatial dependencies, and adaptive responses to significant traffic state variations. To capture abrupt disturbances, we introduce an impulse-like modulation mechanism that adaptively adjusts the continuous dynamics when significant traffic variations occur, without introducing discontinuous state jumps or explicit hybrid system assumptions. Furthermore, ST-GINDE integrates multi-scale temporal feature extraction and hybrid dynamic graph learning to jointly model short-term fluctuations, long-term periodic patterns, and time-varying spatial dependencies across traffic networks. We further analyze the mathematical properties of the constructed dynamic system to verify the rationality of the proposed modeling framework. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world traffic datasets demonstrate that ST-GINDE achieves highly competitive performance in traffic forecasting tasks, with notable improvements in prediction accuracy and robustness under complex traffic conditions and sudden disturbances.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Truck-drone collaborative routing under road damage and dynamic demand for humanitarian logistics
Authors: Liang YOU, Lei ZHANG, Mingfa ZHENG, Chuhan MA, Bowu WEI, Chen YANG
Abstract: Efficient delivery of humanitarian supplies is crucial for disaster loss reduction. The Truck-Drone Collaborative Routing Problem (TDRP) has mostly been studied under static demand and ideal road networks, neglecting the dynamic revelation of demand points and nonlinear road capacity degradation from disaster damage. This paper introduces the TDRP with Road Damage and Dynamic Demand (TDRP-RD-DD) to minimize global delivery completion time. We build a full-chain model linking disaster intensity, road capacity, and truck travel speed, and develop an event-driven two-layer rolling optimization framework with locally optimal selection criteria for supply and replenishment modes. To solve this NP-hard problem, we design a Rolling Replenishment-aware Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (RR-ALNS) with three specialized destroy-repair operators, a capacity- and mode-aware Warm-start strategy, and a replenishment-prioritized repair mechanism for infeasible solutions. Experiments on Solomon instances and a real-world disaster-relief case in Hubei Province show that RR-ALNS closely matches CPLEX on CPLEX-proven small-scale instances, with a 0.47% average gap for the default simulated-annealing setting, while scaling effectively to larger dynamic settings. Compared with three baseline algorithms, RR-ALNS achieves stronger feasibility and overall lower makespan in both benchmark and real-world tests. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further support the value of truck-drone collaboration, collaborative replenishment, and explicit road-damage-to-speed modeling. This work extends dynamic truck-drone routing to post-disaster settings with road damage and demand revelation, and provides quantitative support for emergency logistics decision-making.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The economics of abduction marriage: Evidence from Ethiopia
Authors: Jorge García-Hombrados, Lindsey Novak
Abstract: A sizable share of marriages in several Asian and African countries are initiated by the man abducting the woman he wishes to wed. In this paper, we use quantitative and qualitative methods to characterize the practice of abduction marriage in Ethiopia. We first present the results from in-depth qualitative interviews with community leaders and abducted women in the Gambella region of Ethiopia to gain a deeper understanding of how the practice functions in these communities. These interviews suggest that abduction is typically used to overcome the refusal of the woman's family. Second, we use Demographic and Health Survey along with ethnographic data to characterize women and ethnic groups affected by this practice in Ethiopia. Finally, we empirically examine the central hypothesis about the persistence of this practice and find evidence consistent with the hypothesis that men often use abduction to improve bargaining power in marriage negotiations and reduce the size of the bride price payment. Specifically, we demonstrate that droughts—a proxy for income shocks in this setting—increase the probability of abduction marriage only for women from ethnic groups that traditionally exchange a bride price.

Title: Incentivizing environmental public goods: Evidence from urban greening in China
Authors: Ding Ma, Zhiren Hu, Xintong Li
Abstract: China’s recent surge in urban greening presents a puzzling deviation from global patterns. We document three empirical patterns. First, urban greening was stable from 2001 to 2013 but expanded rapidly afterward, coinciding with China’s air pollution control efforts. Second, more polluted cities experienced faster growth in urban greening. Third, greening expansion was disproportionately concentrated near air quality monitoring stations. These patterns suggest that urban greening expansion in China after 2013 was largely driven by political pressure induced by air pollution control. The economic benefits of the urban greening expansion exceed the associated costs. Our results suggest that top-down air pollution control reshaped local government incentives, thereby improving the provision of environmental public goods and social welfare.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: The difficulty of telling signal from noise when noise lingers
Authors: Bhagwan Chowdhry
Abstract: How many observations does it take to detect a fixed signal when the noise has long memory? For a sample-mean detector applied to a constant signal buried in fractionally integrated noise of order (Formula presented), I give a closed-form expression for the sample size required to reach a target power at a fixed size: (Formula presented). The exponent (Formula presented) is the whole story: the required sample size is a power function of detection difficulty whose exponent diverges as (Formula presented). A doubling of detection difficulty that costs four times the data under independence costs 210 times the data at (Formula presented). A Monte Carlo confirms the formula delivers the target power and size.

Title: Agent-based analysis of competitive robotaxi operations: Variable pricing and multi-service strategies
Authors: Priyanka Paithankar, Navjyoth Jayashankar, Krishna Murthy Gurumurthy, Kara M. Kockelman
Abstract: This study examines shared autonomous vehicle (SAV or robotaxi) fleet performance with service-specific variable fares in a competitive ride-hailing market. It calibrates operator-specific fare models using New York's ride-hailing dataset, enabling fare adjustments based on real-time demand fluctuations and hour of the day. Agent-based POLARIS simulations of two SAV operators (Operator 1 and Operator 2) across Bloomington, Illinois show how a variable-fare strategy allows operators to adjust quickly to demand variations, improving fleet usage and turning underperforming fixed-fare services into profit centers. Under fixed fares, Operator 1 remained modestly profitable (with an 11% profit margin) by deploying only standard, 4-seat SAVs, while Operator 2′s mixed-fleet strategy incurred steep losses in premium tiers ($66 daily loss per 4-seater premium SAV and $278 daily loss per 6-seater premium SAV), yielding just a 2% overall profit margin. In contrast, variable pricing strategies generate substantial economic and efficiency gains: daily profit per SAV rose almost tenfold, from $35 to $348, and total fleet profit rose more than eightfold, while fleet vehicle-miles travelled (VMT) fell 17%, empty VMT share fell from 34% to 31%, and vehicle occupancy levels improved, all after reducing fleet size from 455 to 385 SAVs. When holding fleet size fixed at 455 SAVs, variable pricing alone raised profits per SAV by 57%, showing how gains come mainly from the pricing strategy itself rather than from a smaller fleet size.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The global cost of automobility
Authors: Nadja Schweiggart, Stefan Gössling, Mark Nieuwenhuijsen, Felix Creutzig
Abstract: This study quantifies the private and social costs of global automobility and evaluates the potential economic benefits of a transition to shared electric autonomous mobility-as-a-service (E-AV-MaaS). Using comprehensive cost components, including accidents, emissions, air pollution, noise, infrastructure, land use, and resource impacts, it is estimated that private car travel currently incurs approximately USD 0.16 per vehicle-kilometer in private costs and USD 0.55 per vehicle-kilometer in social costs. Scaled globally, these unit costs translate to roughly USD 2.1 trillion in private and USD 7.2 trillion in social costs per year under an internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV)-dominated system, totaling approximately USD 9.3 trillion annually, equivalent to 8.3% of global GDP. Under a full E-AV-MaaS scenario with 25% reduced vehicle-kilometers traveled, social costs fall to approximately USD 0.30 per kilometer and USD 2.4 trillion in total. Private costs are estimated between USD 0.7 and 1.9 trillion, as lower parking expenditures are offset by the higher per-kilometer cost of autonomous electric vehicle services; private cost comparisons do not account for mode-specific utility derived from car ownership. This scenario reduces the global cost of automobility by roughly USD 5.6 trillion, driven almost entirely by social cost reductions. The results underscore that 77% of the cost of automobility is currently externalized.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Cost overruns in Sweden’s transport infrastructure investments: evidence against the Planning Fallacy and the Hiding Hand
Authors: Paul Chapman, Jonas Eliasson
Abstract: There is a dearth of evidence on whether Planning Fallacy or Hiding Hand explains cost overruns. We analysed all Swedish road and rail infrastructure investments finalized 1998–2025. 3% of roads and 6% of rail fit the Planning Fallacy narrative of failing both with respect to cost and benefits. 14% of road and 12% of rail projects fit the Hiding Hand narrative of going over budget but also delivering higher than planned net benefits. Many projects, 52% of roads and 40% of rail, fit neither the Planning Fallacy nor the Hiding Hand; they are, instead, successful. Overall, the results provide little support for the strong Planning Fallacy narrative and only limited support for the Hiding Hand, suggesting instead that most Swedish transport infrastructure projects perform broadly as expected when assessed against estimates at the final go-ahead decision.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: New solutions for the multi-skilled resource-constrained project scheduling problem with a satisfiability solver
Authors: Mario Vanhoucke, José Coelho
Abstract: This paper presents a SAT-based algorithm for solving the multi-skilled resource-constrained project scheduling problem (MSRCPSP). The proposed approach translates the problem’s precedence, resource and skill constraints into a Boolean satisfiability formulation, enabling both lower- and upper-bound strategies to efficiently explore the solution space. Comprehensive computational experiments are conducted on four benchmark datasets, comparing fast heuristics, consisting of 18 lower bounds, several priority-rule-based upper bounds and a simulated annealing algorithm, with three intensive optimization procedures consisting of a CPLEX model and a genetic algorithm from the literature and the proposed SAT procedure of the current study. The results show that the SAT-based algorithm is particularly effective in improving lower bounds and can also refine upper bounds. When combined with other optimization methods, it significantly tightens both bounds for a large portion of instances. Despite these improvements, a number of challenging open instances remain, suggesting opportunities for further research. All data and updated solutions, including both lower and upper bounds for the four datasets, are publicly available.

Title: Emission reduction potential of freeway stop-and-go wave smoothing
Authors: Junyi Ji, Derek Gloudemans, Gergely Zachár, William Barbour, Jonathan Sprinkle, Benedetto Piccoli, Daniel B. Work
Abstract: The real-world potential of stop-and-go wave smoothing at scale remains largely unquantified. Smoothing freeway waves requires opening a gap large enough for them to dissipate, but that gap is often impractically large. We propose a counterfactual wave-smoothing benchmark that reconstructs a smooth, feasible trajectory from each empirical trajectory by solving a quadratic program with fixed boundary conditions and a maximum-gap constraint, and we use the MOVES model to estimate the resulting emission reduction potential. Applying the framework to nine weeks of weekday peak-period data from the I-24 MOTION testbed, which exhibits rich day-to-day variation in wave dynamics, we find meaningful potential for passenger cars under a 0.1-mile maximum-gap constraint: average CO 2 reductions of 9.80% to 14.08% across lanes, with 12.94% to 25.70% in CO, 24.29% to 29.76% in HC, and 29.40% to 36.03% in NOx. Trucks emerge as particularly attractive targets, showing roughly twice the reduction potential of passenger cars.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: An integrated simulation and optimization framework for mixed-fleet public transit decarbonization
Authors: Majid Gholami Shirkoohi, Walter Mérida
Abstract: Public transit agencies face growing pressure to decarbonize operations while maintaining reliable service. Planning and operating mixed fleets of diesel, battery-electric, and hydrogen buses requires modelling tools that capture interactions among vehicle energy use, charging and refueling infrastructure, and network operations. This paper presents MLTransit, an integrated simulation-optimization framework that links general transit feed specification preprocessing, agent-based operational modelling, and multi-stage optimization to evaluate transit decarbonization strategies under realistic service patterns. The framework represents vehicle energy consumption, nonlinear charging behavior, queueing at charging facilities, battery degradation, emissions, and grid constraints. A two-stage optimization assigns service blocks to feasible vehicle types and determines cost-efficient charging infrastructure and policy parameters, while detailed charging schedules emerge endogenously through simulation. Applied to the Metro Vancouver bus network, MLTransit evaluates trade-offs between depot-only and combined depot-opportunity charging, showing that combined charging improves operational feasibility and service reliability at the cost of higher infrastructure investment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Editorial Board
The effect of job loss on labor supply, wealth, and spousal labor supply for older workers
Authors: Anne Katrine Borgbjerg
Abstract: Abstract I study the effect of job loss due to mass layoffs on labor supply, wealth, and spousal labor supply among older workers using high-quality Danish administrative data. Job loss reduces labor earnings, disposable income, and employment across all ages, but short-run losses are largest for older workers. Displaced workers aged 60 to 64 earn 32% less one year after displacement compared to similar non-displaced workers and are more likely to retire and less likely to be homeowners. Job loss also affects partners. While younger partners increase labor supply, older partners are more likely to retire.

Title: Single-machine hierarchical scheduling with deadlines: minimising the total completion time and other objectives
Authors: Rubing Chen, Michael L. Pinedo, Jinjiang Yuan
Affiliations: Zhengzhou University; New York University

Title: High-efficiency operation of hybrid diesel-electric construction machinery collaborative system: configuration, scheduling and parameter analysis
Authors: Xiaohui Huang, Wanbin Yan, Guibao Tao, Min Cheng, Fengze Qin, Huajun Cao
Affiliations: Chongqing University; Guangxi Liugong Machinery Co., Ltd.

Title: An integrated mixed-integer programming and metaheuristic approach for ergonomic cobot-assisted assembly line balancing
Authors: Hilmiye Betül Dikmen, Adil Baykasoğlu, Zeynel Abidin Çil

Title: Implementation of OR in healthcare services: a systematic review
Authors: Guillaume Lamé, Coco Newton, Luca Grieco, Sonya Crowe, Tom Bashford, Saba Hinrichs-Krapels
Affiliations: CentraleSupélec; TU Delft; University College London; University of Cambridge; Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
