Title: Efficiency and environmental performance evaluation of the water industry: a dynamic four-stage network data envelopment analysis
Authors: Kim Huat Goh, Kok Fong See, Bo Hsiao
Abstract: Water sustainability, which is the effective management of water resources to meet growing demand while mitigating environmental impacts, is imperative for fostering a resilient and thriving future. To mitigate the increasing risk of water shortages and associated greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, recycled water offers an alternative source. To address the dual challenges of resource scarcity and environmental sustainability, this study develops a circular internal structure by categorizing water utility into four operational divisions while introducing recycled water as a carryover product and considering GHG emissions as undesirable outputs within the evaluation framework. This proposed dynamic four-stage network based on the directional distance function (DDF) was employed to measure the technical efficiency of 47 integrated water and wastewater utilities in Australia from 2019 to 2023. The results reveal an aggregated overall efficiency score of 0.8080, suggesting a potential 19.2% improvement in resource utilization, water output, and emission performance across utilities. Among the four divisions, the nonresidential customer water consumption division has the lowest efficiency, indicating substantial room for improvement in industrial and commercial water use practices. Moreover, compared with small and medium-sized utilities, major utilities exhibit more consistent overall efficiency levels, highlighting structural advantages in achieving water sustainability and GHG mitigation objectives.

Title: Optimisation models for the design of multiple self-consumption loops in semi-rural areas
Authors: Yohann Chasseray, Mathieu Besançon, Xavier Lorca, Éva Petitdemange
Abstract: Collective electricity self-consumption gains increasing interest in a context where localised consumption of energy is a lever of sustainable development. While easing energy distribution networks, collective self-consumption requires complementary prosumers’ profiles. Before determining the proper energy exchanges happening between these prosumers, one must ensure their compatibility in the context of collective self-consumption. Motivated by real use cases from a solar power producer, this article proposes network flow-based linear models to solve both the design aspect of the problem and the attribution of distribution flows between involved prosumers. Two main models are proposed, handling (i) single collective self-consumption loop creation and (ii) multiple loop creation. One of the objectives of this work is to provide models that can be applied at a strategic level which implies their extension to large time scale and large spatial scale. To do so, associated Benders and Dantzig-Wolfe decompositions are proposed to ensure model scalability along temporal and spatial dimensions. Proposed models are tested on realistic use cases to assess their performances.

Title: Agents of collaborative adaptation: modelling temporal resilience in supply chains
Authors: Ari Carisza Graha Prasetia
Abstract: Abstract Supply-chain disruptions vary in intensity, scale, and frequency, producing temporally heterogeneous impacts on network viability. The emphasis on exposure and topology has anchored resilience in network structure, obscuring how collaboration and trust govern its phase-specific temporal dynamics, including resistive capabilities, adaptation speed, containment, and recovery. This study thus develops an agent-based simulation of the Netherlands logistics network, in which nodes operate as autonomous agents that redistribute load under capacity, link, and trust constraints. Cascading failures are simulated with trust-gated, capacity-aware, and collaboration-dependent load reallocation, capturing both immediate contagion and multi-step redistribution dynamics. The framework compares rule-based heuristics with adaptive AI agents trained using supervised imitation, online multiplicative adaptation, and cross-entropy policy search. Temporal resilience is then measured across each phase specific metrics of absorptive, adaptive, and recovery phases across the collaboration structure. This points to the main contribution of this article, in which AI agents improve adaptation and cascade containment through targeted use of high-trust, high-capacity links, while recovery dynamics remain bounded by structural and exogenous constraints. This points to a layered view of resilience, where performance depends on the interaction between network configuration, trust-mediated coordination, and agent-level adaptation.

Title: Exploring Spatial Patterns in Inefficiency Using a Stationary Gaussian Random Field
Authors: Ioannis Skevas
Affiliations: Department of International and European Studies University of Macedonia Thessaloniki Greece
Abstract: ABSTRACT This article presents a semiparametric stochastic frontier model that accounts for unobserved spatial heterogeneity in inefficiency by incorporating a stationary Gaussian random field based on geographic coordinates into the inefficiency scaling function. This approach captures spatial patterns in inefficiency at a fine scale. The proposed model is validated using simulated data and applied, within a Bayesian framework, to a panel dataset of Dutch dairy farms with precise geographic coordinates. For comparison, several alternative specifications are also estimated, excluding the spatial component, the inefficiency covariates, or both. The results confirm the presence of spatial heterogeneity and indicate that spatial dependence in inefficiency persists over relatively long distances. The estimated spatial effects reveal variation across locations, including areas with relatively higher and lower inefficiency. Model comparisons further show that omitting the spatial component and/or the scaling covariates affects the distribution of inefficiency across observations and leads to a worse model fit.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Do Teachers Boost Test Scores in Public High Schools in Delhi?
Authors: Deepti Goel, Bidisha Barooah
Affiliations: Pitzer College Claremont California USA; Asian Development Bank Manila Philippines
Abstract: ABSTRACT We measure teacher effects by their ability to raise test scores in high‐stakes examinations. We present estimates for value‐added teacher effects from public high schools , while prior work in developing countries has focused on primary and middle schools or private high schools. Our data come from 22 schools and represent the cohort of public‐school students in Delhi who took their end of grade 12 examinations in 2016. We estimate teacher effects using within‐student and across‐subject variation in test scores, and additionally account for contemporaneous student inputs. We find substantial variation in teacher quality that contradicts the perception that most public‐school teachers are ineffective: over the course of two years, namely grades 11 and 12, being assigned a one standard deviation better than average teacher from the same school moves a student at the median to the 63rd percentile of their cohort's test score distribution. Furthermore, being female is the only teacher attribute that positively predicts teacher effectiveness; training, experience, and personality traits are uncorrelated with teacher effectiveness. Lastly, we find low correlation between value‐added teacher effects and principals' ratings of teachers implying that principals' ratings cannot function as a proxy for value‐added estimates when deciding teacher compensation.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Cooperative green innovation in platform supply chains under asymmetric market information
Authors: Jianghua Wu, Yinuo Zhao
Abstract: Amid the growing emphasis on corporate environmental responsibility, some e-commerce platforms provide financial support to help manufacturers invest in green product development. This study examines cooperative green innovation through cost-sharing within a platform supply chain considering both selling mode choices and asymmetric market information. A game-theoretic framework is employed to analyze mechanisms influencing manufacturers' green investment decisions, the platform's optimal cost-sharing strategy, and choices of selling modes and information-sharing strategies. First, our analysis demonstrates that platform-enabled information sharing facilitates manufacturers in aligning greenness with realized demand, thereby amplifying the value of information disclosure. Contrary to conventional wisdom, by strategically augmenting its green cost-sharing proportion, the platform may have an incentive for voluntary information disclosure under the reselling mode. This incentive intensifies as consumer green awareness rises. Second, with low greenness competition intensity, the platform's willingness to undertake green cost-sharing increases with price competition intensity, and agency mode is more advantageous for sharing green costs than reselling when the commission rate is high. Third, higher green cost-sharing proportions and greater consumer green awareness enhance the platform's incentive to adopt the agency mode. Specifically, when consumer green awareness is high and the platform bears a substantial share of green investment costs, the agency mode with information sharing leads to a win-win outcome under weak price competition; in contrast, the reselling mode with information sharing is mutually beneficial under intense price competition. This study provides significant managerial insights into collaborative green research and development operations within platform supply chains.

Title: A tractable model and heuristic for vessel routing with multiple unmanned aerial vehicles
Authors: Bo Ren, Yantong Li, Hairui Sun, Danyu Bai, Kang Chen
Abstract: Offshore parcel delivery is essential for ensuring the sustained operation of offshore oil and gas platforms by providing timely access to essential supplies, spare parts, and emergency materials. We study a vessel routing problem emerging from a novel delivery paradigm in which a vessel and multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) collaborate to complete delivery tasks. The studied problem extends the carrier–vehicle traveling salesman problem by allowing a vessel to carry multiple UAVs. We first formulate a mixed-integer second-order cone program that effectively captures the interdependent vessel–UAV operations by representing take-off and landing constraints using two operational points for each platform. To handle practical-sized instances, we design a tailored parallel adaptive large neighborhood search (PALNS) algorithm. The PALNS algorithm begins with a heuristic procedure to generate initial feasible solutions, incorporates problem-specific destroy and repair operators, and integrates local search mechanisms that explore various take-off and landing modes for multiple UAVs during the iterative process. Computational experiments on randomly generated instances show that CPLEX is effective for small-sized instances but fails to obtain feasible solutions for larger instances within the 3-hour time limit. Compared with the improved simulated annealing (ISA) baseline algorithm, PALNS reduces the average objective value from 27399.47 to 26286.25 on large-sized instances, corresponding to an average improvement of approximately 4.1%, while also requiring less computational time. In addition, we conduct a sensitivity analysis to evaluate the impacts of key parameters, including the number of UAVs, UAV endurance, and the speeds of both the vessel and UAVs. Finally, a case study is conducted to illustrate the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed method in offshore logistics.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: From LinkedIn to labor statistics: Using Revelio microdata for labor market research in developing economies
Authors: Samuel Chang, Hans B. Christensen, Ziang Zhang
Abstract: We explore the use of Revelio data—obtained primarily from LinkedIn profiles—as a source of labor force microdata in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where large-sample, high-frequency, employer-linked alternatives are largely unavailable. To address the selection inherent to LinkedIn usership, we employ ILO labor statistics to construct five sets of country-year-specific weights that alleviate non-representativeness across occupation, industry, occupation × education, industry × education, and industry × firm-size cells. We further validate these weights using national census data where they are available and not used for ILO labor statistics. The weighted dataset provides a balanced monthly panel with coverage across most LMICs. We also discuss remaining limitations of the dataset, including within-cell selection and self-reporting errors, and suggest techniques to alleviate them. Despite imperfect coverage, Revelio offers improved temporal and geographical resolution as well as cross-country comparability and is especially useful for studying the role of firms in economic development.

Title: Allocation of foreign aid in emerging economies: Investment in new vs maintenance of old infrastructure
Authors: Rolando A. Escobar-Posada, Goncalo Monteiro, Stephen J. Turnovsky

Title: Idle monetary policy? Evidence from monetary policy shocks for Pakistan
Authors: M. Ali Choudhary, Vasco J. Gabriel
Abstract: We challenge the narrative of idle monetary transmission in Pakistan. By cleansing conventional policy measures of anticipatory and endogenous motives à la Romer and Romer (2004), and using local projections in long differences (Jordá and Taylor, 2025; Piger and Stockwell, 2025), Piger and Stockwell, 2025], we trace the effects of monetary shocks on macroeconomic and financial outcomes while controlling for the global financial cycle (Miranda-Agrippino and Rey, 2020). A contractionary shock generates a large and persistent output contraction and a significant, non-monotone response of year-on-year inflation, with disinflation on impact and again after eight to nine quarters. The policy rate rises in the short run, while term-spread and credit responses are economically coherent but less precisely estimated. US monetary spillovers are small and statistically imprecise. Monetary policy works in Pakistan; only its measurement was idle.

Title: On the bracketing relationship in staggered treatment designs
Authors: Joonho Hwang
Abstract: Researchers often use fixed-effects and lagged-dependent-variable (LDV) estimates as upper and lower bounds on a treatment effect. This paper studies this comparison in staggered-treatment designs and shows that the conventional ordering of the two estimates is not generally preserved. The direction of the difference depends on cohort- and event-time-specific treatment effects, outcome persistence, and the alignment of treatment timing with unit and time heterogeneity. Thus, either estimator may serve as the lower or upper bound, and the ordering may vary across group-time cells. Monte Carlo simulations further show that the interval formed by the two realized point estimates frequently fails to contain the true group-time average treatment effect in finite samples. The results suggest that fixed-effects and LDV estimates should be viewed as a descriptive comparison rather than as guaranteed bounds.

Title: Cryptocurrency uncertainty and bank intermediation
Authors: Whelsy Boungou, Alhonita Yatie
Abstract: The rapid expansion of cryptocurrency markets has intensified interactions between digital assets and traditional financial institutions, raising important questions about the implications of cryptocurrency-related uncertainty for banking activities. This paper investigates how cryptocurrency uncertainty shapes banks' funding, lending, and risk-taking decisions. Using a panel of 8330 banks across 129 countries over the period 2009–2018, we examine the relationship between cryptocurrency uncertainty and key dimensions of banks' balance-sheet decisions. We find that heightened cryptocurrency uncertainty increases customer deposits while reducing lending activity, non-performing loans, and risk-weighted assets. These findings suggest that banks respond to cryptocurrency uncertainty by adopting more conservative balance-sheet decisions characterized by stronger funding positions, lower credit expansion, and reduced risk exposure. The results remain robust to alternative measures of cryptocurrency uncertainty and lending activity. Our findings highlight that cryptocurrency uncertainty generates significant spillover effects on traditional financial intermediation and should be incorporated into macroprudential surveillance frameworks.

Title: Going the extra mile — By design: Generating road networks with target values of travel impedance via bi-level optimization
Authors: Steven Parks, Selene Silvestri, Matthias Winkenbach
Abstract: The inherent characteristics of a road network impact transportation system design, performance, and user behavior. However, systematically evaluating their impacts on vehicle routing, facility location, and other transportation decisions is challenging. In this work, we propose a methodology to generate stylized road networks that satisfy user-defined values of average network circuity and inefficiency, two graph characteristics that, respectively, describe the closeness of spatial locations in terms of shortest travel distance and time. We refine an exact solution approach consisting of two novel bi-level mixed-integer Road Network Design Problems solved in succession. We concoct a suite of test instances to evaluate their computational performance and demonstrate that our proposed linearizations, valid inequalities, and warm start heuristics significantly improve model tractability. The resulting method enables the generation of road networks with prescribed values of average travel impedance. As such, it lays a groundwork for future research on the impacts of road network structure and connectivity on transportation systems.

Title: Corrigendum to “Public or private? A unified demand–supply coupled framework for EV infrastructure investment” [Trans. Res. Part D: Trans. Environ. 159 (2026) 105501]

Title: AI or human live sales? Live sales model selection and pricing strategies in a competitive market
Authors: Jianjian Chen, Wenfan Zhao, Lili Liu, Wei Yu, Sihua Chen
Abstract: In recent years, live sales have surged tremendously. Some retailers are increasingly hiring human streamers to reduce product uncertainty among consumers, while others, equipped with virtual streamers, are developing artificial intelligence (AI)-based live sales models to overcome problems such as weak streamer control and high live sales costs. This study develops a three-stage game model to investigate the live sales selection between AI and human live sales, as well as their pricing strategies in a competitive market. It elucidates how the live sales strategies vary with the network effect, market expansion effect, erosion effect, and consumer acceptance of AI live sales. Notably, as the scale of the consumer market softens retailer competition, a low or high degree of consumer acceptance of AI live sales can lead the retailer that adopts AI live sales to set a higher price. In a competitive live sales scenario, retailers should adopt AI live sales when the erosion effect is moderate and the network effect is weak, whereas human live sales become the equilibrium strategy when the erosion effect is weak or the network effect is strong; otherwise, competing retailers should adopt different live sales models. Finally, as consumer acceptance of AI live sales increases, the AA, HN, and NN strategies become more likely to be equilibrium strategies, while HA and HH are less likely to occur. Although the AN strategy initially becomes more likely to emerge as the equilibrium strategy, its likelihood ultimately decreases. The extension models confirm the robustness of the underlying conclusions.

Title: Timeliness-driven routing and scheduling for infrastructure rush repairs with cascading time uncertainties
Authors: Xinhao Cui, Penghao Qi, Bo Li, Yi Ren, Yiyong Xiao
Abstract: Post-disaster restoration of interdependent infrastructure networks demands rapid and coordinated rush-repair operations under severe resource constraints and pronounced time uncertainties. This paper proposes an integrated mixed-integer linear programming framework for timeliness-driven technician routing and scheduling under cascading time uncertainties, where stochastic deviations in repair durations and technician arrivals accumulate sequentially along repair routes and amplify schedule risk through successive tasks. The framework jointly optimizes unit-to-technician assignment and collaborative routing to maximize cumulative service restoration throughout the planning horizon. The cascading propagation of uncertainties is characterized through a mean-variance formulation with an ε-accurate linearization technique. To address the combinatorial complexity, we develop a matheuristic algorithm that synergistically combines Variable Neighborhood Search with ILP-based local optimization, featuring adaptive neighborhood operators and a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach attains proven optimal solutions on small-scale instances and the best solutions among the tested algorithms on larger instances, while reducing computation time by up to 96% compared with the commercial solver. Out-of-sample comparisons against deterministic and robust counterparts then validate the modeling choice, confirming that the mean-variance formulation effectively navigates the fundamental trade-off between realized timeliness and scenario feasibility. Sensitivity and effect analyses translate these methodological advantages into actionable insights for emergency decision-makers on workforce deployment and risk tolerance calibration. Ultimately, the proposed framework advances rush-repair optimization by integrating cascading-uncertainty modeling, technician routing and scheduling, and timeliness maximization within a unified, tractable optimization paradigm.

Title: Editorial Board
Product variety, alcohol purchases, and the role of excise taxes
Authors: Aljoscha Janssen
Abstract: This study explores how product variety affects alcohol purchasing in the U.S., using store-level and household scanner data. By analyzing households that relocate to areas with different product availability and controlling for destination-specific consumption patterns, I document a positive relationship between increased product variety and higher alcohol purchases. I complement the household-level evidence with an analysis of two state-specific policy changes, the 2012 Washington liquor deregulation and the 2009 Illinois excise tax increase, to document that policies that raise prices, particularly the Washington liquor deregulation, are also associated with expanded product variety, which may partially offset the intended reduction in consumption. The results have important implications for public health: policymakers should be aware that alcohol market reforms can inadvertently increase product assortment and thereby stimulate consumption, particularly among the heaviest purchasers.

Title: Impacts of in-person school days on student outcomes and inequality: Evidence from Korean high schools during the pandemic
Authors: Youjin Hahn, Hyuncheol Bryant Kim, Hee-Seung Yang
Abstract: We investigate the effects of in-person schooling on high school students’ outcomes by leveraging variation in school days within regions induced by the COVID-19 pandemic in Korea. Using nationally administered standardized test scores linked to standardized student survey measures collected as part of the same assessment system, we find that while additional in-person schooling does not significantly affect average test scores, it reduces educational inequality and improves selected school-related attitudes and behaviors, such as class participation, school satisfaction, and career aspiration. The changes in test score distributions are primarily driven by boys rather than girls. The findings emphasize the need to address educational inequality in policy responses to pandemic-related learning loss.

Title: An environmentally sustainable feasible policy for dynamic lot sizing model with remanufacturing and separate setup costs: time complexity and optimality
Authors: Chee-Khian Sim
Affiliations: University of Portsmouth

Title: Shockproof or exposed? The moderating role of tariff shocks in the link between artificial intelligence and firm supply chain resilience
Authors: Zhisheng Li, Tachia Chin, Francesco Caputo, Hanrong Xu
Affiliations: Zhejiang University of Technology; University of Naples Federico II; Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia

Title: Striking a Bargain: Narrative Identification of Wage Bargaining Shocks
Authors: Žymantas Budrys, Mario Porqueddu, Andrej Sokol
Affiliations: Lietuvos Bankas and Vilnius University Vilnius Lithuania; European Central Bank Frankfurt am Main Germany; Bloomberg LP Frankfurt am Main Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT Wage markup shocks, an important driver of business cycles, are hard to pin down. We quantify the importance of exogenous variation in wage bargaining power, one source of those shocks, from German minimum wage introduction episodes and strikes. This disciplines the impulse responses of unemployment and output, and sharpens inference for other variables, which behave consistently with predictions from search‐and‐matching models. We find that wage bargaining shocks meaningfully contribute to aggregate fluctuations in unemployment and inflation, exhibit substantial pass‐through to prices, and imply plausible dynamics for the vacancy rate, firms' profits, and the labor share.

Title: Efficient Forecast-Based Routing and Dynamic Time Window Management for Attended Home Deliveries
Authors: Mohammad Abdollahi, Xinan Yang, Michael Fairbank
Abstract: Abstract In light of the escalating popularity of online shopping and the urgent need to reduce unnecessary driving to mitigate environmental impacts, it has become increasingly important to provide cost-effective solutions for attended home deliveries. Extensive research efforts have been dedicated to addressing challenges related to integrating demand management and vehicle routing with time windows. In this paper, we present two key contributions. Firstly, we propose an enhanced method for estimating opportunity cost, by leveraging a dynamic-routing and distribution approach that incorporates forecast orders. This approach allows for more accurate revenue-loss assessments, ultimately leading to improved decision-making on the delivery charges. Secondly, we introduce a dynamic slot-combination strategy, aiming to fully exploit the flexibility that customers possess in receiving their delivery, which enhances overall route efficiency and customer satisfaction. Importantly, our proposed augmented time-windows approach can be easily implemented within existing systems, employing standard time windows, without necessitating any strategic changes or complex computational modifications to the routing system. To assess the performance of our proposed approach, we conducted exhaustive experiments on real data. The results demonstrate that our generated solution outperforms both recent and current state-of-the-art approaches in terms of profitability and delivery efficiency. This signifies the effectiveness and practicality of our proposed methodology in addressing the challenges associated with attended home deliveries.

Title: Dynamic allocation and index policies in bandit problems: celebrating the contributions of Michael N. Katehakis
Authors: Wen Chen
Abstract: Sequential decision-making under uncertainty lies at the core of operations research, statistics, and modern machine learning. Among its most influential formulations is the multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem, which formalizes the exploration-exploitation trade-off through adaptive allocation of uncertain alternatives. This article presents a comprehensive festschrift in honor of Michael N. Katehakis, whose work has played a central role in shaping the structural and information-theoretic foundations of bandit theory and its applications. We trace the development of project index theory and discounted bandits, highlighting the structural decomposition principles that reduce complex stochastic control problems to scalar index comparisons. We then examine the Lai-Robbins lower bound and the Burnetas-Katehakis asymptotic optimality framework, which constructs allocation rules attaining the exact logarithmic regret constant dictated by Kullback–Leibler divergence. These contributions establish a unified perspective in which dynamic programming, large deviations theory, and statistical efficiency converge. Building on this foundation, we survey extensions to constrained, restless, contextual, combinatorial, non-stationary, and adversarial bandits, as well as connections to reinforcement learning. Across these generalizations, a common structural paradigm persists: optimal exploration is governed by quantified uncertainty, and complex allocation problems admit tractable solutions through indexability and Lagrangian relaxation. We further examine applications in adaptive clinical trials, dynamic pricing and revenue management, inventory control with learning, online recommendation systems, finance, and service operations. In each domain, index-based and regret-optimal policies provide computationally implementable decision rules with provable long-run efficiency guarantees. By situating these developments within the broader evolution of sequential decision theory, this article highlights the enduring influence of Katehakis’s contributions and underscores the continuing relevance of structural and information-theoretic principles in modern data-driven optimization.

Title: Enhancing data envelopment analysis: a comprehensive calibration with random forests
Authors: Zhichao Wang
Abstract: Abstract This paper proposes an algorithm integrating random forests (RF) and data envelopment analysis (DEA), termed RF-DEA, to address several methodological challenges commonly encountered in DEA applications, e.g., sensitivity to outliers and the ‘curse of dimensionality’. We show that by leveraging the strengths of RF, the DEA estimator with a calibrated frontier and input/output vectors can effectively mitigate the influence of outliers, identify redundant variables, and account for the influence of environmental variables. Evidence from Monte Carlo simulations demonstrates that these properties of RF-DEA yield substantial improvements in estimation accuracy compared to the conventional DEA. Through an empirical application to global production efficiency, we illustrate that this easy-to-implement method constitutes a viable alternative DEA estimator, capable of disentangling some practical challenges in efficiency analysis.

Title: Tracking Shifts in U.S. Monetary Policy: Comparing Multiplicative Indicator Saturation With Three Alternatives
Authors: Josh R. Stillwagon
Affiliations: Economics Division Babson College Babson Park Massachusetts USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This article applies Multiplicative Indicator Saturation (MIS), for automated coefficient break selection, to a Taylor rule estimated with real‐time data and the shadow federal funds rate from 1972 to 2025. MIS is compared with sample splitting by Fed Chair, Bai–Perron break tests, and Markov‐switching. MIS offers advantages by controlling for outliers and allowing parameters to vary flexibly over time. Across methods and specifications, several breaks emerge as robust, most notably Volcker's and Greenspan's appointments. Surprisingly, once interest rate smoothing is incorporated, no test rejects a constant policy ‘rule’ after 2000, despite this period's reputation as a ‘new discretionary era’.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: The Effects of Induced Emotions on Leading‐By‐Example
Authors: Michalis Drouvelis, Zeyu Qiu
Affiliations: Department of Economics University of Birmingham Birmingham UK; CESifo Munish Germany; Department of Economics and Public Policy Imperial College London, South Kensington Campus London UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates the effects of induced emotions on leading‐by‐example. Using an online sample of more than 1000 participants, we observe behaviour in a one‐shot sequential voluntary contribution mechanism game where leaders and followers are induced to be either happy or angry. Our findings show that angry leaders contribute less than happy leaders. The same effect is observed when considering followers' behaviour. A follow‐up study using the strategy method, where followers make conditional contribution decisions without observing the leader's actual contribution, detects no statistically significant differences between angry and happy followers' conditional contribution schedules. This suggests that the effect of induced emotions on followers' behaviour operates primarily through the leader's behaviour, highlighting the importance of leader emotions in shaping team outcomes. More broadly, our findings highlight the role of emotions as a causal force, suggesting that negative changes in well‐being can bring about adverse effects on team cooperation.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Operationalizing ocean equity in a multi-use marine protected area: Management practice and stakeholder perspectives from the Marine Nature Park of Iroise, France
Authors: Pierre Scemama, Diana Burbano, Marie Guingot, Océane Darmandieu, Frédérique Alban
Abstract: As global commitments to marine conservation intensify under the Kunming-Montréal Global Biodiversity Framework, there is growing recognition that Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) must deliver not only ecological outcomes but also social equity. This study examines how equity is operationalized in the governance of the Marine Nature Park of Iroise (MNPI), one of France's largest multi-use MPAs, by comparing institutional management actions with stakeholder perspectives. Using the Ocean Equity Framework—comprising Recognitional, Procedural, Distributional, Environmental, Management, and Contextual dimensions—this study combines analysis of MNPI institutional reporting with stakeholder perspectives elicited through Q-Methodology. Institutional reporting suggests that MNPI governance primarily emphasizes the Management and Environmental dimensions of equity through actions largely focused on knowledge production, commercial fishing, and environmental protection. In contrast, the Q-methodology reveals greater consensus around Management and Recognitional dimensions of equity, while Procedural and Contextual dimensions remain more contested. Comparing institutional actions with stakeholder perspectives enables a more integrative assessment of the trade-offs shaping MPA governance. The Q-analysis identified four perspectives on equity-related tensions: (i) the knowledge paradox, reflecting gaps between scientific knowledge production and local needs; (ii) the protection paradox, reflecting competing conservation priorities among ecosystem services; (iii) the process-without-capacity tension, reflecting cross-sectoral governance challenges across horizontal and vertical governance scales; and (iv) path dependency, reflecting persistent tensions between biodiversity conservation and economic development. Overall, this study advances the assessment of equity in MPAs by integrating institutional analysis with stakeholder perspectives through a mixed-methods approach, providing insights to support more inclusive, context-sensitive, and socially grounded marine governance.

Title: Enhancing flood impact assessment accuracy: A comparison of IRIO-Flood predictions using HAZUS- and insurance claims-based business interruption estimates
Authors: Jlenia Di Noia, Alessandro Caiani, Luigi Cesarini, Marcello Arosio, Mario Martina
Abstract: While input–output models are widely used to assess the economic impacts of natural disasters, their results strongly depend on how disaster shocks are specified. This paper examines two alternative characterizations of flood-induced business interruptions, and their effect on total economic losses. We compare restoration time estimates derived from the Hazus-Flood framework with a novel approach based on micro-level insurance claims data, which allows for partial reductions in plants’ productive capacity during the restoration phase, rather than assuming full inoperability.Using georeferenced plant-level data and high-resolution flood maps, we calibrate flood shocks for four major Italian flood events and simulate their propagation through the economy using the IRIO-Flood model. We find that Hazus-based specifications generally produce larger and more dispersed estimates of productive capacity contractions, leading to greater GDP and sectoral output losses – particularly in the short term – and to stronger spillovers to regions not directly affected by the flood. Despite these substantial differences in magnitude, both approaches identify broadly similar patterns in terms of the most affected sectors and regions, with discrepancies emerging more frequently when considering the medium-term propagation of losses.These results highlight the importance of accurate shock specification and suggest that the two proposed methods can be viewed as complementary tools for flood impact and risk assessment.

Title: From climate vulnerability to elite capture: the hidden pathways linking inequality to climate adaptation readiness
Authors: Cong Minh Huynh, Nam Hoai Tran
Abstract: Asia faces intensifying climate risks, yet its capacity for adaptation remains uneven across countries. This study examines how income inequality influences national climate adaptation readiness in 35 Asian economies from 1996 to 2023, focusing on two mediating mechanisms: climate vulnerability and elite capture. Integrating adaptation-readiness theory with perspectives from environmental justice and elite theory, we estimate a panel mediation model combining country fixed effects with an instrumental-variable two-stage least squares approach to identify the causal pathways linking inequality to adaptation readiness. In the empirical analysis, elite capture is operationalized using a corruption-based proxy derived from the Worldwide Governance Indicators' control of corruption index, reversed so that higher values indicate greater corruption and thus stronger elite capture. Results show that income inequality significantly reduces adaptation readiness both directly and indirectly. Inequality increases vulnerability and elite capture, and both mechanisms substantially undermine adaptation readiness. Decomposition indicates that the direct effect explains about 65.23% of the total impact, while elite capture (22%) and vulnerability (12.77%) form the main indirect pathways. Robustness checks using two-stage least squares with instrumental variables confirm the findings. The analysis demonstrates that inequality is not only a social problem but also a structural barrier to national adaptation capacity, operating through both social exposure and governance capture. The study contributes new evidence on the inequality-adaptation nexus and highlights the need for redistribution, anti-corruption, and participatory governance to make adaptation finance and policy more equitable and effective.

Title: Coordinated bus service design and response for resilient bus-metro transit systems under metro disruptions
Authors: Zhiya Su, Enoch Lee, Hong K. Lo, Joseph Y.J. Chow, Jiayang Li
Abstract: Metro systems are central to urban mobility in dense cities, yet service disruptions often occur as partial capacity degradations whose impacts propagate through the network and depend on system design and operations. Existing studies mainly follow two perspectives: ex-post recovery, which reacts after disruptions but is constrained by fixed designs and resources; ex-ante planning, which embeds resilience in advance but abstracts from operational flexibility. This paper proposes an Event-Adaptive Resilience-Aware (EARA) framework for coordinated bus service design and response in multimodal transit systems. The framework provides a single implementable baseline design while enabling flexible adjustments once a disruption is identified. To avoid the computational burden of a full two-stage stochastic program, we embed disruption risk into planning through service-reliability-based effective capacity constraints and prepare event-specific frequency adjustments and shuttle deployment without changing the network structure. Disruption uncertainty is represented by a finite set of events specifying jointly affected metro segments, allowing heterogeneous disruption patterns to be captured without enumerating detailed capacity realizations. A Hong Kong Island case study compares four planning and response strategies. Results show that reactive adjustments cannot compensate for disruption-blind baseline designs, while disruption-aware planning without event differentiation leads to conservative capacity allocation. By combining disruption-aware planning with event-adaptive response, EARA substantially reduces unmet demand and improves overall system performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Robust indoor automated guided vehicle navigation for logistics applications via imitation-augmented hierarchical reinforcement learning with a memory-attention generalized network
Authors: Weidong Xie, Zhiyong Wang, Peiqun Lin, Yingying Ma, Yueying Zhang, Zhaoyu Lin, Runze Huang
Abstract: Robust navigation of automated guided vehicles (AGVs) in indoor logistics environments remains challenging, as AGVs must operate in confined, cluttered, and dynamically changing spaces while satisfying strict requirements for safety and efficiency. This paper focuses on three key problems: (1) balancing fast goal-directed motion with collision avoidance, (2) extracting transferable spatiotemporal representations from heterogeneous LiDAR and kinematic observations, and (3) improving the generalization of learned policies from simulation to unseen and real-world indoor logistics scenarios. To address these problems, an imitation-augmented hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework with a Memory-Attention Generalized Network, termed IAHDRL-MAGNet, is proposed. It decomposes navigation into a low-level goal-directed motion policy and a high-level safety-aware option selector to balance rapid target approaching and obstacle avoidance. MAGNet integrates angle-aware multi-head attention, GRU-based temporal fusion, and D2RL feature propagation to extract compact spatiotemporal representations from multimodal LiDAR and kinematic observations. An augmented imitation learning mechanism further combines state-dependent expert guidance, prioritized experience replay, and limited randomization of LiDAR and kinematic observations to improve convergence efficiency and policy transferability. Simulation experiments in training and unseen indoor environments show that IAHDRL-MAGNet outperforms baseline methods by achieving higher success rates, fewer collisions, and shorter navigation times in successful trials. Ablation studies provide supporting evidence for the contributions of MAGNet and the augmented imitation learning mechanism. Real-world tests further show that the learned policy can be deployed without additional real-world fine-tuning under the tested settings. These results indicate that IAHDRL-MAGNet shows promise as a practical navigation framework for safe and efficient AGV navigation in indoor logistics environments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Emotional and physical burdens of water poverty: evidence from the drinking water service ladder in Mozambique
Authors: Terrence Kairiza, Wanglin Ma, Abbi Kedir
Abstract: Access to safe and reliable drinking water remains uneven across sub-Saharan Africa, yet existing evidence largely focuses on health outcomes and binary measures of access, overlooking how different service levels affect everyday well-being. This study examines how the water service ladder shapes the emotional and physical burdens of water poverty and whether these effects differ by household head gender in Mozambique. Using nationally representative data from the 2022–2023 Mozambique Demographic and Health Survey and a multivalued treatment effects framework, we estimate the impacts of unimproved, limited, basic, and safely managed water services on water-related worry, anger, hygiene deprivation, and insufficient drinking water. Results show that limited services, i.e., improved sources located more than 30 min away, do not significantly reduce water-related distress relative to unimproved sources. In contrast, both basic and safely managed services substantially reduce emotional and physical burdens, with no additional gains from on-premises access beyond the 30-minute accessibility threshold. Female-headed households are more likely to access improved services, but the well-being benefits of improved water access do not differ by household head gender. These findings highlight the importance of service proximity rather than source type alone and suggest that progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 6 may be overstated when measured using binary indicators of improved access. The results emphasize the need for policy strategies that prioritize reducing collection time to deliver meaningful well-being gains from water infrastructure investments.

Title: Corruption and capital investment: Worldwide evidence
Authors: Wei-Fong Pan
Abstract: Can international anti-corruption monitoring stimulate private investment? We examine staggered reviews across jurisdictions under the United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC), using firm-year observations from 84 economies over 2003–2023. We document that reviews are followed by improvements in economy-level corruption-control indicators. Local-projections difference-in-differences estimates indicate that reviews raise firms' capital expenditure relative to assets by 1.2126 percentage points, equivalent to 20% of the sample mean. Dynamic estimates show no systematic pre-review adjustment, and the result is robust to influential-economy exclusions, economy-level reweighting, alternative sample restrictions, lagged-outcome controls, and alternative staggered-adoption estimators. Investment responses are stronger in high-corruption economies and developing economies and among firms that are more financially constrained, government dependent, domestically concentrated, or reliant on irreversible capital. These patterns are consistent with international oversight reducing corruption-related institutional risk, financing frictions, and the value of delaying investment. UNCAC reviews are also followed by increases in employment, R&D investment, and leverage. Additional analyses provide no evidence that the increase in investment is accompanied by a systematic decline in investment efficiency. Overall, the findings show that a non-punitive international peer-review mechanism can affect firms’ real activity, particularly where initial institutional frictions are greater.

Title: Under pressure: High-Stakes exams and media-reported student suicides in India
Authors: Subarna Banerjee, Gitanjali Sen
Abstract: We estimate the temporal association between high-stakes exam timing and media-reported student suicides in India using geocoded news data. Student suicides are 17.5 percent higher during months in which NEET-UG or JEE-Mains examinations are held, with no comparable pattern around lower-stakes board exams or among adults. The association is concentrated when national entrance exams coincide with board exams, suggesting the salience of cumulative exam burden. These patterns are stronger among girls, in states with higher exam participation, and in urbanised districts. Event-study estimates show suicides increasing immediately before and during exams, while movements around result announcements are weaker and less precisely estimated. We find no evidence that broad shifts in media attention during cyclone or election months account for the pattern, although exam-specific reporting bias cannot be ruled out. In the absence of mental health data, we generate an alternative database to address a policy question and spur future research.

Title: Coal phase-out in a second-best setting: Evidence from China’s coal-to-gas transition
Authors: Antonio M. Bento, Ruozi Song, Bing Zhang
Abstract: As countries phase out coal, natural gas is often promoted as a transitional fuel, but incomplete policies and price distortions can cause emissions leakage, undermining coal reduction efforts. This paper examines China’s 2017 coal-to-gas transition policy, which banned coal in central heating across 28 northern cities, triggering a 70% increase in natural gas prices while coal prices remained stable due to price distortions. Using a comprehensive dataset of hourly pollution measures from 1563 monitors and firm-level data covering around 50% of coal consumption in China, we find that instead of reducing coal consumption, the policy led to substantial leakage. Baseline industry composition, the stringency of environmental regulations, and uneven enforcement across polluting firms all contribute to leakage. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest that for every ton of coal reduced in the heating sector, coal use increased by 0.19 tons in targeted cities, 2.18 tons in northern non-targeted cities, and 2.32 tons in southern cities. We estimate that 42.9% of the coal consumption rebound could have been prevented if coal prices had been liberalized to fluctuate with natural gas prices, as in European markets. Alternatively, a carbon price of 16.61 RMB (approximately 2.4 USD) per ton of CO 2 would achieve an equivalent reduction in coal use while preventing leakage. These findings highlight the importance of addressing market distortions to enhance the effectiveness of coal phase-out policies.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Why did air conditioning adoption accelerate faster than predicted? Evidence from Mexico
Authors: Lucas W. Davis, Paul Gertler
Abstract: A common theme in the vast literature on climate change is the estimation of models using historical data to make predictions many decades into the future. Although there is a large and growing number of these types of studies, researchers rarely return later to check the accuracy of their predictions. In this paper, we perform such an exercise. In Davis and Gertler (2015), we used household-level microdata from Mexico to predict future air conditioning adoption as a function of income and temperature. Revisiting these predictions with 12 years of additional data, we find that air conditioning in Mexico has accelerated, significantly exceeding our predictions. This large prediction gap is not explained by income growth, rising temperatures, migration patterns, or an overly restrictive model. Instead, the evidence points to decreased electricity prices and technological change in air conditioning as potential explanations.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Dealing with the dilemma of digitalization asymmetry within buyer-supplier relationships: The dual-edged moderating effects of governance mechanisms
Authors: Wei Yang, Zeze Song, Yin Zhou, Xihan Gao, Fangmin Yin
Abstract: The increasing prevalence of supply chain digitalization has widened the digital divide between firms and their partners, posing a significant collaboration challenge. Previous studies predominantly emphasize the negative effect of digitalization asymmetry on focal firms, with limited attention to its effect on dyadic performance. This study investigates how digitalization asymmetry affects buyer-supplier relationship (BSR) performance, with particular attention to the mediating role of joint learning and the moderating effects of trust and monitoring as two distinct governance mechanisms. Using a sample of 170 matched buyer-supplier dyads from China, this study tests the proposed model through regression analyses. The results reveal the double-edged role of digitalization asymmetry in BSRs, demonstrating an inverted U-shaped relationship between digitalization asymmetry and dyadic performance. The instantaneous indirect-effect analysis indicates a significant negative indirect effect through joint learning at a relatively high level of digitalization asymmetry. Furthermore, trust strengthens, whereas monitoring weakens, the effect of digitalization asymmetry. These findings provide theoretical insights for supply chain literature by advancing our understanding of the nonlinear dynamics of digitalization asymmetry in BSRs. For practitioners, this study provides practical insights on how to engage in effective collaboration with partners at varying levels of digitalization and implement governance strategies to address the digitalization asymmetry dilemma.

Title: What ties us together? Explaining synchronized GDP volatility
Authors: Javier Adrián López Artero, Lorenzo Ductor, Danilo Leiva-León
Abstract: Amidst heightened policy uncertainty, understanding the drivers of global macroeconomic instability becomes increasingly critical. This paper studies the determinants of output volatility synchronization using data for 42 economies worldwide. We construct a bilateral time-varying index of volatility synchronization and infer its drivers using Bayesian Model Averaging, complemented by Weighted Average Least Squares and LASSO. We find that differences in Total Factor Productivity, interest rate, and fiscal policy volatility robustly explain cross-country synchronization, with nuances between developed and developing countries. Overall, the results highlight the role of technological divergence and macroeconomic policy uncertainty in shaping the international co-movement of output volatility.

Title: Do stock markets price words or actions? President Donald Trump´s geopolitical signals and conflict risk
Authors: Boris Pastén-Henríquez, Carlos P. Maquieira
Abstract: Geopolitical tensions and military threats increasingly shape global financial markets. Using geopolitical threat signals associated with President Donald Trump, we distinguish between threats that later escalated into military action and those that did not. We find a clear asymmetry in stock market responses. Threats that do not materialize are associated with positive abnormal returns, whereas threats followed by military escalation generate weaker or negative effects, particularly in Latin American stock markets, while responses in G7 economies remain muted. These findings suggest that markets price not only geopolitical threats themselves, but also their perceived credibility and eventual realization, highlighting the role of credibility in asset pricing.

Title: Common ownership with a location leader
Authors: Kenneth Fjell, John S. Heywood, Debashis Pal
Abstract: We investigate the impact of common ownership in a spatial price discrimination model with sequential location choice. In contrast to simultaneous location choice, an increase in common ownership need not reduce locational efficiency. Common ownership by the location leader improves locational efficiency, even restoring the first best.

Title: Different institutions, different finance: Evidence from early twentieth-century China
Authors: Wanda Wang
Abstract: Institutional legacies are associated not only with the scale of finance but also with the organizational forms that emerge. Using prefecture-level data from early twentieth-century China, where indigenous money houses based on relational contracting coexisted with modern banks operating under codified law, we document that prefectures more deeply embedded in the imperial administrative system had more money houses and lower private borrowing costs, consistent with lower information and enforcement costs in relational finance. Treaty-port prefectures instead had more modern banks, with this concentration widening from 1910 to 1935. The analysis is descriptive and does not establish causality.

Title: Uneven carbon pricing signals in shipping: Regulatory overlap, abatement costs and fuel choice
Authors: Jing Wang, Lei Liu, Xun Yang, Dong Yang, Ran Yan
Abstract: Carbon pricing is increasingly positioned as a key instrument for decarbonizing international shipping. However, the coexistence of global and regional carbon pricing mechanisms is reshaping the economics of maritime decarbonization, while also raising concerns about overlapping compliance burdens and uneven transition incentives. This study develops a voyage-level framework to examine the combined impacts of the IMO net-zero framework, the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), and FuelEU Maritime on container shipping. Using high-resolution Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, TEU-level carbon pricing costs and alternative-fuel competitiveness are assessed across four representative shipping corridors with different levels of regulatory exposure. For conventional fuel operation, carbon pricing costs remain relatively limited compared with the overall market freight level. Substantial heterogeneity emerges across vessel sizes and routes. Corridors exposed to overlapping EU-related regulations experience significantly higher carbon costs, while vessel scale acts as the dominant moderating factor, with large vessels consistently diluting carbon liabilities more effectively than smaller vessels. For alternative fuel pathways, hydrogen exhibits the strongest cost competitiveness under uncertainty, with WinProb values reaching up to 45.1% by 2035, whereas methanol remains below 2.54% across most scenarios. The uncertainty structure also differs substantially across fuel pathways. Methanol and ammonia competitiveness is primarily driven by fuel-price uncertainty, whereas hydrogen depends more strongly on policy-support mechanisms. We further compare the e-fuel pathways with biofuel-blend scenarios to analyze short-term transition options. Waste/residue-based hydrotreated vegetable oil blends appear more readily deployable and cost competitive before 2035, but their emission-reduction potential remains limited. Overall, the findings suggest that current carbon pricing levels alone are unlikely to trigger large-scale fuel switching. Effective maritime decarbonization will require not only stronger and more coordinated carbon pricing signals, but also sustained reductions in green fuel costs and long-term policy support for alternative fuel deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Ready to begin: driving towards the best and steering away from the worst in road pricing policy reform
Authors: Matthew J. Beck, Michiel C.J. Bliemer, John M. Rose
Abstract: Declining revenue from traditional road funding sources, rising infrastructure costs, and the transition to electric vehicles have increased the urgency of road user charging reform as a key demand management strategy. While such schemes can improve transport system efficiency by pricing congestion and other externalities, their implementation requires careful balancing with concerns around fairness and affordability. Public acceptability therefore remains a critical constraint on policy adoption. This paper examines which policy features most strongly influence support for road user charging and how these preferences can inform the design of policies that advance efficiency, fairness, and affordability objectives. A best worst scaling approach is used to elicit the relative importance of policy features, with choices modelled using a hybrid choice framework that captures both observed preferences and underlying attitudes. Three distinct behavioural classes are identified, reflecting differing priorities related to efficiency, fairness and consistency, and broader public benefit. Across these groups, governance and institutional arrangements are central to perceived legitimacy. Features such as public ownership, not for profit operation, independent investment decision making, and transparent revenue use are strongly preferred, while more complex pricing mechanisms are viewed less favourably. The findings highlight the importance of trust, fairness, and affordability in supporting effective and acceptable reform.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: From awareness to perceived savings: the role of consumer understanding in vehicle-to-grid benefit expectations
Authors: Andrea Pellegrini, Elisabetta Cherchi, John M. Rose
Abstract: Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) has been widely promoted as a mechanism for integrating electric vehicles (EVs) into electricity markets by enabling bidirectional energy flows. While much of the existing literature focuses on technical feasibility and system-level value, comparatively less attention has been paid to how EV owners perceive the private financial benefits associated with participation. This study examines how awareness and conceptual understanding of V2G are associated with EV owners’ subjective perceptions of annual electricity bill savings. Using data from a nationwide survey of 1,794 Australian EV owners, we distinguish between awareness of V2G and correct conceptualisation of the technology. We estimate a sample-selection endogenous ordered probit model that jointly accounts for awareness and potential endogeneity in correct understanding when modelling perceived savings. Results indicate that awareness and understanding are distinct phenomena and that, after accounting for awareness and shared unobserved factors, correct conceptualisation remains strongly associated with a higher propensity to report larger perceived savings. Approximate midpoint-based summaries of the predicted ordinal distributions suggest higher perceived annual savings among respondents who correctly define V2G. At the same time, overall perceived savings remain modest, with most EV owners selecting categories consistent with incremental rather than substantial bill reductions. Significant heterogeneity emerges across segments, particularly by solar panel ownership, battery storage ownership, home charging access, and age. The findings suggest that informational frictions, subjective beliefs and incomplete understanding may shape perceived private benefits of V2G, which are likely to be relevant for future participation decisions, even in a context characterised by high residential solar uptake and widespread home charging. From a policy perspective, the results underscore the importance of clear communication, contract transparency, and targeted program design that accounts for heterogeneity across user segments in scaling V2G participation. Integrating behavioural insight into energy–transport policy may therefore be critical to realising the flexibility potential of electrified mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Quality or convenience? Behavioral evidence on how facility grade influences urban destination choice
Authors: Yang Zhou, Sicheng Wang, Chaofan Wang, Quan Yuan, Tianren Yang
Abstract: Modeling non-work activity destination choices is essential for urban transportation planning, as these activities involve greater flexibility and more complex behavioral decision-making than mandatory activities. However, existing studies often treat all facilities within the same activity category as homogeneous and have rarely examined how facility-grade heterogeneity shapes individuals’ destination preferences. To address this gap, this study develops a hierarchical location choice modeling framework that explicitly incorporates facility-grade distinctions into the destination choice process. Four common non-work activity categories—shopping, dining-out, recreation, and medical care—are analyzed, with urban facilities classified into high-grade and low-grade types. Destination choice sets are generated using fuzzy logic inference and stratified importance sampling that account for both travel distance and facility grade. Conditional logit (CL) and nested logit (NL) models are then estimated to capture alternative-specific utilities and within-grade correlations. Results show that (i) destination choices exhibit distinct decision-making logic across facility grades, with high-grade facilities usually planned for quality-seeking purposes and low-grade facilities primarily serving convenience-oriented needs; (ii) facility-grade heterogeneity significantly shapes destination choice behavior, with preferences varying across activity purposes and population groups; (iii) the nested logit results reveal correlated destination choices within facility-grade categories, highlighting the importance of accounting for within-grade substitution patterns when modeling non-work destination choices; and (iv) the effects of accessibility improvements vary across activity types, with stronger impacts observed for shopping and recreation and comparatively limited impacts for dining-out and medical-care. These findings highlight the critical role of facility-grade heterogeneity in shaping non-work travel behavior and offer new insights for demand analysis and facility planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Self-adaptive interval strategies for exact line search: Application to traffic assignment problems
Authors: Zhengyang Li, Anthony Chen
Abstract: Step size determination in optimization is often performed via line search. Interval reduction methods, such as golden-section and bisection, are widely used for exact line search but require multiple function and/or derivative evaluations at each outer iteration of the optimization algorithm (e.g., Frank–Wolfe). In this paper, we propose two simple yet effective self-adaptive interval strategies, one based on zero-order information and the other on first-order information, that adaptively determine the search interval at each iteration using step size information from the previous iteration. We integrate these strategies into the exact line search procedure commonly used in the Frank–Wolfe algorithm and apply them to three traffic assignment problems with different complexities: classical user equilibrium (UE), bi-criteria user equilibrium (BUE), and multiclass bi-criteria user equilibrium (MBUE). Numerical results demonstrate that the self-adaptive interval strategies considerably accelerate classical exact line search methods, reducing the number of function and/or derivative evaluations by up to 52%. This translates into considerable CPU time reductions when function and derivative evaluations are computationally expensive.

Title: Switching macroeconomic growth and volatility: Evidence from a mean-variance Markov-switching dynamic factor model
Authors: Catherine Doz, Laurent Ferrara, Pierre-Alain Pionnier
Abstract: As illustrated by the Great Recession, the COVID-19 pandemic and the global decline in GDP growth since the mid-2000s, economists need to account for sudden and deep recessions, shifts in macroeconomic volatility, and longer-term fluctuations in GDP growth. This paper puts forward a Mean-Variance Markov-Switching Dynamic Factor Model (MV-MS-DFM) that accounts for these stylised facts by allowing the mean and the volatility of macroeconomic variables to switch abruptly, and trend GDP growth to vary smoothly over time. We show that allowing for different volatility regimes improves the detection of turning points in the US business cycle, that the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic only led to temporary increases in volatility, and that US trend GDP growth has declined by around 1 percentage point since the early 2000s. Information criteria and marginal likelihood comparisons support our model specification. The model also provides a unified framework connecting the literature on turning-point detection to the more recent literature on Growth-at-Risk in macroeconomic forecasting. While tightening financial conditions are shown to increase the probability of falling into recession, the model can generate left-skewed density forecasts without including any financial variable in the information set. The paper finally discusses how to deal with the COVID-19 period when estimating the model.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: The long-term effects of military occupations: Evidence from post-world war II Austria
Authors: Christoph Eder, Martin Halla, Philipp Hilmbauer-Hofmarcher
Abstract: What are the long-run economic consequences of short-lived but intense institutional shocks? We study the post-World War II occupation of Austria, where the country was divided into Soviet and Western Allied zones for ten years before reunification. Using a spatial regression discontinuity design combined with a difference-in-differences approach, we show that areas initially occupied by Soviet forces remain significantly less economically developed today. These regions are less populated, host fewer and lower-paying jobs, and exhibit substantially higher rates of out-commuting than comparable areas in the former Western zones. We show that these persistent differences are driven by a large population flight triggered by the onset of the Soviet occupation, which durably shifted the spatial distribution of economic activity. This initial migration shock altered local agglomeration forces, leading to sustained regional divergence despite the restoration of a unified institutional framework. Our findings highlight how even temporary institutional shocks can have long-lasting economic effects.

Title: Routine-biased technical change, structure of employment, and cross-country income differences
Authors: Werner Peña, Christian Siegel
Abstract: We investigate links between routine-biased technical change, the structure of occupational employment, and cross-country income differences. To implement this, we combine several data sources, including national labour force surveys and the Penn World Tables. In our novel dataset spanning 92 countries, we document a negative relationship between the employment share of routine occupations and GDP per hour worked. We then conduct a development accounting exercise in which we differentiate labour inputs by occupation and allow for occupation-specific technologies. We find a systematic relationship between occupation-specific productivities and development. Labour in routine occupations tends to be much more productive in richer countries, with effective productivity in the top 25 percent being about 14 times higher than in the bottom 25 percent of countries ranked by GDP per hour worked. Cross-country gaps in routine technology alone account for about 17 percent of the 90–10 ratio of GDP per hour worked, whereas differences in abstract labour technology do not contribute to the observed GDP dispersion. Eliminating all occupations’ and capital’s technology differences would compress the GDP distribution by 32 to 40 percent.

Title: Comparative research and analysis on third-party governance based on market effects
Authors: Zuliang Lu, Junman Li, Mingsong Li, Zhihui Cao, Zhuran Xiang
Abstract: With the tightening of environmental regulations, traditional command-and-control pollution approaches have proven inadequate. Specifically, they fail to align with the incentives of polluting enterprises, relying on coercion rather than motivation, and suffer from low treatment efficiency due to insufficient technical expertise. Specifically, they fail to align with the incentives of polluting enterprises, relying on coercion rather than motivation, and suffer from low treatment efficiency due to insufficient technical expertise. While prior research highlights its potential to enhance environmental governance, empirical validation remains limited. This study applies evolutionary game theory to compare two models, investigating the efficacy of third-party institutions in regional pollution control and the impact of key system parameters. Notably, we integrate external market and consumer factors as dynamic parameters. Our findings demonstrate that third-party participation yields significantly better evolutionary outcomes. Furthermore, stakeholder strategies exhibit strong interdependence, sensitive to parameter variations. Based on this comparative analysis, we offer evidence-based policy implications for optimizing third-party governance mechanisms.

Title: Dual channel mixed frequency forecasting for carbon prices: Informer-BiLSTM deep features embedded in Grey-MIDAS framework
Authors: Qi Ding, Xinping Xiao, Lizhong Yang, Zhuang Yang, Zhiwei Xu
Abstract: As global climate governance accelerates and carbon markets become increasingly financialized, carbon prices link macro level mitigation targets with micro level firm decision making. However, mixed frequency explanatory variables and recurrent structural breaks constrain forecasting performance, leaving econometric models with limited robustness. Using carbon prices in the EU Emissions Trading System and the China Emissions Trading System and incorporating 14 explanatory variables, this study develops a dual channel, feature driven mixed frequency grey forecasting model (GMIB) that combines the Informer model and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) to handle variable heterogeneity and frequency alignment. Trend dominated variables enter the Informer model to extract global features, whereas fluctuation dominated variables enter the BiLSTM model to capture high frequency shocks; both feature sets are integrated into a grey system based mixed data sampling (MIDAS) framework (Grey-MIDAS) to strengthen mixed frequency modeling capability. GMIB is evaluated against machine learning baselines, single frequency deep learning baselines, and mixed frequency deep learning baselines, and residual bootstrap intervals are constructed to quantify uncertainty and tail risk. Empirical evidence shows that GMIB delivers the most accurate point forecasts in both markets, achieving mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) of 1.10% and 1.05%. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) indicate that the China market is anchored by energy cost trends, whereas the EU market is more sensitive to financial sentiment shocks. Overall, the framework improves carbon price discovery, supports regulatory monitoring, corporate compliance, and financial institutions' risk management, and promotes the sustainable operation of carbon trading markets.

Title: Understanding the heterogeneity of willingness to share: Ridesplitting’s adoption and usage frequency
Authors: Yite SUN, Xiaobing LIU, Yufeng ZHANG, Hua ZHONG, Xuedong YAN, Ziyou GAO
Abstract: Ridesplitting, a shared urban mobility service, is widely regarded as a promising way to alleviate the negative impacts of ride-hailing, yet its market penetration remains low. Existing studies provide limited understanding of spatiotemporal and user heterogeneity in willingness to share (WTS). To fill this gap, we conduct a questionnaire survey in Beijing and apply latent class analysis to identify user segments based on psychological factors related to ridesplitting. Binary logit model and scenario analysis are then used to examine sharing behavior and mode conversion across segments. Results show that both ridesplitting and non-ridesplitting users exhibit substantial heterogeneity in WTS. Moderately satisfied users show strong potential for more frequent use, while improving travel time reliability and cost savings can convert likely adopters into active participants. These findings inform policies and platform strategies to promote sustainable urban mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Immigration and local inflation: Evidence from US cities
Authors: Philip Barrett, Brandon Joel Tan
Abstract: We estimate the impact of inward immigration on city-level inflation in the United States. We find that doubling the rate of immigration reduces inflation by about 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points. The disinflationary effect is concentrated in goods prices. Effects are larger for working-age immigrants, with suggestive but less precise evidence of stronger disinflationary effects from less-educated immigrants, especially in services. Housing markets respond differently: immigration increases local housing prices, with the largest effects for higher-education immigrants. Our results are jointly rationalized by a simple general equilibrium model where substitutability of capital and labor varies across industries but capital is fixed in the short run.

Title: Cycling cities: Mode choice, car congestion, and urban structure
Authors: Tijl Hendrich, Hans R.A. Koster, Nicole Loumeau, Jos van Ommeren
Abstract: Cycling as a mode of commuting has gained popularity in cities worldwide. This study examines the impact of cycling on the urban spatial structure and welfare through the development of a quantitative spatial equilibrium model that incorporates mode choice and car congestion. We apply this model to the Netherlands, which is known for its extensive cycling infrastructure. Eliminating cycling increases commuting times and distances by 15% and 30%, exacerbates car congestion, and results in a significant reduction in worker welfare. We also show that removing dedicated cycleways leads to similar, although less pronounced, changes in the spatial economy.

Title: Competition and complementarity between online healthcare platform and offline hospital
Authors: Xi Yu, Jizhou Lu, Stephen Shum, Shenghao Zhang
Abstract: Motivated by the rapid expansion of online healthcare platforms, we study a healthcare system with online–offline interactions. We develop an analytical model capturing patient type uncertainty, service differentiation, heterogeneous cost structures of healthcare facilities, and patient flow across channels. This paper shows that the entry of third-party online healthcare platforms may create a diagnosis–treatment mismatch, even as they expand access to healthcare. Our study examines the competition and complementarity between online healthcare platforms and offline hospitals. We show that, under certain conditions, the online healthcare platform entry can increase the offline hospital's patient demand and profitability, leading to a win–win outcome. When the hospital's capacity cost pressure is moderate, the complementary effect dominates, improving both demand and profitability. When the hospital's capacity cost pressure is high, rising costs burden and diagnosis–treatment mismatch reduce both profitability and patient demand. When the hospital's capacity cost pressure is low, the competitive effect dominates, lowering profitability, while the impact on patient demand depends on whether cannibalization or price competition dominates.
