The empirical results show that airline relationships are multidimensional, with different patterns of similarity emerging across carrier types and network characteristics. A longitudinal analysis relative to the 2016 baseline reveals heterogeneous adjustment trajectories across airlines and indicates post-pandemic convergence in some dimensions of network organization alongside persistent differentiation in others. Overall, the proposed OT framework provides a general tool for inferring airline similarity from transport distances, assessing resilience and recovery following shocks, and examining structural change over time. The framework can also support the construction of airline peer groups for benchmarking, and the medium- to long-term monitoring of structural network recovery following major market shocks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Global airport connectivity and resilience: a data-driven approach and inverse-U relationship, 1996–2024
Authors: Yilin Zhang, Tommy Cheung, Anming Zhang
Abstract: This study analyzes the long-run evolution of global airport connectivity from 1996 to 2024 and examines how resilience to major shocks varies across the connectivity distribution. Using an extended Global Airport Connectivity Index (GACI) panel covering 101,049 airport–year observations and 5428 airports, it documents steady expansion punctuated by crises, a redistribution of connectivity across continents, and an increasingly multipolar hub hierarchy. The paper then develops a reproducible, multi-crisis resilience index with three components: depth (magnitude of loss), speed (pace of recovery), and adaptability (post-shock upgrading in the global hierarchy). The index aggregates realized airport performance across multiple major shocks, applies empirical-Bayes regularization to improve comparability across airports with uneven shock histories, and filters micro-fluctuations below 1% to reduce noise. Relating resilience to connectivity uncovers a consistent inverse-U relationship: resilience increases with connectivity up to a mid-scale range and declines among the most globally connected hubs. This pattern is consistent with greater exposure to synchronized shocks and scale-related operational frictions, although the analysis identifies the relationship rather than its underlying mechanisms. Robustness checks include alternative component weightings, pre-COVID estimates, crisis-specific recovery horizons, alternative adaptability definitions, region-specific COVID timing, an alternative fixed-scale connectivity construction, and non-overlapping crisis windows. These checks confirm the stability of the pattern. By embedding airport-level recovery behaviour in a three-decade network context, the GACI–resilience framework provides a systematic basis for comparing hub types and benchmarking realized resilience, and for informing route-development, infrastructure-planning, and policy strategies during pandemics, geopolitical disruptions, and other major shocks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The economic gains from breaking boundaries: Reformulating index insurance zones to maximize lower tail dependence
Authors: Enrique Estefania-Salazar, Michael R. Carter, Eva Iglesias, Álvaro Escribano
Abstract: Index insurance intended to help low-wealth households manage risk is hampered by downside basis risk, meaning that the insured suffers a loss, but the insurance index fails to signal a loss. Existing index insurance contracts use statistically ad hoc administrative boundaries to demarcate insurance zones. We develop an algorithm that creates zones that maximize lower tail dependence amongst individual units included in each zone. Breaking boundaries in this way minimizes basis risk. Using data from a satellite-based index insurance program in Kenya, we show that replacing administrative with optimized zones can as much as triple the value of insurance using an expected utility-based metric of insurance quality.

Title: Picking winners: Local land allocation and bottom-up industrial policy in China
Authors: Wenjia Tian, Zhi Wang, Qinghua Zhang
Abstract: This study examines the industrial preferences of local governments in China through the lens of land allocation. We analyze industrial land transactions from 2007 to 2019, a period marked by both expanding industrial policy and intensifying land market competition. Using a border discontinuity design that compares land transactions near county borders, we separate local government preferences from firm demand. We find systematic industrial favoritism: localities offer deeper price discounts to industries aligned with their existing specialization. This favoritism persists over time, is more pronounced in industries with substantial unrealized agglomeration potential, and is stronger in regions with well-developed market institutions. We further show that local governments comply with upper-level industrial policy only when it aligns with their own specialization. Together, these findings point to a bottom-up process in which local governments use land allocation to attract firms that reinforce local industrial strengths through agglomeration spillovers.

Title: Window-dressing in environmental regulation: Short-term incentives and temporary abatement
Authors: Zhengwen Liu, Hong Ma, Fangrui Zhang
Abstract: We study how short-term political incentives affect firms’ compliance with environmental regulation. In China, city mayors face a sharp drop in promotion probability after age 57, creating a transitory enforcement window. Using a regression discontinuity design, we find that firms governed by promotion-eligible mayors reduce sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) emissions substantially more than under the same mayors after the threshold. These reductions are concentrated among firms without end-of-pipe abatement equipment and are driven by temporary cuts in operating hours and output rather than technological upgrades. We further document that government subsidies increase during the promotion window and are disproportionately directed to unequipped firms that curtail production, consistent with coordinated short-run compliance. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that these transitory incentives account for 5.2% of the national SO 2 decline during the Eleventh Five-Year Plan, but at a cost of 0.9% of total industrial output. We develop a dynamic model of firm compliance showing that such short-lived incentives induce inefficient output-based responses. Our findings highlight the limits of episodic regulatory pressure.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Correction: Application of a disaster related emergency response model to a food bank network
Authors: Faith Idoko, Lauren Davis, Chrysafis Vogiatzis
Abstract: While disaster management and preparedness has seen significant developments in both theory and practice in recent years, there is still a shortage of operations research and decision science strategies specifically for food banks and their operations. This manuscript aims to fill that void by investigating how a disaster-related emergency response model can be used to improve food bank preparedness and decision-making for food bank operations during disasters. Using realistic projections of food bank operations, this study evaluates various strategies to address unmet demand and minimize operational costs across different scenarios that depict the network’s potential state following a disaster. A framework is designed to facilitate effective decision-making by considering different levels of risk tolerance. The implementation of mobile pantries is highlighted as an effective way to meet demand with minimal increases in operational costs when the network is disrupted. This framework provides food bank managers with an array of possible solution approaches, enabling them to make optimal decisions based on their specific objectives.

Title: Bounded rationality, monetary policy, and the scars of supply shocks
Authors: Dario Bonciani, Frantisek Masek, Paolo Nanni, Giulio Tarquini
Abstract: Bounded rationality reshapes monetary-policy trade-offs in response to supply shocks in a New Keynesian model with endogenous growth. A negative supply shock depresses innovation and future productivity, which gives rise to long-run scarring and persistent inflationary pressures. Under rational expectations, tighter monetary policy eases the initial rise in inflation but amplifies the fall in demand, innovation, and productivity. Under bounded rationality, households underreact to future income losses. This weakens the negative wealth effect and mitigates the decline in demand and growth. As a result, tighter monetary policy can contain inflation without generating large scarring effects.

Title: Do you remember? Prosocial behavior declines in memory-based decisions
Authors: Sebastian Olschewski
Abstract: Many economic decisions affect other stakeholders, yet information about these consequences is often not directly available at the moment of choice and must instead be recalled from memory. Here, three studies examine how memory processes shape social behavior and whether their behavioral effects are better explained by motivated memory or rational accounts of memory allocation. In Study 1, participants made binary dictator-game decisions in which the consequences for themselves and another player were represented by pictures whose monetary outcomes had to be learned and later recalled from memory. Compared with the control condition in which all outcome information was available on the decision screen, participants chose less prosocially when decisions relied on memory. Studies 2 and 3 showed that prosocial choice in memory-based dictator games did not reliably increase either when strategic encoding of outcomes was made impossible or when accurate recall was monetarily incentivized. A structural model with a social utility function indicates that memory-based decisions reduce the weight placed on the other player’s outcome in unequal allocations that are advantageous to the dictator. Across choices, recall patterns, structural modeling, and individual differences, the results are most consistent with motivated forgetting during decision making: participants appear to selectively fail to retrieve information about social consequences when this information would make selfish choices harder to justify. These findings suggest that making consequences for other stakeholders salient at the moment of choice can promote socially beneficial behavior.

Title: Train scheduling with variable running speeds and multiple train compositions
Authors: Hanchuan Pan, Siqi Guo, Fan Xiao, Wei Liu, Zhe Liang
Abstract: In recent years, frequent small-scale emergencies, such as extreme weather events, have often led to significant passenger flow fluctuations in metro systems. To better accommodate this fluctuated demand, the operators are required to design irregular timetables where both train arrival/departure times at each station and composition modes for each train service vary dynamically. Accordingly, this paper investigates an integrated train scheduling problem that simultaneously addresses (1) the train running speed optimization strategy that seeks to find the best train trajectories for a series of trains, and (2) the multiple train compositions optimization strategy that provides sufficient transport capacity with the least rolling stock units. To this end, we propose a novel nonlinear mixed integer optimization model for minimizing the total costs of energy consumption and service quality for passengers, where the train running speed is innovatively treated as a decision variable. A conic reformulation technique is proposed, such that the nonlinear parts of the developed model can be reformulated as second-order cone constraints, which can be efficiently handled by commercial solvers. Two computational experiments involving a relatively small- and large-sized cases derived from the subway line 17 in Shanghai are tested to assess the quality of our method. The results suggest that this approach can be used by operators to derive a high-quality energy-efficient train timetable.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Truck-drone collaborative routing with flexible cross-truck operations and slot constraints
Authors: Hang Fan, Zhuxi Zhang, Tong Guo, Wenbo Du, Xuechen Gu, Tao Song, Defu Lin
Abstract: Truck-drone collaborative routing faces critical operational bottlenecks in realistic logistics scenarios due to strict return constraints and limited physical recovery slots. We address these challenges by proposing a novel Mixed-Integer Linear Programming model for the Flexible Assignment Vehicle Routing Problem with Drones and Slot Constraints (FA-VRPDSC). By decoupling drones from specific launch vehicles, the model enables flexible cross-truck operations and dynamic task assignments across the entire fleet under strict slot capacity limits. To efficiently solve this complex combinatorial problem, we develop a tailored Memetic Algorithm with Adaptive Large Neighborhood Perturbation (MA-ALNP). The algorithm leverages a dual-chain representation to jointly encode routing sequences and collaboration states. To navigate the tightly coupled temporal and spatial constraints, we integrate specialized repair operators and an adaptive destroy-and-repair shaking mechanism that effectively prevents premature convergence. Computational results confirm the algorithm’s exact optimality on small instances and its structural superiority on large-scale benchmarks, significantly outperforming advanced heuristics in minimizing total makespan. Our sensitivity analysis ultimately highlights that extended drone endurance is pivotal for activating flexible cross-truck docking and maximizing fleet coordination.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Experimental study on low-carbon supply chain management using symbolic award
Authors: Junjun Liu, Lifang Gao, Ning Li
Abstract: Symbolic awards, such as low-carbon supplier certification, actively motivate suppliers to strengthen their carbon reduction initiatives and advance sustainable supply chain management. Yet, when low-carbon suppliers remain scarce, these awards intensify buyer competition and raise the costs of maintaining supplier relationships. Notably, several suppliers leverage awards to build reputations that improve their bargaining power, creating strategic dilemmas around public disclosure. This study develops a two-stage game model and tests its predictions through controlled experiments to examine how alternative award formats influence supplier and buyer outcomes. Our results show that a symbolic award significantly encourages suppliers to reduce emissions and improve buyers’ bottom lines. However, award format shapes buyer utility in critical ways: public awards compel buyers to invest more in retaining suppliers, while private awards deliver greater financial value to buyers. In markets with few low-carbon suppliers, buyers often need to allocate more resources to relationship management, while suppliers may resist private incentives if they perceive reputational drawbacks. These findings highlight the need for carefully designed disclosure strategies to balance costs and benefits for both sides, thereby fostering more effective and sustainable supply chains.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Integrating minimum cost flow and capacitated location in global supply chains under uncertainty
Authors: Yi Zhang, Hari Nandan Nath, Stefan Nickel
Abstract: Modern supply chain networks face significant challenges in balancing operational efficiency and resilience under diverse real-world uncertainties such as demand fluctuations and disruptions. To address these complexities, this study proposes an Integrated Capacitated Facility Location and Minimum Cost Flow Problem under Multi-Uncertainty (ICLMF-MU). The integrated multi-objective optimization model simultaneously optimizes total cost, service utility, and total risk while accounting for unmet demands and disruptions in supply chain network design. To deal with the NP-hardness of the problem, we propose an enhanced hybrid non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II). A novel bi-level evaluation strategy couples an exact linear programming (LP) solver to maintain flow balance with a greedy heuristic as a fallback mechanism. Through a three-stage benchmarking process, the algorithm demonstrates strong convergence and consistent performance. A large-scale numerical study (100 nodes) evaluates performance under diverse global trade environments, contrasting cost-sensitive goods against strategic resources prone to export controls. Pareto frontier trade-off analysis identifies a distinct Criticality Premium, confirming that strategic sectors require a substantially greater investment to withstand sanctions compared to commercial scenarios. Furthermore, regret analysis exposes a Robustness Paradox: the min-risk strategy exhibits the highest operational regret and lowest real-world resilience by limiting network scope. In contrast, the max-utility and balanced strategies demonstrate superior robustness. Sensitivity analysis confirms this implicit redundancy provides the structural capacity needed to absorb large demand surges, with the medical strategy demonstrating superior overall resilience under extreme demand. These findings imply that for critical supplies, true robustness is an emergent property of sufficient capacity investment rather than the optimization of theoretical risk indicators alone, offering guidance for designing resilient networks in an unstable global trade landscape.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Effective policies and behavioral adaptations toward climate-neutral mobility: Introduction to the special issue
Authors: Feixiong Liao, Yacan Wang, Maarten Kroesen, Huiyu Zhou, Tim Schwanen
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: When safety is not free: mitigating the transportation pink tax through safety-oriented policy interventions
Authors: Caiyin Dong, Chenyang Wu, Hyungchul Chung, Sisi Jian, Tiantian Chen
Abstract: Influenced by sociocultural norms and ongoing safety shortcomings in urban transportation systems, women frequently perceive a higher personal risk during routine travel. Building on the concept of the “pink tax” in consumer markets, this study introduces the notion of a transportation pink tax as a gendered safety-compensation burden, the additional expected monetary cost that women incur when safety concerns prompt compensatory behaviors, such as choosing more expensive travel modes. Using a stated preference (SP) experiment conducted in Shanghai (N = 785; 391 females and 394 males), we examine mode choice among metro, ride-hailing, and autonomous robotaxi services. Both multinomial and mixed logit models are employed to estimate gender-differentiated preferences, derive willingness-to-pay (WTP) for safety-related attributes, and account for unobserved heterogeneity. The results indicate that women place significantly higher marginal utility on safety-enhancing features, including female ride-hailing drivers, advanced in-vehicle security systems, and improved lighting in robotaxi access segments, reflecting a greater safety-compensation premium in their utility functions. For example, women's WTP for advanced security measures in robotaxi services exceeds that of men by 3.90, 26.05, and 27.86 CNY for short-, medium-, and long-distance trips, respectively. Importantly, we show that this marginal safety premium translates into a tangible cost burden when women shift toward higher-cost modes under unsafe conditions. Policy scenario simulations indicate that enhancing metro safety, through measures such as shorter walking distances, upgraded in-carriage CCTV, additional security staff patrols, and improved lighting, could raise women's metro usage and reduce their monthly travel expenditures by approximately 26–121 CNY, thereby alleviating the gendered safety-compensation burden. These results suggest that transportation gender inequities arise not from inherent preference differences, but from structural safety externalities that disproportionately impact women. Implementing safety-by-design principles in public transit and emerging autonomous mobility services can therefore lower gendered cost burdens and foster more equitable urban mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Can community policing improve police-community relations in a low-income country setting?
Authors: Robert A. Blair, Guy Grossman, Anna M. Wilke
Abstract: Community-oriented policing (COP) is one of the most widely touted mechanisms for building bridges between police forces and the communities they serve. But evidence on the effectiveness of COP is surprisingly scant. We present results from one of the first randomized controlled trials to evaluate the impact of COP in the Global South. The COP initiative we study was locally designed and funded by the Ugandan government. Contrary to our expectations, we find no evidence that the program reduced crime, enhanced citizens’ perceptions of safety, improved their attitudes towards the police, increased crime reporting, or strengthened other norms of citizen cooperation with the police. Nor do we find evidence that the program generated greater empathy or accountability among participating police officers themselves. We explore a variety of potential explanations for these null results, including both supply-side factors (e.g., resource constraints within the Ugandan police force) and demand-side factors (e.g., citizens’ fear of engaging with the police). We find no evidence that overcoming these obstacles would make COP more effective. Taken together, our findings point to potential limitations of COP in low-income countries.

Title: Assessing the sensitivity of poverty to inequality: A method and an application to Brazil, 1981–2022
Authors: Florent Bresson
Abstract: This paper proposes an analytical approach to assess the sensitivity of poverty to inequality variations. It introduces a general transform of the Lorenz curve that delivers point Gini elasticities of poverty corresponding to observed distributional changes. This overcomes the limitations of existing methods, due to reliance on rigid and inadequate redistribution processes or dependence on the magnitude of inequality changes. The proposed framework enables pro-poorness benchmarking via extremely regressive and progressive counterfactual redistribution scenarios. A Changes-in-Changes construction is also considered for comparisons across time or space while holding the initial income distribution fixed. Finally, the paper investigates the relationship between inequality changes and the incidence, intensity, and inequality dimensions of poverty. An empirical illustration for Brazil (1981–2022) shows that an increasing share of poverty reduction was associated with inequality variations; inequality fell and poverty declined sharply, notably between 2003 and 2014. Moreover, irrespective of initial conditions, the sensitivity of poverty to inequality increased over the four decades. Yet, distributional change remained below pro-poor benchmark frontiers, reflecting insufficient relative gains for the worst-off.

Title: The skill premium across countries in the era of industrial robots and artificial intelligence
Authors: Marcos J. Ribeiro, Klaus Prettner
Abstract: How do new technologies affect economic growth and the skill premium? To answer this question, we analyze the impacts of industrial robots and artificial intelligence (AI) across 52 countries using counterfactual simulations. In so doing, we simulate the nested CES production function framework of Bloom et al. (2025) with low-skilled workers, high-skilled workers, traditional capital, robots, and AI. Our contribution lies in documenting substantial heterogeneity across income groups: the inequality-increasing effect of robots and the inequality-reducing effect of AI are particularly strong in high-income countries, while they are less pronounced among upper-middle and lower-middle income countries. In addition, we show that both technologies boost economic growth. In terms of policy recommendations, our framework suggests i) balanced investment in both types of automation technologies to increase economic growth while keeping wage inequality subdued, and ii) investments in education and skill-upgrading to mitigate negative effects of robot use on wage inequality.

Title: How does the availability of alternative coping strategies influence households’ reliance on charcoal as a coping strategy?
Authors: Protensia Hadunka, Vinicius Okada Da Silva
Abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa experiences some of the world's highest deforestation rates, partly because households turn to charcoal production when agricultural shocks reduce farm income. Yet the extent to which alternative coping strategies can offset this pressure on forests remains unclear. This study examines how access to other livelihoods shapes household responses to the first appearance of the Fall Armyworm (FAW) in Zambia. Using four years of household panel data and exploiting spatial variation in FAW intensity, we estimate the causal effects of FAW on charcoal production and local deforestation. We find that low, medium, and severe FAW exposure raise the likelihood of charcoal production by 4.8, 8.6, and 12.3 percentage points, respectively, and are associated with increases in surrounding deforestation of approximately 7.3%, 18.9%, and 26.2%, respectively. However, these effects are substantially smaller among households that diversify crops and use pesticides. In contrast, households engaged in off-farm work are more likely to participate in charcoal production. Our findings show that the environmental consequences of agricultural shocks depend critically on the availability of alternative coping strategies, highlighting the importance of policies that expand non-forest-based livelihood options.

Title: Staying in power: how does political continuity shape debt?
Authors: Jaime Bonet-Morón, Jhorland Ayala-García, Jorge Guerra-España
Abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between political continuity and public municipal debt in Colombia, highlighting how political cycles influence fiscal behavior at the subnational level. Unlike national cycles, local political dynamics, marked by consecutive electoral victories of the same party, significantly impact fiscal policy and debt accumulation. Using a Kink Regression Discontinuity design, we explore the effects of these electoral outcomes on public financial debt. Our findings reveal that municipalities governed by the same party or coalition across successive elections exhibit a 0.25% increase in debt levels for every percentage point increase in their election win margin. This trend becomes more pronounced over time, with debt levels peaking in election years. The robustness of our results is confirmed through various bandwidths and placebo tests, which include random shuffling of electoral outcomes and reassignment of electoral results from different years. Our study contributes to the understanding of how political stability or continuity can shape fiscal outcomes at the regional level, a topic that has received limited attention in the political economy literature.

Title: From care-takers to breadwinners? Gendered livelihoods’ dynamics under climate change: Implications for resilient livelihood planning
Authors: Francis Dakyaga, Fuseini Waah Salifu, Samuel Z. Bonye, Emmauel K. Derbile
Abstract: Gender and climate change scholars have demonstrated how gendered livelihood (re)produces unequal vulnerabilities between men and women shaped by differentiated adaptive capacities. In response, human-nature interaction scholars underscore the reciprocal relationship between human beings and the environment by highlighting their mutual agency and the ability of environmental change to shape the formation and transformation of gendered livelihoods. Inspired by the human-nature interaction studies, we explore how communities’ responses, coping and adapting to climate change, shape the formation and transformation of gendered livelihood strategies. Drawing on the gendered lens, we explored the everyday lived experiences of rural communities under climate change; analysed gendered livelihood formation (resource access, control and power relations); examined gendered livelihood transformation under climate change; and offered reflections on the implications for resilient livelihood planning. The study found that gendered livelihood practices are transforming as communities’ respond to climate change. Women were found engaged in farming, out-migration, livestock and poultry rearing, complementary but contradictory to livelihood strategies perceived as feminine. The constellation of livelihood activities and strategies practised by women enhanced their resilience capacities to climate change but increased their domestic and economic burdens through simultaneous engagement in productive and reproductive roles. Men were perceived as more vulnerable in adapting their livelihoods to climate change. We argue that policy planning interventions toward rural livelihood enhancement should focus on improving the productive adaptive capacities of both men and women towards fostering resilient livelihoods.

Title: The price of progress: Causal evidence on the health, economic, and gendered costs of construction-driven air pollution
Authors: Shaokang Xu, Yeyi Liu, Qiuyun Zhao
Abstract: This study examines the health and welfare costs of construction-driven air pollution in a rapidly urbanizing context. We exploit the predictable, nationwide cessation of construction during China's Spring Festival holiday, combined with cross-city variation in construction intensity, as a quasi-natural experiment identifying the causal effect of construction on air quality and mortality. Using city-level panel data from the China National Environmental Monitoring Centre matched with official construction statistics, we show that a 10,000-square-meter increase in annual construction area widens the Air Quality Index (AQI) gap between active-construction and holiday-shutdown periods by 0.772 points, raising annual respiratory and cardiovascular mortality rates by 0.173 and 0.737 per 100,000 inhabitants, respectively. These health costs fall disproportionately on women. We propose and test a gendered time–space exposure mechanism: socially structured differences in caregiving responsibilities and labor force participation increase women's daytime exposure to localized construction pollution. Consistent with this mechanism, the female mortality effect is larger in cities with heavier childcare burdens and lower female labor force participation. We estimate annual welfare losses of $84.32 billion, equivalent to a gross health externality of $9.01 per square meter of annual construction. We interpret these estimates as pricing an urban-development externality, pointing to targeted mitigation through dust control, work scheduling, and residential-area protection.

Title: Evaluating sensitivity of distributionally robust optimization models
Authors: Yi Zhao, Jun Li, Shuming Wang
Abstract: This paper develops a sensitivity computation framework for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) models with event-wise ambiguity set, quantifying how the worst-case loss responds to perturbations of the ambiguity-set parameters, including mean bounds, dispersion radii, and scenario probabilities. This framework covers many commonly-used loss functions and dispersion measures and therefore accommodates extensive well-studied DRO applications in the operations management community such as portfolio optimization and chance-constrained program. We first exploit the decomposable structure of the event-wise ambiguity set and derive a scenario-wise dual reformulation of the worst-case loss. We then establish the compactness of the optimal dual solution set for two common loss functions. Leveraging this dual reformulation together with the compactness of the optimal dual set, we next derive directional derivative of the worst-case loss and derive its computationally tractable formula, obtained by solving a small convex optimization subproblem. To achieve meaningful comparisons across heterogeneous parameters, we introduce scenario-wise and globally averaged normalized sensitivity indices that convert the directional derivatives into dimensionless, elasticity-like measures. Furthermore, we establish a rigorous first-order expansion of the worst-case loss under arbitrary parameter perturbations. Finally, we validate the practical efficacy of our framework through extensive numerical experiments on a redundancy allocation problem, demonstrating how the sensitivity map identifies critical ambiguity-set parameters, and how the choice of dispersion measure affects robustness to data outliers.

Title: Task assignment and multi-AGV collision-free path planning considering integrated picking and replenishment in robotic mobile fulfillment systems
Authors: Xuefang Han, Kunpeng Li, P.N. Ram Kumar
Abstract: Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) are essential to the logistics frameworks within contemporary e-commerce warehouses. These systems involve three primary aspects of decision-making: rack-to-AGV assignment, AGV path planning, and conflict mediation for multiple AGVs. While substantial research has been dedicated to these elements in isolation, comprehensive integrated studies addressing the problem holistically are still relatively few. This study introduces a co-optimization problem for task assignment and global path planning for multiple AGVs in RMFS, effectively integrating dispatching, conflict-free routing, and scheduling of these vehicles. We formulate this problem as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model, aimed at minimizing the total operational time of AGVs and the maximum picking completion time. Given that the problem is NP-hard, efficiently solving the MILP model for realistic-scale instances presents significant challenges. To address this issue, we developed a two-echelon K-Means and an enhanced conflict-based search algorithm. This approach allocates racks to AGVs using the K-Means algorithm while planning conflict-free paths for AGVs through an enhanced conflict-based search method. Furthermore, we rigorously analyze key structural properties of the problem, revealing several theoretically grounded properties embedded within the algorithm’s logic. To ensure high-quality lower bounds, we propose a relaxation model that does not involve planning paths for AGVs. Our experimental results indicate that: (i) our algorithm achieves solutions with minimal optimality gaps compared to the high-quality lower bounds developed; (ii) it outperforms existing benchmark algorithms in terms of solution quality and demonstrates superior computational efficiency; and (iii) the proposed properties significantly enhance the algorithm’s performance. In conclusion, this paper presents a robust and tailored approach to RMFS, providing valuable managerial insights to empower warehouse operators in their decision-making processes.

Title: Market size, trading frictions, and selling pressure in experimental over-the-counter asset markets
Authors: Shuze Ding
Abstract: This paper investigates market outcomes and trading behavior in experimental over-the-counter (OTC) asset markets. By reducing market size from 9 to 4 participants, the experiment induces changes in trading frictions and selling pressure that produce distinct effects at both the market and individual levels. The results show the emergence of positive price bubbles in both treatments, even though the fundamental value remains constant. The findings further demonstrate that the lower traded prices and narrower bid-ask spreads observed in smaller OTC markets are largely attributable to the decrease in ask prices. This pattern can be interpreted as a consequence of the increased difficulty sellers face in executing trades within a smaller OTC market, where fewer potential buyers heighten overall trading frictions and amplify selling pressure. Consequently, sellers lower their ask prices to complete transactions.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Editorial Board
Stochastic sequential screening
Authors: Hao Li, Xianwen Shi
Abstract: We study a sequential screening model with discrete ex ante types and continuously distributed ex post values. The approach — solving a relaxed problem by pointwise maximization and focusing on deterministic cutoffs — relies on strong regularity conditions and can fail when they are violated. We develop an alternative method that retains local incentive constraints, allowing deterministic and stochastic mechanisms, and derive surplus-to-slack ratio tests that identify each case. We propose the weak alignment condition, a strengthening of first-order stochastic dominance that guarantees stochastic allocations respect global incentive constraints, and the strong alignment condition, under which the gap between deterministic and stochastic conditions closes. We extend the analysis to a continuum of types and solve for optimal mechanisms in the three-type case under additional shape restrictions on the surplus-to-slack ratios. Our results show that randomization can be essential and tractable in optimal dynamic mechanisms when regularity fails.

Title: Impacts of speed limits on emissions, energy consumption and traffic efficiency
Authors: Shi-Teng Zheng, Junfang Tian, Rui Jiang, Bin Jia, Ying-En Ge
Abstract: A field experiment is conducted to investigate operational benefits of speed-limit control in platooning traffic, where the leading vehicle travels at a constant cruise speed while an additional speed-limit control is imposed on following vehicles. First, the effects of speed limits on traffic oscillation dynamics and traffic flow performance are analyzed. Results indicate that restricting the maximum speed of vehicles can stabilize traffic flow, reduce oscillation frequency, and lower emissions and energy consumption (EEC), but may reduce traffic throughput due to an increase in platoon length. A simulation framework is then developed to extend this investigation to broader speed levels and bottleneck scenarios. The results show that speed-limit control should vary with cruising speed to balance EEC and traffic efficiency, and that the proposed solutions apply to traffic management strategies. These findings enrich our understanding of traffic dynamics under speed-limit control strategies and provide practical insights for their real-world implementation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Development of regional heavy-duty vehicle driving cycles based on optimized Markova chain
Authors: Yitao Shen, Peng Guan, Shuojin Ren, Zheyu Wang, Sen Chen, Xiao Ma, Jianfu Zhao, Shijin Shuai
Abstract: Driving cycles are essential for vehicle energy and emission standards, but standard cycles often overlook regional variations. This study proposes a novel framework for constructing representative driving cycles for heavy-duty vehicles by optimizing a Markov chain with a hybrid Multi-Population Genetic Algorithm and Wavelet Threshold Denoising (hMPGA-WTD). The methodology involves: (1) spectral clustering of 1.27 million telematics data points to identify operational scenarios; (2) generating scenario-specific cycles using a two-dimensional Markov chain; and (3) enhancing driving cycle fidelity with hMPGA-WTD to reduce feature distortions. The method achieves a mean relative error of 4.61% across key parameters, with velocity standard deviation error below 1%. It outperforms micro-trip concatenation and conventional Markov approaches. Fuel consumption is validated via real-world and chassis dynamometer tests under identical loads, showing a 4.26% deviation, better than the 7.71% under CHTC-TT. The framework offers a robust basis for efficiency assessment and standard development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Slow and steady wins the race: How autonomy facilitates long-haul truck electrification
Authors: Anthony Wiskich
Abstract: This paper examines how autonomy affects the competitiveness and operations of battery-electric long-haul trucks. We model fleet operations between Sydney and Melbourne—Australia’s busiest long-haul corridor—using a parameterised cost-minimisation framework. By lowering travel-time costs, autonomy leads to slower optimal speeds and reduced energy use. This enables smaller, lighter battery packs or reduces the number of charging stops en route, lowering total costs. Autonomy thus enhances the economic case for battery-electric trucks, improving their cost competitiveness relative to diesel trucks commensurate with an AUS$34/kWh reduction in battery pack price (ranging from about AUS$10 to AUS$75/kWh across sensitivities).
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Strategic adoption of additive manufacturing in edible product supply chains: a resource-based view on sustainability
Authors: Wenqi Li, Banu Yetkin Ekren, Emel Aktas
Affiliations: Cranfield University School of Management, , Cranfield; Yasar University Department of Industrial Engineering, , Izmir, , and School of Management, Cranfield University, Cranfield, UK
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how the strategic value of additive manufacturing (AM) is created in edible product supply chains, using the resource-based view (RBV) as a theoretical lens. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on 29 semi-structured interviews with experts from the food, pharmaceutical and AM sectors, this research refines an initial, literature-based conceptual model and develops an empirically grounded framework. Findings AM’s VRIN attributes are necessary but not sufficient for strategic value; value depends on deployment within supply chain configurations. Three pathways are identified: supply chain transformation, product innovation and operational improvement. SMEs integrate AM strategically, while large incumbents often contain it within R&D. Sustainability outcomes remain conditional on economic viability, which acts as a gatekeeper for environmental and social value. Practical implications The framework offers decision guidance for practitioners: SMEs are shown the organisational prerequisites for pursuing supply chain transformation through AM, while large firms are given concrete signals for when to migrate AM from R&D into core operations. Policy levers for lowering adoption barriers are also identified. Originality/value This study extends the RBV by revealing that resources generate competitive advantage through multiple independent pathways, and that organisational context determines resource strategic status, not merely moderating effectiveness but fundamentally shaping whether resources function strategically or operationally. It provides the first interview-based evidence of these dynamics in the previously underexamined context of edible product supply chains.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Tabu search for proactive multi-skilled resource-constrained project scheduling problem
Authors: Yong Ma, Zhengwen He, Nengmin Wang, Erik Demeulemeester
Affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong University; KU Leuven

Title: AI and blockchain-enabled optimising information disclosure in live-streaming supply chains
Authors: Yu Tian, Yuting Meng, Daoping Wang, Liukai Wang
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing

Title: Rail vehicle assembly job shop scheduling via hierarchical multi-agent deep reinforcement learning
Authors: Peng Guo, Haichao Shi, Xiangheng Meng, Feng Chu, Jianbin Xin
Affiliations: Southwest Jiaotong University; Univ-Évry, Université Paris-Saclay; Zhengzhou University

Title: How to match rescue teams to disaster zones under uncertainty? An evidential two-sided matching framework
Authors: Anlin Song, Liguo Fei, Tao Li, Pengyu Jiang
Affiliations: Shandong University
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The paradox of strategic altruistic behaviour in a low carbon supply chain
Authors: Yu Xia, Xu Chen, Xiaojun Wang
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Chongqing Jiaotong University; School of Economics and Management, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Birmingham Business School, University of Birmingham
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Reinforcement Learning for decision support in defense and security: A systematic review
Authors: Maarten P. D. Schadd, David S. Berman, Carolyn Chen, Mika Cohen, John Dorsch, Alexander Gegov, Maximilian Moll, Oliver Rose, Anna Rösner, Kalle Saastamoinen, Thomas Schiller, Andreas Strand, Lauri Vasankari, Mark Rempel
Abstract: Sequential decision making with imperfect knowledge of the environment and adversary lies at the heart of defense and security. As such, contemporary reinforcement learning methods which are well adapted to these sorts of problems have the potential to provide the key tools to support decision makers in a military context. This paper presents a literature review of reinforcement learning for decision support in a defense context with a focus on recent work produced by NATO member states. To aid the reader, we provide the prerequisite background in military decision making; decision support systems in general; reinforcement learning basics; simulation; and explainability. Through a systematic review of the literature and using tools such as UMAP, we construct the research landscape and study the emergent trends and research gaps that are present. This allows us to examine the challenges for exploiting this work in reality and finally, we look to the future and how these challenges can be overcome.

Title: Reliability optimization of tethered high-altitude platform systems through hysteresis-controlled battery management
Authors: Arya P.S., Manikandan Rangaswamy
Abstract: This paper develops a stochastic framework for analyzing reliability and cost optimization in tethered High-Altitude Platform Systems (tHAPS) through integrated battery repair and replenishment strategies. The system is modeled as a k -out-of- n : G , WARM configuration with identical and independent battery units, where failure, repair, and replenishment dynamics are governed by a continuous-time Markov chain. Three distinct operational policies are proposed to capture the interaction between repair and replenishment decisions: repair-priority, replenishment-priority, and coordinated strategies. For each model, steady-state probabilities are explicitly derived, and key performance measures are obtained to evaluate system reliability and operational efficiency. A cost optimization problem is formulated with threshold-based control parameters, and the global optimal solution is determined using an exhaustive search over the finite decision space. The analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off between reliability and operational cost, driven by repair, replenishment, and holding mechanisms. Numerical experiments and sensitivity analysis using the Morris method are conducted to compare the models and assess the impact of system parameters. The results demonstrate that coordinated repair–replenishment strategies can significantly improve system performance while minimizing cost, providing actionable insights for optimal battery management in tHAPS operations. The proposed framework also opens avenues for future research in extending the model to non-Markovian dynamics, dependent failure structures, and more general optimization schemes under realistic operational constraints.

Title: Unequal hiring wages and their impact on the gender pay gap
Authors: Tho Pham, Daniel Schaefer, Carl Singleton
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Related Studies University of York York UK; Department of Economics Johannes Kepler University Linz Linz Austria; Economics Division Stirling Business School University of Stirling Stirling UK
Abstract: Abstract Payroll data from Great Britain reveal that men are paid more than women upon entry into firms. Although this hiring wage gap has narrowed over the past two decades, it still accounts for over two‐thirds of the steady‐state gender pay gap—the wage gap that would eventually prevail under constant employment levels. A significant part of this hiring wage gap is not explained by men and women working in different firms and occupations. Even when hiring men and women into the same job, there remains an unexplained hiring wage gap that favors men by 2.4 log points.

Title: Farmers' preferences for the design of an agglomeration bonus in the context of peatland restoration
Authors: Nils L. Langanke, Michael H. Grunenberg, Uwe Latacz-Lohmann
Abstract: This paper investigates how the design of an agglomeration bonus influences farmers’ participation in a stylised peatland restoration scheme. Results from a discrete choice experiment with 110 farmers in Germany indicate that the bonus has only limited influence compared to land-use restrictions. In the mixed logit and latent class estimations the bonus is statistically insignificant and mostly ignored in the decision-making process. Only when preferences are adjusted for attribute non-attendance does the bonus enhance willingness to participate and the scheme’s cost-effectiveness. Overall, voluntary schemes appear insufficient for ambitious peatland restoration goals, suggesting a need to complement incentives with regulatory measures.

Title: Environmental conditions and the conversion of economic and relational resources into subjective well-being in China
Authors: Mengdie Ruan
Abstract: Environmental conditions shape the conditions under which human well-being is produced, yet limited attention has been paid to how ecological conditions influence the conversion of economic resources (household income) and relational resources (community social trust) into subjective well-being. Drawing on the capability approach, this study conceptualizes environmental quality as a contextual conversion factor through which resources are translated into well-being. Using five waves of the China Family Panel Studies and individual fixed-effects models, the analysis examines how the well-being returns to income and social trust vary across pollution conditions in contemporary China. The results show that the well-being returns to income and social trust vary systematically across pollution conditions. Social trust is positively associated with life satisfaction, whereas income exhibits comparatively limited well-being returns. Under moderate pollution, both resources exhibit their strongest associations with life satisfaction, with social trust contributing more strongly than income. By contrast, neither association remains statistically significant under either low or high pollution, suggesting that well-being returns are strongest under moderate environmental stress. The findings suggest that environmental conditions matter less through their average association with subjective well-being than through their role as contextual conversion factors linked to differences in the well-being returns to material and relational resources. The study contributes to ecological economics by showing that environmental conditions are associated with differences in both the well-being returns to material and relational resources and their relative importance for subjective well-being.

Title: Editorial Board
Do Ryder Cup captains randomize? Evidence from Sunday singles orders
Authors: Daniel A. Dias
Abstract: Professional sports offer rare field tests of game theory with observed choices, sharp incentives, and expert competitors. Ryder Cup Sunday singles is a simultaneous permutation game where captains order twelve players and pairings form slot by slot. Under Hurley (2002)’s benchmark, uniform random ordering is a mixed-strategy equilibrium of the constant-sum game, and therefore also a minimax strategy. Using Sunday singles orders from 1981–2025 and, where available, Data Golf and OWGR ranks before each Cup, I test whether within-team ability is assigned uniformly at random across lineup slots. Permutation tests reject uniform random assignment. The data indicate that stronger players appear earlier than random shuffles within teams predict, with the pattern more pronounced in later Ryder Cups.

Title: Modeling and solving the two-echelon open vehicle routing problem with autonomous delivery vehicles
Authors: Wenhui Bai, Peng Liu, Tianyu Wang, Wenchao Wei
Abstract: With the rapid advancement of driving automation technology, the logistics industry is increasingly adopting autonomous delivery vehicles (ADVs), particularly within hybrid logistics modes. This study investigates a novel delivery system that integrates traditional trucks and ADVs within a two-echelon distribution framework, formalized as the two-echelon open vehicle routing problem with autonomous delivery vehicles (2E-OVRP-ADVs). A defining characteristic of this system is that ADVs can depart from one satellite and return to another, an open-route structure that reduces empty deadhead trips but creates vehicle flow among satellites. The core novelty of this work is the joint consideration of open routes and vehicle imbalance management. We introduce the concept of tolerance for imbalance (TI), which explicitly bounds the post-delivery number of ADVs at each satellite, thereby constraining the vehicle redistribution induced by the open-route mechanism. The problem is first modeled as a mixed-integer linear program using an arc-based formulation. To improve computational efficiency, a path-based reformulation is solved via a branch-and-price algorithm. An adaptive large neighborhood search metaheuristic is used to generate initial solution pools and assist in the pricing subproblem before invoking the exact pricing procedure. For the exact pricing, both a commodity-flow formulation and a Dantzig-Fulkerson-Johnson formulation with a lazy-cut separation procedure are solved concurrently, with the one yielding the smaller optimality gap adopted. Extensive numerical experiments validate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and provide managerial insights into how open routes and TI impact total routing costs, offering valuable guidance for optimizing ADV-enabled logistics systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Energy-aware drone-based parcel delivery problem with multi-charging mode availability
Authors: Yanfang Ma, Mengdi Yuan, Zhinan Wu, Rui Qiu, Feng Li
Abstract: As drone delivery moves toward practical logistics operations, smart parcel lockers can be extended from parcel storage facilities to drone-supporting infrastructure with multi-charging mode capabilities. However, charging modes differ in charging speed and operational cost, and charging-mode availability varies among smart parcel lockers in practice. To minimize the total cost, this paper proposes an energy-aware drone-based parcel delivery problem with multi-charging mode availability (EDPDP-MCMA). For realism, we develop a comprehensive nonlinear drone energy consumption function related to payload, the entire flight process, wind, and pitch angle. Furthermore, we formulate the EDPDP-MCMA as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model (MINLP) and reformulate it as a mixed-integer linear programming model through the discretization of the payload values. To address large-scale problems, an improved local-adaptive large neighborhood search (ILALNS) algorithm is designed. Numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the computational performance of the ILALNS, and to analyze the effects of charging-mode availability, energy consumption function, and wind conditions on the total cost. In addition, a real-world case study in Hangzhou, China, is conducted to demonstrate the practical applicability of multi-charging mode availability. The results indicate that the proposed model and algorithm can effectively support drone routing and provide insights into charging-mode availability for smart locker-based drone delivery systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Population-weighted transport pressure and its inequality causally shape global socioeconomic development
Authors: Xianmin Ye, Chenyang Shuai, Xi Chen, Bu Zhao
Abstract: Rapid urbanisation, population growth and continued economic expansion have placed many national systems under rising supply pressure. However, how transport infrastructure supply pressure and its inequality within countries relate to socioeconomic development outcomes remains unclear. Here we develop two globally comparable indices, a Transport Infrastructure Supply Pressure index (TISP) and a Transport Infrastructure Supply Pressure Inequality index (TISPI), to quantify population-weighted supply pressure and its internal inequality for 180 countries in 2020 and to examine their associations with key socioeconomic indicators. On average, TISP in the Global South is about 3.5 times that in the Global North, while TISPI is about 1.4 times higher. Moreover, TISP and TISPI are closely linked to socioeconomic outcomes, with higher TISP associated with a lower economic development level and higher TISPI associated with greater income inequality and faster urbanisation, and these relationships exhibit directional evidences. These findings underscore the necessity of optimising transport infrastructure allocation to relieve supply pressure and improve supply–demand matching, thereby guiding transport investment towards more inclusive and sustainable growth.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Distributional incidence of car feebates with spillovers to the second-hand market
Authors: Quentin Hoarau
Abstract: Feebates applied to new vehicles are widely used to reduce emissions from the automobile sector, yet most vehicles are traded in second-hand markets. This paper studies how interactions between new and used car markets affect the distributional incidence of a car feebate. Using comprehensive French administrative data on vehicle transactions over the period 2008–2019 and detailed information on used car prices, we develop an accounting framework linking the feebate spillover to vehicle depreciation. We find that over half of the initial feebate is redistributed through used car markets within five years, with important consequences for incidence. Corporate buyers, who face the largest direct tax on new cars, recover approximately two-thirds of their burden through resale and end up close to neutral overall. Among private households, the burden shifts further towards high-income groups, who purchase both more new and more recent used cars. Yet the feebate remains progressive: the net burden as a share of income increases with household income, whether accounting for used car markets or not. These results suggest that the distributional effects of vehicle regulations cannot be assessed on the basis of new car markets alone, and that corporate buyers play a key role in transmitting feebate costs across the car lifecycle.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Factors associated with discrepancies between scheduled and actual flight block times: evidence from U.S. domestic airline operations
Authors: Yi Gao, Zhi Dou, Sen Wang, Jiayu Liu
Abstract: Scheduled block time (SBT) represents the planned gate-to-gate duration of a flight and serves as a key element of airline schedule planning. In practice, actual block times (ABTs) frequently differ from scheduled values due to operational and environmental conditions. This study investigates factors associated with relative block time discrepancy between ABT and SBT using a dataset of approximately 7.13 million U.S. domestic flights in 2024, integrating flight operations data with airport characteristics, aircraft information, origin-airport weather observations, and airport traffic measures. The analysis combines descriptive exploration with multiple empirical modeling approaches, including robust linear regression, LASSO regression, multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS), generalized additive models (GAM), Random Forest, and XGBoost. Results reveal systematic patterns in block time discrepancies across time of day, airport categories, and aircraft types. Weather and airport traffic variables remain important correlates, with precipitation, wind speed, humidity, and visibility showing relatively consistent associations across model specifications, while the role of temperature is more sensitive to fixed-effect controls. Regional jet operations show greater sensitivity to weather conditions, while congestion-related factors play a stronger role in wide-body operations. A common time-blocked out-of-sample comparison shows that all fitted models outperform a simple historical operational benchmark, with tree-based machine-learning models providing the strongest predictive performance. However, the incremental gains over other fitted models are modest, and overall explanatory power remains limited. Overall, the findings provide large-scale empirical evidence on the operational conditions associated with discrepancies between scheduled and actual block times and offer diagnostic insights for schedule reliability, congestion management, and operational performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A longitudinal analysis of user acceptance of electric car-sharing services
Authors: Senkai Xie, Feixiong Liao
Abstract: Electric car-sharing services (ECS), which have been expected to address the negative externalities of owning and using private cars, remain relatively small in the mobility market. Existing research on ECS adoption has relied on cross-sectional designs and models. This study marks the first longitudinal extension of the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) to analyze the dynamic process of ECS adoption. With a two-wave online panel survey, results from autoregressive cross-lagged structural equation modeling confirm that psychological factors and behavioral intention to adopt ECS show stable autoregressive effects. It is found that the behavioral intention established earlier significantly strengthens psychological factors afterwards, revealing a feedback mechanism and cross-lagged effects. The relative importance of social influence grows over time and ultimately surpasses performance expectancy, reflecting a shift in the power of the influencing factors. These findings demonstrate the value of longitudinal perspectives in adoption research. The extended model also reveals a critical role of attitudes toward sharing, innovativeness, and mobility-related factors. Policymakers and ECS operators are recommended to continuously monitor user motivations and apply dynamic adjustments to strategies to promote durable shifts toward on-demand and climate-neutral mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Enhancing financial inclusion measurements: A comparative analysis using unsupervised machine learning methods across Mexican municipalities
Authors: René Cabral, Salvador Ulises Cadena Espinoza, Jong-Min Kim
Abstract: While several different statistical methods have been employed to measure financial inclusion, two of the most frequently used in the literature are the adaptation of the Human Development Index (HDI) methodology proposed by Sarma (2008) and, more recently, the two-stage Principal Component Analysis (PCA) suggested by Cámara and Tuesta (2014). Employing a unique dataset on the access and usage of financial services across Mexican municipalities, this paper proposes the alternative use of two unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) methods: Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and Kernel PCA (KPCA). To contrast the performance of the four different methods, we first cluster the municipalities using the K-Means algorithm. Thereafter, we focus our comparison of the indices produced by the four methods on the most financially excluded clusters, using standard ML performance metrics: precision, recall, F1 score, and accuracy. Our results show that both HDI and NMF significantly outperform PCA-based methods across different thresholds at the bottom of the distribution. Several robustness checks confirm our findings. This result is particularly significant, as poverty alleviation, one of the primary targets of financial inclusion, can only be achieved successfully if policymakers accurately identify individuals and regions that are excluded or underserved by the financial sector.

Title: Enhancing sustainability and cost-efficiency in urban rail-road bridge: A Bayesian-optimized surrogate-assisted framework
Authors: Sentayehu Lelisa Dirirsa, Yan Gao, Qing He, Paul Schonfeld, Jianping Hu
Abstract: Cities increasingly require sustainable and land-efficient transportation infrastructure. While Integrated Rail-Road Bridge (IRRB) optimizes urban land use by combining rail and road into a single bridge, integration alone is insufficient to minimize environmental and economic burdens. Consequently, as horizontal alignment is the primary determinant of economic and environmental footprints, optimizing horizontal geometry is imperative for developing land-efficient and sustainable urban corridors. To address this, we propose a Bayesian-optimized surrogate-assisted Multi-Objective Horizontal Curve Optimization (MOHCO) framework. It comprises a data-driven phase for initial impact datasets, a Bayesian-optimized surrogate model for rapid, high-fidelity impact predictions across high-dimensional design spaces, and a Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II) multi-objective optimization incorporating CO 2 emissions and contribution to local temperature. Applied to a real-world case, the framework achieved high predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.98), reduced cost by 5.64%, environmental impact by 38.90%, and improved safety by 44.40% compared to manual designs, supporting sustainable urban transportation development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The strategic value of platform encroachment: Seller entry and network effects
Authors: Salvatore Piccolo, Shiva Shekhar, Jorge Padilla, Marco Pagnozzi
Abstract: In a platform market where user participation is endogenous and shaped by direct network effects, we compare the competitive and welfare effects of two alternative business models: pure intermediation and ‘encroachment’ — a hybrid model where the platform competes with third-party sellers by selling its own private-label products. There are two groups of sellers: entrants, who must pay a specialization cost to access the marketplace, and incumbents, who have already paid it. With encroachment, the platform has no incentive to entirely foreclose their downstream rivals if there are positive network effects. Surprisingly, although encroachment restricts entry, it increases consumer surplus, total welfare, and the incumbents’ profit when there is a sufficiently large number of incumbents in the marketplace.

Title: Cyber-physical systems and AI-enabled decision architecture for smart agricultural production and logistics
Authors: Puwadol Oak Dusadeerungsikul, Francisco Munoz, Shimon Y. Nof
Affiliations: Chulalongkorn University; Pontificia Universidad Javeriana Cali; PRISM Center and Edwardson School of Industrial Engineering, Purdue University

Title: A constraint programming-based decomposition procedure for shop scheduling problems
Authors: Francisco Yuraszeck, Gonzalo Mejía, Daniel Alejandro Rossit, Armin Lüer-Villagra
Affiliations: Universidad Andres Bello; Universidad de La Sabana; Universidad Nacional del Sur (UNS); INMABB, Universidad Nacional del Sur (UNS)-CONICET
Abstract: In this paper, we propose a two-phase constraint programming (CP) based algorithm to obtain high-quality lower and upper bounds for classical scheduling problems under the makespan minimisation criterion. The method relies on a resource-constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP) formulation that incorporates a decomposition approach and a warm-start mechanism exploiting the problem structure to derive competitive bounds. We evaluate our approach on 280 instances of the non-permutation flow shop scheduling problem (NPFSSP) and the job shop scheduling problem (JSSP), comprising 120 and 160 instances, respectively. A comprehensive computational analysis shows that the proposed decomposition approach (DA) is highly competitive in terms of optimality gap and relative percentage deviation with respect to both the lower and upper bounds, outperforming a direct solution (DS) approach commonly used in industrial practice. DA consistently dominates DS across most instance subsets, both in average performance and in variability. We further validate our approach on 20 real-world industrial instances featuring non-rectangular job structures, job recirculation, and unbalanced machine workloads, reaching the optimal makespan on all instances in an average of 251 s. By obtaining highly competitive bounds, our proposed decomposition procedure increases managerial confidence when committing to due dates, allocating workloads, or evaluating whether additional capacity is required.

Title: Closed-loop supply chain network design in the tire industry: a review of recent work, opportunities and unexplored directions
Authors: Ehsan Solgi, Amir M. Fathollahi-Fard, Igor Averbakh
Affiliations: Amirkabir University of Technology; University of Toronto Scarborough; Laurentian University; University of Toronto

Title: Simulating team dynamics with generative agents: a case study on data science teams from digital platforms
Authors: Libo Li, Huan Yu, Martin Kunc
Abstract: Abstract Team-based collaboration is central to tackling complex analytics challenges, yet such collaboration involves intricate and dynamic social interactions. Factors such as collaboration duration, power imbalances in communication, trust levels, and instances of dishonesty have been shown to influence team chemistry in varying contexts. Managing team dynamics remains inherently difficult, prompting increasing interest in using generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools to support analytical work. However, the effectiveness of these tools in real-world team settings is still debated. To better understand and evaluate team dynamics in analytics-driven projects, we develop a multi-agent team dynamics model that leverages large language models as generative agents. This approach allows us to simulate team interactions in the context of open innovation challenges, revealing key insights into the relationship between team behaviours and performance outcomes. Our contributions are twofold: (1) we propose a unified model to holistically understand team dynamics, and (2) we develop a novel simulation framework using generative AI to model text-based team interactions. These contributions offer new perspectives for managing collaboration in analytics-intensive environments and inform the evolving role of AI in supporting innovation and decision-making.

Title: Coordinated Effects in the American Airlines‐US Airways Merger
Authors: Douglas C. Turner
Affiliations: Department of Economics University of Florida Gainesville Florida USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT I study the potential for collusion before and after the American Airlines‐US Airways merger. Results suggest the merger increased major airlines' incentives to coordinate their pricing decisions. US Airways was disinclined to collude prior to the merger due to its unique route structure which was highly dependent on connecting products. The merger, by combining the networks of US Airways and American Airlines, reduced US Airways' dependence on connecting products and enhanced its incentives to collude. Absent US Airways' unique premerger network structure, the merger would not have substantially increased major airlines' incentives to collude.

Title: Minimax-Optimal Reward-Agnostic Exploration in Reinforcement Learning
Authors: Gen Li, Yuling Yan, Yuxin Chen, Jianqing Fan
Affiliations: Department of Statistics and Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China; Department of Statistics, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53706; Department of Statistics and Data Science, Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08540
Abstract: This paper studies reward-agnostic exploration in reinforcement learning (RL)—a scenario where the learner is unaware of the reward functions during the exploration stage—and designs an algorithm that improves over the state of the art. More precisely, consider a finite-horizon inhomogeneous Markov decision process with S states, A actions, and horizon length H, and suppose that there are no more than a polynomial number of given reward functions of interest. By collecting an order of[Formula: see text]without the guidance of the reward information, our algorithm is able to find [Formula: see text]-optimal policies for all these reward functions, provided that [Formula: see text] is sufficiently small. This forms the first reward-agnostic exploration scheme in this context that is nearly minimax optimal. Furthermore, once the sample size exceeds [Formula: see text] episodes (up to log factor), our algorithm is able to yield [Formula: see text] accuracy for arbitrarily many reward functions (even when they are adversarially designed), a task commonly dubbed as “reward-free exploration.” The novelty of our algorithm design draws on insights from offline RL: The exploration scheme attempts to maximize a critical reward-agnostic quantity that dictates the performance of offline RL, whereas the policy learning paradigm leverages ideas from sample-optimal offline RL paradigms. Sloan Foundation, the Air Force Office of Scientific Research [Grant FA9550-22-1-0198], the National Science Foundation [Grants 1907661, 2210833, 2221009, and 2433450], and the Office of Naval Research [Grants N00014-22-1-2340 and N00014-22-1-2354].

Title: Can women's participation in decision making promote sustainable fisheries management? Evidence from a choice experiment with fishermen and their wives
Authors: Krishanthan Gnanapragasam, Shyama Ratnasiri, Christopher Fleming
Abstract: Despite the crucial role of fishermen's wives in small-scale fisheries, fisheries management research often relies on fishermen as sole household representatives. As a result, limited attention is given to how household fisheries management decisions are formed and how wives contribute to shaping these decisions. This study addresses this gap by engaging both fishermen and their wives to examine household preferences for sustainable fisheries management decisions. Using a split-sample choice experiment, we compared the individual preferences of fishermen and their wives alongside couples' joint preferences. Results show that couples' joint preferences for fisheries management attributes tend to fall between the individual choices of fishermen and their wives, suggesting that household fisheries management decisions are shaped through intra-household negotiation and compromise between husbands and wives. Couples' joint choices were also more aligned with sustainable fishing practices than those of fishermen alone, indicating that wives may play an important role in encouraging more sustainability-oriented household decisions. In addition, wives' involvement in intra-household joint decision-making influenced compensation trade-offs and contributed to greater certainty in decision-making. These findings highlight that wives already influence fisheries-related household decisions, yet their contributions remain insufficiently recognised within fisheries management research and formal governance processes. We therefore urge researchers and policymakers to recognise households as joint decision-making units and to engage more directly with wives in fisheries research, data collection, and management processes, rather than relying solely on fishermen as household representatives.

Title: Market versus state in driving growth: An institutional interpretation of TFP changes in China
Authors: Harry X. Wu, Xiang Li
Abstract: By institutionally rethinking the Solow residual in light of how the interplay of policy interventions and market forces affects factor income shares, we attempt to interpret China’s TFP performance from an institutional perspective. To explore the growth–efficiency paradox inherent in the China model of growth, we apply the Jorgensonian APPF–Domar growth accounting framework to the revised and updated CIP/China KLEMS dataset. The framework coherently integrates industry productivity accounts with national accounts to distinguish TFP growth caused by changes in factor utilization within industries from TFP growth caused by changes in factor reallocation between industries. By regrouping 37 Chinese industries according to their distance from state controls (or, conversely, their proximity to final demand) and dividing the entire 1978–2023 period into subperiods to reflect major policy and institutional changes and external shocks, we show that capital reallocation brought about strong TFP gains when both the government and the market happened to address similar structural problems, but policy efforts toward growth inevitably led to efficiency losses and ultimately hindered China’s growth.

Title: Deep reinforcement learning for optimizing mobile depots allocation and hybrid order dispatch in last-mile delivery under multi-participants behavioral uncertainty
Authors: Shixuan Hou, Chengming Hu, Annabathuni Sandeep Chowdary, Bissan Ghaddar, Joe Naoum-Sawaya, Jie Gao
Abstract: As last-mile delivery demand continues to grow and customer preferences become increasingly diverse, traditional single-mode logistics systems are inadequate in addressing the complexity and variability of modern urban delivery environments. In this paper, we propose an innovative hybrid last-mile delivery system that leverages mobile depots as intermediate hubs, integrating crowd-shipping, and customer self-pickup, to enhance cost-effectiveness. However multiple stakeholders in the system have conflicting interests, ignoring their behavioral uncertainties can impair operational efficiency and increase delivery costs. For example, customers and crowd-shippers may compete for the limited storage capacity of mobile depots, and crowd-shippers may be unwilling to deliver orders that customers decline to pick up.
