Specifically, the study captures crowd-shippers’ order-acceptance behavior and customers’ self-pickup choice through two binomial logit models, and embeds these behavioral components into a stochastic mixed-integer programming model. This model jointly optimizes mobile depots allocation and order dispatch decisions, aiming to minimize the expected total operational cost. Considering computational complexity of this model, we propose PRiME-DQN, a reinforcement learning framework that incorporates behavior-prioritized resource filtering, action biasing, and model-efficient temperature tuning to accelerate convergence and improve solution quality. A case study on Amazon’s last-mile delivery in Seattle shows that the proposed hybrid model achieves up to 49.5% cost reduction in low-shipper settings and 11.3% in higher-shipper settings compared to a crowd-shipping system, while also consistently surpassing the self-pickup baseline by 3–6%. Extensive scaling experiments show that PRiME-DQN produces high-quality feasible solutions efficiently. For the largest instances, it achieves delivery costs 1.97% lower than Gurobi’s best incumbent solution obtained within the 3,600-second time limit, while reducing the solution time to approximately 1400 seconds.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Customized first-and-last-mile ridesharing services with electric modular autonomous vehicles
Authors: Bo Sun, Qiang Meng
Abstract: This study proposes an interesting and viable first-and-last-mile ridesharing service (FLMRS) that leverages electric modular autonomous vehicles (EMAVs) to enhance public transportation (PT) accessibility. A platoon advantage of assembled EMAVs to form a fully connected EMAV (CEMAV) can reduce the operational cost and simultaneously satisfy customized ridesharing needs. Specifically, passengers can select whether to accept ridesharing with others, which are assigned to adaptable EMAVs within a CEMAV. Given the electric nature of a CEMAV fleet, we formulate the FLMRS problem as a set-covering model that accounts for time-dependent energy consumption, partial charging operations, nonlinear charging functions, restricted charging times, and capacitated public charging infrastructures. To consider the unknown availability of limited public chargers, we propose a predict-then-optimize approach that first forecasts charger availability using both endogenous and exogenous features and converts the prediction results into uncertainty-adjusted charger capacities before optimization. We then incorporate the charger capacities as input parameters to tackle the FLMRS by optimization methods. A data-driven column generation (DDCG) method within a rolling-horizon framework is developed to solve the real-time optimization problem with dynamic request arrivals. To enhance computational efficiency in solving the pricing subproblems of DDCG, we utilize two advanced acceleration techniques to reduce label exploration. Extensive computational experiments using real-world data from Singapore validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods in obtaining high-quality solutions. The experimental results demonstrate the advantages of the predict-then-optimize framework in improving capacity utilization and matching personalized travel needs with suitable CEMAV configurations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A dual-phase spatio-temporal deep reinforcement learning approach for the time-dependent green multi-depot vehicle routing problem with time windows
Authors: Yang Zou, Xiaokun Huang, Yunqiang Yin, T.C.E. Cheng
Abstract: In time-varying traffic conditions, departure timing affects travel duration, arrival schedules, and environmental performance, making temporal decisions an important component of green multi-depot vehicle routing. This study investigates the Time-Dependent Green Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows. It incorporates proactive node-level waiting into spatial route planning, whereas conventional immediate-departure approaches treat temporal scheduling as an implicit consequence of the selected route. We propose a Dual-Phase Spatio-Temporal Policy (DPSTP) framework based on deep reinforcement learning. The framework adopts a route-first, schedule-second decision paradigm, where spatial route construction and route-conditioned departure scheduling are sequentially determined and jointly optimized to minimize a total cost comprising operational duration, emission-proxy costs, and lateness penalties. Computational experiments on synthetic benchmark instances (n=100) show that DPSTP achieves the lowest mean total cost among the compared methods; Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search, POMO, and the OR-Tools solver incur 22.38%, 12.66%, and 8.79% higher total cost, respectively. A case study on a large-scale Cordeau instance further shows that proactive waiting with an expanded temporal action space (a relaxed-window reference scenario) reduces the emission-proxy cost by 10.4% and total cost by 18.1% relative to immediate departure, with a moderate increase in lateness penalties, while the default bounded policy reduces total cost by 14.0%. These results provide empirical evidence that route-conditioned temporal scheduling can improve objective performance under the time-varying traffic conditions and benchmark settings considered in this study.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The ontological dimensions of coastal mangrove reserve conflicts——insights from China
Authors: Shuning Zhu, Annah Lake Zhu, Weiye Wang
Abstract: In the context of escalating anthropogenic pressures on coastal ecosystems, this article employs a case study of one of China’s southeastern coastal mangrove reserves to interrogate the interplay between local communities and state authorities in natural resource governance from an ontological perspective. Through qualitative research involving 30 semi-structured interviews conducted between 2019 and 2023, we reveal how state, market, and community actors operate from fundamentally different – and often incompatible – understandings of mangroves. We trace a historical shift from a community ontology, where mangroves were perceived as socio-ecological commons buffering against flooding, to a market ontology through which mangroves were seen as barriers to marketized aquaculture development. While state intervention later curtailed market overexploitation, its regulatory, ecological ontology clashed with both the eroded community framework and the persistent market logic. Consequently, state governance, though justified by ecologically necessity, proved ontologically irreconcilable with the community’s original, relational approach. This study demonstrates that environmental governance conflicts are not merely about resource distribution but are rooted in conflicting ontologies and clashes between divergent world-making practices. It thus contributes a novel analytical lens for understanding governance conflicts in socio-ecological systems under competing state and market pressures, revealing that effective and just governance requires recognizing and navigating deep ontological divides, not just negotiating resource claims.

Title: Advanced probabilistic tabu search for the fair max-min diversity problem
Authors: He Zheng, Anna Martínez-Gavara, Rafael Martí, Fred Glover
Abstract: The concept of fairness in optimization models has opened up a wide range of practical applications, ranging from the equitable access to services in location, to team formation problems in human resources. Recently, the concept of fairness has found applications in the important area of maximizing diversity, giving rise to the Fair Max-Min Diversity (FMMD) problem which incorporates group fairness constraints. In this paper, we target this novel variant of the well-known Max-Min Diversity Problem (MMDP) that constitutes a challenge for today’s solvers. We explore two metaheuristic paradigms to develop new solution methods for the FMMD problem: Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP) and Probabilistic Tabu Search (PTS). A computational study reveals that incorporating memory mechanisms makes PTS particularly effective in solving FMMD instances. To further enhance performance, we propose an advanced version of PTS that integrates memory-based perturbation and strategic oscillation mechanisms. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate that our advanced PTS consistently outperforms basic metaheuristics on all problems and achieves significantly superior performance relative to the exact approaches for larger problems. Additional analysis highlights the contributions of each proposed component, offering insights into the design of efficient methods for diversity optimization under fairness constraints.

Title: Procedural rationality, endogenous sampling, and the instability of defection
Authors: Srinivas Arigapudi, Jonathan Newton
Abstract: We examine cooperation and defection in populations where individuals use both procedural rationality and imitation to choose their strategies. For a broad class of sampling-based choice procedures that encompasses both procedural rationality and imitation, we characterize the conditions under which universal defection is unstable. The results highlight that for cooperation to emerge and persist, the manner in which agents generate and share information can be as important as the underlying payoff incentives.

Title: Banking on carbon: modeling intertemporal equilibrium in China's rate-based emissions trading system
Authors: Limin Du, Huiying Peng, Zheng Wang
Abstract: China's emissions trading system (ETS) is a key market-based strategy to meet its ambitious “dual-carbon” targets of peaking emissions and reaching neutrality. Unlike “cap-and-trade” markets that limit total pollution, China's “rate-based” system adjusts permits based on production intensity. To understand how this unique design and “allowance banking”—saving permits for future use—influence long-term stability, this paper develops a discrete-time equilibrium model for the power sector. Theoretically, we show that China's rate-based approach better balances industrial growth with emissions abatement than traditional caps. The numerical simulations show that, under the rate-based approach, allowance prices rise steadily, carbon emissions decline continuously, thermal power output contracts moderately, and trading volume exhibits an overall upward trend. These results remain robust across alternative discount-rate assumptions. A comparison between cap-and-trade and rate-based approach further reveals that, when cumulative allowance allocation is held constant across regulatory regimes, rate-based approach results in higher allowance prices and greater thermal power output in most periods. These findings clarify the dynamics of intensity-based markets, providing a vital roadmap for policymakers to manage price stability and ensure the market's long-term success.

Title: Getting there and feeling better: mechanisms from perceived accessibility to subjective well-being
Authors: Jiahang Liu, Qiyang Liu
Abstract: Accessibility matters for subjective well-being, yet its underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Using survey data from 5591 respondents in ten Chinese cities, this study examines how perceived accessibility relates to hedonic and eudaimonic well-being through domain-specific travel satisfaction and social exclusion. After accounting for the indirect pathways, the structural equation modeling results show that perceived accessibility remains positively associated with flourishing and negatively associated with negative affect, whereas its total effect on positive affect is not significant. The mediation effect varies across travel domains and well-being outcomes. Leisure travel satisfaction emerged as the most important mediator for flourishing, while shopping travel satisfaction played a mediation role across all outcomes. Commute travel satisfaction was particularly salient for affective well-being. Social exclusion, meanwhile, constituted a strong and consistent pathway. The findings highlight that accessibility contributes to well-being not only through reaching destinations, but also through satisfying travel experiences and social inclusion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Bus fleet electrification: A comprehensive review of charging, operations, planning and sustainability
Authors: Federico Silvestri, Seyed Mahdi Miraftabzdeh, Michela Longo, Dario Zaninelli
Abstract: Battery Electric Buses (BEBs) are increasingly adopted by Local Public Transit (LPT) companies to support the sustainable mobility transition, at the cost of introducing new challenges and constraints. This paper presents an up-to-date review of more than 100 studies published between 2019 and 2025 on bus fleet electrification. The analysis identifies four major research directions: Charging Infrastructure and Methods, Bus Fleet Operations, Electrification Planning, and Sustainability. Recurring themes emerge, including the central role of optimized charging strategies on total cost of ownership and the need for integrated planning models that jointly consider infrastructure, battery sizing, and operations. The review also reveals persistent gaps related to uncertainty modeling, scalability for large transport networks, and careful consideration of battery degradation. Finally, a functional framework is proposed to synthesize how current research contributions map onto the practical decision layer, providing a consolidated foundation for future studies and supporting practitioners in large-scale BEB deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A multi-criteria readiness assessment of cities for sustainable autonomous vehicle infrastructure
Authors: Ertugrul Ayyildiz
Abstract: This study develops an integrated decision-support framework for assessing the readiness of major Turkish cities for sustainable autonomous vehicle (AV) infrastructure. İstanbul, Ankara, İzmir, Bursa, and Antalya are evaluated using 16 sub-criteria grouped under Physical Infrastructure, Smart Mobility, Sustainability, and Adaptive Capacity. Expert judgments are consolidated through the Modified Delphi method and analyzed using Pythagorean Fuzzy Indifference Threshold-based Attribute Ratio Analysis (PF-ITARA) and Pythagorean Fuzzy Measurement of Alternatives and Ranking according to Compromise Solution (PF-MARCOS). The results identify Economic Feasibility, Municipal Capacity, and R&D Ecosystem as the most influential criteria. İzmir ranks first, followed by İstanbul, Ankara, Bursa, and Antalya. Sensitivity analyses confirm that İzmir remains the leading city under alternative threshold structures and 32 criterion-weight perturbation scenarios. The findings show that autonomous vehicle readiness depends on balanced technological, financial, institutional, and sustainability capabilities and provide practical guidance for urban infrastructure planning and phased deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Integrated intelligence, autonomous operations, and trusted autonomy: AI-driven SCM performance in 2040
Authors: Wolf Frenkler, Manuel Wimmer, Christoph Küffner, Evi Hartmann
Affiliations: Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg Chair of Supply Chain Management, , Erlangen
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven advancements may enhance supply chain management (SCM) performance across SCOR-DS processes by 2040, addressing the lack of systematic, long-horizon, cross-process evidence on AI-related performance effects. Design/methodology/approach A foresight-oriented real-time Delphi study assessed 13 projections developed from desk research and 12 semi-structured expert interviews, then refined in internal and expert workshops. Seventy experts rated each projection’s expected probability, impact and desirability, providing qualitative rationales. Results were analyzed using descriptive and consensus statistics, stakeholder comparisons, dissent diagnostics, qualitative coding and fuzzy c-means clustering, discussed through a complex adaptive systems lens. Findings Experts expect substantial AI-enabled SCM performance gains by 2040. Results indicate layered AI integration. Integrated intelligence emerges as the most plausible and impactful pathway, reflecting deeply embedded, predominantly assistive AI across planning, sourcing, fulfillment and returns. The autonomous operations pathway captures more selective, contested moves toward AI-led training, shared AI infrastructures, unmanned production and autonomous mass customization. Trusted autonomy is less directly impactful yet enables adoption by stabilizing data protection, contractual delegation and safety-related AI use. Assessments vary across SCOR-DS stakeholder groups, while country-based differences are negligible. Originality/value This study offers a SCOR-DS-wide, Delphi-based analysis of how AI-driven SCM performance enhancement is expected to unfold by 2040 as a layered, process-uneven configuration rather than a single linear trend. Through a complex adaptive systems lens, it shows that these trajectories operate through distinct mechanisms: schema and network-connectivity changes, shifts in agent composition and self-organization and governance-based boundary setting, thereby advancing theorizing on AI as an adaptive agent in supply networks.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Hybrid discrete–continuous optimisation of material and energy flows in steel enterprises for flexible grid interaction
Authors: Huan Ma, Yu-Qi Zhao, Heng-Yu Liu, Jia-Zheng Sun, Nan Meng, Qun Chen
Affiliations: North China University of Technology; Electric Power Research Institute of State Grid Liaoning Electric Power Co., Ltd.
Abstract: The strategic exploitation of demand-side flexibility in energy-intensive industries such as steel enterprises, is critical for advancing decarbonisation efforts. However, a fundamental challenge arises from the operational conflict between continuous-time material flow scheduling and discrete-time energy management. This study resolves this challenge with a hybrid framework for co-optimising material and energy flows in steel enterprises. The framework incorporates an improved material flow model that adjusts production makespan in continuous time domain, integrates refining furnace power regulation, and accounts for the nonlinear energy consumption of reheating furnaces relative to waiting time and temperature drops. Wherein, a novel bridging mechanism is introduced that translates the Lagrangian trajectories of individual discrete material entity into a Eulerian perspective for plant-wide, discrete-time energy consumption profiles. Synchronisation of material and energy flows enables co-optimised production and energy scheduling responding to electricity tariffs. The method shows superior computational performance, cutting solution time by 88% compared to conventional resource-task network models. Validated by a case study, this framework enabled a 4.3% reduction in total system cost, and a 7.85 MW improvement in demand response capability, accounting for 44.38% of the maximum load, thereby providing a practical paradigm for evolving steel industry into a flexible, grid-interactive virtual power plant.

Title: To be generous or spiteful? A bilateral exploration of fairness preferences in supply chains with downstream competition
Authors: Yanan Song, Libo Sun, Yangyang Guo, Wei Gu, Xiangbin Yan
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management University of Science and Technology Beijing Beijing China; School of Management Hefei University of Technology Hefei Anhui China; Key Laboratory of Process Optimization and Intelligent Decision‐making Philosophy and Social Sciences Laboratory for Data Science and Smart Social Governance, Ministry of Education, Hefei, 230009 China; Douyin Life Services ByteDance Beijing China; School of Business Guangdong University of Foreign Studies Guangzhou Guangdong China
Abstract: Abstract Fairness breeds long‐term partnerships in supply chains, yet stakeholders may differ in their perceptions of fair profit allocation. This study examines how fairness preferences, categorized as generosity and spite, affect ordering decisions and profit allocation between one supplier and two competing retailers. Supported by our exploratory survey confirming that firms actively monitor their relative profit shares in routine operations, our analytical results reveal that the impacts of fairness on supply chains differ in different power structures. Under supplier‐led scenarios, supplier spite harms all parties, whereas supplier generosity benefits both retailers and the overall supply chain. Importantly, while supplier generosity can lead to win–win outcomes if matched by retailer generosity, lose–lose situations are more common, especially when suppliers act spitefully. Therefore, influential suppliers should spearhead efforts to cultivate a productive environment, due to their central role in supply chains. In retailer‐led settings, however, retailer fairness preferences do not influence equilibrium outcomes, as retailers can directly control outcomes via procurement decisions. While supplier generosity still benefits the overall supply chain, it precludes the potential for win–win outcomes, leading to situations where only the supplier suffers. That is, suppliers in retailer‐led contexts should secure their positions rather than feel pressured to always display generosity. Lastly, we examine asymmetric retailer behavior and perception biases regarding fair profit shares. Moderate generosity by one retailer can ease competition and benefit supply chains, while perception biases may trigger shifts for others. These findings explain how fairness preferences and downstream competition reshape supply chain partnerships and outcomes.

Title: Weathering hard times with bushmeat: rural household coping under rainfall shocks
Authors: Prachi Jhamb, Susana Ferreira, Martin Reinhardt Nielsen
Abstract: While bushmeat can be a crucial protein source for food insecure households, its consumption and trade raise significant concerns for both human health and wildlife conservation. Here we investigate how rainfall shocks influence rural households’ income from and reliance on bushmeat hunting. Drawing on data from nearly 8,000 rural households across 24 low- and middle-income countries, matched to gridded rainfall records and detailed agricultural season calendars, our study distinguishes between the effects of shocks depending on their type, intensity and timing of occurrence within the agricultural cycle. We mitigate endogeneity concerns faced in prior studies relying on self-reported shocks and cross-sectional data, by constructing a quarterly household panel survey integrated with objective, high-resolution data on climatic moisture stress. We find that dry conditions increase both bushmeat income and its share in total household income, particularly during critical agricultural periods. Conversely, wet conditions have the opposite effect, often decreasing hunting due to improved agricultural yields. However, these effects vary depending on the intensity of wet conditions. Additionally, we find heterogeneity in responses across socio-economic strata, as wealthier households tend to have higher bushmeat income during dry periods, likely due to better access to resources. The study increases our understanding of when and by whom climate stressors induce greater wildlife offtake, providing important insight for targeted development and conservation policy.

Title: A novel tri-individual memetic search algorithm for the set orienteering problem
Authors: Mu He, Qinghua Wu, Jin-Kao Hao, Yongliang Lu, Yuning Chen
Abstract: The Set Orienteering Problem is a generalization of the popular Orienteering Problem, where customers are grouped into mutually exclusive clusters, and the profit of each cluster is collected by visiting at least one customer in the respective cluster. For this NP-hard problem, we develop a novel heuristic algorithm rooted in the memetic search framework. This algorithm incorporates a pre-processing phase to accelerate the search, an inherit-mutate-repair crossover operator for generating high-quality offspring solutions, and a local search that integrates strategic oscillation to adaptively explore both feasible and infeasible regions of the search space. Other innovative features of our method include a fast tri-individual population, a solution-based tabu strategy based on hashing techniques, and an adaptive mutation operator. Extensive experimental results on two sets of 496 large benchmark instances demonstrate the strong competitiveness of the proposed approach in comparison to state-of-the-art heuristics documented in the literature. Specifically, for the 192 large original benchmark instances, the proposed algorithm outperforms the current best-known solutions for 27 instances, while matching all other established results. For the 304 new larger benchmark instances, the proposed algorithm improves the best-known solutions for 138 instances. Further experiments are carried out to provide deeper insights into the performance of the algorithm by analyzing its primary elements.

Title: Editorial Board
Transparency in Supply Chain Service Design: Assessing the Impact of Country of Seller and Country of Fulfillment Information
Authors: Rowan Hilend, Simone T. Peinkofer, Yao "Henry" Jin
Affiliations: Department of Management, College of Business Colorado State University Fort Collins Colorado USA; Department of Supply Chain Management, Eli Broad College of Business Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA; Department of Management, Richard T. Farmer School of Business Miami University Oxford Ohio USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT To combat counterfeit or unsafe products in retail supply chains, regulations require large online retailers to disclose seller‐specific information including the country of seller (COS) and the country of order fulfillment (COF). This supply chain transparency aims to empower consumers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Yet, the impact of disclosing such supply chain information to consumers—particularly toward the policy goal of deterring counterfeit purchases by informing consumers—is unclear. Drawing on signaling theory, we conducted a scenario‐based experiment to examine how COS and COF disclosures impact consumer perceptions regarding the likelihood of receiving a counterfeit product and willingness to purchase. Our results reveal the benefits of disclosing COS or COF information in reducing consumer expectations of receiving a counterfeit product and increasing purchase intentions. Yet nuanced insights reveal that consumer perceptions of a country influence their interpretation of COS and COF information. Specifically, the presence of a country associated with low product quality as either COS or COF negates the positive effects of a high‐quality country affiliation.

Title: Immigration and crimes against natives: the 2015 refugee crisis in Germany
Authors: Yue Huang, Michael Kvasnicka
Abstract: Abstract During the 2015 refugee crisis, nearly one million refugees arrived in Germany, raising widespread concern that crimes against natives would rise. Using novel county-level data, we study this question empirically in first-difference and two-stage least squares (2SLS) regressions. Our results do not support the view that Germans were victimized in greater numbers by refugees, as measured by their rate of victimization in crimes with refugee suspects. Our findings are of great policy and public interest, and also of material relevance for the broader literature on immigration and crime, which mostly considers crimes per capita or variants thereof. We show that such aggregate measures may be insufficiently informative about the actual victimization patterns of specific groups.

Title: Field experiments to reduce inequality: Introduction to the special issue
Authors: Michèle Belot, Henning Hermes, Philipp Lergetporer, Frauke Peter, Simon Wiederhold

Title: The rhythm of reliability: diagnostic patterns of quality-control gaps in manufacturing
Authors: Andrea Chiarini
Affiliations: Department of Management, University of Verona
Abstract: Manufacturing companies face a persistent challenge: maintaining quality stability amidst fluctuating process conditions and material variability. While traditional quality management emphasises technical standardisation, this paper argues that quality is actively stabilised through distributed routines and human sensemaking on the shop floor. Using an inductive, multiple-case study of four manufacturing firms and 32 interviews, we employ the Gioia methodology to identify seven core dimensions of quality stabilisation: Process-Input Fit, Ripple Effects of Small Process Changes, Real-Time Quality Sensemaking, Tacit-to-Standard Translation, Precision Drift Anticipation, the Reliability-Intervention Loop, and Machine–Human Synchronisation Routines. We develop a diagnostic framework that identifies recurring patterns associated with possible gaps in formal process control. The seven dimensions do not constitute a new control system. Nor do the interview data demonstrate that local interventions improved performance. The framework indicates when managers should examine an existing SOP or Process Quality Control Plan for unvalidated adjustments or possible statistical tampering risks.

Title: A two-stage stochastic approach to fixed-income multi-portfolio optimization with deep-learning scenario generation: an investment bank case study
Authors: Mojtaba Azizian, Mohammad Ali Izadi, Mohammad Ardestani, Salman Jobeiri, SeyedehMohaddeseh Ghoreishi, Mohammad Hassan Siamak
Abstract: Complex decision-making processes within a model investment bank can lead to challenges in managing its internal funds. This study addresses this challenge by developing a novel multi-portfolio two-stage stochastic optimization model to optimize fixed-income asset allocation in multi-periods for such a bank. The paper first analyzes the complexities faced by real-world investment banks. It then details the parameter estimation process, which includes forecasting risk-free rates using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model, generating scenarios with a novel residual bootstrapping method, and estimating yield-to-maturities based on yield curve analysis. These parameters are subsequently integrated into the linear optimization model, and solved to optimality. The two-stage framework is presented mathematically, followed by the development of constraints that ensure budget feasibility, logical consistency, and regulatory compliance across different periods. Real-data analysis from a leading Iranian investment bank demonstrates the model’s effectiveness in dynamically adjusting portfolio maturities in response to market scenarios, while also providing valuable managerial insights regarding fund return distribution and the bank’s holdings in its own funds. This research signifies the potential of two-stage stochastic optimization for optimizing investment strategies in a dynamic market environment.

Title: A multi-objective stochastic home health care routing and scheduling problem under demand and service time uncertainty
Authors: Khaoula Besbes, Houda Alaya, Fouad Ben Abdelaziz
Abstract: This paper studies a stochastic Home Health Care Routing Problem (HHCSRP) that integrates routing, assignment, and scheduling decisions under uncertainty. The problem considers heterogeneous caregivers, skill requirements, time windows, and patient-career preferences. Unlike most existing works, we jointly model stochastic patient demand and stochastic service times within a multi-objective framework. We formulate the problem as a bi-objective stochastic mixed-integer program that minimizes total operational costs while maximizing service quality. To address uncertainty, we propose a hybrid approach combining chance-constrained programming and recourse modeling, and derive an equivalent deterministic formulation using goal programming techniques. Computational experiments in benchmark and real-world-inspired cases demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in producing robust and cost-effective schedules. The main contribution lies in the integrated treatment of multiple uncertainty sources within a unified multi-objective HHCSRP and the development of a tractable chance-constrained recourse framework.

Title: Cost-effectiveness of centralized versus decentralized decision-making in agri-environment schemes for biodiversity conservation: Insights from an ecological-economic model
Authors: Caterina De Petris, Martin Drechsler, Frank Wätzold
Abstract: The cost-effectiveness of agri-environment schemes (AES) depends, among other things, on spatial dimensions. Extensive research has been conducted on how to incentivize habitat connectedness, but far less attention has been given to how the spatial level of decision-making affects the outcome of AES. This article contributes to filling this research gap by analyzing the cost-effectiveness of multiple AES under two levels of decision-making, namely centralization and decentralization. For this purpose, a generic ecological-economic model is developed. The model considers two regions, two levels of decision-making, two species, and two AES, each targeting one of the two species under consideration. We analyze different policy scenarios: the central government can either implement a uniform policy, whereby both regions are offered the same compensation payment for the same conservation measure, or it can coordinate the regions by targeting one species per region, exploiting the regions' relative cost-advantages. Under decentralization, the AES are managed purely at the regional level, meaning that the regions design their AES independently. This study aims at identifying how different ecological and economic parameters affect the relative cost-effectiveness of AES under different levels of decision-making. Our model shows that the cost-effective level of decision-making is highly dependent on the ecological and economic context. We find, among other things, that centralized approaches are potentially more suitable for conserving combinations of species with similar environmental requirements, while decentralized approaches are potentially better for combinations of species with different environmental requirements.

Title: Smart and sustainable production, logistics, and supply chain: trends, challenges, methods, and best practices II, part 2
Authors: Beata Mrugalska, Paulina Golinska-Dawson, Youngchul Shin, Gerhard-Wilhelm Weber

Title: Editorial Board
A full-sample longitudinal trajectory reconstruction framework for signalized intersection approach lanes in a vehicle-infrastructure cooperation environment
Authors: Tingting Ren, Chengxin Fu, Yangsheng Jiang, Zhihong Yao, Yunxia Wu, Kefan Chen
Abstract: Vehicle trajectories contain abundant spatial–temporal information that can be utilized for traffic state estimation and parameter optimization. In the vehicle-infrastructure cooperation environment, connected automated vehicles (CAVs) can provide their trajectory data and perceive the trajectory data of nearby vehicles within a specific range. Moreover, these trajectory data can be shared and cross-validated with fixed detectors, offering a novel solution for reconstructing full-sample vehicle trajectories at the signalized intersection. Based on the car-following (CF) model, this paper proposes a trajectory reconstruction framework that integrates CAVs sensing data and camera detection data. This framework can solve the trajectory reconstruction problem for regular vehicles (RVs) between any two consecutive CAVs on the lane. It comprises four key modules: the trajectory reconstruction model (TRM) based on the trailing CAV (TTRM), the TRM based on the leading CAV (LTRM), the Modified LTRM, and the fusion algorithm (FA). Furthermore, NGSIM and simulation data are utilized to validate and analyze the performance of the proposed framework under various CAV penetration rates (PRs) and traffic demands. Results indicate that: (1) compared to the state-of-the-art CF-based algorithms, the proposed framework significantly reduces in terms of position error, queuing position error, moving position error, time error, speed error, and acceleration error with average RMSE reductions of 83.45%, 20.97%, 90.87%, 85.54%, 30.39%, and 28.64% in NGSIM data, respectively, and even more substantial decrease in simulation data. (2) The framework maintains acceptable error rates across different PRs of CAVs and varying traffic volumes. (3) The framework is robust for different CF model parameters in simulation data. The findings can support signalized intersection management and control in the vehicle-infrastructure cooperation environment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Latent paths in mode choice models: incorporating street-level environment features for active travel policy
Authors: Corin Staves, Qin Zhang, Aruna Sivakumar, Ismail Saadi, SM. Labib, Belen Zapata-Diomedi, James Woodcock
Abstract: There is growing empirical evidence that walking and cycling are influenced by street-level environment features such as greenness and traffic stress. To assess active travel policy, these features are increasingly incorporated into mode choice models through predictors that aggregate spatial information along the route. However, this requires assumptions about which routes decision-makers evaluate. Simple assumptions (e.g., fastest path) can produce unrealistic routes and therefore inaccurate predictors, potentially biasing estimated street-level environment coefficients. We present a practical estimation process to evaluate plausible paths without prior route choice knowledge. In this proof of concept, we introduce a latent path selection mechanism in which routes are optimised together with mode choice. Implementations in Manchester (England) and Melbourne (Australia) produced plausible estimates comparable to existing mode and route choice literature. For example, cycling on high-stress paths was utility-equivalent to travelling 94–177% longer on low-stress paths for males, and this was higher for females (up to 389%) and children (up to 768%). Furthermore, using latent paths improved log-likelihoods and produced larger street-level environment coefficients versus fastest paths. For scenario forecasts, our methodology produced similar mode shifts at the population level, but with substantial variations at the trip-level by evaluating more decision-relevant routes. Latent path estimation could therefore be advantageous for forecasting applications where reliable chosen route data is unavailable. With growing availability of micro-spatial data and policy focus towards sustainable transport, this methodology can enhance how street-level features are represented in empirical literature and forecasting models.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Corrigendum to “Locus of control, climate change adaptation and perception: Evidence from rural Ethiopia” [World Dev. 208 (2026) 107525]
Authors: Halefom Yigzaw Nigus, Martin Paul Jr Tabe Ojong, Kibrom A. Abay
Abstract: The authors regret that the acknowledgment in the originally published version is incorrect. The correct acknowledgement is provided below:

Title: Location choice when the number of jobs matters: matching in spatial equilibrium
Authors: Anthony J. Venables
Abstract: The idea that people want to go to where the jobs are is intuitive, yet is absent from the standard quantitative spatial modelling approach in which location choices are guided by prices, without reference to quantities (the number of jobs in a place). The purpose of this paper is to fill this gap by making jobs, as well as places, the objects of household choice. This involves minor change to the modelling approach used in the literature and provides a simple description of labour market matching. Similar modification of the modelling of firms’ location choices captures the idea that these are shaped by both wage costs and the availability of workers with appropriate skill. These modifications yield powerful agglomeration forces, as workers’ location choices become positively influenced by the number of jobs in a place, and firms’ decision are shaped by the number of workers with appropriate skills. Results are established analytically and in a regional model in which the equilibrium distributions of workers and sectors are demonstrated.

Title: Explainable AI and decision analytics for early disease detection: a systematic synthesis of healthcare information systems
Authors: Md. Talha Mohsin, Ismail Abdulrashid, Dursun Delen, Mohamed Khalafalla
Abstract: Early disease detection constitutes a complex decision problem marked by heterogeneous evidence sources, high levels of uncertainty, and substantial clinical and operational implications. Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced predictive accuracy in this domain, yet the integration of AI into healthcare information systems (HIS) remains hindered by the lack of transparency, fragile trust, and weak decision governance. This study provides a systematic, decision-analytic synthesis of explainable AI (XAI), repositioning explainability as a functional component of optimal decision infrastructure rather than a retrospective interpretability layer. Reviewing 60 peer-reviewed studies, we examine how XAI contributes to decision justification, uncertainty reduction, multimodal evidence integration, and trust calibration within clinical decision processes. Findings reveal a heavy concentration on point-estimate, image-based applications, with limited attention to longitudinal decision processes, workflow alignment, and operational governance. By mapping XAI techniques to core decision-analytic mechanisms rooted in operations research, we surface critical capability gaps and propose a research agenda for designing explainable, operationally deployable, AI-enabled analytics to support early detection decisions within healthcare systems.

Title: Good Unsystematic Mistakes
Authors: Lina Lukyantseva, Alex Suzdaltsev
Affiliations: Omnifold AI San Francisco California USA; HSE University St. Petersburg Russia
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study the effects of consumers' unsystematic perception mistakes on market outcomes and consumer welfare. In the model, two firms produce goods of different quality and compete by choosing prices. Consumers observe the qualities and/or the prices with noise and make choice mistakes as a result. When the magnitude of mistakes grows, the lower‐quality firm increases its price while the higher‐quality firm initially reduces its price before increasing it. We show that this price reduction effect is so strong that consumers eventually benefit from making a small amount of unsystematic mistakes despite the sub‐optimal choices and the increasing price of the lower‐quality firm.

Title: Supporting learning in and out of school: Experimental evidence from India
Authors: Martina Björkman Nyqvist, Andrea Guariso
Abstract: Although targeted educational interventions for primary school children in low-income countries have led to substantial improvements in learning, the extent of their effectiveness varies considerably across studies, raising questions about how to adapt them to different settings. This paper examines a novel primary education program that combines a conventional in-school targeted pedagogical intervention with an out-of-school study group initiative facilitated by the community. We use a cross-cutting randomized experiment design across 200 villages in Assam, India. Our results show that standalone implementation of either component has no significant effect on learning outcomes, but when the components are combined in the full program they improve children’s test scores in mathematics and language by 0.11 and 0.09 standard deviations, respectively. The analysis highlights that the combined program increases program awareness and take-up, thereby increasing program effectiveness.

Title: Is drug-related violence fueling emigration from Central America?
Authors: Leonardo Bonilla-Mejía, Jessica Bracco, Andrés Ham, Leonardo Peñaloza-Pacheco
Abstract: We examine how drug-related violence influences emigration choices in Central America, a region that has experienced a sharp increase in migration to the United States. Combining multiple data sources, we leverage an instrumental variables strategy that exploits local variation in proximity to drug-trafficking routes and coca production in Colombia. Our results show that rising violence increases intentions, plans, and preparations to emigrate, particularly to the United States. These migration responses are strongest among young and higher-skilled individuals. Mediation analysis suggests that these migration responses operate predominantly through declining economic activity and worsening labor-market conditions in Central America, rather than through a direct response to insecurity.

Title: Risk assessment of relief food delivery delays from a cross-disaster perspective
Authors: Manyi Yang, Shao jian Qu, Zhuohua Qu, Rameshwar Dubey, Guoqing Zhao, Massoud Mohsendokht, Ying Ji, Zaili Yang
Abstract: Delays in relief food delivery critically threaten post-disaster survival, yet existing studies lack a systematic approach to identifying and assessing these risk factors across different disaster contexts. Focusing on floods and storms, this study develops a two-stage risk analysis framework tailored to relief food delivery delay risks across disaster contexts. Using multi-source real-world data and grounded theory, it identifies 24 risk factors, including previously overlooked institutional political risks such as geopolitical conflicts, political considerations, and bureaucratic approval redundancy. Methodologically, this study integrates failure mode and effect analysis (FMEA), a belief-rule-based Bayesian network, and evidential reasoning to assess and prioritise risks, while employing spherical fuzzy set-based social network analysis and the best-worst method to determine expert and risk factor weights. The results show that the key risk factors differ between disaster types: bureaucratic approval redundancy, traffic paralysis, and concentrated warehouse distribution dominate in floods; severe weather, bureaucratic approval redundancy, and communication infrastructure breakdown prevail in storms. This study contributes to delay risk assessment by applying an integrated FMEA–BBN–ER framework to the underexplored context of relief food delivery under floods and storms, while refining its weighting architecture through combined background–SFS–SNA expert weighting and BWM-based risk factor weighting to account for expert and risk factor heterogeneity. It further provides disaster-specific insights by cautiously interpreting how contextual factors, including governance capacity, institutional settings, and cultural value orientations, may help explain these differences and inform targeted mitigation strategies.

Title: Bank market power and fire-sale amplification under earnings-based constraints
Authors: Panit Wattanakoon
Abstract: This paper analyzes the macroeconomic consequences of bank market power under corporate earnings-based borrowing constraints. By embedding a Cournot banking structure within a Kiyotaki-Moore framework, we uncover a sharp structural reversal: while credit market power dampens the fire-sale multiplier under traditional asset-backed constraints, it amplifies that multiplier under earnings covenants. The endogenous lending markup directly inflates debt-service obligations, tightening borrowers’ cash-flow constraints, forcing deeper asset misallocations and severe aggregate output contractions. Fostering banking competition and relaxing countercyclical covenants act as structural complements, compressing spreads and maximizing real capital retention during financial distress.

Title: Does slow strategizing indicate optimal behavior or uncertainty?
Authors: Ian Krajbich
Abstract: In simple choice, slower decisions tend to indicate proximity to indifference and thus less predictable choice. In complex situations, some studies have argued that slower decisions indicate more reasoning and thus more optimal decisions. However, those studies rely on games where the optimal responses are debatable – they depend on agents’ beliefs or social preferences. Thus, it is unclear whether being slow is a good or bad sign. Here, we examine whether fast decisions are more or less optimal in high and low complexity, zero-sum games with dominant strategies and limited social-preference concerns. We study repeated 2-person p-beauty contests, where halfway through the experiment we switch the multiplier, changing the dominant strategy. Only 33% of subjects correctly adjusted after the switch, an indication of understanding the dominant strategy. Those who continued to play the dominant strategy showed a decrease in response time (RT) upon playing the dominant strategy, while those who later switched away from the dominant strategy did not. Contrary to the predictions for complex games, subjects exhibited negative correlations between RT and optimal choice, both in the early rounds and after the switch. Thus, we find no support for the notion that slower decisions result in better choices.

Title: No impact without details: Quasi-experimental evidence on carpooling regulations and usage
Authors: Yite Sun, Xiaobing Liu, Yu Duan, Yun Wang, Chun Zhang, Xuedong Yan
Abstract: Carpooling is widely regarded as an effective approach to mitigating urban traffic congestion and environmental pollution. However, adoption remains limited, and rigorous causal evidence on carpooling regulatory policies (CRP) is scarce. Using high-resolution order data from 28 cities in three major Chinese urban agglomerations in 2017, this study exploits staggered city-level CRP implementation as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate its effects on carpooling activity. We develop a spatiotemporal feature-based classification algorithm (SFBCA) to distinguish LF-HSC drivers, characterized by lower carpooling frequency or higher spatiotemporal concentration, from HF-LSC drivers, characterized by higher carpooling frequency and lower spatiotemporal concentration. We estimate average effects using a two-way fixed-effects staggered difference-in-differences model and dynamic effects using heterogeneity-robust event-study estimators, supplemented by robustness checks. Under the monthly specification, SFBCA achieves consistency rates of 93.8% for LF-HSC drivers and 73.0% for HF-LSC drivers, yielding a harmonic consistency of 82.1%. CRP reduce total carpooling orders by 10.2% and HF-LSC drivers’ orders by 25.0%, while having no statistically significant average effect on LF-HSC drivers’ orders. These findings suggest that CRP primarily constrain more intensive and potentially quasi-commercial carpooling activity without producing a detectable average reduction in lower-frequency or more spatiotemporally concentrated carpooling. Heterogeneity analyses reveal variation across urban agglomerations, policy designs, and market environments, with statistically detectable effects concentrated in cities with standalone and detailed regulations. Overall, the findings provide implications for governments and transportation network companies (TNCs) to refine carpooling regulation through targeted and context-sensitive implementation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Small and large neighborhood search for the on-demand bus routing problem: A bus stop assignment and transportation problem
Authors: Jorge Mortes, Martin Cousineau, Fabien Lehuédé, Jorge E. Mendoza, María I. Restrepo
Abstract: This article investigates a static on-demand transportation problem in which users are picked up and dropped off at existing bus stops. Specifically, the selection of bus stops for each request, along with the bus routes, is simultaneously determined by the booking system using an optimization algorithm. We focus on service quality by lexicographically minimizing request travel time (including both walking time and time spent on the bus) and total route length. We introduce a matheuristic algorithm based on small and large neighborhood search, incorporating state-of-the-art operators and a set covering component. The algorithm is tested on a new set of instances, based on real data from New York City, which we propose as a future benchmark. On our New York City instances, this algorithm outperforms prior approaches by finding feasible solutions for all instances and reducing user ride time by more than 5%; it also performs well on related benchmark problems. Additionally, we discuss implementation details for decision-makers and practitioners.

Title: Sailing in calmer waters: Trade policy uncertainty and product quality
Authors: Xin Chen, Kailin Gao, Difei Ouyang
Abstract: This paper examines a novel channel through which trade agreements affect product quality upgrading. Specifically, we analyze the impact of the US granting Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR) status to China — a policy shift that effectively eliminated trade policy uncertainty (TPU) on imports from China. Using a triple-difference estimation strategy, we find that eliminating TPU encourages Chinese incumbent exporters to improve product quality. This quality-enhancing effect is particularly pronounced among low-productivity firms, firms in industries with high sunk costs, and firms located in regions with favorable market conditions. Quality upgrading by incumbents drives aggregate quality improvement, and ignoring this adjustment would underestimate the benefits for US consumers.

Title: Oil price shocks and private equity versus unicorns: transmission channels and policy implications
Authors: Rayenda Khresna Brahmana, Adnan Aslam
Abstract: This study examines how oil price shocks (supply, demand, and risk) are transmitted to private markets (Private Equity and Unicorns), an area largely absent from the literature that has focused almost exclusively on public financial markets. To test the hypothesis, we utilize Morningstar private market indices, including developed market private equity and unicorn indices across Asia, Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, India, and China, and apply vector autoregressions, Markov-switching models, and wavelet quantile methods. Overall, oil price shocks transmit asymmetrically across private market segments, with developed market private equity exhibiting systematic sensitivity while unicorn markets remain largely insulated. Results show that developed market private equity is systematically responsive across all three shock types: supply and demand shocks lower returns, while risk shocks deepen losses during crisis regimes, with transition probabilities confirming prolonged distress following supply disruptions. Impulse response functions confirm demand shocks produce the broadest immediate effects, while wavelet analysis reveals short-term vulnerabilities in unicorn markets that dissipate over longer horizons. Only China and US unicorns register partial sensitivity under supply shocks, suggesting that growth dynamics and appraisal-based valuation dampen oil shock transmission broadly. For practitioners, the findings indicate that oil shocks alter private equity risk premia but carry limited implications for unicorn assets, offering novel insights for asset allocation, diversification, and systemic risk monitoring.

Title: A framework for sustainable robotaxi infrastructure in emerging cities
Authors: Orhan Engin, Ömer Kaya
Abstract: This study proposes an integrated planning framework for robotaxi deployment in medium-sized cities by combining MCDM, GIS-based spatial analysis, and robustness assessment. Intended primarily for local governments and urban transport authorities, the framework also provides operators and investors with an analytical baseline for fleet sizing and charging-infrastructure planning. Seven main criteria and 32 sub-criteria were weighted using FWZIC and RANCOM, with strong agreement confirmed by Pearson correlation (r = 0.9620), Spearman correlation (ρ = 0.9643), and MAD (0.00728). A normalized [0–1] suitability map was used to delineate feasible service areas. The baseline scenario assumes 200 robotaxis, including 150 active and 50 standby vehicles, with rem-based allocation for staging. Using Tesla Model Y Juniper data as a proxy, total grid-side fleet energy demand was estimated at 9.96 MWh/day. Peak-period sizing indicates that at least nine DC fast-charging units are required for the daytime DC charging component.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Investigating and comparing user experiences at EV charging and petroleum fueling stations
Authors: Aaron I. Rabinowitz, Vaishnavi Karanam, Sina Nordhoff, Scott Hardman, Gil Tal
Abstract: Light duty electrification requires DC charging stations to take over the current role of petroleum stations. However, charging and fueling systems differ substantially in technology, user behavior, and business models. This study analyzes thousands of reviews for petroleum stations and DC charging stations. Using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative rating, sentiment analysis, and Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted topical classification, factors that shape user experience are identified. Charging and fueling are perceived as fundamentally different activities. Fueling reviews are dominated by fuel price and staff interaction, while charging reviews emphasize equipment reliability, location convenience, and access to nearby amenities. Manufacturer-owned charging networks are perceived more positively than open networks. Open networks suffer from small station sizes and higher outage rates which reduce effective capacity and generate negative feedback. Across networks, proximity to amenities strongly influences perceived convenience and satisfaction. These findings identify actionable pathways for improving charging experiences and perceptions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A negotiation-based multi-agent reinforcement learning for dynamic scheduling of reconfigurable manufacturing systems
Authors: Manonmani Sekar, Nasim Nezamoddini
Affiliations: Oakland University
Abstract: Reconfigurable manufacturing systems demand scheduling decisions that respond in real time to dynamic job arrivals, machine breakdowns, and module-level reconfiguration constraints. This paper proposes a negotiation-driven multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which enhanced deep Q-network agents are trained centrally and deployed in decentralised execution. Conflicts over machines and shared modules are resolved through an attention-based bidding mechanism incorporating due-date-sensitive features. Experiments in a simulated RMS environment show that the proposed method outperforms the entire multi-agent reinforcement learning family (QMIX, VDN, QTRAN, QPLEX, Weighted QMIX, and MAPPO) by 25% in makespan, matches the strongest single-agent baseline, and attains the lowest reconfiguration overhead of all 15 methods evaluated. Classical metaheuristics achieve marginally better makespan under static conditions, but their reliance on repeated re-optimisation, requiring tens to hundreds of seconds, limits their use in dynamic settings. The proposed framework instead generates decisions within milliseconds and maintains full job completion under a single-machine failure representing a 20% capacity reduction, without retraining. These results establish explicit negotiation as an effective alternative to value decomposition for resolving competitive resource contention, and the framework as a viable solution for real-time scheduling in RMS environments.

Title: Livestreaming or advertising? Managing livestreaming supply chain modes under a competitive contract farming environment in the digital era
Authors: Junbin Wang, Yangyan Shi
Affiliations: Suzhou University of Technology; Capital University of Economics and Business; Macquarie University

Title: Towards optimised perishable inventory systems: integrating time-temperature indicators with deep reinforcement learning
Authors: Sirine Taleb, Chaaben Kouki, Lama Moussawi-Haidar
Affiliations: Business Information and Decision Systems, Suliman S. Olayan School of Business, American University of Beirut; Department of Operations Management and Decision Science, ESSCA School of Management
Abstract: Time-Temperature Indicators (TTIs) can improve the control of perishable temperature-regulated products in cold-chain operations. Companies monitor product quality and temperature over the full cold-chain process, and TTIs provide visual signals indicating product freshness. This study develops a periodic-review temperature-sensitive perishable inventory model that integrates TTIs and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) within a high-dimensional Markov decision process. We implement Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to learn ordering policies that capture multi-period inventory aging and demand uncertainty. Through numerical experiments, we compare PPO against a base-stock policy and a projected inventory level policy in TTI-enabled and non-TTI settings. PPO achieves the highest mean performance overall and in almost all tested configurations, with the PPO advantage increasing as deterioration becomes faster. Comparing systems with and without TTIs shows profit gains up to about 45%. The value of TTI information depends on deterioration rate, green/yellow demand mix, and whether replenishment responds to the green/yellow stock mix. TTIs are more beneficial when the deterioration-generated stock mix is close to demand. Profit may decrease when this alignment breaks down, either because too many items move to yellow while demand remains mainly green, or because yellow demand arises before enough stock has moved from green to yellow.

Title: A multi-level analysis of Digital Twin implementation challenges using RAMI 4.0 and LASFA frameworks
Authors: Pedro A. Boareto, Eduardo F. R. Loures, Fernando Deschamps, Eduardo A. P. Santos, Anderson L. Szejka, Hervé Panetto, Marcelo F. F. Calixto
Affiliations: Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná; Federal University of Technology – Paraná; Universidade Federal do Paraná; Federal University of Paraná; Université de Lorraine
Abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology is a key enabler of Industry 4.0 (I4.0), yet its implementation remains challenging. Organisations face obstacles such as low digital readiness, skill gaps, complex system integration, and cultural resistance. This study conducts a systematic review of high-impact literature using the ProKnowC method to map these challenges and propose solutions. A novel six-category taxonomy is introduced: Data Handling, Systems, Implementability, Regulatory, People, and Culture & Strategy, extending prior classifications by incorporating socio-technical dimensions. These categories are then mapped across the organisational layers of RAMI 4.0 and LASFA, revealing where these reference architectures offer actionable guidance and where gaps persist. While data and systems challenges dominate the literature, technical skills, costs, and strategic alignment are also frequently cited. The analysis shows that RAMI 4.0 and LASFA provide strong technical support at the Integration, Communication, and Operational layers, but fall short in addressing socio-technical factors such as people, culture, governance, and leadership, which are critical for sustained, large-scale DT deployment.

Title: Supply chain viability: Foundations, perspectives, and future research agenda
Authors: Dmitry Ivanov
Affiliations: Department of Business Administration, Berlin School of Economics and Law
Abstract: The concept of supply chain viability (SCV) has emerged in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, framing a novel context of survival, performance persistence, and adaptation under prolonged uncertainty. SCV represents a rapidly growing research area, recognizing that responding to isolated, bounded disruptions differs from sustaining structural adaptability and flexible reconfiguration across many and over a long-term time horizon. This paper reviews the foundations and perspectives of SCV and conceptualizes it across several methodological dimensions, grounding the analysis in key system properties and the existing literature. We examine the relationship between SCV and resilience and identify a set of attributes that frame SCV as a distinct research area. Furthermore, we propose a future research agenda that includes, but is not limited to, the synergetic effects between resilience and viability, large-scale systemic shocks, SCV assessment, the evolution from reactive responses toward network survival- and adaptation-centric management, and the role of digital twins. This paper positions SCV as a novel research area in industrial and systems engineering, offering substantial opportunities for future research and providing a common reference point for scholars and practitioners interested in viability.

Title: Soft actor-critic facilitated algorithm for maintenance optimization considering reliability
Authors: Jianyi Zhao, Lu Zhen, Jiawen Hu
Affiliations: School of Management, Shanghai University; School of Aeronautics and Astronautics, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Abstract: This paper studies a maintenance optimization problem considering reliability for the engines equipped on a fleet of airplanes. During operations, engines inevitably encounter the risk of in-flight alerts, which can significantly impact maintenance decisions and flight scheduling. Therefore, we formulate a mathematical model to jointly optimize flight-to-engine assignments, the timing of shop visits, and the depth of modular maintenance based on in-flight alert reliability analysis. To solve this comprehensive optimization problem, we propose a soft actor-critic (SAC) facilitated algorithm. The algorithm integrates a graph attention network based dual stabilization strategy to accelerate convergence, alongside an improved SAC method incorporated with a reward shaping mechanism to further enhance computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm reduces the computational time by 34% compared to the traditional column generation method. Finally, we derive several managerial insights for airline operations. For instance, constructing flight portfolios with moderate heterogeneity can balance engine flight hour and flight cycle consumption to extend operational time between maintenance events, and given the uneven degradation across engine modules, differentiated flight assignments prevent simultaneous shop visits, thereby reducing total maintenance costs.

Title: Managing the effort-value tradeoff for integrating human judgment into surgery duration predictions
Authors: Laura Maria Poreschack, Andreas Fuegener, Dominik David Walzner, Ulrich Thonemann, Christof Denz
Abstract: Abstract For surgery duration prediction, it has been shown that integrating human judgment into algorithmic prediction models results in a higher accuracy than machine learning based approaches can achieve alone. However, since humans are a scarce resource in healthcare, their involvement in surgery duration prediction has high opportunity costs as their time could be spent more effectively on patient care and other medical tasks. This raises the question of how these costs should influence human involvement in tasks where algorithms perform reasonably well at minimal cost. This paper introduces a framework for selectively integrating human judgment based on the costs of human involvement and prediction uncertainty, which is captured using algorithmic meta features. Our framework identifies instances in surgery duration prediction where human judgment should be integrated in algorithmic predictions and those where it should not. We evaluate our framework using a data set containing 70,610 surgeries from a large university hospital. We observe that while always integrating human judgment leads to an overall higher accuracy than never integrating human judgment, employing the framework can lead to an even higher accuracy with lower human workload. In our case study planning costs could be reduced by 27% compared to the current status quo. Our results indicate that a cost-sensitive allocation policy that excludes human judgment for task instances that are easy for the algorithm allows humans to focus on medical tasks.

Title: Forecasting the impact of the viral ‘Kia Boys’ social media trend on car thefts to 2050
Authors: P. Jeffrey Brantingham, Craig D. Uchida, Fred Morstatter, George Mohler
Abstract: In 2022, Hyundai Sonatas became the most frequently stolen car model in Los Angeles, mirroring a nationwide trend. The sudden popularity of this mid-sized sedan among car thieves has, according to some, been linked to the viral spread of videos on TikTok and YouTube that showcased a security vulnerability that made certain Kia and Hyundai models easy to steal. These videos later acquired the moniker ‘Kia Boys’ or ‘Kia Challenge.’ In this work, we show that the surge in Hyundai Sonata thefts in Los Angeles was only weakly tied to the ‘Kia Boys’ trend, having begun much earlier during COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns. Any lasting effects of the viral social media trend were fully absorbed into offline car theft dynamics by the time social media interest peaked in 2022. We use historical data on Honda Civics and Toyota Camrys, car models popular among pre-social media generations of car thieves, to develop a model for the offline temporal and spatial evolution of theft preferences. The model suggests that the effects of the ‘Kia Boys’ vulnerability are likely to persist for decades, irrespective of the role social media played in its inception, and that these effects will be increasingly concentrated in low-income communities over time.

Title: Improving the simple average combined forecast via factor-adjusted regularization
Authors: Saerom Lee, Tae-Hwy Lee
Abstract: This paper addresses the forecast combination puzzle — the empirical observation that the simple average forecast combination often outperforms complex weighting schemes — by employing a factor-adjusted regularization framework. In this framework, the simple average is treated as a common factor. We identify and incorporate idiosyncratic components, defined as the deviations of individual forecasts from the simple average. Our approach effectively manages the high correlation among forecasts by focusing on idiosyncratic components that enhance predictive content beyond what is captured by the simple average. Empirical applications in macroeconomic forecasting show that this factor-adjusted approach yields significant accuracy gains over the simple average.

Title: Compositional zero-shot demand forecasting in retail via disentangled demand drivers
Authors: Zefree Lazarus Mayaluri, Sasmita Mishra
Abstract: Retail demand forecasting is central to assortment planning, replenishment, and promotion design, but many global forecasting models are evaluated mainly on configurations similar to those observed during training. This paper studies Compositional Zero-Shot Demand Forecasting (CZDF), where individual demand-driver values are observed in training but selected joint configurations are held out and appear only during evaluation. We propose DD-CZFormer, a driver-disentangled encoder–decoder that represents seasonality, price, promotion, product/category, region, and weather-related drivers in separate latent subspaces and composes them through cross-driver attention. The model is trained with forecasting, contrastive, orthogonality, and masking losses to encourage reusable driver representations. We evaluate DD-CZFormer on M5-CZDF and an anonymised Industrial-CZDF dataset using temporally ordered splits with held-out Region × Product × Month and Region × Product × Promotion configurations. On CZDF splits, DD-CZFormer reduces aggregate WRMSSE by 11.0% on M5-CZDF and 13.8% on Industrial-CZDF relative to the strongest non-proposed baseline in the reported mean results. Median series-level analyses further show lower WRMSSE in all twelve CZDF pairwise baseline comparisons.

Title: The ecological externalities of climate governance: Evidence that solar land use harms bird biodiversity
Authors: Xi Ji, Jie Lin, Pengfei Liu, Xiaoxue Zong
Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) energy is widely promoted as a cornerstone of climate change mitigation, yet its land-intensive deployment may impose unintended ecological costs. This study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of the impact of PV land use on bird biodiversity in China, using high-resolution county-month panel data. Using an instrumental-variable strategy with rich fixed effects, we find that a 1% increase in PV panel area is associated with a 0.659% decline in bird abundance and a 0.473% decline in species richness. Evidence on mechanisms suggests that these effects operate primarily through the loss of surface vegetation, which reduces habitat availability. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the negative impacts are most pronounced on forest land, followed by cropland and grassland. Low-density, large-scale centralized installations have larger adverse effects than more spatially distributed installations, and the estimated impacts are most pronounced in autumn, a period that overlaps with intensive bird migration. Furthermore, we find no evidence that Key Ecological Function Zones mitigate the adverse ecological effects of PV development on birds. Our findings highlight an underappreciated trade-off between renewable energy expansion and biodiversity conservation, and underscore the importance of incorporating ecological externalities into energy planning.

Title: Green debt for nature-based solutions: aligning municipal budgeting and banking practices
Authors: Axelle Vincent, Tara Op de Beeck, Heleen Van Hecke, Tine Compernolle, Jan Cools, Tom Coppens
Abstract: Local governments face growing risks from climate change, which require substantial investments in climate adaptation to safeguard future generations. Nature-based solutions (NBS) have been recognized as a cost-efficient strategy to redevelop public space, to create greener and more climate adaptive urban environments. However, development of NBS is hindered by a lack of financial resources to fully scale up the transformation. To overcome this barrier, literature calls for clear sustainable finance frameworks and business model approaches to include private financing in the development of public NBS. In our research we consider the perceptions of municipalities and banks, as institutional lenders, towards using green debt-financing to finance NBS. We draw on sustainability transitions literature to theorize NBS as a niche innovation within established banking-municipal relations. Using qualitative interviews with Belgian banking experts and urban and financial planners from Flemish cities, we reveal competing financial logics between municipal financing practices and banking requirements, limiting the uptake of green debt for NBS. While NBS are mostly absorbed in traditional municipal deficit financing, this conceals their value and prevents market development. Alternatively, project finance remains difficult due to capacity constraints and differing valuation logics. Emerging sustainable finance frameworks create opportunities but shift administrative burdens onto municipalities. Overall, current practices mainly support NBS to fit and conform, rather than transform established debt-practices. Substantial upscaling of NBS will require changes in both banking practices and municipal financing approaches, including explicit integration of physical climate risk and collective financing mechanisms.

Title: Race-to-the-bottom dynamics in industrial land pricing: Asymmetric effects of China’s 2009 price floor adjustment policy
Authors: Ran Tao, Jialin Yu, Zhejin Zhao
Abstract: Minimum price floors are a common but understudied instrument for regulating industrial land markets in developing economies. We exploit China's 2009 adjustment of minimum industrial land prices, which lowered the minimum land price in some counties and raised it in others. Combining parcel-level land transactions with county characteristics in a difference-in-differences design, we find a striking asymmetry: easing counties experienced a 9.15% decline in industrial land prices and a 23.12% expansion in transferred area, whereas tightening counties showed no detectable change. The asymmetry reflects the floor's initial binding status: it was binding in easing counties, where competition for mobile manufacturing capital pushed prices down and expanded land supply, but non-binding in tightening counties, where the raised floor either stayed below market prices or was offset through rebates and subsidies. Easing counties also gained 15.53% more large-scale industrial enterprises relative to the sample mean and 7.90% in fiscal revenue, yet new land sales concentrated in low- and medium-low-tech, land-intensive sectors, a pattern that persisted through 2022 with no shift toward higher-tech industries. Relaxing a binding industrial land price floor thus brings short-run gains in firm entry and fiscal revenue but leaves these counties specialized in low-tech industries, consistent with race-to-the-bottom competition operating through industrial land pricing.

Title: Beyond the early era of EVs: Evidence from the staggered rollout of the HOV lane network in California
Authors: Eric Avis, Jing Li, Katalin Springel
Abstract: Local policies like high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lane exemptions play an important role in encouraging electric vehicle (EV) adoption, a key component of climate programs. Using tract-level vehicle registrations and detailed data on HOV lane openings from 2012 to 2024, we study the causal effect of HOV policies on EV adoption in California. We find that HOV exemptions significantly increased EV uptake, with effects that were stronger in later years as EV technology and markets advanced. The impact is also greater in more congested areas with longer commutes and concentrated in higher-income tracts, highlighting both the effectiveness and distributional implications of HOV incentives.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Local charger availability and electric vehicle adoption: Evidence from Norway
Authors: Costanza Cincotta, Øyvind Thomassen
Abstract: We examine the effect of local public charging infrastructure on electric vehicle (EV) adoption using microdata from Norway between 2010 and 2023.
