Such information could be extracted from an analysis of history or a forecast of the future. In fact, the financial markets are driven mainly by the expectations of market investors and by exogenous sources. An explicit way for market investors to make clear their expectations about a certain asset is to define the implied volatility of the options that are written on that asset. Moreover, the literature proposed tools that generate the state price density of the underlying by observing the implied volatility of the options. The combination of the implied volatilities and the state price density can give deep insight into investors’ expectations about the short-term movements of the underlying and, thus, can represent a reliable source of information to perform a market timing strategy or to select a portfolio for a risk-neutral investor with a short-term horizon. To avoid adjusting the procedure for dividend-paying assets, we develop our approach considering market price indexes. This approach constitutes a completely new technique to establish both a market timing strategy and a ranking among the considered indexes. In the empirical analysis, we considered both the market timing problem for a single index and the portfolio selection problem when multiple indexes are available.

Title: Streaming platform games: construction of the core
Authors: Bas Dietzenbacher, Iago Núñez Lugilde, Estela Sánchez-Rodríguez
Abstract: Abstract Streaming platforms offer subscribers unlimited access to content against a periodic subscription fee. To address the problem of dividing the revenues of the platform in a stable way among the content creators, we model these situations as cooperative streaming platform games and analyze the structure of the core. In particular, we study the construction of the core of a streaming platform game from the cores of its so-called marginal games, dominated games, and utopia games.

Title: Alumni relationships and judicial bias
Authors: Tianwang Liu, David Zhang
Affiliations: Independent Researcher San Francisco California USA; Jones Graduate School of Business Rice University Houston Texas USA
Abstract: Abstract We examine whether law school alumni relationships between lawyers and judges are correlated with case outcomes. We show that, in the context of medical malpractice lawsuits filed in Florida, having a plaintiff's attorney who attended the same law school as a randomly assigned judge increases the chances of recovery by about 2 percentage points. We further show that the effect is more pronounced between lawyers and judges with a larger age gap, consistent with an age‐dependent effect. Our results suggest that case outcomes can be biased when lawyers and judges are part of the same affinity group.

Title: Road to resilience: Floods, highways and Indian informal manufacturing
Authors: Dixit Poudel, Munisamy Gopinath
Abstract: Road infrastructure is widely recognized as a driver of economic development, but can it also aid in disaster resilience? This study addresses the resilience question in the Indian context by examining the output effects of dual and staggered treatments: national highway construction – the Golden Quadrilateral, and the North-South and East-West highways – and extreme flood exposure. Employing a production-theoretic framework, this study focuses on India’s informal manufacturing, the largest in the world without any formal safety nets. It combines geospatially matched, staggered flood exposure data from the Dartmouth Flood Observatory with phased highway rollout timelines from the National Highways Authority of India and repeated cross-section plant-level survey data (1990–2016). Exploiting quasi-random variation in the timing of flood exposure and road construction, a stacked difference-in-differences design is implemented, matching treated districts to future-treated counterparts. Results show that floods significantly reduce gross output and value added, while access to completed highway segments nearly offsets the average 8 percent flood-related output loss through higher output and reduced input expenditures. These effects are magnified for plants that own transport assets, highlighting a complementarity between internal logistics and external infrastructure. Off-highway plants exhibit similar resilience only when they possess transport assets. Heterogeneity analysis by market orientation reveals that resilience benefits are higher among non-tradable industries through local market stabilization. These findings reveal that roads are not only engines of development but also critical to disaster resilience. Designing infrastructure with dual function— development and resilience —is essential for building a climate-smart and resilient economy.

Title: Operational metrics in derivatives adoption: Evidence from China's chemical industry
Authors: Wubo Zhang, Qi Zhang, Gangshu (George) Cai
Abstract: ABSTRACT Manufacturers face severe raw-material price volatility. Inventory represents both a core operational asset and their primary source of risk exposure. The operations-finance interface literature links these operational realities to financial hedging. However, large-sample evidence on what drives the decision remains scarce. Drawing on 289 listed Chinese chemical firms from 2016 to 2022, we address this gap. We examine how operational exposure, measured by inventory level and inventory turnover, compares against traditional financial determinants. Specifically, we evaluate their relative impact on firms’ derivations adoption. Our empirical strategy integrates probit estimation, moderation analysis, and k-means clustering. We find that operational metrics are the primary drivers of derivatives adoption. Inventory level and turnover outweigh traditional financial indicators, including liquidity, leverage, and growth. Among financial factors, only pre-tax profit remains consistently significant. Furthermore, the firm’s financial capacity moderates these effects. Operational exposure dominates the hedging decisions of cash-constrained firms. Conversely, well-capitalized firms hedge more selectively. These findings remain robust to rigorous endogeneity tests and controls for geographic heterogeneity and pandemic shocks. Building on these empirical patterns, we develop a managerial decision framework. This framework maps a firm’s operational exposure and financial capacity to specific hedging stances and derivative instruments. Finally, this study contributes large-sample empirical evidence on the relative importance of operational versus financial drivers of derivatives adoption, bridging the operations-finance interface with industrial practice.

Title: Farmer self-returning or outsourcing? An agricultural product supply chain network operation and straw returning mode selection strategies
Authors: Caiquan Duan, Shan Liu, Fengmin Yao, Yan Sun
Abstract: Ensuring sustainable operation of agricultural product supply chain networks while safeguarding cultivated land is essential to advancing agricultural green transformation. This study integrates straw returning into an agricultural product supply chain network, recognizing its role in enhancing soil organic matter and reducing reliance on chemical fertilizer. Drawing on noncooperative game theory and variational inequality, an agricultural product supply chain network equilibrium model is developed under two straw returning modes: farmer self-returning and outsourcing returning. The equilibrium results and straw returning mode selection strategies are explored under the influence of single- and dual-factor scenarios, including straw returning subsidy, outsourcing fee, chemical fertilizer cost, under-fulfillment penalty, and straw nutrient release rate. Results show that increases in the other factors generally promote the returning rate under both returning modes, whereas an increase in the straw nutrient release rate does not boost the returning rate under the outsourcing mode. However, their impacts on profits differ significantly. Comparative analyses indicate that both farmers and retailers gain greater profits when straw returning is implemented by other-tier entities. Nevertheless, the preferable straw returning mode in terms of whole system profits and the straw returning rate mainly depends on the interactions among the above factors. Notably, the outsourcing returning mode proves to be the more viable strategy for achieving a win-win situation between whole system profits and cultivated land protection in most scenarios. In contrast, only when the subsidy level is low and the chemical fertilizer cost is high does the self-returning mode become the dominant strategy.

Title: A note on the asymptotic unbiasedness of Akaike information criterion
Authors: Yong Li, Zhou Wu, Jun Yu, Tao Zeng
Abstract: This note revisits the standard derivation of the asymptotic unbiasedness of Akaike information criterion (AIC). The existing literature has shown that AIC is an asymptotically unbiased estimator of the predictive risk. However, there is a technical issue in these justifications. In this note, we bridge the gap and establish the asymptotic unbiasedness of AIC under certain regularity conditions, which are applicable in various scenarios. Our result suggests that AIC should be used with caution if the moment conditions on the parameter estimators may not hold. When model misspecification is allowed, our result can be extended to Takeuchi information criterion (TIC).

Title: When patents become collateral: Intellectual property financialization and corporate venture capital investment
Authors: Hao Zhang, Lina Shi
Abstract: This paper examines whether patent-backed financing reforms affect firms’ external technology acquisition strategies. Using the staggered rollout of China’s Patent Pledge Financing Pilot (PPFP) across cities, we employ a difference-in-differences design to study its effect on corporate venture capital (CVC) investment. We find that PPFP significantly increases firms’ CVC activity, with the effect concentrated in high-tech CVC, and weaker for state-owned enterprises. These findings are consistent with the view that increasing the financial value of patent assets strengthens firms’ incentives to engage in technology-oriented CVC for external technology sourcing.

Title: Annual overseas migration and housing markets: Evidence from Australian neighborhoods
Authors: Marcel Peruffo, Madeleine Check
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of net overseas migration (NOM) on residential property marketsusing annual, neighborhood-level data for Australia. We leverage an instrumental variableapproach based on historical immigrant settlement patterns to isolate plausibly exogenousvariation in migration flows. We find that a 1% increase in NOM, as a share of the local population,raises unit rents and prices by 5.0% and 1.3%, respectively, and increases house rents by3.6%. These effects are more pronounced in areas with low rates of dwelling approvals, suggestingthat housing supply constraints amplify the response of prices and rents to migration.In contrast, house prices decline by 1.3%, a pattern concentrated in older neighborhoods andconsistent with displacement dynamics, for which we present supporting evidence.

Title: Conformity and silence: Experimental evidence on social pressure and free speech
Authors: Juan S. Morales, Margaret Samahita
Abstract: This paper studies the public expression of opinions on polarized topics (race and gender). In a series of pre-registered online experiments conducted in the United States in 2021 and 2023, we elicited participants’ views on these topics and their willingness to publish their views online. We find an asymmetric U-shaped relationship between ideological stance and willingness to share views publicly: moderates were least willing to speak up, willingness rose toward both ideological extremes and was highest among respondents with progressive views. Participants also perceived publicly expressed opinions as more left-leaning than underlying private opinions. A priming treatment highlighting the risk of negative social media backlash had modest and statistically insignificant effects. A social-information treatment informing respondents that many others were willing to speak up significantly reduced self-censorship.

Title: An equity-constrained two-stage distributionally robust optimization model for urban disaster preparation
Authors: Xihui Wang, Zikai Chen, Yu Fan
Abstract: Natural disasters are becoming more frequent and complex and are characterized by greater uncertainty. Urban areas are especially vulnerable because high population density and concentrated infrastructure can amplify disaster impacts. Two-stage distributionally robust optimization is a widely adopted method to deal with the uncertainty in disaster logistics problems. However, most existing studies lack precise demand assessment and general equity concerns. To fill the research gap, we first propose a more precise demand assessment method with the consideration of urban environmental information (e.g., fine-grained urban building features), and then incorporate an explicit equity constraint into the second-stage resource allocation. Through applying affine decision rules and copositive programming reformulations, we solve this complex random recourse problem by deriving a computationally tractable approximation. With a numerical experiment based on real-world data in Hefei, China, we find that our approach outperforms the deterministic model and sample average approximation model in both average cost and robustness. Compared to the model without equity consideration, our solution narrows community satisfaction rates gaps with a marginal cost increase and enhances urban resilience by increasing pre-positioned inventory. This work provides a decision-making tool for achieving equitable and resilient urban disaster logistics.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Robust trajectory optimization for communication-constrained drone logistics under wind and payload uncertainty
Authors: Xia Zhou, Jianpeng Ding, Yuanbo Li
Abstract: The rapid expansion of drone delivery services has created an urgent need for planning tools that can guarantee mission feasibility under physical uncertainties and strict communication constraints. However, existing approaches treat these factors in isolation or rely on deterministic assumptions that fail at deployment, leaving a critical gap between nominal planning and operational reliability. Motivated by this gap, we propose a unified robust optimization framework for multi-drone pickup and delivery systems that simultaneously addresses wind disturbances, payload variability, and strict communication rate requirements. Our model integrates aerodynamic power consumption, Shannon-capacity constraints, leg-based budgeted wind uncertainty sets, and polyhedral payload uncertainty sets into a single mixed-integer second-order cone program (MISOCP). Theoretically, we prove that the robust flight speed constraint admits an exact SOCP representation and derive exact linear duals for the payload constraints via strong duality. Because spatial coupling constraints invalidate traditional decomposition approaches, we design a multi-start hybrid (MSH) algorithm. This algorithm employs a stochastic master problem with Log-normal perturbations to generate diverse routing skeletons and a continuous SOCP subproblem for rigorous physical feasibility verification, coupled with a bottleneck-directed local search. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate substantial performance improvements over existing methods. Compared to exact solvers, the MSH algorithm significantly reduces computation time while maintaining near-optimal solution quality. Crucially, for large-scale instances where exact solvers completely fail, it remains a non-trivial method capable of producing feasible solutions. These results confirm that the framework bridges the tractability gap between exact optimization and heuristic dispatch, establishing it as a highly practical tool for real-world drone fleet deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A dual-channel model integrating wavelet denoising and multi-head self-attention mechanism for predicting train travel times of China-Europe railway express
Authors: Yongxiang Zhang, Liting Gu, Jingwei Guo, Xin Hu, Xu Yan, Zhen-Song Chen
Abstract: The China-Europe Railway Express (CRE) is an important logistics corridor linking China and Europe. However, due to various influencing factors during transportation, existing prediction models generally fail to correctly represent the complex nonlinear spatio-temporal aspects of the CRE train travel times, leading to incorrect train travel time predictions. To overcome this challenge, this study proposes a Multi-scale Wavelet Denoising (MWD)-Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) dual-channel model incorporating a Multi-head Self-attention Mechanism (MHSA) (MWD-CNN-GRU-MHSA) to forecast CRE train travel times. The MWD is first employed to extract features and reduce the noise in the historical train travel times, aiming to improve data quality. Then, a dual-channel model combining CNN and GRU is established, where the CNN learns local spatial patterns and the GRU handles time-dependent features, processing the input time series in parallel. MHSA is introduced into the dual-channel model to flexibly allocate weights on salient fused features derived from the two branches. A series of comparative experiments are conducted to evaluate the proposed method based on real-world CRE round-trip train travel time data. The experimental findings show that the MWD-CNN-GRU-MHSA framework outperforms thirteen mainstream baseline models in forecasting performance and generalization. Specifically, the MWD-CNN-GRU-MHSA model exhibits robust performance in CRE train travel time estimation, with root mean square error (RMSE) of 7.516 hours, mean absolute error (MAE) of 5.053 hours, mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 1.259%, and coefficient of determination ( R 2) of 0.907. In conclusion, the MWD-CNN-GRU-MHSA model demonstrates strong stability and robustness, with good adaptability to complex transportation data. It offers reliable technical support for rail dispatching optimization and CRE service quality improvement.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Truck-drone routing problem under time-dependent traffic congestion: A novel variable neighborhood search metaheuristic
Authors: Shaorui Zhou, Xiaorui Liu, Jihong Chen, Lingxiao Wu, Zhou Xu, Min Zhao
Abstract: Urban last-mile delivery faces growing demand, stricter delivery-duration requirements, and persistent road congestion. Truck-drone coordination offers a promising response, but most existing studies simplify either truck travel conditions or drone endurance by assuming constant truck speeds or fixed drone flight capability. This paper studies a truck-drone routing problem with time-dependent traffic congestion and load-dependent drone endurance, termed TDC-LDE-TDRP. We formulate a mixed-integer linear programming model that jointly optimizes truck routes, drone flights, customer assignment, and service timing, while capturing time-dependent truck travel and nonlinear payload-dependent drone energy consumption. To solve large-scale instances, we develop PRS-VNS, a novel variable neighborhood search metaheuristic that integrates parallel exploration, structured restart, and decomposition-based re-optimization to improve search stability and solution quality. Computational experiments show that PRS-VNS outperforms benchmark heuristics in solution quality, robustness, and convergence behavior. Using real customer locations and road congestion data from Shenzhen, China, we further show that truck-drone coordination is economically viable and can mitigate the cost impact of congestion. The results also reveal that the marginal value of drones depends jointly on delivery duration and congestion intensity, that jointly modeling TDC and LDE produces a positive complementary effect, and that improved drone endurance may alter the coordinated delivery structure.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Credit-driven quality coordination in cross-regional fresh-food supply chains: A tripartite dynamic game and policy optimization
Authors: Chao Zhao, Yongmei Chi, Nini Gao, Shunshu Bao
Abstract: Cross-regional fresh-food supply chains expand market access, but they also make quality governance more challenging as product deterioration, transportation delays, information asymmetry, and fragmented regulation interact over time. This study examines how credit supervision can be integrated with supply-chain contracts and public policy to coordinate quality investment, logistics timeliness, and fiscal sustainability. We develop a tripartite differential game model involving a manufacturer, a retailer, and a government regulator, in which product quality, corporate credit, and policy instruments co-evolve as state variables. The Markov perfect equilibrium is approximated using relaxed best-response iteration with GPOPS-II. The numerical results yield four insights into supply-chain governance. First, under baseline calibration, the effective decision cycle is approximately 11 days; longer planning horizons sharply reduce profits and welfare because logistics and quality-adjustment frictions accumulate over time. Second, quality improvement and credit accumulation reinforce each other, but credit ratings respond with a lag, making early operational decisions particularly important. Third, subsidies and penalties are effective only within appropriate ranges: weak penalties fail to deter firms’ low-quality behavior, whereas excessive subsidy effectiveness crowds out firms’ own quality-improvement and freshness-preservation efforts. Fourth, upstream quality improvement generates downstream spillovers through demand and logistics-cost channels, making government welfare more sensitive to source-side quality efficiency than to several downstream policy parameters. These findings suggest that regulators should adopt strong early intervention with gradual withdrawal, while firms should align quality-improvement investment, freshness-preservation effort, and transportation-cycle decisions within the perishability window of fresh-food logistics.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Low-altitude delivery path planning for unmanned aerial vehicles based on optimal energy consumption
Authors: Xiaowen Sha, Shuang Qiu, Zhihao Xu
Abstract: In low-altitude logistics, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) energy consumption exhibits strong nonlinear characteristics due to complex micro-meteorology and dynamic payloads. Traditional geometric routing algorithms struggle to maximize true endurance. This paper proposes a global energy-optimal path planning framework for micro-meteorological environments. First, an AttnHeadLSTM network integrating physical coupled features and temporal attention is constructed to capture the high-dimensional hysteresis effects of energy consumption. Second, a steady-state sequence replication mechanism and a spatial cost tensor map are introduced to seamlessly embed the deep kinematic model into a heading-aware A* search. Under predefined wind field scenarios and payload loads, experimental results verify the framework’s capability to autonomously formulate scenario-adaptive optimization tactics, opting for wind-assisted detours when unloaded and straight trajectories at maximum payload. The approach achieves up to 41.05 % energy savings, offering an effective energy optimization method for mission planning in low-altitude logistics UAVs. Open-source link: https://github.com/Shaxiaowen/UAV-Path-Planning .
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Take it to the streets: Spatial and sociodemographic determinants of e-commerce demand in the Netherlands
Authors: Sanne Wolf, Paul Buijs, Dirk Pieter van Donk
Abstract: E-commerce has transformed freight systems by shifting goods distribution from a limited number of retail locations to millions of individual households. This shift poses challenges for transport policy and practice, because demand for goods is increasingly generated in residential areas not designed for high levels of delivery activity. At the same time, existing research offers no clear consensus on how sociodemographic and spatial characteristics shape e-commerce demand, limiting the ability of transport and land-use planners to anticipate where delivery activity is most likely to arise. Using unique fine-grained e-commerce order data from the Netherlands, combined with fine-grained sociodemographic and spatial characteristics, this study examines how e-commerce demand varies across space. We model non-linear relationships and examine whether these relationships differ across five levels of urbanisation. The results show that demand is highest in areas with larger shares of middle-aged and middle-educated residents and rises with income at a diminishing rate. Demand is also lower in more urbanised areas and highest in rural areas. Beyond urbanisation, demand is higher where many stores are located nearby, but lower where residents have many retail options across the wider surrounding area. By showing that several relationships are non-linear and depend on the spatial scale at which retail access is measured, the results help reconcile mixed evidence and provide a basis for anticipating where freight activity is likely to concentrate. The findings support more targeted transport and land-use planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: An exact pruned route-enumeration and set-partitioning approach for the multi-pickup and delivery problem with time windows
Authors: Conor Kikkert, Michael Forbes
Abstract: The multi-pickup and delivery problem with time windows (MPDPTW) arises in on-demand logistics applications where each delivery corresponds to one or more pickups, all of which must be completed before the delivery. Existing exact methods for the MPDPTW typically rely on large mixed-integer programming formulations with extensive branching and cutting. This paper proposes PRE-SP, an exact pruned route-enumeration and set-partitioning framework that evaluates candidate single-vehicle request subsets a priori , discards infeasible subsets using pruning rules that preserve exactness, and then solves a set-partitioning master problem over the resulting feasible routes. Computational results on the 120 classical MPDPTW benchmark instances show that PRE-SP solves 116 instances to proven optimality within a 1-hour time limit, and all 120 when the time limit is extended to 24 hours for the remaining four cases, outperforming existing exact approaches on this benchmark set. Additional analysis of the explored search space shows how instance size, request length, and time-window structure affect the practical behaviour of the enumeration procedure. Experiments on 30 larger 200-node instances provide additional insight into the scalability limits of the framework. Overall, the results show that route enumeration with exactness-preserving pruning, combined with set partitioning, is a competitive exact solution framework for the MPDPTW on the benchmark classes studied.

Title: Coupling-aware destruction with large-language-model guidance for energy-efficient blocking hybrid flow shop scheduling
Authors: Shikun Chen
Abstract: The blocking hybrid flow shop with sequence-dependent setup times and time-of-use electricity pricing presents a bi-objective scheduling problem that requires simultaneous minimization of makespan and energy cost. Blocking constraints create hidden couplings between these two objectives, where a single constraint affects makespan and energy cost through different mechanisms, and the dominant coupling effect varies across regions of the Pareto front. Standard evolutionary baselines do not explicitly model this region-specific coupling structure. Our approach embeds a coupling-aware iterated greedy algorithm within a decomposition-based multi-objective framework, where a large language model (LLM) serves as a constraint-objective coupling analyzer. Rather than replace evolutionary operators, the LLM identifies which coupling dominates in each Pareto region and provides subproblem-specific destruction–construction strategies through a three-level phase-adaptive architecture. In the tested configuration, this design uses roughly thirty-one to forty-three LLM invocation opportunities per run. Computational experiments on adapted benchmark instances and steelmaking-continuous casting instances with real scheduling structure and representative energy parameters show that the proposed method attains higher hypervolume and lower inverted generational distance than nine comparison algorithms, including non-LLM variants with the same destruction-mode action space.

Title: Machine learning for detecting collusion and capacity withholding in wholesale electricity markets
Authors: Jeremy Proz, Martin Huber, Ivan Marin
Abstract: Collusion and capacity withholding in electricity wholesale markets are important mechanisms of market manipulation. This study applies a refined machine learning-based cartel detection algorithm to two cartel cases in the Italian electricity market and evaluates its out-of-sample performance. Specifically, we consider an ensemble machine learning method that uses statistical screens constructed from the offer price distribution as predictors for the incidence of collusion among electricity providers in specific regions. We propose novel screens related to the capacity-withholding behavior of electricity providers and find that including such screens derived from the day-ahead spot market as predictors can improve cartel detection. We find that, under complete cartels - where collusion in a tender presumably involves all suppliers - the method correctly classifies up to roughly 95% of tenders in our data as collusive or competitive, improving classification accuracy compared to using only previously available screens. However, when trained on larger datasets including non-cartel members and applying algorithms tailored to detect incomplete cartels, the previously existing screens are sufficient to achieve 98% accuracy, and the addition of our newly proposed capacity-withholding screens does not further improve performance. Overall, this study highlights the promising potential of supervised machine learning techniques for detecting and dismantling cartels in electricity markets.

Title: Private ownership and pricing: Evidence from the Swedish district heating sector
Authors: Erik Lundin
Abstract: I examine the pricing behavior of municipal and private firms in the unregulated Swedish district heating market, characterized by geographically bounded local monopoly networks. Nearly all firms employ two-part pricing. Conditional on exogenous cost factors, private ownership is associated with a fixed-fee premium equivalent to 6.5 percent of the municipal average total price. Consistent with standard monopoly theory, the price difference is concentrated in the fixed fee, while the estimated difference in the unit price is statistically insignificant. The estimated total-price premium is nevertheless smaller, because the point estimate for the unit price is negative. Further, there is suggestive evidence that foreign-owned private firms charge an additional fixed-fee premium relative to domestically owned private firms, although this estimate is less precise. A descriptive analysis of financial statements indicates that private firms report higher profit margins, despite municipal firms being legally required to operate in a business-like manner. These findings are consistent with private firms exercising more market power than public firms in this market, so that the resulting upward pressure on prices appears to outweigh any downward effects from the potential cost efficiencies associated with privatization.

Title: Tracking sustainability dynamics in EU transport sector: Bayesian latent change-score analysis study
Authors: Alexandru Constăngioară, Olimpia Ban, Mirela Bucurean, Adriana Mirela Constăngioară
Abstract: This dataset contains harmonized longitudinal data for the EU-27 covering the period 2007–2023, designed to support empirical analysis of transport-sector greenhouse gas emissions dynamics. It includes transport-related greenhouse gas emissions per capita (GHG), road freight activity measured in tonne-kilometres (TK), and Logistics Performance Index (LPI) scores. GHG emissions and freight activity data were sourced from Eurostat, population data from the UN World Population Prospects (via Our World in Data), and LPI scores from the World Bank. The dataset integrates these sources into a consistent country-level panel structure. All variables were log-transformed and standardized prior to analysis to address skewness and scale differences. Time alignment was performed to match the availability of LPI waves, resulting in harmonized observation periods suitable for longitudinal and latent change score modeling. The dataset includes the processed wide-format file (DATA_wide.xlsx) used in the empirical analysis, along with associated metadata required for replication. It is intended for use in studies on transport emissions, logistics performance, sustainability transitions, and dynamic panel or structural equation modeling.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Correction
Abstract: Article title: Innovative approaches in reshaping the supply chain for societal challengesAuthors: Fornasiero, R., and Zangiacomi, A.Journal: Production Planning & ControlDOI: https://doi.org/10.10...

Title: Modelling and multi-objective scheduling of an energy-efficient hybrid flow shop with multiple heating-forging cycles
Authors: Chai Bingbing, Zhang Yongjun, Sun Yanguang, Gu Jiachen, Li Shaobin
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing; Automation Research Institute of Metallurgical Industry Co., Ltd.
Abstract: This study addresses the characteristics of forging production scheduling and investigates an energy-efficient hybrid flow shop scheduling problem considering multiple heating-forging cycles (EEHFSP-MHFC). The problem is formulated as a multi-objective optimisation problem with two objectives: minimising the makespan and minimising the total energy consumption. A mathematical description model is proposed by considering the characteristics of forging production, including multi-resource constraints, mixed production modes, and multiple heating-forging cycles. A dual-archive hybrid cultural genetic algorithm with knowledge transfer (DAHCGA) is developed to solve the scheduling problem, building upon the Memetic Algorithm framework and NSGA-II. It adopts two hybrid initialisation rules and a dual-archive mechanism to achieve coordinated optimisation of solution-set convergence and diversity. The effectiveness of the proposed model and algorithm is demonstrated through experiments on instances of different scales, as well as comparative analyses and numerical evaluations against alternative algorithms.

Title: Lagrangian framework fusion with deep learning for steelmaking-continuous casting scheduling
Authors: Liyi Yu, Xirang Hao, Liangliang Sun, Zhenghao Song, Mengshuang Li, Yunpeng Li, Natalia M. Matsveichuk, Yuri N. Sotskov
Affiliations: Northeastern University; Belarusian State Agrarian Technical University; National Academy of Sciences of Belarus
Abstract: Steelmaking–continuous casting (SCC) production scheduling is a critical step for optimising charge combinations, enhancing process compactness, and reducing energy consumption, thereby influencing the production efficiency and economic benefits of steel enterprises. However, the small batch sizes and extensive product variety inherent in modern steelmaking substantially increase scheduling complexity, making it difficult to rapidly generate feasible production plans. Therefore, we incorporate deep learning (DL) into the surrogate Lagrangian relaxation (SLR) framework to accelerate the acquisition of scheduling schemes by replacing the costly process of accurately solving subproblems with predicting ‘good-enough’ subproblem solutions. First, we propose a novel pointer network (GDPN) that integrates gated recurrent unit (GRU) with dot-product attention (DPA) to predict subproblem solutions in the Lagrange decomposition-coordination process. Subsequently, a dual-phase masking (DM) mechanism is developed during both the training and inference of GDPN to enforce the feasibility of the surrogate subproblem constraints caused by the continuous casting process in SCC. Finally, extensive numerical experiments and an industrial study with different scales demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DM-GDPN-SLR method.

Title: A comprehensive sustainability-based framework for locating net-zero manufacturing facilities
Authors: Melike Cari, Betul Sasmazturk, Ertugrul Ayyildiz, Betul Kara
Affiliations: Karadeniz Technical University; Hasan Kalyoncu University; Industrial Policy and Development Center, Istanbul Ticaret University, Istanbul, Türkiye
Abstract: Achieving net-zero manufacturing requires robust strategies that balance environmental, economic, and operational priorities while aligning with global sustainability targets. Integrating advanced decision-making methodologies with comprehensive sustainability frameworks is crucial for guiding climate-neutral industrial transformation. This study develops a modular decision-aid model, namely the Net-Zero Manufacturing Location Decision-Aid Model, for evaluating net-zero manufacturing facility locations from a production-system and logistics-readiness perspective. The model systematically incorporates ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) and HSE (Health, Safety, Environment) criteria and operationalises them through Picture Fuzzy Stepwise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis (PiF-SWARA) and Picture Fuzzy Additive Ratio Assessment (PiF-ARAS). Expert judgments are aggregated through picture fuzzy logic, capturing uncertainty and subjectivity inherent in real-world decision environments. Results demonstrate that environmental and safety dimensions are the most influential factors in site selection for net-zero manufacturing, while governance and health play a moderate role, and social criteria are relatively less impactful. Sensitivity analysis confirms the stability and robustness of the model across various weighting scenarios. The proposed framework provides actionable insights for decision-makers and policymakers aiming to enable climate-neutral manufacturing investments. This study contributes a scalable, transparent, and replicable methodology, supporting the strategic alignment of industrial development with circular economy principles and smart production technologies.

Title: Unrelated parallel machines with release times and job rejection
Authors: Jianming Dong, Weitian Tong, Yao Xu, Kaizhou Gao
Affiliations: Contemporary Business and Trade Research Center, Zhejiang Gongshang University. Hangzhou; Georgia Southern University; Macau University of Science and Technology
Abstract: We study the problem of scheduling on unrelated parallel machines with release times and job rejection. We design a simple greedy algorithm that achieves an (m+1)-approximation ratio, where m is the number of machines. We further develop a linear-programming-rounding algorithm with a 3-approximation guarantee. Then we present a pseudo-polynomial time dynamic programming algorithm that computes exact optimal solutions. Building upon this framework, we develop a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) that combines scaling with dynamic programming to produce (1+ε)-approximate solutions when m is a fixed constant. Notably, when m=1 our FPTAS achieves a running time of O(n2/ε), improving upon the earlier O(n3/ε)-time FPTAS of Zhang et al. [European Journal of Operational Research, 198, 975 (2009)]. To evaluate the effectiveness of our methods, we design extensive computational experiments. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that develops both exact and approximation algorithms for unrelated machine scheduling with release times and job rejection.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Incorporating data drift to perform survival analysis on credit risk
Authors: Jianwei Peng, Stefan Lessmann
Affiliations: Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin; Bucharest University of Economic Studies
Abstract: Survival analysis has become a standard approach for modelling time to default by time-varying covariates in credit risk. Unlike most existing methods that implicitly assume a stationary data-generating process, in practise, mortgage portfolios are exposed to various forms of data drift caused by changing borrower behaviour, macroeconomic conditions, policy regimes and so on. This study investigates the impact of data drift on survival-based credit risk models and proposes a dynamic joint modelling framework to improve robustness under non-stationary environments. The proposed model integrates a longitudinal behavioural marker derived from balance dynamics with a discrete-time hazard formulation, combined with landmark one-hot encoding and isotonic calibration. Three types of data drift (sudden, incremental and recurring) are simulated and analysed on mortgage loan datasets from Freddie Mac. The experimental evidence shows that the proposed landmark-based joint model consistently outperforms classical survival models, tree-based drift-adaptive learners and gradient boosting methods in terms of discrimination and calibration across all drift scenarios, which confirms the superiority of our model design.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Sustainable supplier selection in the textile and apparel industry: an integrated fuzzy multi-criteria approach
Authors: Yunxiang Ge, Zhongyi Zhu, Zhebin Xue, Guangtao Chang
Affiliations: College of Textile and Clothing Engineering, Soochow University
Abstract: Sustainable supplier selection in the textile and apparel industry is hindered by generic criteria and the difficulty of balancing expert cognitive efficiency with ranking robustness. This study develops a textile-specific indicator system with 23 indicators, screened from 42 candidates via the Content Validity Ratio (CVR) by 13 industry experts, and proposes an integrated fuzzy MCDM framework combining Fuzzy Best-Worst Method (Fuzzy-BWM) and Triangular Fuzzy Number-MULTIMOORA (TFN-MULTIMOORA). In a case study of a Chinese apparel trading enterprise and six core suppliers, the economic dimension received the highest weight (0.453), followed by the social (0.279) and environmental (0.267) dimensions, while product quality (0.068) and strategic decision-making and execution ability (0.058) were the most influential sub-indicators. Supplier S3 ranked first across the Ratio System, Reference Point and Full Multiplicative Form. Cross-method validation with four alternative fuzzy MCDM methods yielded a mean Spearman rank correlation of 0.903, and sensitivity analysis under 16 weight variation scenarios produced a mean Spearman correlation of 0.966. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides a textile-specific, cognitively efficient and robust alternative to existing sustainable supplier selection approaches.

Title: Fault root cause tracing in complex mechanical systems via probabilistic logic and reinforcement learning
Authors: Rui He, Xin Ye, Yujie Wei, Haiyan Xu, Zhi-Sheng Ye
Affiliations: School of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Center for System Reliability and Safety, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Department of Industrial Systems Engineering and Management, National University of Singapore; Joint Laboratory of Data Science and Business Intelligence, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics; School of Statistics and Data Science, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics; China COSCO Shipping Corporation Limited; Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing, Agency for Science, Technology and Research
Abstract: When a failure occurs in a large-scale mechanical system such as a marine engine, the maintenance team typically conducts a sequence of inspections on various system components to progressively gather fault information and ultimately localize the root cause, a process known as fault root cause tracing. This process requires the inspection sequence to be planned efficiently. We formulate fault root cause tracing as a Markov decision process (MDP). This MDP is challenging to solve as its system dynamics are unknown. To capture the logical relationships between symptoms and root causes, we construct a Markov logic network (MLN) by integrating historical fault data with expert knowledge from failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) tables. Parameters in the MLN are estimated using a variational expectation-maximization algorithm, in which the variational distribution is flexibly parameterized by a neural network. The constructed MLN facilitates the inspection sequencing for fault root cause tracing problems. The MLN-based reasoning enables efficient root cause inference by updating the posterior probabilities of root causes as new information is obtained through sequential inspections. We integrate the constructed MLN into a reinforcement learning framework to train a policy for fault root cause tracing problems. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through both simulation experiments and a real-world case study involving starting air system failures of harbor tug engines. Our method outperforms benchmark approaches in both inference accuracy and inspection efficiency.

Title: Statistical monitoring of censored lifetime data: Insights into two special alarm phenomena
Authors: Chenglong Li, Xun Xiao, Piao Chen
Affiliations: School of Management, Northwestern Polytechnical University; Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Otago; ZJUI Institute, Zhejiang University
Abstract: Monitoring lifetime variation of mass-produced products is a central objective of process quality control in industrial settings. Unlike classical quality-control problems, sequential monitoring of lifetime data poses a unique challenge because failure-time information must be obtained through life tests, which inevitably introduce time delays. This paper delves into the monitoring of type-I censored lifetime data, focusing on two previously underexplored alarm phenomena: competing alarms and predetermined alarms. They have distinct generation mechanisms: competing alarms exhibit a “later comes, first alarms” pattern, in which a sample drawn later may complete its life test earlier, and the earliest among all alarm-triggering samples ultimately determines the detection delay; predetermined alarms occur when an alarm can be anticipated before a sample’s life test is completed, serving as a proactive mechanism to expedite decision-making. We develop statistical models to characterize the underlying generation mechanisms of both phenomena. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we evaluate their occurrence probabilities and effects on control-chart performance metrics. Our findings reveal that although incorporating these alarms is expected to reduce the out-of-control average time to signal, predetermined alarms yield notable improvements in certain cases, whereas competing alarms have no discernible effect on the optimal censoring time. Two industrial examples further illustrate the practical benefits of accounting for these alarms. Our research offers actionable insights for decision-making in the statistical monitoring of censored lifetime data.

Title: Cancer clinical decision support system: the case of osteosarcoma stages recognition with gene data
Authors: Yuchen Wang, Ying Cao, Xianghui Peng, Robert Pavur
Abstract: Genetic testing has emerged as a powerful tool for cancer diagnosis, but its widespread adoption is constrained by challenges, including the lack of standardized protocols and insufficient genetic counseling. A scalable and standardizable gene-testing-aid cancer diagnostic procedure is needed to support clinicians and genetic counseling and promote broader integration into medical systems. This study aims to advance such a procedure by using gene testing and healthcare service operations within a decision support system (DSS) to facilitate the diagnosis and stage recognition of osteosarcoma, a bone cancer with high fatality rates, predominantly in children and teens. We develop models using machine learning (ML) algorithms to identify cancer stages for patients with the DSS. These predictive models leverage information from the large-scale genomic project of the National Cancer Institute. This database is the only available public data source for osteosarcoma with comprehensive genomic profiles in the USA. The study contributes to the collective efforts to enhance the technological scalability of gene testing, which is crucial for integrated diagnostic and treatment procedures and emerging preventive health strategies. This research conducts two model types, one for each algorithm: a comprehensive model employing 18,000 chromosome characteristics and a simplified model based on nearly 100 representative predictors. The resulting comprehensive models are highly precise, and the simplified model fits into limited data. The resulting models specifying features, such as probes and the length of cuts of chromosomes, provide significant indicators of the cancer stages. Reducing the number of tested chromosomes generates a more cost-effective and time-saving gene testing diagnosis. As part of a clinical DSS, the proposed diagnostic process benefits efficiency, responsiveness, and operations of healthcare, optimizes treatment steps, and enhances patients’ quality of life. The research results highlighted the transformative potential of advanced genomic analytics in improving healthcare operations management. The study also highlights the potential of ML in bridging predictive and prescriptive analytics in high-stakes environments and resource optimization within operations research (OR), particularly in the healthcare context.

Title: When exports decelerate: The mental health consequences of China’s export slowdown
Authors: Chuan He, Yuting Li, Hong Ma, Mingzhi (Jimmy) Xu
Abstract: This paper examines the mental health consequences of China’s export slowdown from 2010 to 2016. Using nationally representative individual-level panel data and a shift-share instrument for city-level export exposure, we find that export slowdown significantly increased psychological distress. The effects are most pronounced in export-reliant regions and among middle-aged, less-educated individuals, production and manufacturing workers, and married women. We further show that export slowdowns operate through both level and distributional channels: they deteriorate labor market conditions and widen income inequality. At the household level, export slowdowns increase reliance on short-term borrowing, amplifying forward-looking financial stress, particularly for families with young children. Institutional and technological forces shape these impacts: stronger local social safety nets mitigate mental distress among vulnerable groups, while accelerated workplace automation exacerbates stress for employed workers. A one-standard-deviation decline in export exposure is associated with 44,686 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and mental health-related costs equivalent to 0.34% of China’s GDP in 2013. These findings reveal the uneven psychological costs of adverse trade shocks and highlight the importance of distribution-sensitive trade adjustment policies.

Title: The macroeconomic and biophysical impacts of decarbonization and circular economy strategies. A scenario analysis for Austria
Authors: Ina Meyer, Sommer Mark, Baumgart André, Eisenmenger Nina, Virag Doris, Kratena Kurt, Haas Willi
Abstract: Growth in resource use is a key driver of climate change and environmental degradation. In recognition of this, a few governments have set targets to reduce their countries' per capita resource use while striving to achieve the goals set out in the Paris Agreement. In this context, the concept of the circular economy (CE) has attracted mounting interest as a means of mitigating climate change, reducing resource use and waste generation, while advancing economic performance. This paper uses a mass-balanced biophysical model (CeAT) linked to a macroeconomic model (DYNK) of the Austrian economy to analyze different stock-flow scenarios, combining a decarbonization scheme with CE strategies at varying levels of ambition. The analysis examines Austria's buildings, transport, and electricity sectors, evaluating economic impacts by employment, GDP, and disposable income results. The framework incorporates two stylized indirect rebounds effects arising from CE strategies of narrowing, i.e. reduced growth in infrastructure, buildings or car fleets. These rebound effects, driven by the reallocation of financial resources, manifest through two distinct consumption pathways: service-oriented and goods-oriented expenditure patterns. Findings indicate, the strong CE scenario can achieve substantial dematerialization. At the same time, it shows potentially the highest average growth rates in disposable income when combined with a service-oriented rebound. First order CE strategies (refuse, rethink, reduce) are therefore of key importance for the triple agenda of climate mitigation, resource use reductions and economic growth. Particularly, demand-side reductions can enhance economic performance if the rebound effects are constrained by reallocating the freed-up expenditure to low-material-intensity services.

Title: Environmental values, climate awareness and willingness to pay for green savings: The direct and moderating effect of perceived greenwashing
Authors: Maxime Merli, Tristan Roger
Abstract: The transition to a low-carbon economy depends critically on mobilizing household savings toward green financial products. Using a survey experiment on a representative sample of 1061 French adults, we examine how perceived greenwashing shapes willingness to pay for a green savings account and whether environmental impact disclosures influence it. We find that individuals are, on average, unwilling to pay a premium to green their savings, and that willingness to pay does not increase when the stated environmental impact is scaled up. Perceived greenwashing plays a dual role: it directly reduces willingness to pay and moderates the relationship between pro-environmental attitudes and financial behavior. Green consumption values raise willingness to pay only when sustainability claims are perceived as credible; climate awareness follows the same pattern. When perceived greenwashing is high, these relationships become statistically insignificant, even among environmentally motivated individuals. At the individual level, willingness to pay declines with subjective financial literacy, whereas climate-related emotions play no robust role. These results suggest that impact disclosure alone is insufficient to shift household financial behavior, and that the perceived credibility of environmental claims is a necessary condition for translating pro-environmental values into green financial choices.

Title: The green credentials of benefit corporations and sociétés à mission: Property rights and the prevention of greenwashing
Authors: Alejandro Agafonow, Marybel Perez, Ana Cristina O. Siqueira
Abstract: This research inquires whether the property rights templates of US benefit corporations (BCs) and French sociétés à mission (SaMs) are credible protections against greenwashing. By dissecting their unique legal structures (dubbed their “legal DNA” by B Lab), we aim to find whether these firms' environmental and social claims are truly backed by robust corporate governance. The importance of this lies in the “credence” nature of environmental and social claims, which makes their verification difficult while increasing the likelihood of fraud. This vulnerability is further exacerbated by ambiguous missions and third-party assessments weakened by the freedom BCs and SaMs have to select and pay auditors. Rooted in the tradition of institutional ecological economics, this research emphasizes institutional realism by leveraging a mechanism-based methodology. Qualitative institutional data, derived from the model benefit corporation legislation, société à mission legal status, case law, and company filings, are then analyzed through manifest coding using the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), which adheres to the ISO/IEC 21838–1 standard. Findings reveal a fundamental bargaining power imbalance favoring shareholders in BCs and SaMs, leaving non-equity stakeholders with limited countervailing powers (e.g., costly exit, no voting, ineffective legal recourse). Formal stakeholder protection proves ineffective, leading to weak practical accountability and heavy reliance on owner altruism for mission fulfillment. The implications are that ensuring credible protection against greenwashing necessitates a fundamental structural redesign of BCs and SaMs. This involves shifting bargaining power towards stakeholders and establishing governance independent of selfless owners, thereby creating imperative credible commitments.

Title: Air pollution and conflict in West Africa: The effects of the Harmattan dust
Authors: A. Delgerchuluun, K. Kis-Katos, K. Perlik
Abstract: We study the impact of dust-driven pollution on social conflict in West Africa, exploiting exogenous variation in PM 2.5 concentrations caused by Saharan dust transported by Harmattan winds. Using a monthly panel covering 16 West African countries from 2003 to 2017, we combine satellite-derived PM 2.5 data with geo-referenced conflict events. We instrument PM 2.5 using dust emissions from the Bodélé Depression interacted with northeasterly Harmattan winds. We find that a one standard deviation increase in PM 2.5 reduces the likelihood of conflict by 0.13 percentage points. The effects are concentrated in riots, one-sided violence, ethnic and religious conflict, and conflicts involving non-local actors. Similarly, we find that resource-related conflicts increase. The findings suggest that severe dust episodes constrain mobility, visibility, and social interaction, thereby reducing opportunities for violent confrontation, even as they intensify competition over scarce resources.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Joint product-service innovation in EV battery-swapping supply chains under alternative service leadership structures: Insights from the Chinese market
Authors: Qiuting Li, Ying Li, Feifan Li
Abstract: With the rapid diffusion of electric vehicles, battery-swapping has emerged as a replenishment alternative that converts time savings into potential market adoption. Battery-swapping represents a product-service system, whose diffusion hinges on complementary innovations between product-side compatibility and service-side capacity. As battery-swapping networks attract investment from battery suppliers, vehicle manufacturers, and third-party firms, differences in capital commitment and control over service assets bring service leadership structures to the forefront of strategic analysis. Accordingly, we investigate product-service innovation and pricing decisions under three leadership regimes, and examine equity-based coordination through cross-shareholding. To capture demand heterogeneity arising from time-based competition between charging and swapping, we develop a circular Hotelling model of a swapping supply chain comprising a battery supplier, a manufacturer, and a service provider. Our results highlight three key findings. First, higher users time value generally expands swapping adoption under decentralized leadership, but may reduce adoption when the manufacturer self-operates service, unless coordination efficiency is sufficiently high. Second, leadership advantages are stage contingent. When time advantages and differentiation are strong, regimes that better internalize cross-stage gains achieve higher innovation levels, lower effective service prices, and greater penetration; as fast charging technologies converge and substitution intensifies, performance becomes increasingly sensitive to cost efficiency and asset turnover. Third, cross-shareholding can mitigate innovation spillovers and improve both supply-chain performance and consumer welfare, but its incentive effects depend on leadership structure: under third-party leadership, innovation is inverted-U in equity intensity, whereas under supplier leadership, stronger equity alignment more consistently promotes innovation, particularly in time-sensitive markets.

Title: The value of advance demand information for shipment consolidation under customer behavioral responses
Authors: Haiwei Lu, Gudrun P. Kiesmüller
Abstract: This paper studies how warehouses should price advance demand information to maximize its value in shipment consolidation systems. Unlike existing research that assumes exogenous demand, we explicitly model customer ordering behavior as influenced by discount rates, delivery lead times, and order cancellation risks. We develop three shipment consolidation policies: a Bayesian-optimized approximate threshold policy, a layered decision policy, and a cost-based myopic policy, to determine optimal discount rates under various operational conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the layered policy achieves near-optimal performance with only 0.05% average optimality gap. Our analysis reveals that optimal discount rates exhibit an inverted-U relationship with demand lead time. Price sensitivity significantly amplifies optimal discounts, while high cancellation costs and severe late-delivery penalties constrain discount strategies. In addition, incorporating cancellation behavior significantly improves system performance. These findings provide actionable guidance for pricing advance demand information through discount strategies under different operational conditions.

Title: The Phillips multiplier and the two sides of inflation
Authors: Ricardo Quineche
Abstract: The inflation-unemployment trade-off faced by a central bank can be characterised non-parametrically by the Phillips multiplier of Barnichon and Mesters (2021). Because the multiplier is linear in inflation, it inherits any exact decomposition of it. We split it into the two directional margins of price adjustment of Quineche and Zapata (2026). Before 1990, a policy-induced one-percentage-point rise in the cumulative unemployment gap raises cumulative deflationary pressure by 0.4pp: the identified trade-off runs through price cuts. After 1990, excluding the zero lower bound, nothing is identified: neither the multiplier nor either margin. The instruments carry too little exogenous variation.

Title: A decision-support framework for selecting new energy bus technologies: Assessing battery electric and hydrogen fuel cell buses
Authors: Mohammad Sadrani, Mirko Giagnorio, Alejandro Tirachini
Abstract: New energy bus (NEB) technologies, including battery electric buses (BEBs) and hydrogen fuel cell buses (FCBs), offer pathways to support decarbonisation strategies in public transport. Selecting the most suitable technology represents a multi-dimensional decision problem encompassing trade-offs across different criteria. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the factors influencing the choice of BEBs or FCBs, grouped into technological, economic, managerial, social, environmental, and institutional categories. We address this NEB technology selection problem using a hybrid multi-criteria decision-making framework integrating the Best-Worst Method (BWM) and the Measurement of Alternatives and Ranking according to Compromise Solution (MARCOS). Evaluation criteria are identified and refined through a structured expert interview process, and their weights are determined using BWM based on assessments from 34 international experts with diverse backgrounds. The MARCOS method is applied to evaluate and rank NEB alternatives, including BEBs, FCBs, and mixed fleet configurations. Results indicate that economic factors (e.g., vehicle, energy, and infrastructure costs) are the most influential, followed by institutional (e.g., political will and funding) and technological (e.g., driving range and energy system resilience) dimensions. BEBs are identified as the most suitable option for current urban systems, while FCBs remain competitive where operational flexibility is critical. Interestingly, a divergence is observed between academic and industry perspectives, with the former prioritising economic and environmental factors, whereas the latter prioritise institutional and technological factors. This is also reflected in the ranking of alternatives, with academics favouring BEBs and industry experts favouring FCBs, highlighting the importance of incorporating stakeholder perspectives into decision-making.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Understanding user responses to incentives in shared micromobility with LLM-based digital twins
Authors: Rui Guan, Arijit De, Yaoming Zhou
Abstract: Shared micromobility has emerged as a crucial component of urban transportation, yet high operational costs remain a significant bottleneck. User incentives, primarily offered as fare discounts, are widely adopted to mitigate these issues; however, their effectiveness relies heavily on a thorough understanding of user choice behaviors. This study investigates user responses to incentive mechanisms in shared micromobility using a novel large language model (LLM)-based behavioral simulation framework. Profile-based user digital twins are developed to emulate responses under incentive scenarios at scale. Two types of incentives are analyzed: station-based incentives (spatial relocation) and vehicle-based incentives (battery adjustment). The fidelity of these digital twins is evaluated across dimensions of stability (consistency testing), rationality (rationale analysis), and validity (empirical benchmarking), suggesting their ability to capture key stated preference patterns under controlled scenarios. Findings highlight user heterogeneity, with younger, lower-income, and non-commuting individuals showing greater acceptance than older, higher-income, and commuting users. Past interactions influence incentive effectiveness, as prior acceptance promotes engagement and negative experiences deter it, with both effects initially strengthening before diminishing. However, exposure frequency has no significant impact on incentive acceptance. Vehicle-based incentives can serve as an efficient baseline mechanism for routine operations with lower adoption barriers. In contrast, station-based incentives encounter greater initial resistance, but are more responsive to financial rewards and suited for targeted rebalancing. The work offers practical insights for incentive design in shared micromobility and demonstrates the potential of LLMs in behavioral simulation for transportation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A frequent pattern mining-based hybrid evolutionary algorithm for the k-clustering minimum biclique completion problem
Authors: Dawei Wu, Zhiying Zhang, Qing Zhou
Abstract: The k[jls-end-space/]-clustering minimum biclique completion problem (k[jls-end-space/]-CMBCP) is a challenging combinatorial optimization problem with important applications in areas such as multicast network design and supply chain management. Given a bipartite graph (Formula presented), the k[jls-end-space/]-CMBCP aims to partition U into k disjoint clusters Ui[jls-end-space/], and each cluster (Formula presented) contains all vertices in V that are adjacent to at least one vertex in Ui[jls-end-space/]. For each bipartite cluster (Formula presented), the induced subgraph is completed into a biclique by adding edges as needed. The objective is to minimize the total number of edges added across all clusters. This study proposes a frequent pattern mining-based hybrid evolutionary algorithm (FPMHEA) to effectively address the k[jls-end-space/]-CMBCP by exploiting structural information inherent in the problem graphs. The FPMHEA features a frequent pattern-based population initialization to generate high-quality and diverse initial solutions, a frequent pattern-guided crossover operator to strengthen search guidance during recombination, and an attribute-based tabu search with fast incremental evaluation for efficient local optimization. Extensive computational experiments on three widely used benchmark sets of 63 instances demonstrate that FPMHEA is highly competitive in both solution quality and computational efficiency compared with several state-of-the-art algorithms. Specifically, it improves the best-known upper bounds in literature for 44 instances and fails to match the best-known results on only 4 cases within short running times. Additional analysis further confirms the substantial contributions of the main algorithmic components to the overall performance of FPMHEA.

Title: Timetables, attendance and academic achievement in higher education
Authors: Adeline Delavande, Emilia Del Bono, Angus Holford, Kevin Williams
Abstract: We identify the impacts of a student's timetable on their attendance, study time and academic achievement using administrative and survey data from a public UK university across a broad range of degree programmes using quasi-random assignment of students to their timetables. Timetable measures include back-to-back classes, single-class days, time-of-day, day-of-instruction and long hours. We observe hourly attendance decisions. Findings indicate that student attendance at the event level is highly dependent on the timetable structure. Single-class days reduce attendance and back-to-back classes raise it. We are able to show that students compensate for marginal non-attendance at some events with increased attendance at other events on the same module, or among more conscientious students, with increased study time. Net of all behavioural responses to the timetable, these features have little impact on academic attainment.

Title: Preferential trade agreements and non-tariff measures
Authors: David J. Kuenzel, Rishi R. Sharma
Abstract: We study the product-level effects of Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs) on the implementation of non-tariff measures (NTMs) using a global database spanning the 2000-2017 period. Employing an instrumental variable strategy, we provide evidence that an increase in the import share of PTA partners leads to a reduction in the application of NTMs. Exploring several mechanisms, we find that these effects are driven by products with higher preferential margins, the gap between MFN and preferential tariff rates. This result is consistent with what we call a “rent preservation effect,” whereby PTA partner countries push to limit the imposition of NTMs in order to preserve their preferential rents. Importantly, higher PTA import shares contribute to multilateral liberalization by lowering both the usage of NTMs against PTA members and non-PTA partners.

Title: Entrepreneurial heterogeneity, financial development, and business cycle dynamics
Authors: Hanjo Terry Kim
Abstract: This paper studies how financial development affects business cycles through entrepreneurial composition. Using Argentine microdata, I show that self-employed entrepreneurs are concentrated below the median of the income distribution and have countercyclical population shares, while employer entrepreneurs are concentrated above the median and have procyclical shares. Motivated by these patterns, I develop a dynamic occupational choice model with aggregate risk in which endogenous sorting across occupations shapes macroeconomic fluctuations. In the calibrated model, financial development raises aggregate output volatility by 8 percent because relaxing collateral constraints shifts economic activity toward employer entrepreneurs, who are more sensitive to aggregate shocks. These findings show that while financial development raises long-run output, it may also increase short-run instability.

Title: Trading off capacity factors, location, storage, access charges and curtailment for renewable electricity
Authors: David Newbery
Abstract: Variable renewable electricity (VRE, wind and solar PV) is typically located far from load centres. As marginal curtailment is 3+ times average curtailment, VRE curtailment rises rapidly, demanding costly transmission expansion. Efficiency requires trading-off curtailment to reduce transmission against the value of curtailed VRE. This article develops novel closed-form formulas for the efficient transmission expansion, renewables capacity and voluntary curtailment in a simplified model of distant VRE. Given VRE entry equilibrium in demand centres, the solutions depend only on cost and technology parameters. If local grid-connected storage covers most of its cost, co-located storage increases the profit of onshore wind, reducing optimal export capacity. Calibration for Scottish wind shows overhead lines have little effect on desirable levels of curtailment/congestion but proposed costly subsea links increase efficient curtailment to the point where most Scottish wind expansion becomes unprofitable.

Title: Enhancing transportation system resilience under earthquake-induced geohazards: a framework for cross-regional rescue
Authors: Damin Zhou, Li Peng, Rui Guo, Zhousong Jiang, Muzi Li
Abstract: In mountainous areas, earthquake-induced geohazards frequently fragment road networks, isolating dispersed rural settlements and overwhelming local disaster response. Resource allocation constrained by fixed administrative boundaries often fails to adapt to the connectivity of road networks. We propose a coupled simulation framework that integrates an agent-based model with network science to strengthen the resilience of transportation systems in response to earthquake-induced geohazards. This framework simulates cascading failures in transportation system functionality that affect human mobility, enabling the assessment of how physical disruptions constrain organizational decision-making. Sensitivity and robustness analyses addressing macrolevel environmental constraints, microlevel behavioral attributes, and conditions under cross-factor scenarios revealed that this approach substantially enhances system resilience, particularly under high disaster intensity and limited resources. This study shows that improving transportation system functionality during disasters requires aligning emergency management strategies with the topological realities of networked mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Contested transparency: Digital monitoring technologies and worker voice
Authors: Gabriel Burdin, Stefano Dughera, Fabio Landini, Filippo Belloc
Abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence and data analytics have notably expanded employers’ monitoring and surveillance capabilities. While new digital monitoring (DM) technologies facilitate the accurate observability of work effort, their productivity and broader welfare implications remain subject to debate. In this context, many countries confer information, consultation and co-determination rights to employee representation (ER) bodies on matters related to workplace organization and the introduction of new technologies, which could potentially discourage employers from making DM investments. Using a cross-sectional sample of more than 21,000 European establishments, we find instead that establishments with ER are more likely to utilize DM technologies than establishments without ER. We also document a positive effect of ER on DM utilization in the context of a local-randomization regression discontinuity analysis that exploits size-contingent policy rules governing the operation of ER bodies in Europe. We rationalize this unexpected finding through the lens of a theoretical model in which shared governance via ER creates organizational safeguards that mitigate workers’ control-averse responses to monitoring.

Title: Do Voluntary and Mandatory Clean Truck Programs Improve Air Quality Around Ports?
Authors: Chinedu Ufodike, Alex Scott, Yemisi Bolumole
Affiliations: College of Business Valparaiso University Valparaiso Indiana USA; Stokely Management Center The University of Tennessee Knoxville Tennessee USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT States and port authorities have implemented “Clean Truck” programs (CTPs) to encourage trucking companies to transition to newer, cleaner trucks to reduce the emissions around ports. We examine the comparative effectiveness of mandatory and voluntary CTPs implemented across major United States ports. Leveraging insights from the awareness‐motivation‐capability framework, we theorize how environmental regulatory programs shape carrier behavior under different regulatory structures in the trucking industry. Using a difference‐in‐differences design and a database containing detailed truck and trailer information and air quality measures, we find that mandatory programs significantly accelerate truck model‐year upgrades, narrowing pre‐existing disparities in fleet upgrades across carriers, whereas voluntary programs show no measurable effects. Mandatory CTPs are associated with reductions in nitrogen dioxide concentrations, while effects on particulate matter are less consistent. Air quality improvements are most pronounced in inner harbors and decrease with distance from port activity. Our findings contribute to supply chain and regulatory policy literature by highlighting the effectiveness of mandatory environmental programs in driving industry‐wide change and the limited impact of voluntary initiatives.

Title: The Three R's of Powerful Research: Rigor, Relevance… and Resonance!
Authors: Rodney Thomas, Terry Esper, Christian Hofer, Mehrdokht Pournader, Damien Power, Judith Whipple, Scott Grawe, Chad W. Autry, Matthias Klumpp, Maria Keil, Randy V. Bradley, Bryan Ashenbaum
Affiliations: Supply Chain Management Walton College of Business, University of Arkansas Fayetteville Arkansas USA; Marketing and Logistics Ohio State University Fisher College of Business Columbus Ohio USA; Supply Chain Management Sam M.
