Walton College of Business, University of Arkansas Fayetteville Arkansas USA; Business and Economics University of Melbourne Melbourne Victoria Australia; University of Melbourne Melbourne Victoria Australia; Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA; Mississippi State University Starkville Mississippi USA; Department of Supply Chain Management University of Tennessee Knoxville Tennessee USA; Chair for Production and Logistics Management Georg‐August‐Universitat Gottingen Gottingen Germany; Institute for Logistics and Service Management, FOM University of Applied Sciences Essen Germany; Politecnico di Milano Milano Italy; University of Bremen Bremen Germany; Supply Chain Management The University of Tennessee Knoxville Tennessee USA; Belmont University Nashville Tennessee USA; New Mexico State University Las Cruces New Mexico USA

Title: Polygyny as a determinant of migration
Authors: Ruud Koopmans, Daniel Meierrieks
Abstract: Abstract We hypothesize that polygyny acts as a significant push factor for migration in sub-Saharan Africa because it is associated with competition within polygynous families and on the marriage market, while also contributing to unfavorable economic and political outcomes at the societal level. Using cross-country data from 46 sub-Saharan African countries, we show that higher polygyny prevalence is associated with increased international emigration. We complement this macro-level evidence with original survey data from Senegal, the Gambia, and Nigeria. We show that polygyny is also associated with higher migration aspirations and observed migration of survey respondents’ siblings at the individual level. Respondents from polygynous families tend to report stronger economic motives for migration, while those concerned about the marriage market effects of polygyny—regardless of family background—are more likely to consider migrating for marriage. This highlights two distinct pathways—competition within polygynous families and on marriage markets—linking polygyny to migration.

Title: Quantifying the effects of accounts payable automation on technology adopters and their suppliers: A difference-in-differences study
Authors: Wanling Rong, Morgan Swink
Abstract: Accounts Payable (AP) Automation promises significant cost reductions for an adopting firm by automating many manual and repetitive tasks. However, AP automation may also enhance supplier satisfaction by enabling faster payments, greater transparency, and more consistent communication, ultimately contributing to stronger buyer-supplier relationships (BSRs). The literature lacks a rigorous assessment of the claimed benefits of this technology for adopters and for their suppliers. Using financial data from 135 publicly listed U.S. companies and employing a difference-in-differences (DiD) approach, this study quantifies the effects of AP automation on both technology adopters and suppliers for which they are a major customer. The results show improved liquidity and decreasing Days Payable Outstanding (DPO) for adopters in comparison to otherwise similar firms. These effects are moderated by industry characteristics. However, there is no consistent evidence of cost reduction or improved profitability. Suppliers of adopting firms benefit from a decline in doubtful receivables and reduced reliance on short-term debt, suggesting reduced uncertainty from the buyers and potential enhancement in supplier satisfaction. These benefits are moderated by the degree of buyer-supplier interdependence. While providing evidence of working capital efficiencies for AP automation adopters, our findings also highlight AP automation's relational value in enhancing supplier satisfaction through prompter payments, improved operational execution, and reduced uncertainty.
Journal: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management

Title: Too efficient to stop: the power of digital manufacturing in product customisation and market competition
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Shu Tao, Zihao Mu
Affiliations: South China University of Technology; Northwestern Polytechnical University
Abstract: Digital manufacturing technologies such as additive manufacturing significantly improve manufacturers' ability to customise products, but they also reshape competitive dynamics in markets with heterogeneous consumer preferences. This study examines how digital manufacturing influences firms' strategic decisions through its impact on product customisation. We develop a multi-stage decision model in which two competing manufacturers decide whether to adopt digital manufacturing, choose customisation levels, and compete in prices. Digital manufacturing improves customisation efficiency and reduces the disutility consumers experience from imperfect product fit, thereby altering demand allocation and market competition. When only one manufacturer adopts digital manufacturing, it offers better-fitting products and attracts consumers. However, when both manufacturers adopt, improved customisation expands the overlap between their effective product offerings, intensifying market competition. As a result, mutual adoption may reduce manufacturers' profits even though average product fit improves. We further show that manufacturers may face a Prisoner's Dilemma in technology adoption. From a welfare perspective, digital manufacturing increases consumer surplus through improved product fit, while its effect on social welfare depends on the balance between these benefits and intensified competition. These findings highlight that the value of digital manufacturing extends beyond operational benefits and depends critically on competitive responses and market structure.

Title: Joint optimisation of quality-dependent production and economic-dependent maintenance for a degradation system under online and offline inspections
Authors: Jingjing Wang, Lingyun Luo, Dandan Song, Xinqiang Tang
Affiliations: Qingdao University of Technology
Abstract: The relationship between quality-dependent production and economically dependent maintenance is generally ignored during the production process, especially for multi-unit degradation production systems. To bridge this gap, an improved Weibull distribution with two scale parameters and shape parameters is employed to depict the ‘bathtub curve’ characteristic of nonconforming product rates. Moreover, an acceleration factor related to product quality is considered to describe the effect of unqualified products on the degradation process of the downstream machine. New quality-based maintenance and condition-based opportunistic maintenance are proposed, and the opportunity originates from safety inventory capacity and the deterioration level of other machines. A comprehensive optimisation model of production, maintenance and inspection policy, is formulated under online and offline inspections, respectively. The aim is to minimise total costs that consist of falsely rejecting qualified products and accepting unqualified products under inspection errors by optimising the sampling proportion, the inventory capacity and the thresholds of maintenance. Furthermore, a Quadratic Particle Swarm Optimization with Local Search (QPSOL) algorithm is developed to effectively solve the optimisation problem. Finally, spiral grooves for air conditioning compressors are used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model, and we further prove that online inspection is more cost-effective than offline inspection.

Title: Bundling or breaking apart? Mixed mergers, innovation effort, and pricing power in logistics systems
Authors: Netnapha Chamnisampan
Affiliations: National Chin-Yi University of Technology
Abstract: Logistics systems are increasingly organised around complementary services and platform-based bundles. In this setting, mixed mergers between firms in related logistics segments have become a key strategic option, yet their implications for innovation and pricing remain unclear. This study develops a game-theoretic model of two complementary logistics firms that choose R&D effort, decide whether to form a mixed merger, and then compete under three configurations: no merger, a mixed merger with bundling, and a mixed merger without bundling. In a baseline with symmetric, commonly known R&D costs, the preferred structure depends on how strongly customers value service quality: bundling is attractive when quality sensitivity is low, while independent operation dominates when quality is central. An extension with privately known R&D costs and surplus sharing shows that bundled mixed mergers become a more robust source of profit, but shift innovation effort and pricing power towards the advantaged firm.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: From words to vision: Imaginability, attention, and investment decisions in innovation disclosures—Experimental evidence from humans and LLMs
Authors: Yuqian He, Xinyi Huang, Xiaoming Jiang, Lu Li, Yihang Li, Yating Ye, Hongjun Zhu
Affiliations: Shanghai Normal University; Durham University Business School; Shanghai International Studies University; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; Anhui University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: Innovation is sold in stories long before it appears in numbers. Decision-support processes often begin with narrative disclosures. We ask a basic question: whether the representation of narrative inputs changes human judgements and whether large language models (LLMs) react in the same way. We construct paired disclosures in which informational content is held constant, but wording varies in imaginability, defined as the ease with which readers can form mental images of the innovation unfolding. In a lab study, financially literate participants exposed to high-imaginability wording see the same projects as less risky and more worthy of investment. Eight LLMs interface detect these linguistic shifts yet reproduce only about 15-20% of the human response. Eye-tracking provides process evidence consistent with this account: high-imaginability wording redirects and sustains visual attention on innovation-diagnostic text, revealing an attention-related pathway from language to judgement and decision making that is present in humans but only weakly reflected in current model interfaces. Overall, our study contributes to behavioural OR by showing that pre-model narrative representation is a design variable, and by proposing role‑specific validation for AI that processes unstructured information.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The Role of Demand Information for Price‐Setting Newsvendors: A Monotone Comparative Statics Approach
Authors: Junjie Zhou, Chen‐Nan Liao, Yu‐Ping Chen, Ying‐Ju Chen
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China; Department of Business Administration National Taiwan University Taipei Taiwan; Department of International Business National Taiwan University Taipei Taiwan; School of Business and Management (ISOM) The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Kowloon Hong Kong
Abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, we examine the role of demand forecast information for price‐setting newsvendors. In our model, the newsvendor faces stochastic, price‐sensitive demand, has discretion over the retail price, and receives an informative signal that aids the quantity decision. Focusing on a class of signal structures that satisfy the scale‐location property, We analyze the model using a monotone comparative statics approach, which does not require uniqueness of the solution and substantially relaxes the regularity conditions commonly assumed in the literature, and we show that as the quality of demand forecasts improves, the optimal retail price may increase, decrease, or remain unchanged. We provide sufficient conditions on the primitives under which each type of monotonicity arises. We offer a comprehensive analysis across a broad spectrum of information structures, whereas the existing literature focuses primarily on the comparison between full‐information and no‐information benchmarks. Finally, we also discuss applications to food waste in the Grab‐and‐Go food market and illustrate our results using several commonly adopted demand distributions.

Title: How risk preferences and perceived yield distributions affect farmer adaptation to climate change
Authors: Natalie R. Loduca, Scott M. Swinton
Abstract: Agricultural producers' risk preferences and perceptions of climate change risks play a role in shaping their adaptation decisions. This research elicits farmers' subjective crop yield distributions and links farmers' risk preferences and subjective beliefs to adaptation decisions under changing weather conditions. Based on detailed interviews with 44 Michigan corn farmers, this exploratory study finds that in the absence of water management practices and holding crop genetics constant, farmers anticipate increases in both the mean and variance of corn yields. They expect that adopting irrigation and, to a lesser degree, tile drainage will further increase mean yields. Adopting drought-resistant seed varieties, by contrast, will only slightly increase the mean while also reducing variance. Even though all the farmers interviewed were risk averse, when choosing water management technologies to adapt to weather risk, they preferred ones that offered perceived yield gains. Reduction in crop yield variance and degree of risk aversion played minor roles. These findings suggest that policies and extension programs promoting climate adaptation technologies should emphasize potential yield gains ahead of production risk reduction.

Title: The power of words: Adult literacy campaign and intergenerational transmission of human capital
Authors: Shuo Chen, Zhuoer Lin, Xian Xu, Yanfei Yin
Abstract: We examine the intergenerational impact of China's 1950s adult literacy campaign, one of the largest anti-illiteracy efforts in history, reaching 150 million people. While direct effects on adult literacy remain debated, we document significant long-term benefits for the next generation's education. Using an original dataset compiled from county gazetteers and the population census, we find a notable increase in educational attainment for children whose parents were more strongly exposed to the campaign. We attribute these results to extensive government propaganda that likely shifted population attitudes toward education. Our findings suggest that education campaigns can be a viable strategy in developing countries for improving human capital.

Title: Stochastic modeling of labor supply and discouraged worker behavior
Authors: John K. Dagsvik, Tom Kornstad, Terje Skjerpen
Abstract: Discouraged workers are those who have given up searching for work because of the (perceived) low chances of obtaining it. In this paper we develop a stochastic structural econometric framework for analyzing discouraged worker behavior based on the theory of job search and the notion of probabilistic rationality and risky choice. Subsequently, we conduct an empirical analysis of immigrant women from non-Western countries and women born in Norway, using microdata on labor force participation and unemployment. We find that the discouraged worker effect is particularly high among immigrant women with low wage rates and many children.

Title: A robust optimization approach for scheduling with uncertain start-time dependent costs
Authors: Sofía Rodríguez-Ballesteros, Javier Alcaraz, Laura Anton-Sanchez, Marc Goerigk, Dorothee Henke
Abstract: In this work, we study a single-machine scheduling problem that aims at minimizing the total cost of a schedule subject to start-time dependent costs. This framework naturally captures scenarios where costs fluctuate throughout the day, such as time-varying energy or labor prices. To model more realistic scenarios, we assume that these costs lie within a budgeted uncertainty set and propose a two-stage robust optimization approach. In a first stage, the order in which activities should be executed is decided. After a cost scenario has been revealed, the starting times for each activity are established, subject to the ordering from the first stage. We demonstrate that the proposed problem is NP-hard and not approximable, implying the complexity of its robust counterpart. Furthermore, we show that already evaluating a first-stage solution is NP-hard when the uncertainty set is discrete. We develop models and solution methods for both continuous and discrete budgeted uncertainty. In computational experiments, we compare these approaches and demonstrate the advantages of including uncertainty beforehand.

Title: The long shadow of typhoons: Prenatal exposure and adult mental health
Authors: Yu-Ting Huang, Elaine M. Liu, Jin-Tan Liu, Tzu-Yin Hazel Tseng
Abstract: This paper examines how poor in utero conditions caused by severe typhoons affect psychological well-being later in life. We exploit variation in the timing and location of severe typhoon landfalls. Our design compares individuals with higher expected fetal exposure in landfall counties to those with no such exposure. A one-unit increase in expected in utero exposure raises the likelihood of an adult mental illness diagnosis by 2.2 percentage points, or 11 percent relative to the mean. The incidence of mood disorders such as depression and the use of antidepressants has risen by more than 50 percent. The adverse effects are concentrated among women. In a fully interacted model, we reject equality of the male and female effects for our main outcomes. This gender gap is not driven by differential healthcare-seeking behavior. We discuss several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms that could generate a genuinely female-concentrated effect, including sex-specific fetal programming and mortality selection.

Title: Macroeconomic effects of carbon pricing: The role of bank credit
Authors: Yunsang Kim, Givi Melkadze
Abstract: This paper quantifies the role of bank lending in shaping the short-run effects of climate policy on the economy. Using carbon price surprises from the EU Emissions Trading System we document that higher carbon prices, while successfully reducing emissions, lead to lower economic activity, lower bank capital and higher credit spreads. We further show that banks with greater exposure to emission-intensive industries reduce credit supply more strongly in response to an increase in carbon price. We interpret these empirical facts through the lens of a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model with polluting and non-polluting sectors, nominal price rigidities, and a bank credit channel. The model matches well the empirical impulse responses of key aggregates to a carbon policy shock. Counterfactual simulations suggest that the bank credit channel plays a quantitatively meaningful role in the transmission of carbon policy shocks. Finally, implications for the design of macroprudential and monetary policies are explored.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: The distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem with tool transfers to minimize the total tardiness
Authors: Martin Schönheit, Tristan Becker, Rainer Lasch
Abstract: Competitive pressure and economic growth have driven firms to diversify their production locations to access customer and raw material markets. The resulting production networks require coordinated planning across multiple factories, leading to distributed scheduling problems. In industrial production networks, processing at certain machines requires specialized and costly tools that are only available at a subset of factories, thereby inducing factory-eligibility constraints. Despite their practical relevance, such constraints have been largely overlooked in the scheduling literature over the past 15 years. We address this gap by extending the distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem to incorporate eligibility constraints arising from tool availability, evolving dynamically through tool transfers between factories. To support on-time delivery while accounting for geographically dispersed factories, the model incorporates factory-dependent due dates and minimizes total tardiness. Accordingly, we develop three solution approaches: a novel network-flow-based mixed-integer programming model, a constraint programming formulation, and a tailored Iterated Greedy algorithm that reduces total tardiness by an average of 7.7% compared to the constraint programming approach for large instances. Computational experiments further show that tool transfers reduce total tardiness by 21.67% on average compared with static tool allocation. A sensitivity analysis confirms that tool transfers remain beneficial across varying tool redundancy levels and geographic network configurations.

Title: Maximising profit in a stochastic capacitated hub location problem with flow-dependent economies of scale
Authors: Dung Tran, Nader Azizi, Thomas Welsh Archibald
Affiliations: The University of Edinburgh
Abstract: In this study, we investigate the interactions between a number of important factors that affect network profit including uncertain demand, pricing and flow dependent unit transportation cost in the capacitated single allocation hub location problem (HLP). We first present a deterministic formulation in which economies of scale on inter-hub connections are modelled using the FLOWLOC formulation (O’Kelly and Bryan, 1998). The deterministic HLP model with flow dependent discount factor is then extended to a two-stage stochastic program under demand uncertainty. The stochastic formulation is solved using a hybrid Lagrangian relaxation and Benders decomposition algorithm. We present extensive computational results using a large number of benchmark problems derived from the three well-known HLP datasets and discuss managerial insights.

Title: Single or hybrid? manufacturers' live-streaming mode selection considering virtual streamers
Authors: Gaoke Wu, Wensheng Yang, Xinru Hou, Mengze Chen
Affiliations: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
Abstract: The emergence of AI-generated virtual streamers in live-streaming commerce has complicated manufacturers' mode selection. In response, this study develops a game-theoretic decision-aid framework to analyze manufacturers' optimal strategies across both single live-streaming modes (self-streaming, streamer, and virtual streamer) and hybrid live-streaming modes (‘self−streaming+streamer’ and ‘self−streaming+virtual streamer’). It further incorporates different slotting fee structures and the platform's drainage effect to evaluate how these factors shape the manufacturer's mode choice. The findings show that: (i) consumer distrust may reduce demand for virtual streamers and the return on AI customisation, but a sufficiently strong drainage effect can offset this disadvantage; (ii) as streamer traffic effects strengthen, or drainage effects rise when traffic effects are still weak, the optimal strategy shifts from self-streaming to external or virtual streamer live-streaming, and eventually to hybrid modes; (iii) manufacturers prefer a single mode when both traffic and drainage effects are weak, but hybrid modes when these effects become stronger; and (iv) these results remain robust under different slotting fee structures and platform drainage strategies, while the manufacturer–platform equilibrium depends on drainage costs and off-peak incremental gains. Overall, the threshold-based framework guides manufacturers and platforms in allocating human and AI-enabled live-streaming resources across channels and periods.

Title: Policies for the operation of an ambulance fleet under uncertainty based on a new preparedness metric
Authors: Vincent Guigues, Anton J. Kleywegt, Victor Hugo Nascimento
Affiliations: School of Applied Mathematics, FGV; School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology
Abstract: Two important decisions in the management of an ambulance fleet are ambulance selection decisions and ambulance reassignment decisions. Ambulance selection decisions determine what to do when an emergency call arrives (such as choosing what ambulance to dispatch to the emergency or putting the emergency in a queue of emergencies waiting for an ambulance to be dispatched). Ambulance reassignment decisions determine where to send an ambulance next when it has finished service for an emergency. Making good ambulance selection decisions and ambulance reassignment decisions is challenging because a decision made at a point in time affects the ability of the emergency medical service to respond to future emergencies (that are typically not known when the decision is made). We propose a new preparedness metric that quantifies the ability of the emergency medical service to respond to future emergencies. The preparedness metric can be used to make ambulance selection decisions and ambulance reassignment decisions by solving a tractable optimisation problem each time that a decision has to be made. We compare the performance of the resulting method with 9 methods that have been proposed in the literature, based on data from a real emergency medical service for a large city.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Quantile forecast combination: An application to forecasting US GDP growth
Authors: Knut Are Aastveit, Saskia ter Ellen, Giulia Mantoan
Abstract: We propose an easy-to-implement framework for combining quantile forecasts, applied to forecasting GDP growth. Using quantile regressions, our combination scheme assigns weights to individual forecasts from different indicators based on quantile scores. Previous studies suggest distributional variation in forecasting performance of leading indicators: some indicators predict the mean well, while others excel at predicting the tails. Our approach leverages this by assigning different combination weights to various quantiles of the predictive distribution. In an empirical application to forecast US GDP growth using common predictors, forecasts from our quantile combination outperform those from commonly used combination approaches.

Title: Modeling uncertainty in the covariance matrix for probabilistic forecast reconciliation
Authors: Chiara Carrara, Dario Azzimonti, Giorgio Corani, Lorenzo Zambon
Abstract: In minimum trace (MinT) forecast reconciliation, the covariance matrix of the base forecast errors plays a crucial role. Typically, this matrix is estimated and then treated as known. This can lead to an underestimation of the variance of the predictive distribution. To address the problem, we propose a Bayesian reconciliation model that accounts for uncertainty in the estimation of the covariance matrix. By adopting an Inverse-Wishart prior and assuming Gaussian residuals, the reconciled predictive distribution follows a multivariate t-distribution, obtained in closed form, rather than a multivariate Gaussian distribution. We evaluate our method on three tourism-related datasets, including a new publicly available dataset. Empirical results show that our approach consistently improves prediction intervals compared to MinT reconciliation.

Title: Accessible Complexity Bounds for Restarted PDHG on Linear Programs with a Unique Optimizer
Authors: Zikai Xiong
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208
Abstract: The restarted primal-dual hybrid gradient method (rPDHG) has recently emerged as an important tool for solving large-scale linear programs (LPs). For LPs with unique optima, we present an iteration bound of [Formula: see text], where [Formula: see text] is the target tolerance, [Formula: see text] is the standard matrix condition number, [Formula: see text] is the norm of the optimal solution, and [Formula: see text] is a geometric condition number of the LP sublevel sets. This iteration bound is “accessible” in the sense that computing it is typically no more difficult than computing the optimal solution itself. Indeed, we present a closed-form and tractably computable expression for [Formula: see text]. This enables an analysis of the “two-stage performance” of rPDHG: we show that the first stage identifies the optimal basis in [Formula: see text] iterations, and the second stage computes an [Formula: see text]-optimal solution in [Formula: see text] additional iterations, where A is the constraint matrix, B is the optimal basis, and [Formula: see text] is the smallest nonzero in the optimal solution. Furthermore, computational tests are consistent with our iteration bounds. We also show a reciprocal relation between the iteration bound and stability under data perturbation, which is also equivalent to (i) proximity to multiple optima, and (ii) the LP sharpness of the instance. Funding: Part of this work was performed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and was supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR) [Grant FA9550-22-1-0356]. Another part of this work was performed at Georgia Institute of Technology and was supported by the Office of Naval Research (ONR) [Grant N00014-25-1-2088].

Title: An adaptive, resilient, regenerative life-based economy? Using structure-mapping theory to enhance the conceptual clarity of bio-inspired economic models
Authors: Christos Makriyannis
Abstract: Disagreement and conceptual vagueness continue to characterize the use biological metaphors in economics, including its bio-inspired, sustainability-oriented subfields. This paper suggests that these challenges may be addressed by asking whether and how the structure, function and dynamics of complex organisms are analogous to those of economies. Aligning with educational and scientific standards in biology, we explore this question by comparing the structure, function, and dynamics of economies against an established standard by which scientists distinguish living from non-living systems: the eight, well-established characteristics of complex organisms: Hierarchical Organization (HO), Metabolism, Homeostasis, Response to Environmental Stimuli, Growth and Development, Reproduction, Evolutionary Adaptation, and Order. To identify deep, structural-functional parallels – rather than flexibly-interpreted metaphorical similarities – we apply the formal criteria of structure-mapping theory which underlie the cognitive alignment process that drives scientific model-building. This analysis suggests that economies are not just metaphorically similar to organisms, but that the properties, principles or laws underlying the structure and abilities of complex organisms apply to economies. More simply, although economies may not resemble complex organisms in appearance, they are organized and function as if they are. This supports shifting from the mechanistic to a biological paradigm. Importantly, shared characteristics – particularly with respect to HO – may enhance the conceptual clarity of vague ecological metaphors, offering potentially a novel, scientifically grounded framework for understanding economies in terms of the structure, function, and dynamics of complex organisms. The paper concludes with limitations and directions for future research.

Title: Refugee immigration and natives’ fertility
Authors: Aya Aboulhosn, Cevat Giray Aksoy, Berkay Ozcan
Abstract: Research and policy debates on population ageing typically assume that immigration matters only through immigrants’ own fertility and its impact on total population size, ignoring effects on natives’ fertility. We study this margin in the context of the large inflow of Syrian refugees into Türkiye after 2011. Using an instrumental-variables strategy, we provide evidence that greater local exposure to refugees increases native fertility. Drawing on complete birth histories from the Demographic and Health Surveys, we find that the response operates primarily through earlier entry into motherhood and is concentrated among younger women. The result holds across three independent datasets, including administrative birth registers, and is mirrored in women's stated ideal number of children. Examining potential mechanisms, we find the evidence most consistent with improved household economic security and find no support for channels operating through housing costs or the use of paid childcare.

Title: Smart and sustainable production, logistics, and supply chain: trends, challenges, methods, and best practices II, part 1
Authors: Paulina Golinska-Dawson, Beata Mrugalska, Youngchul Shin, Gerhard-Wilhelm Weber

Title: Synchromodal bi-objective two-stage stochastic optimization for container and power unit allocation
Authors: Milton Caballero, Andrés D. González
Abstract: Container repositioning and power-unit deployment are typically planned in isolation, despite being operationally coupled in practice. Moreover, these processes are continually affected by diverse uncertainties-such as fluctuating demand and variable availability of containers and other resources-which further increases the complexity of planning and operations. To address these challenges, we propose an integrated Bi-Objective Two-Stage Stochastic Mixed-Integer model for the landside component of intermodal container logistics. The model jointly allocates containers across the drayage network and power units across the trucking network under demand uncertainty. In the first stage, the model determines repositioning, leasing, and initial deployment, utilizing leasing decisions as the structural link between the two networks. In the second stage, once scenarios are realized, both networks execute recourse flows. We employ the ε-constraint method to trace the Pareto-efficient frontiers, revealing that, for the modeled instances, sequential “siloed” strategies are mathematically dominated solutions. A numerical study based on the Florida intermodal network exposes a critical economic asymmetry in the value of coordination. We identify a “strategic efficiency zone” where the trucking sector can realize significant cost savings (' 40%) while imposing negligible penalties (' 0.5%) on the drayage sector. This finding challenges the assumption that supply chain integration is a zero-sum game, suggesting that, in this setting, a key barrier to coordination may be not economic incompatibility but the absence of structural mechanisms to align independent objective functions. The results quantify the opportunity cost of decentralized coordination, suggesting that a cooperative mechanism-enabled by minor adjustments to leasing locations-can yield notable systemic value without requiring significant financial concessions from the primary stakeholder.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Two-stage optimization framework for electric vehicle automatic charging stations with differential charging strategies in photovoltaic-energy storage system microgrid
Authors: Jing Liu, Zhou Zhang, Mingyang Pei, Lingshu Zhong, Kun Gao
Abstract: The rapid expansion of the electric vehicle (EV) market has intensified the demand for efficient charging infrastructure, yet conventional fixed-charger paradigms suffer from low utilization rates, pronounced grid peak-valley disparities, and insufficient renewable energy absorption due to the one-vehicle-one-charger binding constraint. This study proposes a two-stage robust optimization framework for Electric Vehicle Automatic Charging Stations integrated with a photovoltaic-energy storage system microgrid: Stage 1 employs a reinforcement-learning-enhanced NSGA-II and TOPSIS to simultaneously optimize economic efficiency, reclassification count, and grid load variance under a budget-of-uncertainty formulation that jointly handles EV arrival/departure time uncertainty and photovoltaic output variability; Stage 2 combines CPLEX-based exact EV grouping with a Wolpertinger-DDPG architecture for dynamic rail-mounted mobile charger (RMC) assignment, enabling a one-charger-serves-multiple-vehicles paradigm through rail-mounted robotic charging arms. A scheduling-flexibility-based EV trichotomy with a formal reclassification safety-net mechanism and a price-inversion-preventing compensation design are embedded to guarantee differentiated yet equitable charging services. Comprehensive validation was conducted across three urban scenarios with 10,000 users. These results confirm that the proposed framework offers a scalable and robust solution for large-scale sustainable EV charging infrastructure deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Data-driven rebalancing support for station-based bike sharing: A hybrid centralized-distributed deployment in Chiba city
Authors: Takahiro Ezaki, Shin Kenjo, Akira Tazawa, Keiji Yamada, Kazuhiro Fujitsuka, Naoto Imura, Katsuhiro Nishinari
Abstract: Station-based bike-sharing systems routinely experience spatiotemporal imbalances that lead to empty and full stations, thereby reducing travel opportunities. Although the literature offers many optimization-based rebalancing models, including dynamic formulations that re-optimize over a rolling horizon, live operations still often depend on field staff’s heuristics because rigid centrally prescribed routes are difficult to maintain under traffic uncertainty and rapidly changing station conditions. A further obstacle is that such methods must be operated continuously: the computational budget, real-time data pipelines, and tight central–field coordination they presuppose are difficult to sustain for many smaller or regional operators, for whom rebalancing must instead be absorbed into routine field work at minimal marginal cost. This study proposes a hybrid centralized–distributed rebalancing framework for HELLO CYCLING, a nationwide shared-mobility platform in Japan, and examines its deployment in the electric bike-sharing network of Chiba City. The proposed procedure computes time-of-day target inventory levels from historical demand and logged empty/full episodes, then prepares a station-level decision table that lists target inventory ranges and associated priorities. Field staff compare these targets with current station inventories and use the table as decision support when choosing which relocations to execute. The scheme adopts relatively simple rule-based calculations rather than large-scale optimization, keeping computational costs minimal and allowing straightforward integration into daily field operations. The framework is examined through a live two-week deployment and compared with a pre-intervention operational baseline and a randomized relocation baseline. The empirical analysis shows spatial and temporal heterogeneity in demand and indicates that many stations face exposure to both empty and full states, motivating intraday repositioning. During the deployment period, the proposed workflow shows higher avoided demand losses per relocated bicycle than both the randomized baseline and routine operations. The results suggest that the proposed support scheme can identify stations requiring near-term intervention and can also reveal stations that were more likely to be overlooked under knowledge- and experience-based operations. Although the present deployment relied on contractor-based execution, the same logic may also provide a basis for more distributed user-side rebalancing schemes in the future.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Revealing the built environment impacts of idling emissions from electric ride-hailing vehicles through explainable machine learning
Authors: Fuqiang Lu, Song Wang, Hualing Bi
Abstract: Understanding how built environment characteristics influence electric vehicles (EV) idling emissions is crucial for designing low-carbon transportation systems, yet this stationary emission source remains largely overlooked. This study fills this gap by integrating high-resolution GPS trajectory data, grid carbon intensity, and explainable machine learning to quantify the nonlinear impacts of the built environment on EV idling emissions. We developed a LightGBM-SHAP framework that achieves robust predictive performance (R2 = 0.889) and systematically identified nonlinear thresholds. Three key findings emerged. First, across the seven observation days, lower daily mean temperatures were generally associated with higher estimated daily CO 2 emissions under the adopted temperature-dependent emission-accounting framework. Second, road network length, residential land, transportation facilities, and population density collectively accounted for nearly 80% of total SHAP importance, with multiple built environment features exhibiting nonlinear threshold effects. Third, feature significance exhibited spatiotemporal heterogeneity, with identical built environment configurations exerting markedly different impacts across varying time periods and spatial scales. These findings should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal planning standards, offering diagnostic evidence for future policy evaluation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Identification of emission characteristics under global shipping decarbonization pathways
Authors: Lang Xu, Lele Li, Jihong Chen, Ran Yan, Yang Zhang
Abstract: Maritime shipping is central to global trade and climate mitigation. We propose an interpretable generative modeling framework to characterize shipping carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions and analyze shipping decarbonization pathways via 1,202 scenarios from the IPCC AR6 database. Climate categories are consolidated into three mitigation groups, and 50 shipping-related variables are converted into cumulative-change features. We then train three generative models to produce synthetic mitigation scenarios and evaluate their performance through bidirectional random-forest (RF) label-transfer tests, distributional realism and structural consistency checks. The results suggest that shipping CO 2 emissions are associated with the joint variation in demand heterogeneity, energy-system conditions, policy stringency, and fuel substitution. The synthetic scenarios further demonstrate that higher carbon prices, greater power electrification, and lower oil-based fuel dependence are consistently associated with lower-emission shipping pathways. These findings offer a data-driven basis for identifying CO 2 emission characteristics and supporting long-term shipping decarbonization strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Aid and armed actors: Collaboration and aid delivery in the DRC
Authors: Haley Swedlund, Marie-Eve Desrosiers, Joshua Fawcett Weiner, Pierre Sosthène Kambidi
Abstract: In conflict-affected contexts, the presence of armed actors—including state security forces, international peacekeeping missions, and non-state armed groups—means that aid organisations may need to cooperate with these actors to deliver foreign aid. Yet the conditions under which this cooperation happens remain underspecified. In this article, we use novel mixed methods data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to study these conditions. Building on qualitative interviews with Kinshasa-based aid practitioners, as well as a survey and survey experiment with Congolese provincial-level aid workers, we provide systematic evidence of the conditions under which humanitarian and development aid workers are more or less likely to collaborate with different types of armed actors across different regions of the country. We test three hypotheses: the type of armed actor, the visibility of cooperation, and the proximity to conflict. Our findings suggest that the type of armed actor and the proximity of the aid workers to conflict matter most. The public visibility of their collaboration is less important than anticipated. For those at the forefront of aid delivery, it is primarily the concrete realities and day-to-day interactions that appear to shape decision-making and behavior.

Title: End-to-end portfolio selection: Leveraging deep learning in Smart Predict then Optimize
Authors: Wenchu Zhang, Zhaolin Hu, Haiqing Yin
Abstract: The end-to-end prediction and optimization paradigm based on Smart “Predict, then Optimize” (SPO) method provides a new approach for portfolio selection. In this paper, we study the end-to-end portfolio selection by leveraging deep learning in the SPO framework. We consider several deep learning models including two linear models, two recurrent neural network models, and two transformer-based models for financial time series forecasting, and incorporate them in the SPO loss functions in the mean–variance models. We train the end-to-end models using the Adam algorithm based on the specific structure of the SPO+ function to directly obtain the optimal portfolio weights. We compare via the real test the end-to-end paradigm with the two-stage prediction and optimization paradigm that uses the conventional Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function, and illustrate the competitiveness of the former. Our tests also suggest that the iTransformer model appears to hold some superiority among the various deep learning models in this end-to-end portfolio selection practice.

Title: FastSC: A fast local search algorithm for the set covering problem
Authors: Jieyu Wu, Shiwei Pan, Yiyuan Wang, Minghao Yin
Abstract: The set covering problem (SCP) is one of the classical combinatorial optimization problems with various applications. In recent years, many algorithms have been proposed for solving SCP, especially local search algorithms have shown outstanding performance in solving ability. In this work, we develop an efficient local search algorithm named FastSC for SCP. First, we propose an improved configuration checking strategy to prevent the search from revisiting previously explored solutions. Second, we propose an adaptive subset selection strategy that dynamically adjusts the selection mode based on instance properties. Third, we implement a perturbation mechanism to help the algorithm escape local optima and explore promising solution spaces. Four, we present a new search mode that incorporates a gap line below the best-found solution to divide the search space into two parts and guide the algorithm toward a high-quality solution by adjusting the gap line. Experimental results show that FastSC is highly competitive with existing state-of-the-art algorithms, and particularly exhibits a distinct advantage on most challenging instances.

Title: Multi-agent collaborative reinforcement learning for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling under machine random failures
Authors: Haoze Wu, Vladimir Golovko, Marta Chodyka, Piotr Lichograj
Abstract: The dynamic flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP) demands improved scheduling efficiency, shortened production cycles, and balanced machining status of job shop machines. To address this, a dual-agent proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm integrating graph neural networks (GNN) and multi-head attention mechanisms, with the objectives of minimizing the maximum makespan, reducing machine idle rate, and enhancing machine load balancing rate is proposed. The DFJSP is modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP) where the state space is constructed in the form of the heterogeneous graph. It defines the state and action spaces of the job and machine, designs a novel multi-objective reward function to minimize completion time, reduce machine idle rate, and improve machine load balancing rate, and establishes a dynamic hierarchical scheduling framework with two-stage collaborative processing of job selection and machine allocation. A novel multi-objective reward function is designed, and a dynamic hierarchical scheduling framework featuring two-stage collaborative processing—job selection and machine assignment—is established. The multi-head attention mechanism is introduced to strengthen the capability of capturing correlation features between job states and machine states, thereby improving the generalization performance of the policy and robustness against dynamic disturbances. Ablation experiments demonstrate that the proposed multi-head attention mechanism, dual-agent approach, and novel advantage estimation all improve the algorithm’s performance. Comparative experiments show that the proposed algorithm has significant advantages in terms of solution quality and generalization performance.

Title: ESG as a mitigator of oil volatility risk
Authors: Ludovico Luce, Elias Demetriades, Alexandros Kontonikas, Athanasios Triantafyllou
Abstract: ESG activities are a forward-looking measure to prevent risks from negative externalities. Linking ESG scores with the crude oil market, we assess their mitigating effect on returns during periods of rising oil price volatility. We examine the interplay between ESG scores and crude oil volatility's impact on returns. Interestingly, this interaction transforms ESG into an insurance-like hedge, protecting returns as volatility increases. Notably, we identify a pivotal turning point at relatively low volatility levels. Below this threshold, ESG activities lack effectiveness, but when volatility surpasses it, their hedging power becomes pronounced. This effect intensifies as volatility rises, rewarding ESG leaders more significantly. Our sectoral and quantile analyses corroborate these findings. Overall, our findings support the role of ESG activities as a "safe haven" in times of financial turmoil, focusing its contribution to the interplay between ESG and oil volatility on periods of heightened uncertainty in the crude oil market.

Title: Coping collectively: Responses to natural disasters in Africa
Authors: Robert Mackay, Astghik Mavisakalyan, Yashar Tarverdi
Abstract: Natural disasters are occurring with increased frequency, significantly affecting the lives of those exposed. We study the coping responses to disasters, matching data on over 1000 disaster locations with individual-level survey data from over 175,000 individuals across 37 African countries in the period 2002-2015. Using a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits spatial and temporal distances to disaster events, we show that disaster exposure is associated with increased economic vulnerabilities. While government support could be critical under such circumstances, we document lower evaluations of government performance in disaster-affected areas. Our analysis of coping responses suggests that disaster-exposed individuals are more likely to contact leaders as a group and participate in community meetings. However, while we document shifts in political interests and democratic attitudes among disaster-exposed individuals, their individual political activism declines. We find considerable heterogeneity in these relationships across countries, suggesting that national context shapes how disasters influence citizen-state relations.

Title: Predicting moose (Alces alces) activity at roadside mineral licks: Implications for moose-vehicle collisions
Authors: Beatrice Penco, Roy V. Rea, Chris J. Johnson, Gayle Hesse, Marco Apollonio
Abstract: Moose-vehicle collisions (MVCs) are a substantial cause of mortality for moose throughout some portions of their range. We investigated a series of factors that explained the timing of moose visits to roadside mineral licks (RMLs) in north-central British Columbia, Canada. Roadside mineral licks are formed by the pooling of road de-icing agents and are attractive to moose, which use them to supplement mineral intake. Moose activity was monitored with camera traps deployed at four RMLs over a 12-year period. Generalized linear mixed models suggested that snowpack and spring green-up best accounted for annual variation in the timing of spring and summer peaks of lick use by moose. Our findings can help to guide road safety planners as they develop site- and season-specific measures for mitigating MVCs which helps to increase public safety and conserve moose.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Socio-technical barriers to electric mobility in India: an expert-based integrated modelling analysis
Authors: Roma Kandpal, Izuru Saizen
Abstract: Electric mobility is central to decarbonising transport; however, developing economies face persistent systemic barriers that limit the transition from fossil fuel-based transport. This study explores India’s case using an expert-based multi-criteria approach to map influences and hierarchical positions among 16 critical socio-technical barriers. These barriers were refined from a set of 29 barriers that were previously identified through a literature review and subsequently prioritised by domain experts. The analysis suggests that, from the perspective of experts, high purchase costs, limited domestic manufacturing capacity, and underdeveloped battery supply chains had the greatest influence on this transition, whereas charging infrastructure constraints and maintenance gaps reinforced these barriers. The cultural attachment to gasoline vehicles is perceived as a deep socio-technical constraint. The findings indicate the importance of leverage points, including cost-reduction strategies, coordinated policies to support domestic manufacturing, and accelerated deployment of charging infrastructure to support electric vehicle transition in India.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Enhancing military load planning: A prioritized 2-D orthogonal packing approach
Authors: William K. Kirschenman, H. Sebastian Heese, Michael G. Kay, Russell E. King, Brandon M. McConnell
Abstract: Military combat loading requires arranging equipment on maritime transport vessels to enable rapid, prioritized off-loading while maintaining unit cohesion and vessel stability. Related maritime deck-loading settings can involve similar access, grouping, and balance requirements. This paper extends a prioritized two-dimensional orthogonal packing framework to incorporate global load balancing requirements alongside existing prioritization objectives. We study three solution approaches for this globally constrained problem: a monolithic mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) approach, a sliding-window matheuristic, and a sliding-window matheuristic with in-stride load balancing penalties. For any sliding-window solution that fails to achieve both feasible packing and load balancing in the initial stage, we develop a universal post-processing strategy that selectively relaxes and re-optimizes item positions to achieve balance with minimal disruption to the prioritized layout. Computational experiments demonstrate that the matheuristic approaches fundamentally outperform the monolithic MILP approach in load balance reliability, solution quality, and computational efficiency, providing practical guidance for integrating automated optimization into military load planning systems. Among these, the simpler sliding-window matheuristic followed by post-processing repair emerges as the recommended practical configuration, offering the strongest overall combination of balance success, solution quality, and runtime, while the in-stride variant remains a narrower alternative when direct first-stage balance attainment is paramount. The matheuristic pipelines generate high-quality, load-balanced solutions for single-vessel scenarios within a few minutes on average, enabling rapid evaluation of multiple loading configurations during time-critical deployment planning.

Title: Contagion, migration, and misallocation in a pandemic
Authors: Qing Chang, Ke Tang, Danxia Xie, Longtian Zhang
Abstract: We study how individuals' migration decisions during a pandemic interact with the spatial allocation of hospital resources, characterizing both the laissez-faire equilibrium and the planner's allocation in closed form. Susceptible individuals leave high-infection cities while infected individuals move toward better-resourced ones, but these private decisions diverge from the planner's along two dimensions. First, the migration of infected agents toward susceptible-rich destinations raises transmission risk, a contagion externality the planner internalizes by restricting such flows. Second, the migration of infected agents toward better-resourced cities relieves hospital congestion at the epicenter, a congestion externality the planner internalizes by encouraging such flows. The two externalities work in opposite directions, and our comparative statics show when each dominates. The framework explains a cross-country pattern that standard misallocation theory cannot: during COVID-19, countries with greater regional dispersion in mortality tended to have lower aggregate mortality. This pattern arises naturally once contagion and endogenous mobility are added to a standard misallocation framework. More broadly, the analysis identifies a setting in which spatial dispersion can raise rather than reduce welfare, reversing the sign of the standard misallocation prescription.

Title: Optimal financing and carbon emission reduction strategies under cap-and-trade and reward-penalty policies
Authors: Peng Ma, Chen Li, Yeming Gong, Henry Xu
Affiliations: Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology; EMLYON Business School; The University of Queensland
Abstract: With the implementation of low-carbon policies, responsible firms have adopted remanufacturing or invested in green technologies to reduce emissions. The sustainability actions, i.e., remanufacturing and investment in green technologies, are significantly influenced by national policies and financial constraints. This study explores optimal production and carbon reduction strategies, as well as financing preferences, in an outsourcing remanufacturing supply chain involving a well-capitalized original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and a capital-constrained outsourced remanufacturer (UR) under cap-trade and reward-penalty policies. We compare three emission reduction approaches – OEM-only, UR-only, and joint emission reduction under two financing options: bank loans and trade credit. Our results show that: (1) The joint emission abatement model generates the highest sales quantities but the lowest retail prices for new and remanufactured products. (2) As the reward-penalty intensities increase, OEMs’ strategies shift from UR-only to joint emission reduction, while URs’ strategies shift from OEM-only to joint emission reduction. (3) When URs face severe capital shortages, OEMs tend to provide trade credit regardless of interest rates, while URs with moderate capital choose between bank and trade credit depending on financing rates. Stronger reward-penalty incentives and higher carbon prices amplify financing needs and further strengthen OEMs’ motivation to support URs through trade credit.

Title: Resilience-oriented integrated optimisation of resource allocation and task scheduling in complex manufacturing networks under risk propagation
Authors: Zian Zhao, Hong Zhou, Zening Song, Xi Vincent Wang, Jiepeng Wang
Affiliations: Beihang University; Marine Design & Research Institute of China; KTH Royal Institute of Technology; University of Shanghai for Science and Technology
Abstract: Uncertainties in manufacturing usually bring about the risk of task failure, which becomes more serious for complex manufacturing service networks (MSN) by cascading effects owing to the complex connectivity and strong interdependence among resources. Hence, the propagation of failure risk throughout the MSN has to be considered in task planning. Typically, resource failures unavoidably lead to the dynamic changes in available capacity, further affect their neighbors, and the effect may propagate throughout the network. So far, fewer investigations on task planning have considered the failure risk propagation among resources. This paper addresses the resource allocation and task scheduling (RATS) considering the propagation of failure risk driven by capacity deterioration/recovery in cloud manufacturing, a typical form of MSNs. A complex-network-based risk propagation and evolution model is first developed to simulate capacity evolution with cascading effects, in identifying and forecasting the risk status of task failure. Then, a resilience-oriented RATS approach is proposed, incorporating flexible scheduling and resilience-enhanced resource grouping to disperse and isolate risk. Three simulation-derived indicators are designed to capture status of risk. A hybrid scatter search algorithm with problem-specific schemes is proposed. Extensive computational experiments and a real-world case have validated the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed method.

Title: Enhanced branch-and-check for extended flexible job shop scheduling problem with arbitrary precedence graphs
Authors: Fuli Xiong, Haojun Shi, Chengfei Xiang, Muming Wu
Affiliations: Xi'an University of Architecture and Technology
Abstract: As manufacturing shifts toward personalised and small-batch production, solving large-scale FJSSP instances remains challenging because existing methods often struggle to balance solution quality and computational efficiency in complex environments. This study investigates the extended Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (e-FJSSP) with arbitrary precedence graphs and proposes a Branch-and-Check (BCH) algorithm enhanced by improved lower- and upper-bound strategies. The problem is decomposed into a master problem for operation-to-machine assignment and a subproblem for operation scheduling, which reduces combinatorial complexity by exploiting the independence between assignment and scheduling decisions. To accelerate convergence, we introduce Path Decomposition-based SSP Relaxation (PDSSR) to strengthen lower bounds and a CP-based warm start (CPWS) to provide strong initial upper bounds. The resulting framework, CP-BCHV, scales more effectively than monolithic exact models. In addition, PDSSR can be embedded into an enhanced MILP variant (MILPV). Computational results on the DAFJS, YFJS, and DAHFJS benchmark sets show that CP-BCHV delivers high-quality feasible solutions together with tight bounds and improves 11 best-known solutions for DAFJS. From a managerial perspective, the proposed framework enhances production planning in flexible manufacturing systems by improving coordination between machine assignment and precedence-constrained scheduling.

Title: The efficiency-equity trade-offs in day-ahead electricity market auctions
Authors: Gökhan Ceyhan, Murat Köksalan, Banu Lokman
Affiliations: Middle East Technical University; University of Michigan; University of Portsmouth
Abstract: European day-ahead electricity markets (DAMs) operate as two-sided auctions where market operators solve a market clearing problem to match the supply and demand bids and determine the price of electricity for the following day. These markets are typically designed to maximise the total surplus of buyers and sellers. However, there is usually no market-clearing price maximising the surpluses of all participants simultaneously. Under these typical circumstances, considering only the total surplus leads to inequity as some bidders experience negative surplus or missed surplus. In this paper, we address these equity-efficiency concerns by developing a multi-objective optimisation approach to European DAMs. We characterise the nondominated set and explore the trade-offs among market loss, missed surplus, and market surplus. Through experiments on data representative of the Turkish DAM, we derive insights that can inform more equitable market designs across all DAMs. We also explore combinatorial auction variants of the problem to observe the characteristics of the nondominated sets under these settings.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Optimizing tactical project planning with a resource-leveled RCCP model
Authors: Anis Noureddine, Robert Pellerin, François Soumis, Raphaël Boudreault
Abstract: Efficient resource leveling is a critical challenge in ship refit and maintenance planning, where fluctuating labor demand leads to costly subcontracting, overtime, and risks of project delay. To address this issue, this paper presents a continuous-time mixed-integer linear programming approach to Rough Cut Capacity Planning (RCCP) for tactical project planning, which integrates resource leveling by treating work package execution intensities as decision variables. The model allows greater flexibility in execution intensities and enforces a single-peaked resource usage profile, in which demand rises to a peak and then declines, thereby reducing repeated hiring and rehiring while assessing impacts on overall project duration. Computational experiments on specially generated instances show that allowing reduced coupling between resource-specific intensities improves workload leveling by up to 35.16% compared with the classical RCCP, at the cost of increased computation time. To accelerate solution times for makespan in the single-peak resource profile formulation, we introduce an incremental lower-bound tightening strategy that yields about a tenfold average speedup on our test instances. When the planning horizon is too constrained to admit a unimodal profile, the model adapts by minimizing inter-period resource fluctuations to avoid costly variations. Roughly 18% of cases required horizon extension to accommodate unimodality. Finally, a bi-objective $$\varepsilon $$ -constraint analysis quantifies the trade-off between project duration and resource stability for instances with extended horizons. The analysis considers three factors: the total project duration, the variation of workload between periods, and whether or not the workload profile is unimodal.

Title: Dynamic learning in strategic games
Authors: Matthew Stern, John R. Birge
Abstract: Abstract Practical decision-making in business and government regularly involves interaction with competitors (and other agents such as suppliers and customers). These interactions can have a significant effect on optimal decision making. To determine optimal prices, for example, a monopoly firm may need to vary prices to learn consumer demand, but, with competition, varying prices may provide information to competitors that is counterproductive. This paper shows that, while firms in competition may be able to learn optimal best-response strategies over time, in some settings, this result is not an ex ante optimal strategy for the competitors when actions reveal information to others. In this situation, the firms can achieve a collaborative outcome in equilibrium by not fully exploring and learning the environment with both firms earning more than they would in a competitive equilibrium with full information. The result has implications for policies (such as price or production controls) that restrict firm actions or that require disclosures.

Title: On the use of flexible rolling-window estimation for macroeconomic forecasting
Authors: M. Artemova, F. Blasques, S.J. Koopman, Z. Zhang
Abstract: We propose a flexible rolling-window estimation procedure which improves the forecasting accuracy of misspecified linear autoregressive models. The method assigns different weights to data points in the observed sample, which can be useful in the presence of data generating processes featuring structural breaks, complex nonlinearities, or other time-varying properties not easily captured by model design. We show how the window can be regularized by means of cross-validation. In a series of Monte Carlo experiments, we reveal that the estimation method can significantly improve the forecasting accuracy of misspecified models. In our empirical study, we show for a set of key macroeconomic indicators that we improve forecasting accuracy by assigning greater weight to periods with similar business-cycle regimes.

Title: Inflation, innovation, and technology transfer in an open economy with variety expansion
Authors: Hung‐Ju Chen, Hao Guo, Chien‐Yu Huang, Yibai Yang
Affiliations: Department of Economics National Taiwan University Taipei Taiwan; Li Anmin Institute of Economic Research Liaoning University Shenyang China; Research Institute International University of Japan Niigata Japan; Department of Economics University of Macau Taipa Macau
Abstract: Abstract This study explores the cross‐country effects of inflation on innovation and technology transfer in a North–South variety‐expansion model. We find that higher southern inflation causes a permanent increase in the North–South relative wage ratio, a temporary decrease in the northern innovation rate, and a permanent decrease in technology transfer. Higher northern inflation causes a permanent decrease in the North–South relative wage ratio, a temporary decrease in the northern innovation rate, and a permanent decrease (increase) in technology transfer if the southern population is sufficiently small (large). We calibrate the model to the China–US data to justify the model implications.

Title: An Irreversible Investment Problem with a Learning-by-Doing Feature
Authors: Erik Ekström, Yerkin Kitapbayev, Alessandro Milazzo, Topias Tolonen-Weckström
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, Uppsala University, Uppsala, 75105 Uppsala, Sweden; Mathematics Department, Khalifa University of Science and Technology, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates; Department of Economics, Social Studies, Applied Mathematics and Statistics (ESOMAS), School of Management and Economics, University of Turin, 10134 Torino, Italy
Abstract: We study a model of irreversible investment for a decision maker who has the possibility to gradually invest in a project of unknown value. In this setting, we introduce and explore a feature of “learning-by-doing,” where the learning rate of the unknown project value is increasing in the decision maker’s level of investment in the project. We show that, under some conditions on the functional dependence of the learning rate on the level of investment (the “signal-to-noise ratio”), the optimal strategy is to invest gradually in the project so that a two-dimensional sufficient statistic reflects below a monotone boundary. Moreover, this boundary is characterized as the solution of a differential problem. Finally, we also formulate and solve a discrete version of the problem, which mirrors and complements the continuous version. Funding: This work was supported by the Swedish Research Council (Vetenskapsrådet) [Grant 2023-04692].

Title: Private wealth ownership and emissions
Authors: Marla Feldwisch, Miriam Rehm, Bruno Brinkmeier
Abstract: This paper estimates the distribution of wealth-related greenhouse gas emissions across the German population, assigning responsibility for emissions to the owners of different asset types. It combines macro-data on the emissions per asset type with micro-data on the asset ownership per individual in Germany in 2019, linking data from national accounts, air emission accounts, and survey data on wealth to capture both direct held assets and indirect ownership of corporations. The results show a distinct inequality in emission responsibilities along the net wealth distribution. The top 10% are responsible for 66% of total wealth-related emissions and hold 62% of the total net wealth in Germany in 2019. Simulations of sectoral differences in emission intensity show a band around these estimates ranging from 38% to 94% of total emissions, and a random sectoral portfolio allocation using bootstrapping finds an emissions share of the top 10% of 66.5%. Wealth-related emissions are thus not only substantially more unequally distributed than emissions distributed by income or consumption, but also even more unequally distributed than wealth.

Title: The political economy of regional development: Evidence from the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno
Authors: Tancredi Buscemi, Giulia Romani
Abstract: Devolution of authority over public investments can lead to agency problems and trigger tactical redistribution between different tiers of government. We test this hypothesis in the context of the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno: a massive development programme for Southern Italy (1950-1984). By 1971, the authority over funds allocation was transferred from a centralised committee to the newborn regional governments. We combine unique historical data on local administrators with detailed information on projects, and find that, after devolution, municipalities aligned with the regional government were assigned a higher number of projects, without producing any positive impact on long-run economic outcomes.

Title: Worker skill assessment in human-centric assembly systems
Authors: Angela Lago Alvarez, Wael M. Mohammed, Jose Luis Martinez Lastra
Abstract: : Accurate assessment of human worker skills is essential for human-centric automation in modern manufacturing systems. However, modelling these skills remains challenging due to variability in human performance and limited high-quality open-access datasets. This study proposes an approach for evaluating individual worker skill levels in assembly systems and assessing the reliability of internal company metrics. It introduces worker-specific learning curves that capture individual skill progression through an exponential model that incorporates three parameters: , representing worker-specific learning rate, , quantifying previous experience and, , correcting inaccuracies in the NMV (Nominal Measured Value) calculations or pre-training effects. An algorithm based on the trust-region method is used to fit the model using task execution data, effectively capturing individualized learning trajectories and distinguishing skill progression across workers. The proposed approach was validated using a real dataset collected from an assembly line over two weeks, where four workers performed tasks at both manual and collaborative workstations. As this dataset can be seen insufficient, a Moving Block Bootstrap (MBB) stability analysis was conducted to assess the robustness of the fitted learning curve parameters under resampling. The MBB results show partial stability, with some parameters remaining consistent under resampling while others vary more substantially. Comparison with company-reported skill levels reveals notable discrepancies, highlighting the need for improved assessment methodologies. Furthermore, the proposed approach was benchmarked against classical learning curve models. The dataset is released as open-access, enabling transparent and reproducible research and fostering advancements in skill modelling.

Title: Unleashing the value of resource orchestration: How supply chain finance enhances corporate ESG performance
Authors: Qiang Lu, Kemu Su, Yudong Yang, Zhongqi Yu
Abstract: Enhancing corporate ESG performance has emerged as a strategic priority for businesses worldwide. However, regardless of whether ESG initiatives stem from regulatory compliance or proactive sustainability commitments, their implementation frequently confronts significant resource constraints. Against this backdrop, this study investigates how supply chain finance (SCF) can serve as an innovative tool for resource orchestration to improve corporate ESG performance. Grounded in resource orchestration theory (ROT), this study elucidates how SCF integrates internal and external organizational resources and transforms them into the key capabilities necessary for the implementation of sustainable strategies, constructing a triple-capability mechanism framework. Drawing on data from Chinese A-share listed companies between 2012 and 2024, this study employs a fixed-effects regression model that accounts for both firm- and year-specific effects to test the proposed research hypotheses. The empirical analysis demonstrates a significantly positive association between SCF and corporate ESG performance. Moreover, this relationship can be mediated by overall operation capability (OOC), green innovation capability (GIC), and social responsibility capability (SRC). Further analysis examines the conditional roles of digitalization and supply chain characteristics as key contextual factors. It indicates that both digital transformation (DT) and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption positively moderate the effects of SCF on OOC and GIC, while showing no significant influence on the relationship between SCF and SRC. Supply chain concentration (SCC) significantly strengthens the impact of SCF on OOC, yet it negatively moderates the relationships between SCF, GIC and SRC. In contrast, the quality of supply chain relationship (SCR) does not affect the SCF–OOC link, but significantly enhances the relationships between SCF and both GIC and SRC.

Title: Protecting employees or replacing them? Paid sick leave mandates and firm automation
Authors: Zhihan Shen, Wenhui Huang
Abstract: Paid sick leave mandates aim to improve employee benefits. This paper examines how firms respond to the additional labor costs caused by PSL mandates. Leveraging the staggered implementation of PSL mandates across U.S. states, we use a difference-in-differences design and find that mandatory PSLs greatly accelerate firms’ adoption of automation. This effect is particularly evident among labor-intensive firms, consistent with the view that rising employment costs drive labor-capital substitution. Overall, by revealing an unintended consequence of PSL mandates, this study contributes to the pertinent literature and has important policy implications.

Title: Estimating intergenerational mobility via a time-varying mixed copula method
Authors: Zongwu Cai, Guannan Liu, Wei Long, Xuehong Luo
Abstract: This paper examines how intergenerational income dependence in the United States has evolved across birth cohorts from 1987 to 2021. We employ a time-varying mixed copula model that combines Clayton, Gumbel, and Frank copulas, with weights and dependence parameters varying smoothly over cohort years, to estimate the full joint dependence structure between parent and offspring permanent incomes. Intergenerational immobility is summarized by the normalized Hellinger distance between the observed joint distribution and the independence benchmark. This index remained stable through the 1990s but increased sharply after 2000, approximately tripling by the 2010s. The copula decomposition associates this increase with upper-tail tightening: the Gumbel copula weight rises substantially, indicating increasing affluence persistence among high-income families, while the Clayton copula coefficient shows no significant trend, implying that lower-tail persistence did not intensify. Subgroup analyses reveal heterogeneous changes in within-group rank dependence, with a particularly sharp increase in the West.

Title: Engineering a win-win: Optimal group buying strategies for food delivery platforms and merchants
Authors: Han Fang, Jinshu Cai, Sisi Jian
Abstract: With the rapid growth of e-commerce, group buying (GB) has become an effective promotional strategy for on-demand food delivery platforms such as Uber Eats and Meituan (e.g., Meituan’s Pin Hao Fan). In this setting, platforms may introduce GB programs that allow consumers to obtain price discounts by waiting for order consolidation and engaging in self-collection. This study examines whether and how GB can create value for platforms and merchants while accounting for consumers’ price-time trade-offs.
